exp.0:51:
This verse says that each Israelite camped with his own tribe, in the place that belonged to him. The words "hosts" and "companies" in the verse refer to the groups or divisions of the people, and "standard" was the banner or sign of each group. Thus, no one camped wherever he wished, but beside his own people and under his own standard.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai while he organizes the people. The Levites camp around the tabernacle to care for it, and the other tribes camp around them. In this way the holiness of the place where God dwelt was protected, and the people were spared from experiencing his judgment.

For today: God wants order and a place for each person. Seek your place in a community of faith, serve with humility wherever you are, and respect the order that helps everyone draw near to God with reverence.
exp.15:23:
God tells Moses to warn the people: "Get away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram." The word "congregation" refers to the whole nation of Israel, and "get you up" means "go away." The tent was the home of these men.

The LORD speaks to Moses. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram had rebelled against the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron had pleaded with God not to punish the whole people for the sin of a few. God responds with mercy: he gives the opportunity to separate from the rebellion before judgment comes.

For today: God gives us the opportunity to move away from evil before its consequences reach us. We must be wise and not join others in attitudes of pride, division, or rebellion, merely out of pressure or habit. Ask God for the courage to step away and do what is right.
exp.25:31:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Gilead, grandson of Manasseh. It names two more sons of Gilead: Shemida and Hepher, from whom the Shemidaites and the Hepherites came. The word "family" here means a clan, that is, a large group of relatives who descend from a common ancestor.

God, through Moses, commands a new census of the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The previous generation had died, and now the new one was counted before entering the promised land. The clans served to divide the inheritance of the land. The next verse mentions the daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Hepher, who would later ask for their share.

God knows each family by name. None is insignificant to him. Today you can rest in the fact that God sees you and knows you personally, and also value your own family and your church as part of his plan.
exp.14:18:
This verse says that when the people of Israel enter the promised land and begin to eat the bread that the land produces, they must set aside an offering for God. The phrase "when ye eat" can be read simply as "when you begin to eat," and "bread of the land" refers to the food made from the grain grown there.

God speaks to Moses so that he will pass these instructions on to the people. They had left Egypt and were in the wilderness, and God promises them that they will arrive in a new land. He teaches them in advance how to thank Him: by giving the first cake from their dough as an offering, acknowledging that the harvest comes from Him.

For today: before we use what we receive, we can give God the first fruits of our time, our money, or our strength. In this way we give thanks and confess that everything we have comes from His hand.
exp.2:6:
It says that the Levites were to carry out their duty: to look after what God entrusted to them and also what belonged to the whole people, beside the tent where God made himself present. "Charge" here means task or responsibility. "Tabernacle of the testimony" is the sacred tent, so called because of the tablets of the law it kept.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness. He has just set apart Aaron and his sons as priests, and now he commands that the tribe of Levi help them. The Levites did not do the priestly work itself, but cared for and attended to the tabernacle, and in this way they represented the whole people in serving God.

Today we can learn that serving God is not always something visible. Faithfully caring for a simple task in the church, such as keeping things in order, teaching children, or helping others, is something God values and that benefits the whole community.
exp.17:12:
This verse says that the firstfruits, that is, the first produce that people gathered from their land and brought to the Lord, belonged to Aaron the priest. Any person in his house who was clean could eat of them, meaning anyone who was ceremonially fit according to the law. The phrase "shall bring unto the Lord" means that these first portions were first given to God, and He then gave them to the priests.

God is speaking, addressing Aaron. The priests and Levites did not receive land like the other tribes, so God arranged that they would live from the offerings of the people while they served in the sanctuary.

For today: God invites us to give Him the first and the best, not what is left over. We can support with generosity and gratitude those who serve in the church, recognizing that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.17:26:
It says that the offering the Levites set apart from the tithe will be counted to them as though it were their own grain, freshly taken from the threshingfloor (the place where grain is threshed), or the produce of the winepress (where grapes are pressed). The word "reckoned" in the verse means to be counted or considered. In other words, God regards that offering as being as valuable as a harvest of their own.

God speaks to Moses to instruct the Levites. They did not receive land in Israel, but lived on the tithes of the people. Even so, God asks them in turn to give a tenth of what they received, for Aaron the priest. In this way they too learn to give and to depend on God.

For today: even when we receive little or depend on others, we can give with gratitude. God looks not only at the amount, but at the thankful heart with which we offer our best.
exp.21:9:
In this verse, Balaam tells God that Balak, son of Zippor and king of Moab, has sent a message to him. The verse stops mid-thought, and Balak's request continues in the next one.

God had just asked Balaam who the men with him were. Balaam answers by explaining who sent them. Balak was afraid of Israel, which had come out of Egypt, and wanted Balaam to curse the people. Notice that God already knew the answer; the question invited Balaam to speak plainly.

For today: when God asks us something in prayer, it is not because he needs the information, but so that we will be honest. Tell him frankly what is being asked of you, what you feel, and what tempts you, and listen to his answer before you decide.
exp.27:15:
This verse says that the Passover of the Lord is kept on the fourteenth day of the first month of the year. The word "Mas," meaning "but" or "now then," and the word "á," an old form of "to," are not part of this verse in English, so there is nothing more to explain about them. After speaking of the offerings for each month, the text moves on to the yearly feasts, and the Passover is the first of them.

God speaks through Moses to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He repeats which offerings and feasts they must keep. The Passover recalled the night when God freed them from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 12). The next day the feast of unleavened bread began.

For today: just as Israel set aside fixed dates to remember their deliverance, we can build regular habits of gratitude. This week, take a moment to remember how God has sustained you and give him thanks. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of the Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).
exp.18:16:
This verse says that for a person made unclean by touching a dead body, ashes were taken from the red heifer that had been burned as an offering for sin. These ashes were placed in a vessel, and living water was added to them, that is, fresh running water from a spring or a river. "Unclean" here means ritually impure under the law, not necessarily guilty of wrongdoing. "Purification" here refers to cleansing.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel in the wilderness. Death made people ritually impure, and God wanted his people, among whom he lived, to have a clear way to be cleansed and return to the community.

For today: death and sin leave their marks on us, but God always offers a path to cleansing. Many Christians see in this a shadow of Christ (Hebrews 9:13-14). We can come to him with confidence, without hiding ourselves.
exp.20:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel settled down to live in the territory where the Amorites had lived before. The word "dwelt" means that they stayed to live there. The verse is the narrator's own sentence, and it comes after Israel's victory over Sihon, king of the Amorites, who had refused them passage. With this, Israel received land east of the Jordan. Shortly afterward, Moses sent men to spy out Jazer, and then came the battle against Og.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often in stages. Israel rested for a moment, and soon after continued on the way. We can give thanks for what God has already given us, without ceasing to walk with confidence toward what comes next.
exp.16:5:
Moses spoke to the people, and each leader of the twelve tribes gave him a staff, one for each of their fathers' houses. In all there were twelve staffs. Aaron's staff was among them.

The word "prince" here means a leader or head of one tribe.

God had commanded Moses to do this because the people were grumbling against Moses and Aaron, after the rebellion of Korah. God wanted to make clear whom he had chosen to serve him as priest. Each staff was placed before God, and the one that sprouted would show his choice.

For today: God is never confused about whom he calls or for what purpose. Instead of grumbling or competing with others for places of service, we can trust that he gives each person their place, and serve with humility wherever he has placed us.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to celebrate the Passover at its appointed time, that is, on the date God had already set.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, a year after the departure from Egypt. The Passover reminded them how God had freed them from slavery. Now, as a people on the way, God wants them not to forget their deliverance. The following verses give the date and ask that it be done according to the instructions.

For today: God values that we remember, with order and gratitude, what He has done for us. We can set aside fixed times, such as Sunday, daily prayer, or the Lord's Supper, to thank Him and not let the busyness erase His work in our lives.
exp.5:25:
This verse is the final part of the priestly blessing. The phrase "The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee" means that God looks at you with attention and favor, never turning his gaze away from you. "And give thee peace" means that God grants you peace; in the original Hebrew the word is one that speaks of complete well-being, not only of calm.

God himself gives these words to Moses so that Aaron and his sons, the priests, may bless the people of Israel. The following verse makes clear that in this way they will place God's name upon the people: the blessing comes from God, not from the priest. Israel was in the wilderness, and this blessing reminded them that God was caring for them.

Today you can ask for this blessing for yourself and for others. When you feel overlooked or anxious, remember that God looks on you with kindness. You can also speak these words over your family or a friend, wishing them the peace that comes from God.
exp.31:13:
Moses tells the tribes of Reuben and Gad that they have risen up in their fathers' place. "Offspring" is the word meaning descendants, and "stood in their fathers' place" means they came after them. Moses compares them to a sinful generation and warns that their attitude could increase God's anger against all Israel. The words "wrath" and "fierce anger" speak of God's righteous anger toward sin.

Moses speaks because these tribes asked to stay east of the Jordan and not cross into the promised land. He feared their decision would discourage the people, as happened when the spies caused fear and that whole generation died in the desert. Then they clarified that they would indeed help in the battle.

For today: before making a decision, let us think about how it affects others. What we choose can encourage or discourage our family, our church, or those around us.
exp.6:71:
This verse says that on the eleventh day of the dedication of the tabernacle, it was the turn of Pagiel, son of Ocran, to present his offering. He was the prince, that is, the leader or head of the tribe of Asher. Here only the one who makes the offering is announced; the details of his offering come right after.

The one narrating is the author of the book of Numbers, traditionally identified with Moses. He tells how each tribal leader brought his offering, one per day, in order. God had commanded that the tabernacle be dedicated in this way. It is remarkable that each tribe gives exactly the same thing, with no one standing out above another.

For today: God values that each person has their own moment and their own place among his people. Serve with what is given to you, without comparing yourself or competing, and do it with steadiness and gratitude.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that when Israel set out on the march, the tabernacle would travel in the middle of the people, surrounded by the Levites. The "tabernacle of the testimony" was the sacred tent where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept. "Set forward" means to start moving. Each tribe was to travel in the same order in which it camped, every man in his place by the standard of his group.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron as he organizes Israel's camp in the wilderness. After counting the tribes, he gives them a clear order: three tribes on each side, with the tabernacle in the middle. In this way, God's presence was at the center of the people's life, and everything moved with order.

For today: put God at the center of your routine, your family, and your decisions. A simple pattern of prayer and Bible reading can help you walk in peace.
exp.9:10:
It says that in the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day, the cloud was lifted from above the tabernacle of the testimony. The "tabernacle of the testimony" was the holy tent where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept. The cloud was the visible sign of God's presence with his people.

The narrator tells this moment after almost a year camped at Mount Sinai. There God gave them the law and organized the people. The instructions about the trumpets prepare the march. Now, as the cloud rises, Israel knows that God is directing them to set out toward the promised land.

For today: God knows when we should stay and when we should move forward. We can ask him for direction in prayer, read his Word, and seek wise counsel. In this way we learn to wait with patience and to move with confidence when he guides us.
exp.7:14:
It says that, after being purified, the Levites could then begin their service in the tabernacle. Moses was to cleanse them, that is, make them clean through the rites that were prescribed, and offer them as an offering, that is, present them to God as wholly dedicated to Him. The tent of meeting was the sacred tent where the tablets of the law were kept.

God speaks to Moses. The firstborn of Israel belonged to Him because He had delivered them on the night of the Passover in Egypt. In place of them, God took the tribe of Levi for sacred service. First they were purified, and then they served.

For today: God cleanses us before He asks us to serve Him. We can serve Him without pride, remembering that we first received His forgiveness and that our lives belong to Him.
exp.18:1:
This verse begins the instructions for a special ritual. God commands the people to bring a reddish-brown cow, without defect and one that has never worn a yoke, meaning one that has never been used for work. The word "ordinance" in the verse means a command or fixed rule.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel was traveling through the wilderness. This cow would be sacrificed, and its ashes would be used to purify anyone who had become unclean by touching a dead body. Scholars explain in various ways why it had to be red, and the Bible does not make this clear.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. It also reminds us that we need to be cleansed, and Christians see in Christ the complete purification (Hebrews 9:13-14). We can come near to God with gratitude, offering him the best of our time and our hearts.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that Moses was to present the Levites before the tabernacle of the congregation, which was the tent where God met with his people. He was also to gather the whole assembly of the children of Israel. The word "bring" in the verse is the one that means bringing them near. "Congregation" refers to the entire community.

God speaks to Moses. The Levites, one of the tribes of Israel, were going to be set apart to serve in the tabernacle. Before that, they were made clean with water, by shaving the body, by washing their clothes, and through offerings. The gathering of all the people shows that this service was something for the whole community, not just for one group.

For today: serving God is both serious and communal. Before serving, it is good to draw near to God with humility, and to remember that the church supports and prays for those who serve.
exp.13:28:
God says that the bodies of the Israelites will fall, that is, they will die, in the wilderness. This applies to everyone who was counted in the census, from twenty years old and up, because they complained against Him. The phrase "your counted ones" refers to the men registered when the army was formed.

God speaks here in reply to Moses. The people had heard the report of the spies, became afraid, wept, and wanted to go back to Egypt, doubting that God would give them the promised land. God answers them according to what they themselves said. Even so, Caleb and Joshua are left out of this judgment, and the children will enter later.

For today: God takes trust in Him seriously. When fears or difficulties come, instead of complaining, speak to Him honestly, remember how He has cared for you before, and take the next step of faith, trusting that He keeps His promises.
exp.24:6:
This verse tells us that Phinehas, the grandson of the priest Aaron, saw what was happening, rose up from among the people, and took a spear in his hand. The words "saw it" mean that he took notice of the act, and "rose up" means that he stood. The verse does not yet say what he did, but it already shows that he had decided to act.

The people of Israel were camped at Shittim, and many had given themselves over to the worship of Baal of Peor and to sexual immorality. God had sent a plague as punishment. An Israelite brought a Midianite woman openly before everyone while the people wept at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The account is from Moses, and Phinehas's action is described in the verses that follow.

For today: when we see something that dishonors God, it is not enough to lament in silence. Today we do not use violence; we act with prayer, truth, and love, seeking the restoration of people, and asking God for wisdom to know when and how to speak or act.
exp.32:7:
This verse tells part of Israel's journey after leaving Egypt. They departed from Pi-hahiroth and crossed the sea (the Red Sea, as we call it today) into the wilderness. They traveled three days through the wilderness of Etham and camped at Marah. The phrase "pitched" simply means they set up their camp.

Here Moses is writing a list of the people's stops during the forty years in the wilderness. It is like a travel journal that remembers each place where God guided them. According to Exodus 15, at Marah the water was bitter. This summary does not describe that in detail, but it shows that God led them step by step.

For today: God can lead us from a great deliverance to a difficult place. If today you are in your own "Marah," remember that it is not the end of the road. God is still guiding you, and after Marah came Elim.
exp.6:6:
It says that Moses gave two wagons and four oxen to the descendants of Gershon, according to the work that belonged to them. The verse notes that the wording is an older form of the verse's "gave." It also says that "ministry" here means their task of service in the tabernacle.

The leaders of Israel had brought wagons and oxen as an offering. God told Moses to receive them and distribute them among the Levites. The Gershonites carried the curtains and fabrics of the tabernacle, which weighed less, so they received fewer. The Merarites, who carried the boards and pillars, received more. The Kohathites carried the holy things on their shoulders, which is why they received no wagons.

God gives what is needed according to each person's task. Not everyone receives the same, and that is not unfair. We can trust that God provides the resources for what he asks of us, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.27:27:
This verse says that, along with the burnt offerings, a grain offering was to be presented: fine flour mixed with oil. It was three tenth deals for each bull and two tenth deals for each ram. The offering of flour is the finest and choicest meal.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, who were close to entering the promised land. Here he gives instructions for the Feast of Weeks, also called the Feast of Firstfruits, a celebration of thanks for the harvest. The amounts were exact and orderly.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. We can give him our time, talents and resources with order and gratitude, recognizing that everything we have comes from him.
exp.34:16:
It says that if someone strikes another person with a stone that fits in the hand, large enough to kill, and the person dies, that man is a killer, that is, a murderer. And the killer was to be put to death. "A stone held in the hand" means a stone that is gripped in the hand; "strike" means to hit.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He was distinguishing two cases: an accidental death, for which there were cities of refuge, and murder committed on purpose. An object capable of killing showed that there was intent to harm. In this way life was protected and injustice was avoided.

For today: God places a deep value on every human life. We can take care of our words, our anger, and our actions, remembering that we are responsible for how we treat others.
exp.16:2:
God commands Moses to write Aaron's name on the staff of the tribe of Levi. Each head of a family of the tribes would have his own staff, with his name on it. "Head of the family of their fathers" means the chief or leader of each house or tribe. The staff was a wooden rod, a symbol of authority.

The LORD speaks to Moses after the people rebelled against Moses and Aaron, questioning who had the right to serve as priest. God wants to settle the complaint with a clear sign: the staff of the chosen one would bud. In this way Israel would see that the choice came from God and not from men.

For today: when there are doubts or arguments about who should lead or serve, instead of grumbling, we can pray and let God show his will. He works with order and not with confusion.
exp.27:12:
This verse says that along with each lamb of the burnt offering, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil was to be offered. That grain offering is called the "meat offering" in the King James wording of this verse. The flour the verse describes is the finest and choicest flour. A "sweet savour" does not refer to a literal aroma, but to an offering that was pleasing to God. The phrase "made by fire" means that it was burned on the altar.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, who were about to enter the promised land. Here the offerings for the beginning of each month are detailed. They were part of a regular order of worship, so that the people would remember that everything they had came from God.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can give Him the best of our time, attention, and resources, with gratitude and consistency.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the army of the tribe of Zebulun, that is, the men who were counted in the census, numbered 57,400. "Host" means an army or an organized group, and "counted" refers to those who were registered.

God spoke to Moses and Aaron to arrange the camp of Israel around the tabernacle. Zebulun camped to the east, alongside Judah and Issachar. With the figures of the three tribes, the total came to 186,400 men. That list showed order, and that each tribe had its place and its leader.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Each person counts and has a place. You can ask him to show you where to serve in your church or your family, and to do it faithfully, even when no one else notices. With God, no service goes unseen.
exp.26:16:
Moses asks God to set a leader over the people. That leader must go out before them and come in before them, meaning he should guide them in everything they do, both in war and in daily life. The phrase about bringing them out and bringing them in means leading them along their way. Moses does not want the people to be like sheep without a shepherd, lost and without care.

Moses speaks with God knowing that he will soon die and will not enter the promised land. He is concerned for the people more than for himself. God answers by pointing to Joshua, a man in whom there is spirit, and presents him before the priest Eleazar and the whole congregation. The handing over of leadership is done publicly and in an orderly way.

For today: pray for those who lead your church, your family, or your work. And if you guide others, do so with a shepherd's heart, caring for people, not only giving orders.
exp.6:80:
This verse lists part of the offering that a leader of Israel brought: one young bullock (a young bull), one ram, and one lamb of the first year, to be burned completely as a burnt offering. This kind of sacrifice was given whole to God, as a sign of total surrender.

Here God is not speaking directly; the narrator of the book is telling the story. He recounts how each tribe, on a different day, brought the same offering for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. This is the twelfth day, the tribe of Naphtali, with Ahira as its leader. The repetition shows that each tribe was taken into account equally.

For today: God values the sincere devotion of each person, no matter whether they come first or last. We can offer him our daily life with steadiness, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.16:8:
Moses brought out all the rods that had been placed before the Lord in the tabernacle and showed them to all the people. The Israelites saw with their own eyes which rod had blossomed, and each tribal leader took back his own. "In the presence of the Lord" means in his presence, in the holy place. The other rods remained dry, and Aaron's rod was alive.

Before this, Korah and others had rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and many had died. The people kept complaining. God himself wanted to make clear, through a visible sign, whom he had chosen to serve as priest, and so to put an end to the complaints.

For today: God does not hide his work; he makes it plain to anyone who has open eyes. When we doubt his direction, instead of complaining, we can stop and humbly look at what he has shown, and trust.
exp.32:34:
This verse says that the Israelites left the place called Ebronah and camped at Ezion-gaber. The word "departed" in this verse means "having set out," and "encamped" means to camp or settle for a time. It is one more of the stops in the wilderness.

Moses writes, by God's command, a list of all the stations of the journey, from Egypt to near the promised land. Ezion-gaber was beside the sea, in the area of the Gulf of Aqaba, as it is commonly understood. The list works as a reminder that God guided his people step by step, even in difficult years.

For today: sometimes our life seems like a list of stops without much sense. God, however, knows every place we pass through. Trust that he guides you also through the ordinary stages, and give thanks for his faithfulness in each one.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that from the first of the dough the people mixed with their flour, they were to give a portion to God as an offering. "First of your dough" means the first and best of the beginning. The dough is the mass of bread before it is baked. "Generations" means that this applied to their children and grandchildren as well.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell Israel. They were still in the wilderness, but God was promising that they would enter the land where they would eat bread from their own harvests. By giving the first cake, they acknowledged that the food came from God. The text also says this instruction would remain in force for a long time.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, such as your wages, your time, or your strength, put God first. You can give with gratitude, pray, and help others, remembering that everything you have comes from His hand.
exp.4:26:
This verse describes what happened when a woman suspected of unfaithfulness drank the bitter waters. If she was guilty, the water would bring harm to her: her belly would swell and her thigh would rot, expressions that probably refer to her reproductive organs. She would become a curse, that is, an example of punishment, before her people. "Defiled" means impure, and "have done trespass against her husband" means to have been unfaithful.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel. It was a ritual for cases of jealousy without proof or witnesses, and it placed the decision in God's hands rather than the husband's. Scholars debate exactly how it worked. Notice that it protected the woman: if she was innocent, she was set free.

For today: when proof is lacking, let us avoid accusing or judging based on suspicion. Let us bring our doubts to God in prayer and seek the truth with patience and justice.
exp.31:12:
This verse says that God became very angry with Israel and made them wander aimlessly through the desert for forty years. In this way, little by little, the whole generation that had acted wrongly before Him died out.

Here Moses is speaking. The tribes of Reuben and Gad wanted to stay east of the Jordan and not cross over with the others. Moses reminds them of what happened when the spies brought back a bad report and the people did not trust God. Only Caleb and Joshua were faithful. Moses fears that they will repeat the same mistake.

For today: disobedience and lack of trust in God not only affect us, they can also affect those around us. Today we can choose to trust God and follow Him faithfully, even when the path is frightening.
exp.4:14:
It says that the husband was to bring his wife before the priest, along with an offering: a tenth part of an ephah (a measure of grain, about two liters) of barley meal. No oil or incense was to be put on it, since these were signs of celebration and joy. It is called an "offering of jealousy" and an "offering of memorial" because it placed the matter before God, who knows the truth.

God gives this instruction to Moses for the people of Israel in the wilderness. It was a case without witnesses, where the husband felt jealous and there was no human way to prove anything. The process prevented personal revenge and left the judgment in God's hands. Scholars explain in several ways how the rite was understood, and the text does not fully detail it.

For today: when you feel suspicion or doubt in your marriage, do not feed them in secret or take justice into your own hands. Bring them before God in prayer and seek honest dialogue and wise counsel.
exp.28:29:
This verse says that on the sixth day of the feast, along with the bullocks, rams, and lambs that were offered, their meat offerings (offerings of flour and oil) and their drink offerings (wine poured out) were also to be presented, in the amount corresponding to each animal. "After the manner" means that everything followed the rules already established.

God gives these instructions to Moses, and Moses passes them on to Israel. This is the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day had its set number of sacrifices, and on this day there were eight bullocks. God wanted worship that was orderly, not left to chance.

For today: God values consistency and order in our relationship with him. We can set aside a fixed time to pray and read his Word, without waiting until we feel inspired, and offer him the best of our day with gratitude.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells us that Aaron did exactly what God had commanded: he lit the seven lamps of the lampstand so that they shone forward, toward the front. "Forward" means toward the place in front, and "as the Lord commanded Moses" means he followed the instruction to the letter.

God spoke to Moses, and Moses passed the message on to Aaron, the high priest. This takes place in the tabernacle, where the golden lampstand gave light to the holy place. The texts do not explain every detail of its symbolism, and Christians have understood it in several ways. What is clear here is Aaron's obedience.

For today: obeying God in the simple and everyday things matters. Aaron did not argue or change anything. We can ask ourselves what small thing God has asked of us, and do it faithfully, even when no one sees it.
exp.30:36:
This verse says that, from the sheep that fell to the soldiers, 675 were set apart for the Lord. "Tribute" means an offering or portion given to God. The word "was" appears in the verse as the form of the verb used for the tally, and its spelling is simply the older form of "was." That number was a small portion of the 337,500 sheep belonging to the half of the fighting men.

It is part of the account of the war against Midian. Moses and the priest Eleazar divided the spoil according to God's instructions: one half for the soldiers and the other for the people. From the soldiers' share, a fraction was given to the Lord (about 1 for every 500), and it was handed over to the priests. The numbers are very detailed, and some scholars discuss how to understand such large figures.

For today: God deserves the first and the best, and also order. We can faithfully and clearly set apart a part of what we receive for Him and for serving others.
exp.24:15:
This verse is brief: it says that the Lord spoke to Moses. It is the phrase that introduces a new instruction from God. The word "spake" reminds us that Moses did not act on his own, but waited for God's direction.

Israel had just sinned at Peor, where many joined in idolatry and immorality with women of Moab and Midian. A plague had punished the people, and Zimri and Cozbi were publicly put to death for their sin. Now God speaks to say how the Midianites are to be treated, since they had been a danger to Israel's faith. The instructions appear in the following verse.

For today: before we react to problems, let us take time to listen to God in his Word and in prayer. His direction helps us act with wisdom and not only on impulse or anger.
exp.31:10:
This verse says that the men who came out of Egypt at twenty years old and older would not see the land that God had solemnly promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The reason is that they did not wholly follow God, that is, they did not keep faithfully and wholeheartedly to him. The word "came up" means they left Egypt, and "sware" refers to God's solemn promise.

Here Moses speaks to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, who wanted to stay east of the Jordan. He reminds them of what happened forty years earlier, when the spies returned from Canaan and discouraged the people. Moses warns them not to repeat that lack of faith, since God was angry and that generation died in the wilderness.

For today: God values a heart that follows him completely. When fear makes you doubt his promises, remember that he is faithful, and ask him for courage to obey him to the end, as Caleb and Joshua did.
exp.31:36:
This verse tells that the tribe of Reuben built up three cities: Heshbon, Elealeh, and Kirjathaim. These cities had been taken earlier, and now the Reubenites were preparing them to live in and to protect their families and their livestock.

The people of Israel were about to cross the Jordan into Canaan. Reuben and Gad asked to stay on the east side, because that land was good for their livestock. Moses allowed them to do so on one condition: they had to help their brothers conquer the land on the other side. This verse describes how they settled while keeping that commitment.

Today we can learn that caring for what God gives us means working with diligence, without forgetting our commitments to others. Building our home and our work is good, but we must not neglect supporting our community and the church.
exp.9:11:
This verse tells that the people of Israel left the wilderness of Sinai, where they had camped for nearly a year, and began to move on. The cloud, which represented God's presence, later came to rest in the wilderness of Paran. The words "took their journeys" simply mean that they set out and continued on their way, stage by stage.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and the scene follows the instructions God had given through Moses, such as the use of the trumpets. Israel had received the law and organized the camp. Now, as the cloud lifted, the journey toward the promised land was beginning, guided by God step by step.

For today: God knows when we should move forward and when we should stop. We can ask him for direction, wait patiently for his sign, and obey him, even when we cannot see the whole road ahead.
exp.30:35:
This verse says that the half of the captured livestock that belonged to the soldiers who went out to battle was 337,500 sheep.

Here the narrator of the book records how the spoils were divided after the war against Midian. By God's command to Moses, everything was split into two equal parts: one for the fighting men and the other for the rest of the people. From the soldiers' share, a small portion was set aside for the Lord. The very exact numbers show that everything was counted with care. Some scholars debate exactly what these numbers were, but the text stresses order and fairness.

For today: God values honesty and order when dividing what we receive. We can practice this by being fair with others and by gladly setting aside a portion of what we have for God and for helping others.
exp.15:8:
Moses asks the Levites whether it seems like a small thing to them that God has set them apart from the rest of the people. God brought them close to Himself so that they would carry out the work of the tabernacle and stand before the congregation to serve them.

Moses speaks to Korah and the Levites who had rebelled. They wanted the priesthood too, which God had given to Aaron and his family. Moses reminds them that they already had a great honor: serving in the tabernacle. The verses that follow show that, at bottom, their complaint was against God, not only against Aaron.

For today: before you desire another person's place, give thanks for the place of service God has already given you. All service done for Him has value, even when it is not visible or famous.
exp.22:22:
This verse says that no "omens" work against God's people, meaning signs or portents used to foretell the future, nor any "divination," which is trying to learn hidden things by forbidden means. Instead, people will say of Israel: "Look at what God has done!"

Balaam speaks here, a prophet from outside Israel. Balak, king of Moab, paid him to curse Israel, but God allowed him only to bless them. Balaam recognizes that no spell can change what God has already decided in favor of his people. The glory belongs not to Israel but to God and to his work.

For today: we do not need to look for horoscopes or omens to feel secure. We can rest in the knowledge that God cares for his own, and when we see his help, we can give him the credit by saying: "What God has done!"
exp.9:16:
It says that, once they had taken down the tabernacle (the sacred tent where God dwelt among his people), the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari set forward, two families from the tribe of Levi. They were the ones in charge of carrying the parts of the tabernacle: the curtains, the boards, the pillars and the sockets.

The book tells how Israel left Mount Sinai toward the promised land. God, through Moses, had ordered the order of march in detail. Here we see that the Levites carried the tabernacle in the middle of the camp, and that each group had its place and its task. From the order of the account, these families went ahead of the standard of Reuben, so that the tabernacle could be set up when the others arrived.

For today: God cares about order and values service that seems small. Ask yourself what simple task falls to you, and do it faithfully, knowing that it helps all of God's people move forward.
exp.28:23:
This verse speaks of the offerings for the fifth day of the feast, although the detail given here refers to the previous day. It says that, along with the bullocks, rams and lambs, their grain offerings (flour mixed with oil) and their drink offerings (wine poured out) were to be presented. Everything was to be done according to the number of the animals and in accordance with the law, that is, following the rule already established.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Israel, in the wilderness, about the Feast of Tabernacles. Each day fewer bullocks were offered, and the animals had to be without blemish. Scholars explain the meaning of that decrease in several ways; there is no single interpretation that is certain.

For today: God values order and sincere dedication. We can give him our best of time, affection and resources with consistency, not only when we have something to spare.
exp.19:0:
This verse tells us that the whole nation of Israel came into the desert of Zin in the first month, and settled at Kadesh. There Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, died, and she was buried in that place. The word "abode" means that they camped there, and the verse's "came" is simply the plain past tense of "come."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He does not say which year this happened, but many think it was near the end of the forty years in the desert. The text is brief about Miriam, even though she had been a prophetess and had accompanied Moses from the time they left Egypt. Right after this comes the lack of water and the people's complaint.

For today: life mixes grief and trials, often one right after another. When we lose someone and another difficulty arrives as well, we can bring everything honestly before God, instead of letting our pain turn into complaint against others.
exp.20:20:
This verse tells that the people of Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites. "Messengers" are people sent to speak on behalf of others. The Amorites were one of the peoples who lived in that region.

The narrator of the book relates that Israel had already come a long way through the wilderness and was approaching the land of Canaan. They needed to pass through the territory of Sihon. Before advancing, Israel chose to ask permission with peaceful words. What follows shows that Sihon refused and attacked, so the conflict did not start with Israel.

For today: before facing a problem, try first respectful dialogue. Seeking peace and speaking with humility does not guarantee that the other person will respond well, but it keeps our conscience clear and shows a heart that prefers understanding over fighting.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that Moses was to count the men of the Gershon family who were between thirty and fifty years old. They were the ones who "enter in to perform the service," meaning those who joined the working group to serve in the tabernacle of the congregation, the sacred tent where God made his presence known among his people. Counting, here, means registering them or taking a census.

God himself speaks to Moses. The Levites were set apart to care for the tabernacle, and each family received different tasks. The Gershonites were assigned to carry the curtains and coverings. God set an age and an order so that the service would be carried out with care and reverence. Some believe the age limit was meant to ensure strong, mature men for heavy work.

Today we can learn that God values orderly service and every task, even the simple ones. Ask yourself what specific responsibility falls to you in your church or family, and carry it out with dedication.
exp.28:30:
This verse says that on the sixth day of the feast, a male goat was also offered as a sin offering. That offering was added to the daily burnt offering, that is, the animal burned completely on the altar, together with its grain offering (the offering of flour) and its drink offering (the wine poured out).

Moses passes on to the people God's instructions for the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day had its own list of offerings, so that Israel would worship God in an orderly way and recognize its need for forgiveness.

For today: even in the middle of the celebration, Israel remembered that it needed atonement. Christians believe that Jesus fulfilled that sacrifice once and for all. We can celebrate with joy, but also with sincere gratitude, and draw near to God each day without carrying guilt that has already been forgiven.
exp.14:17:
God asks Moses to speak with the people of Israel. He tells them that one day they will enter the land to which He is bringing them.

Jehovah speaks to Moses while Israel is still in the wilderness. That generation had doubted and was not able to enter the land (Numbers 14), but God renews His promise for their children. This verse introduces an instruction about offering the firstfruits of the bread to God, once they are living in the land.

God keeps His promises even when we fail or take our time. And when He gives us His blessings, He invites us to acknowledge Him with gratitude. Today we can begin each week or each income by giving thanks and returning to God the first and best of what we receive.
exp.32:44:
This verse says that the people of Israel departed from Iye-abarim and camped at Dibon-gad. "Departed" means "having set out," and "camped" is the sense of the wording here. It is one more stop on the long journey through the wilderness.

The passage is part of the list of stages of the journey that Moses wrote down, at God's command, to record the route from Egypt to the edge of the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). Here Israel is already near Moab, east of the Jordan. Dibon-gad is usually placed in that region, although some of the exact details of the route are debated.

For today: God takes notice of every stage of our lives, even those that seem dull or merely transitional. Remember with gratitude how He has guided you day by day, and trust that He will also lead you to the next stop.
exp.24:9:
This verse is a short transition. It says that the Lord, that is, Jehovah, spoke to Moses. After what has happened, God is going to give his opinion and an answer.

God speaks, and he does so after Israel's idolatry at Peor and the plague that killed twenty-four thousand people. When Phinehas acted, the dying stopped. Now God explains how he saw that act and announces that he will make a covenant of peace with Phinehas. Some readers debate how to apply his violent action today, but the text shows that God took the people's sin very seriously.

For today: God still speaks to those who seek him, especially in difficult moments. Before drawing conclusions, it is wise to listen to his Word with humility and let it interpret what we are living through.
exp.27:3:
This verse commands that two lambs be offered every day: one in the morning and the other at twilight. That older phrase is usually understood to mean evening, although some scholars explain it in other ways. The offering is a command, and the sacrifice was burned up entirely on the altar.

God speaks to Moses and asks him to remind the people of Israel of this. They were already close to the promised land, and a new generation needed to hear the instructions again. This daily sacrifice, known as the regular offering, marked the rhythm of the people's worship from dawn until dusk.

For today: just as Israel began and ended the day by presenting themselves before God, we can set aside a moment in the morning and another at night to pray, give thanks, and entrust the day to him. What matters is faithfulness, not perfection.
exp.0:33:
This verse says that the descendants of Manasseh, one of the sons of Joseph, were counted. They were counted by their generations, their families, and the houses of their fathers, recording each name. Only the men from twenty years old and upward who were able to go to war were included. The result appears in the next verse: thirty-two thousand two hundred.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. He commands a census of the tribes to organize the people before the march toward the promised land. Manasseh and Ephraim were sons of Joseph, and each became a tribe.

For today: God knows his people by name and gives each one a place and a task. You can simply ask yourself what place you are called to serve in your family and in your church, and do it faithfully.
exp.2:19:
This verse ends the list of the sons of Levi. It says that Merari had two sons, Mahli and Mushi, and that from them came the Merarite families. With this, the three branches of the Levites are complete: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The phrase "by their families" means that each family was identified by its ancestor.

Here God, through Moses, orders the count and the organization of the tribe of Levi, which was set apart to care for the tabernacle. Each branch would have different tasks. That is why it was important to record clearly who they were and which family they belonged to.

For today: God knows names and families, not only crowds. Even the services that seem small matter to him. Today you can serve faithfully in the place you have been given, knowing that God sees you, knows you, and values your work.
exp.15:32:
Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, together with their households and everything they owned, are said to have gone down alive into the pit. Here the word refers to Sheol, the place of the dead. The earth closed over them, and they vanished from among the people. The phrase that describes the earth covering them means that it covered them.

This is part of the account in the book of Numbers. These men had rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and they challenged their leadership and their priesthood. Moses had said that God would show whom He had chosen. The text presents this as God's judgment, and the people respond with fear, as the next verse shows.

For today: God takes seriously the pride and ambition that despise the order and the service He gives. We can examine our hearts and ask Him for humility, so that we serve with gratitude instead of competing for positions of importance.
exp.33:8:
This verse finishes describing the northern border of the promised land. The line continues to a place called Ziphron (Ziphon) and ends at Hazar-enan. Today it is not known with certainty where these places were exactly, and scholars propose different locations.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, who are on the plains of Moab, about to enter Canaan. God marks out for them the limits of the land he will give them as an inheritance, so that each tribe would know where to live and there would be no confusion or conflict.

For today: God is a God of order and of concrete promises. You can trust that He has a defined place and purpose for your life. Give thanks for what He has given you, and live with order and contentment within it.
exp.0:49:
God told the Levites to take care of the tabernacle, which is called "of the testimony" here because it held the tablets of the law. They were to look after its utensils and everything that belonged to it. They would also carry it, serve in it, and camp around it. The phrase about setting up their tents means that they would set up their camp.

The Lord speaks to Moses in the wilderness, when the men fit for war are counted. The Levites are not counted with that group, because they had another task: serving in the place where God dwelt among his people. Camping around it also marked a boundary of respect before what was holy.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is not very visible. Ask yourself what simple task He has placed in your hands, in your church or in your family, and do it with reverence and constancy.
exp.27:18:
This verse commands a whole burnt offering to be presented to God: two young bulls, one ram, and seven lambs a year old. The offering was burned completely on the altar, and the sentence about its wording is rewritten to fit the verse your reader sees. "Burnt offering" is what the whole animal was called when it was consumed by fire on the altar. "Young bullocks" are young bulls from the herd, and "without blemish" means without any physical flaw.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He is giving instructions for the yearly feasts. This passage refers to the Passover and to the seven days of unleavened bread, when this offering was presented each day in addition to the daily routine.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. Today we no longer offer animals, because Christians believe that Christ offered himself without blemish for us. We can respond by giving him our best time, affection, and attention, and not only what we have left over.
exp.13:42:
Moses warns the people that the Amalekites and the Canaanites are standing in front of them, and that they will fall by the sword if they advance. He gives them the reason: they have turned back from following the Lord, that is, they have drawn back and refused to obey him. Because of this, the Lord would not be with them.

Moses speaks after Israel believed the bad report of the spies and rebelled against God, who had said that that generation would not enter the land. Now, suddenly, they want to go up on their own. Moses warns them that this is no longer the time, because God would not go with them. They ignored the warning and were defeated.

For today: obeying God at the right time matters. Truly repenting means listening to his direction, not just doing something religious on our own. Before acting, ask yourself whether God is going with you in that decision.
exp.30:18:
This verse says that the Israelite soldiers who had killed someone or touched a dead body were to stay seven days outside the camp. They were to purify themselves on the third day and on the seventh day, together with the captives they had brought. The phrase "purify yourselves" refers to being cleansed according to the ritual of the law.

Moses speaks here after the war against Midian. According to the law, death made impure anyone who came into contact with it, and for that reason the camp had to be protected. This chapter contains very harsh rules of war, and scholars interpret them in various ways. Here the emphasis of the verse is on purification, not on victory.

For today: God takes seriously the weight of death and of sin. When we are stained by mistakes or by living in a broken world, we should not ignore it, but come to God to be made clean. For the Christian, that cleansing comes through Christ (1 John 1:9).
exp.22:1:
Balak, king of Moab, did as Balaam had said, and he prepared seven altars. Together they offered on each altar a young bull (a calf) and a ram (a mature male sheep). Everything was done as a sacrifice to seek God's answer.

The narrator tells us that Balak had hired Balaam to curse Israel, because he was afraid of them. Balaam, a diviner from another land, asks for the altars and the animals before he seeks God. Many believe he wanted to impress Balak, but the Bible does not fully explain his motives. In the end, God meets him, and does not change his plan to bless his people.

We can make grand religious gestures, but God looks at the heart. Balaam's sacrifices looked impressive, but his heart was divided. Today, instead of seeking to impress others, let us ask God for sincerity and obedience.
exp.6:88:
He says that when Moses went into the tent where God met with his people, he heard God's voice speaking to him. The voice came from above the cover of the ark, the mercy seat, right between the two angel figures, the cherubim. The word "testimony" refers to the tablets of the law kept inside the ark. The "peace offerings" are fellowship offerings.

This verse is a note from the narrator, probably Moses himself. It closes the long account of the offerings the tribal leaders brought at the dedication of the altar. After so many gifts, it shows God responding: this is not only ritual, there is real communication. God spoke with Moses and guided him.

For today: sincere worship seeks more than fulfilling duties; it seeks to listen to God. Set aside a moment each day to pray in silence and read the Bible, with a heart ready to hear him.
exp.34:22:
If someone, without seeing the other person, dropped a stone on them that could kill them, and the person died, but they were not enemies and he did not seek to harm them, then he is not to be treated as a murderer.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He established cities of refuge so that the one who killed without intention would not become the victim of an immediate revenge from the dead person's relative. First the congregation was to judge the case with justice, hearing both sides.

Today we can learn not to judge in haste. Before accusing someone, it is wise to ask about their intentions and to know the facts. It also reminds us that our carelessness can hurt others, and we should act with care and responsibility.
exp.32:5:
This verse says that the people of Israel left Succoth and camped at Etham, a place that was at the edge of the wilderness.

This chapter is a record of Israel's stops on the journey from Egypt to the promised land. Moses wrote it at the command of the LORD, as a memorial of each stage. Etham marks the point where what is familiar ends and the wilderness begins. The exact location of these places is not certain, and scholars debate it.

For today: God guides step by step, even when the road leads to the edge of the unknown. If today you are in an uncertain stage, remember that He also records and cares for each stop along your path. Trust Him one day at a time.
exp.26:2:
The daughters of Zelophehad explain their case. They say that their father died in the wilderness during the forty years of the journey, but that he was not part of Korah's group that rebelled against the Lord. He died for his own sin, as happened to many of that generation, and he had no sons. The word "company" in the verse refers to the group that gathered together against the Lord, and the phrase "in the company of Korah" refers to the followers of Korah.

Five sisters speak before Moses, the priest Eleazar, and all the people. Since their father had no sons, the promised land would not pass to their family and his name would disappear. They make it clear that he did not lead any rebellion. They respectfully ask to be given an inheritance.

For today: when something seems unfair, we can bring it forward with courage, respect, and truth, without complaining or rebelling, and leave the matter in God's hands, as Moses did.
exp.0:9:
This verse names the leaders of two tribes: Ephraim and Manasseh, who were the sons of Joseph. Elishama, son of Ammihud, represented Ephraim, and Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, represented Manasseh. The names are the same ones we know today.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to take a census of the men of Israel able to go to war. To help him, each tribe had a leader. This list shows that the people were organized and that each tribe had its place. Joseph receives two tribes, because his two sons were counted as heads of tribes.

For today: God knows people by name and values those who serve in humble places. Ask yourself what small responsibility God has given you, and carry it out faithfully.
exp.8:2:
It says the Passover was to be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, "at even," that is, at evening. That expression is understood in several ways, but it points to the end of the afternoon and the beginning of the night. "In his appointed season" means on the set date. "Rites" are the ceremonies, and "ceremonies" are the rules for carrying them out. Everything was to be done just as God had directed.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, a year after the departure from Egypt. The Passover was a reminder of the people's deliverance. Now God commands it to be kept for the first time since they left, and the people obey, as the verses that follow show.

For today: remembering with gratitude what God has done for us calls for steadiness and obedience. You can set aside a fixed time, each week or each day, to thank him and read his Word, without letting routine or hurry crowd it out.
exp.12:0:
This verse tells of a journey. The people of Israel left Hazeroth, a place where they had camped, and settled in the wilderness of Paran. "Moved" means they set out on the road, and "pitched their camp" means they set up their tents in a new place. It is a short note that marks a change of location.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. His purpose is to orient us: Israel is now very close to the promised land. This stop in Paran prepares the moment when God asks that a leader from each tribe be sent to explore Canaan. Many scholars see here the beginning of a test of faith.

For today: God guides us from place to place, and each stage has a purpose. Even when a season seems like mere passage or wilderness, trust that He is preparing you for what lies ahead.
exp.1:26:
This verse says that the tribe of Asher camped alongside the tribe of Dan, on the north side of Israel's camp. The leader of Asher was Pagiel, son of Ocran. The word "north" here is an old way of saying the direction, and the phrase about where they would pitch their tents describes how they were to set up their tents.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron. After leaving Egypt, Israel needed order to live and march in the desert. Each tribe had its place and its leader, and the tabernacle stood in the center. This showed that God was at the center of the people's life. The names of the leaders show that each tribe mattered.

For today: God cares about order and values each person by name. Look for your place of service in your church, help faithfully, and keep God at the center of your home and your work.
exp.14:37:
God tells Moses to instruct the people to make tassels or fringes on the edges of their clothing, and to put on each one a cord of blue-violet color. The word for the fringe itself is a term for a tassel or fringe, and the color is a shade between blue and purple. This was to be done throughout all their generations.

The Lord speaks to Moses. Just before this, a man was punished for openly disobeying the command about the Sabbath. Then God gives this visible sign, and the next verse explains its purpose: when they saw it, the people would remember the commandments and would not be led astray by their eyes and their hearts.

For today: we all easily forget what God asks of us. You can choose a simple reminder, such as a verse on your phone, a bracelet, or a note on your mirror, to return each day to obeying it with love.
exp.1:6:
This verse names the tribe of Zebulun and its leader, Eliab, son of Helon. Zebulun camped beside Judah and Issachar, on the east side of the tabernacle. The "leader" is the chief or prince of the tribe. The "army" is its fighting force, and those "counted" are the men registered for war.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the people were numbered. He gives them an exact order for camping and marching, with the tabernacle at the center. Judah led, and Zebulun went with it. In this way the camp stayed orderly, and each tribe knew its place.

For today: God knows each person by name and gives them a place among his people. Even when your task seems small or little noticed, it matters. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, and support others with joy.
exp.16:0:
This verse is only the introduction. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses. The phrase "And the Lord spake" appears many times in the Torah and marks that what follows is an instruction that comes from God, not an idea of Moses.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives the message for the people. In the earlier chapters, Korah and others rebelled against the leadership of Moses and Aaron, and the people complained bitterly. For that reason, what comes next, the twelve staffs, aims to make clear and orderly whom God had chosen for priestly service.

For today: before arguing or making decisions, it is good to learn to listen to God. We can set aside a few minutes to pray and read the Bible calmly, ready to obey, instead of being carried away by complaints or the opinions of the moment.
exp.19:7:
God tells Moses to take the rod, gather the whole people together with Aaron, and speak to the rock (the stone) before everyone. In this way water would come out for the people and their animals. The "assembly" means the people gathered together, and the "beasts" are the animals they were carrying.

The LORD speaks. The people are in the desert, without water, and they complain against Moses and Aaron. They go to God, and He answers with a solution. Notice that the command is to speak to the rock, not to strike it. In the next verse, Moses scolds the people and, according to other passages, strikes the rock instead of speaking to it. That is why God corrects him afterward.

For today: when God gives a clear instruction, it is worth obeying it just as it is, even when it seems different from what we did before. Trust that He knows how to supply your need.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel left Ije-abarim and camped in the valley of Zared. The word "removed" here means "having set out," and "pitched" means "camped." A "valley" is a low stretch of land through which a stream runs, which is often dry and carries water only in the rainy seasons.

The writer of the book records the stops of Israel's journey through the wilderness, near Moab, toward the promised land with simplicity. It is part of a list of stages, and it shows that the people moved forward step by step. Scholars do not agree on the exact location of Zared, though it is thought to have been southeast of the Dead Sea.

For today: God also guides our lives in stages, and they are not always striking. Trust Him in the small, ordinary stretches of the road, because He continues to lead you.
exp.28:38:
This verse sums up all the offerings described in chapters 28 and 29. God says that the people were to bring these things to him at their appointed feasts. This was in addition to what each person offered because of a vow they had made, or from their own willing heart. The burnt offerings were offerings completely burned up; the grain offerings were flour and grain; the drink offerings were wine poured out; the peace offerings were offerings of fellowship.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. After describing the calendar of feasts, he closes with this summary. He wanted the new generation to know how to worship God with order and consistency.

For today: God values both regular worship and generous giving. We can have steady habits of prayer and gathering together, and also give with joy and spontaneity, without one replacing the other.
exp.30:43:
This verse is part of a list. It says that from the half of the plunder that fell to the whole community of Israel, 36,000 were cattle. "Congregation" means the people of Israel gathered together, and "set apart" means that Moses separated or divided that portion.

After the war against Midian, God commanded Moses to divide the plunder in half: one part for the soldiers and the other part for the rest of the people. The text records the figures with great care. Some scholars believe the numbers are literal, while others think they could be understood in another way, so there is no single explanation.

For today: God values justice and honest sharing. If you handle money, work, or belongings that belong to others, do so with clarity and fairness, and remember to give thanks, because everything you have comes from Him.
exp.10:14:
Moses tells God that, if things are going to continue this way, he would rather God kill him. He asks this if he has truly found grace, that is, favor, in God's sight. He says "let me not see my wretchedness," meaning that he does not want to have to face his own misery or distress.

Moses speaks out of exhaustion. The people were complaining for lack of meat and weeping for food. Moses felt that the burden was too heavy for him alone. God does not rebuke him for his outburst, but answers him with help: he will gather seventy elders and put of the Spirit upon them so that they share the burden.

For today: when you feel without strength, tell God honestly what you carry inside. And do not carry everything alone; accept the help of others that God places beside you.
exp.6:1:
This verse says that the leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel came forward to offer something to God. They are called "princes," meaning leaders or heads. They were the heads of their fathers' houses, that is, they led their families and tribes. Those who were numbered are those who had been counted in the census.

Moses had just finished setting up the tabernacle and anointing and consecrating everything in it. The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Moses. After the place had been set apart, the leaders responded with freewill offerings. The verses that follow speak of six carts and twelve oxen.

For today: those who lead can take the first step in generosity. When God gives us something, such as a family, a job, or a community, we can answer him with a willing and joyful giving, and so encourage others to do the same.
exp.1:20:
This verse gives the number of the men of the tribe of Manasseh: thirty-two thousand two hundred. "Host" means army, that is, the men fit for war. "Those that were numbered" are the ones who were counted in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while the people are in the wilderness, near Sinai. He gives them instructions for camping in order around the tabernacle, each tribe under its own banner. Manasseh camped beside Ephraim, and the leader of the tribe was Gamaliel son of Pedahzur.

For today: God cares about every person among his people, even when they seem to us to be just a number. He places each one in a place and with a task. Today you can trust that your place in the family, in the church and at work does not go unnoticed by Him. Serve Him faithfully where you are.
exp.6:36:
This verse describes the offering of Shelumiel, prince of the tribe of Simeon. He brought one silver dish weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl of 70 shekels, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. A "shekel" was a unit of weight, and a "present" means a grain offering. "Fine flour" is the finest flour.

Here the account of Moses speaks. Each day, for twelve days, a leader of one tribe presented the same offering for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. This shows that all of Israel took part in the worship. It is repeated in the same way for each tribe, so no tribe was placed above another.

For today: God values each person bringing their own part, without comparing themselves to others. Serve God with what you have, with steadiness and a willing heart, even when your contribution looks the same as everyone else's or goes largely unnoticed.
exp.0:13:
This verse names a man from the tribe of Gad: Eliasaph, son of Deuel. He was one of the leaders chosen to help count the people. That difference is due to variants in the ancient manuscripts.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and orders him to take a census of the men fit for war. To do this, each tribe provides a leader. This list of names shows that the people were organized with order, and that each tribe had someone to represent it.

God knows people by their name, even when they are not famous. Eliasaph barely appears in the Bible, but he was recorded. If today you serve in a humble place, without applause, remember that God sees your faithfulness and values it. Serve gladly wherever He places you.
exp.34:10:
This verse says that Israel was to set apart special cities of refuge. There, a person who had killed someone without meaning to could flee. "Refuge" means shelter or protection. "Killer" is the one who causes a death. "Without intent" means by accident, with no intention of killing.

God is speaking to Moses before the people cross the Jordan into Canaan. He was giving instructions for life in the new land. In that time, a relative of the victim could seek revenge. These cities protected the person who had killed by accident, until the community judged the case fairly. In this way life was guarded and further violence was prevented.

For today: God cares about justice and also about mercy. We can learn not to act with revenge or in haste, and to work so that each person is heard with fairness. We can also be a refuge for someone who has failed and seeks to make things right.
exp.0:26:
This verse gives the result of the count of the tribe of Judah: 74,600 men twenty years old and up, able to go out to war. The phrase "those that were numbered" refers to those who were counted in the census.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commands him to count Israel by tribes, families, and fathers' houses. This was a preparation for organizing the people and their camp as they marched toward the promised land. Judah was the largest tribe on the list. Later from Judah would come King David and, according to the New Testament, Jesus. Some scholars debate how to understand these very large numbers, but the text presents them as the official count.

For today: God knows and counts his people one by one. You are not a lost number in the crowd; your place matters. Serve with courage where God has placed you.
exp.31:19:
Moses answers the tribes who ask to stay on the east side of the Jordan. He tells them: "If ye will do this thing," that is, if they arm themselves and go ahead of the Lord to war. The phrase about making ready means that they must prepare and get themselves ready. It is a condition: their request will be granted only if they keep their word.

Moses speaks. The tribes of Reuben and Gad, and later the half-tribe of Manasseh, saw that those lands were good for their livestock. Moses feared that his brothers would lose heart and that the people would be divided. So here he sets a clear condition: to fight alongside Israel until everyone has their own inheritance.

For today: God gives us rest and blessings, but he also calls us to help others. Before enjoying what is ours, ask yourself whom you can support, and keep what you promise.
exp.33:11:
This verse says that the eastern border of the land goes down to the Jordan River and ends at the salt sea, that is, the Dead Sea. With this the map is closed: "this shall be your land," with its limits all around. The boundary lines and the place where the line ends are what the verse describes.

God speaks through Moses, shortly before Israel enters Canaan. He gives them the limits of the promised land so that they know clearly what they will inherit. Afterward Moses orders them to divide it by lot among nine and a half tribes, because Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh already had their inheritance on the other side of the Jordan.

For today: God is a God of order and of concrete promises. We can trust that what he gives has good limits, and learn to receive with gratitude what falls to us, without living in comparison with others.
exp.34:11:
This verse says that the cities of refuge would serve as protection from the avenger of blood, the family member responsible for avenging a death. A refuge is a place of safety, which is what these cities were. The person who had killed someone would not be put to death before first facing a trial before the community.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to instruct the people on how to organize themselves when they enter the land of Canaan. These were deaths without intent, accidental killings. In that time, family vengeance could cause even more violence, and God set a limit: first, justice through a trial.

For today: before reacting in anger or passing judgment on someone, let us seek the truth calmly and justly. God cares both for the one who was harmed and for the one who is accused, and he calls us not to take revenge into our own hands.
exp.24:4:
Here Moses gives an order to the judges of Israel: each one must put to death the men of his tribe who joined themselves to Baal-peor. The word "joined" means to attach oneself to someone or something; here it describes taking part in the worship of that idol.

Moses speaks after God had shown his anger. Israel, at Shittim, had joined in the worship of Baal-peor, a pagan cult that was tied to sexual immorality. God's command concerning the leaders and Moses' order to the judges are understood in several ways, but both show how serious it is to betray the God of the covenant.

Today, this passage invites us to take seriously everything that pulls us away from God. It is not about judging others harshly, but about examining our own hearts, fleeing what seduces us, and returning quickly to Him.
exp.25:18:
This verse recalls that Judah had sons named Er and Onan, but that both died in the land of Canaan, before founding families of their own within the people. That is why they do not appear as a tribe or family in this census.

The book of Numbers records Israel's second census, taken at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God told Moses to count the men by their families before entering the promised land. In naming Er and Onan, the text recalls their death, which according to Genesis 38 was a judgment from God. Here the cause is not explained; the text only mentions the fact.

For today: God cares for every name and every story, and He also takes our decisions seriously. You can ask Him to help you live with obedience and humility, knowing that He continues to build His people with those who trust in Him.
exp.14:26:
It says that if a person sins without realizing it or without meaning to, they must bring a one-year-old female goat as a sin offering.
