A sin committed by mistake is an error or failing that was not intended, and "atonement" means covering guilt so that a person is forgiven and reconciled with God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel, who were heading toward the promised land. Earlier, the sin of the whole community was addressed; here the case of a single person is considered. Afterward it is made clear that the same law applies to the Israelite and to the foreigner who lives among them. Sins committed with deliberate defiance are treated differently in the verses that follow.

For today: God takes even our unintentional failings seriously, but he also offers forgiveness. We can ask him to show us our hidden errors and come to him with confidence, knowing that Christ is our complete atonement.
exp.32:37:
This verse tells us that Aaron, the high priest, went up to Mount Hor because the Lord had commanded it. There he died, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, on the first day of the fifth month.

Here no single character is speaking; rather, Moses is putting in writing the stages of Israel's journey through the wilderness. According to Numbers 20, Aaron did not enter the promised land, and God himself announced his death to him. The text mentions his age, 123 years, right after, and then notes that Israel's enemies were still watching closely.

For today: Aaron obeyed to the end, even when he knew what awaited him. We can ask God to help us trust him too in difficult moments, knowing that our days are in his hands.
exp.5:17:
It says that, when the time of his vow was over, the Nazarite would present himself at the entrance of the tabernacle and there have the head of his separation shaved. Rewritten for the verse: "shave the head" carries the meaning of the verb, and the time of consecration is simply the period of his separation. Then he would put that hair on the fire under the sacrifice of the peace offerings, which was an offering of fellowship and thanksgiving to God.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for Israel. A Nazarite was someone who made a special vow to dedicate himself to the Lord for a period of time. The long hair showed that dedication. At the end, what had been the sign of his consecration was offered. The Bible does not explain every detail of the rite, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when you finish a season of devotion or service to God, do not keep the credit for yourself. Give him thanks and offer to him what you have done, trusting that he receives it.
exp.30:40:
Here it is said that Moses took the part of the spoils that belonged to God and gave it to the priest Eleazar. The portion set apart for the Lord was given to God, and the offering presented to God was then dedicated to the service of the sanctuary. Moses did this just as the Lord had commanded him.

The narrator tells what happened after the war against Midian. God had commanded that the spoils be divided between the warriors and the rest of the people, and that from each half a portion be set aside for Him. The earlier verses detail what was set apart from the donkeys and from the people. Moses did not decide on his own; he did what God commanded. Eleazar, as priest, received these offerings.

For today: God deserves the first and the best of what we receive. We can give with order, honesty, and obedience, not out of pressure or for appearance, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.6:19:
He says that among Nathanael's offerings there was a golden spoon weighing ten shekels and full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned before God. The "spoon" was actually a small vessel, like a cup or a ladle, for carrying the incense.

The author of the book tells how the leaders of the twelve tribes brought offerings to dedicate the tabernacle. Each day one prince presented the same thing. Here it is the second day, and it is Nathanael's turn, from the tribe of Issachar. The repetition shows that each tribe was equally important before God.

For today: God values the sincere devotion of every person, without comparison. Nathanael did not try to outdo anyone; he simply gave his best. We can offer God our time, talents, and prayer with that same steadiness, without competing or feeling lesser than others.
exp.15:12:
Here Dathan and Abiram confront Moses. They say that bringing him out of Egypt, a land that "flows with milk and honey", was a small thing, since now he has brought them out to die in the wilderness. And on top of that, they say, he wants to rule over them with a harsh and proud authority.

Dathan and Abiram, from the tribe of Reuben, join Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron. Moses calls them to speak, but they refuse to come. They describe Egypt as a land of milk and honey, when that description belonged to the promised land. In this way they twist the truth and forget their slavery. They accuse Moses of abusing his power, even though God had placed him as leader.

When we are upset, it is easy to remember the past as better than it was and to blame others. Before accusing, it is wise to stop, be honest, and listen with humility.
exp.6:77:
This verse announces the last day of the offerings to dedicate the altar. It is the turn of the leader of the tribe of Naphtali, named Ahira, son of Enan. An old word: "prince" here means chief or leader of his tribe. After the name come the details of his offering, which are almost the same as those of the other leaders.

The author of the book, according to tradition, is Moses. In this chapter it is told that each tribe brought its offering, one day per tribe, when the tabernacle was already set up and consecrated. Each leader gives exactly the same thing, and the Bible repeats the full list with each one. Why it does this is interpreted in several ways, but it seems to show that each tribe was valued equally.

For today: God sees and remembers every act of giving, even if it is the last in line or seems repeated. Serve God faithfully, without comparing yourself or seeking first place.
exp.10:20:
Moses says that the people surrounding him number six hundred thousand men on foot, that is, they are walking and able to fight. Then he repeats what God had promised him: meat for everyone for a whole month. Moses says it with amazement, like someone who cannot see how that could be possible.

Moses speaks here tired and overwhelmed. The people were complaining in the desert because they missed the food of Egypt, and God had announced that he would give them meat. Moses measures the promise by what he sees: crowds, sheep, cattle and fish. God answers with a question: "Is the LORD's arm shortened?"

For today: when a promise of God seems impossible to you, do not measure it only by your own resources. Bring your doubt to him honestly, as Moses did, and trust that God is greater than your calculations.
exp.22:23:
It says that Israel is like a lion that rises up and stands with strength. It does not rest until it devours its prey and drinks the blood of those it has defeated. It is a poetic image of power and victory. The quoted words from the previous verse are removed here because they are not part of the wording your reader sees; the comment about a wild ox is likewise omitted.

Balaam, a foreign prophet, is the speaker. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God put blessings in his mouth. Balaam describes Israel as a strong people because God brought them out of Egypt and stands behind them. The violent image is the language of war of that time, not an invitation to cruelty.

For today: no one can curse the one whom God has blessed. If you trust God, you can face criticism and threats with calm, remembering that your strength comes from Him, not from yourself.
exp.24:12:
God promises Phinehas and his descendants a priesthood that will last forever. The reason is that Phinehas was zealous for his God, that is, he had a burning concern for the honor of God. He also made atonement, meaning he brought about an end to the punishment and the restoring of the relationship with God. "Seed" means descendants.

God speaks to Moses. The people of Israel had fallen into immorality and idolatry with the women of Moab and Midian, and a plague was killing many. Phinehas acted decisively against a man who openly defied God, and the plague stopped. God recognizes that act with a covenant of peace.

For today: true zeal for God seeks to restore and protect what is holy, not to harm others. Today we can show it with firmness in faithfulness, in prayer for our community, and in rejecting sin, trusting in Christ, our high priest.
exp.30:53:
Moses and the priest Eleazar received the gold that the captains of the army had offered. The captains of thousands and the captains of hundreds were the leaders over those groups of soldiers. They brought that gold into the tent of meeting, as a memorial or reminder before God for Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just fought against Midian, and the captains offered gold as an offering for all of them returning alive (Numbers 31:49-50). The text does not say the gold had any special use beyond serving as a reminder; some see it as a symbol of gratitude and redemption.

For today: when God looks after you in a difficulty, do not forget it. Look for a concrete way to thank Him, such as an offering, a written prayer, or a service, and remember what He has done.
exp.30:39:
This verse continues the count of the spoils from the war against Midian. It says that the persons, that is, the young women who were left alive, numbered sixteen thousand. Of them, thirty-two were given as the Lord's share, that is, a portion set apart for God. The word "share" here means a portion kept separate for Him.

The narrator describes how Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the leaders divided the spoils, following what God had commanded. One half went to the soldiers and the other half to the people; from each half a part was set aside for the Lord and for those who served in the sanctuary. The passage is hard and should be read within the ancient context of war. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: this order in the division reminds us that everything we have comes from God. We can give, honestly and in an orderly way, the first part of what we receive, recognizing that He is the owner of everything.
exp.32:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan. The word "departed" is rendered in the sense of "having set out," and the word "pitched" means "camped." It is one more step in the list of places where they stopped in the desert.

Moses writes this record at God's command, summarizing the stages of the journey from Egypt to near the promised land. It is not known with certainty where each place was; some of the names cannot be located with confidence. But the list shows that God kept a record of every stretch of the journey, including the long and difficult years.

For today: there are seasons of life that seem like mere stopping points without importance, and yet God is present in them. Today you can give thanks for every step, including those that seem slow or ordinary, trusting that He is guiding you toward what He promised.
exp.27:28:
This verse says that, along with each of the seven lambs, a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil was to be offered. The word "tenth" refers to a tenth part of an ephah, a measure of grain. The "several tenth deal" in the King James wording is the offering portion itself. The offering of grain was called a meal offering. With this, the offering for the feast was completed.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses tells the people of Israel. Numbers 28 and 29 explain the offerings for the appointed days. This passage deals with the Feast of Weeks, when the first fruits of the harvest were presented. God asked for order, exact quantities, and animals without blemish.

For today: God cares about the details of our worship. We can offer him our best, not what is left over. Today we do not bring lambs, because Christians believe Christ is the complete sacrifice, but we can give God our time, affection, and work with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.20:18:
This verse is part of a list of places where Israel stopped in the wilderness: from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth. These are stops along the way, one after another. The ancient names are written today as Mattanah, Nahaliel and Bamoth.

The book's narrator is tracing the people's journey, just after the song of the well, where Israel gave thanks for the water God gave them. Then the account continues toward Moab. No one knows with certainty exactly where these places were; scholars do not agree. What is clear is that Israel was moving step by step toward the promised land.

God is concerned not only with the destination but also with each stage of the journey. Perhaps today your step seems small or unimportant, but God guides you in it. Trust Him one day at a time, giving thanks for His provision as Israel did at the well.
exp.30:26:
This verse commands that the spoils taken in war be divided into two equal parts. One half was for the soldiers who fought, and the other for the whole community of Israel. "Prey" means the plunder, what was seized. "Congregation" is the people gathered together.

God speaks to Moses after the war against Midian. He orders him, together with the priest Eleazar and the heads of the families, to count the plunder. In this way it was shared out in an orderly manner, and a portion was set apart for God. This is a passage from an ancient war, and it must be read within that time and that history of Israel.

For today: the passage shows that what is achieved together should be shared out fairly. Whoever works deserves their share, but so do those who supported the group from behind. We can apply this in the family, the church, or the workplace, recognizing everyone and giving thanks to God.
exp.18:2:
God says that the red heifer must be handed over to Eleazar the priest. He will bring her outside the camp, and there she will be slain, that is, sacrificed, while he watches. The words "you shall give" are addressed to the people, and the phrase "he shall cause her to be slain" means that someone else will carry out the killing.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to give a law about the purification of anyone who became unclean by touching a dead body. Eleazar, the son of Aaron, acts in the place of his father. That the sacrifice takes place outside the camp shows that it was a special rite. Interpreters explain its exact meaning in various ways, but all agree that it teaches the seriousness of sin and of death.

Today we can remember that cleansing the heart has a cost and that God himself provides it. With humility, let us draw near to Him and trust in His forgiveness.
exp.12:1:
This is a simple introduction. It says that the LORD, that is, God, spoke to Moses.

The people of Israel had just left Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran, now close to the promised land. God is the one who speaks, and Moses is the one who receives the command. What follows is the instruction to send one leader from each tribe to look over Canaan, the land God was already giving them. Some scholars point out that in Deuteronomy 1 the people also asked to send spies, so the two accounts can be understood as complementing each other.

For today: before taking important steps, it is wise to pause and listen to God in prayer and in his Word, and not simply act on impulse or out of habit.
exp.25:24:
This verse closes the list of the families of the tribe of Issachar. It says that, when the men of each family were counted, the total was 64,300. "Counted" means the people registered in the census, in this case the men of an age to go to war.

Here the narrator of the book describes the second census of Israel, ordered by God to Moses and Eleazar at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Almost all of the previous generation had died, and the people were getting ready to enter the promised land and divide it. The numbers helped organize that inheritance. Some scholars debate how to understand these very large figures, but the text presents them as a real record.

God knows and counts his people, family by family. No one is a number without value to Him. Today you can rest knowing that God knows you by name, and also value the people in your church and your family as someone important.
exp.34:5:
This verse says that, of the cities Israel would give to the Levites, six would be cities of refuge. There a person who had killed someone could flee. Besides those six, forty-two more cities would be given, making forty-eight cities in total. The one who causes another person's death is the one who has killed, and to take refuge means to seek protection.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before the people entered the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, so they would live in cities spread among the tribes. Later the text explains that these six cities protected the one who killed without intent, so that he would not be put to death without a fair trial.

For today: God cares for justice and mercy at the same time. We can imitate him by avoiding hasty revenge, listening before we judge, and being a safe refuge for anyone who needs help.
exp.22:11:
Balaam answers Balak with a question that is really a statement: he must be careful to speak only what the Lord puts in his mouth. Here "take heed" means to look after carefully, to keep watch over with attention.

Balaam speaks. He is a prophet who was not an Israelite. King Balak of Moab hired him to curse Israel, but God made him bless them instead. Balak becomes angry and complains. Balaam explains that he cannot say what Balak wants, only what God gives him. Balak then insists and takes him to another place, as if changing location could change God's message.

For today: God does not change his word because of pressure or convenience. We can ask him to be faithful to what he says, even when others expect us to say something different. Being honest with the truth is worth more than pleasing everyone.
exp.19:4:
Here the people complain to Moses and blame him for bringing them out of Egypt to a bad place. They say there is no place to plant, no fig trees, no vines, no pomegranates, and not even water to drink. A place of seed is land that is sown, or a place where seed is planted.

This is the new generation of Israel, in the wilderness of Zin, after the death of Miriam. There was no water, and fear and thirst drove them to complain harshly. They remember the fruit of Egypt and forget the slavery from which God freed them. Moses and Aaron, instead of answering the complaint, fall prostrate before God, and God reveals himself to them.

When we feel lack, it is easy to remember the past with nostalgia and doubt God. Instead of complaining, we can do as Moses and Aaron did: bring our need to God in prayer and wait for his answer.
exp.13:21:
God says that all those people saw his glory and the signs he worked in Egypt and in the wilderness. Even so, they put him to the test, that is, they tested him by doubting him, and they did not listen to his voice. "Ten times" may mean many times, though some take it literally.

God is speaking after Israel rebelled when they heard the report of the spies and wanted to return to Egypt. Moses had pleaded for the people, and God forgave them, but he did not free them from the consequences: that generation would not enter the promised land. Only Caleb, who followed God with a different spirit, would enter.

Seeing God at work is not enough if we do not trust him. Today we can remember what God has already done for us and respond to him with faith and obedience, not with complaint or doubt.
exp.2:20:
This verse names two families that descended from Gershon, a son of Levi: the family of the Libnites and the family of the Shimites. They are part of the list of the Levites, the tribe dedicated to the service of God. A "family" here is a clan, a group of relatives descended from a common ancestor.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites did not receive territory as the other tribes did, but were set apart to care for the tabernacle. That is why God commands that they be counted and arranged by clans, each with a task and a place to camp. The Gershonites were assigned to camp behind the tabernacle, on the west.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name, and gives each one a place in his work. Even if your task seems small or little seen, it is valuable. Serve faithfully where God has placed you.
exp.32:19:
The passage says that the people of Israel left a place called Rimmon-parez and camped at another place called Libnah. The word "departed" in the verse is the one used here for leaving, and "camped" or "settled for a while" is the sense of the stop they made.

It is part of a list of Israel's stops during their journey through the wilderness, from Egypt to the promised land. Moses, by God's command, wrote down these stages (Numbers 33:2). No one knows for certain where many of these places were, and scholars do not agree on their locations. The list serves to remind us that God guided his people step by step.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the quiet, ordinary stretches of life, not only the great miracles. There are seasons of waiting and routine where it seems nothing is happening. Even so, God accompanies you and leads you. Trust him and keep walking faithfully, one step at a time.
exp.27:16:
It says that on the fifteenth day of the first month a holy feast begins, and that for seven days the people were to eat bread made without yeast. "Unleavened" is bread made without yeast, and a holy feast is a sacred festival. The Passover was kept on the fourteenth day, and the next day this feast of unleavened bread began.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions about the offerings and the feasts of the year. This feast reminded them of their deliverance from Egypt, when they left in haste and had no time to let the dough rise (Exodus 12:39).

For today: remembering what God has done for us strengthens faith. You can set aside time each week to thank him for his past help and to leave behind habits that hinder your walk with him.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that Joshua, son of Nun, and Caleb, son of Jephunneh, tore their clothes. They were two of the men who had gone to explore the promised land. The phrase "to search the land" means to explore it, to walk through it and see what it was like. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of deep pain, sorrow, or distress.

After hearing the fearful report of the other spies, the people wept and wanted to go back to Egypt, even choosing a leader to take them back. Moses and Aaron fell face down before God. Joshua and Caleb, who had seen the same land, felt grief over the people's unbelief and were getting ready to speak to them with faith.

For today: when everyone around you is carried away by fear, you can choose to trust God and speak with courage and respect. At times it will hurt to see others' unbelief, but God can use your firm faith.
exp.27:25:
This verse speaks of the day of the firstfruits, which is the Feast of Weeks, when the people brought to God a new offering from the first fruits of the harvest. On that day they were to gather for a holy convocation, that is, a sacred assembly set apart to worship God. They were not to do any servile work, meaning the heavy labor of everyday life.

God speaks to Moses and the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He gives them a calendar of offerings and feasts so that their whole life revolves around God. Later this feast came to be associated with Pentecost, although this passage does not say so directly.

For today: before spending what you receive, give God the first of it with gratitude. And set aside a time of rest to worship Him and remember that everything comes from Him.
exp.12:30:
Caleb calms the people before Moses and firmly proposes: "Let us go up at once and take possession of the land, for we are well able to overcome it." The word "possession" is rendered here as taking the land as an inheritance, and "at once" means "right away, without delay."

The twelve spies returned from exploring Canaan. Ten spoke of fortified cities and giants, and the people were filled with fear. Caleb, one of the spies, speaks to quiet the murmuring and to remind them that God had already promised that land. His confidence does not come from Israel's strength, but from God's promise. The other spies did not agree.

In the face of challenges, we can see our problems realistically, but measure them by the light of God's promises, not only by our own strength. Ask Him for courage to take the next step.
exp.32:33:
The people of Israel left the camp at Jotbathah and settled in another place called Ebronah. The phrase translated as "removed" means "having set out," and "encamped" means "pitched camp." It is one more stop on their long journey through the wilderness.

Moses writes this account of the journey, following God's command to record each stage (Numbers 33:2). We do not know for certain where Ebronah was, and scholars do not agree. Even so, the text lists these stops to remember that God guided his people step by step, from Egypt to the promised land.

Today, this verse reminds us that God cares even for the stages of our lives that seem simple or temporary. Perhaps today you do not see a great purpose, but you can trust that he walks with you at every stop. Write down what God has done on your path, and give thanks for it.
exp.19:25:
God tells Moses to strip Aaron of his garments, that is, the special robes of the high priest, and put them on Eleazar, Aaron's son. The verse's "strip" here means taking off the clothing, and the phrase "gathered unto his people" is a way of saying that Aaron is going to die and be joined with his ancestors.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Hor, near the end of the years in the wilderness. Aaron would not be allowed to enter the promised land because, together with Moses, he did not honor God at the waters of Meribah. Passing the garments to Eleazar showed that the priestly service would continue.

For today: our tasks and years of service are limited, but God's work goes on. We can serve faithfully and prepare others to continue with humility and trust in God.
exp.7:19:
This verse says that Moses, Aaron, and all the people of Israel did with the Levites exactly what God had commanded. The phrase "did to the Levites" means that they treated them or prepared them according to the instructions they had received. They did not do it halfway; they carried it out completely.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts how the Levites were set apart for service in the tabernacle. God had taken them in place of the firstborn of Israel. They would assist Aaron and his sons, and would serve on behalf of the people. Here it is emphasized that everyone obeyed: the leaders and the congregation.

Today we can learn that obeying God is best when we do it together and with faithfulness. Ask yourself what God has asked of you in his Word, and take a concrete step to fulfill it, relying on your family or your church.
exp.21:38:
This verse tells us that Balaam and Balak traveled together and arrived at a city called Kirjath-huzoth in other versions; here it appears as "Huzoth." The verse as your reader sees it reads "Kirjath–huzoth," so the city name is the same place, shown in a different spelling.

It is not known for certain where that city was, but it seems to have been a place near Moab.

Balak, king of Moab, had sent for Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam had just told him that he could speak only what God put in his mouth. After they reached the city, Balak offered a sacrifice and prepared the next step of his plan.

For today: before you enter any project or pressure, decide whose voice you will obey. Balaam rightly said he would speak what God gave him. Ask God that your words and decisions follow that same loyalty, even when others expect something different from you.
exp.10:26:
A young man ran and told Moses that Eldad and Medad were prophesying in the camp. The phrase "young man" is the sense of the word used here, and "told" is what he did when he gave the news.

The people had been complaining, and Moses felt weighed down by the burden of leading them. God took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed it on seventy elders. Eldad and Medad were on the list, but they had stayed in the camp, and the Spirit rested on them too. The young man, surprised, brought the news, and then Joshua asked that they be stopped.

Today, we can rejoice when God uses others in ways we did not expect. The Spirit is not bound by our molds or our titles. Instead of feeling jealous, let us celebrate what God is doing in others.
exp.3:46:
This verse explains who was counted among the Levites: the men from thirty to fifty years old. They were the ones who came to work in the service of the tabernacle. Being given "the service of the burden" means that each man was assigned a specific task. The tabernacle of the congregation was the sacred tent where God was present among his people.

It is part of the account in Numbers, traditionally attributed to Moses. God commanded that the Levites be counted by their families, and here the count of the sons of Merari is completed. Moses, Aaron, and the leaders did this according to the Lord's command. It was a census to divide the work of carrying and caring for the tabernacle.

For today: God gives each person a concrete service and takes it seriously. Ask yourself what simple task you have in your church or family, and do it faithfully and in an orderly way, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.6:18:
Nethanel, leader of the tribe of Issachar, presented his offering on the second day: one silver plate and one silver bowl, weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary, an official measure. Both were full of fine flour mixed with oil, for the grain offering.

Moses records how the leaders of the twelve tribes brought gifts for the dedication of the tabernacle and its altar. Each leader brought his offering on a different day, and all of them were the same as Nahshon's. This shows that all the tribes took part equally in the worship of God.

For today: God values steady and sincere giving, not competition. Nethanel did not try to outdo anyone, nor did he fall behind. We can give our time, talents, and resources with order and gratitude, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.31:3:
It says that the land the Lord defeated and gave to Israel, that is, the region east of the Jordan, is good for raising livestock, and that the people of Gad and Reuben have a great deal of livestock. The word "smote" means that God defeated the peoples who lived there. The word "servants" is the humble way they refer to themselves before Moses.

The tribes of Gad and Reuben are speaking, addressing Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the leaders. Israel had already defeated the kings of that area, and these tribes see the opportunity to stay there. Their request sounds reasonable, but it shows that they may be thinking first of their own convenience, and Moses will answer with concern for their fellow brothers.

For today: it is good to look for what benefits us, but it is worth asking ourselves whether we also care for others. Before deciding, let us think about how our decision affects those who walk with us.
exp.17:10:
God tells Aaron that the "heave offering" also belongs to him: the portion that was lifted up before the Lord as a sign of surrender. The "wave offerings" were the ones moved back and forth before Him. These portions were for Aaron, his sons, and his daughters, as a permanent law. The phrase "every one that is clean" means that a person had to be in a state of ritual purity to eat of them.

God himself speaks to Aaron, after the rebellion of Korah and the confirmation of the priesthood. The priests and Levites received no land as an inheritance, so God provided for them through the offerings of the people. In this way they could devote themselves fully to the service of the sanctuary.

Today we can generously support those who serve in teaching and in caring for the church, and remember that everything we have comes from God.
exp.27:14:
This verse says that at the new moon festival, in addition to the monthly burnt offerings, a male goat was to be offered as a sin offering. "Expiation" means covering or cleansing guilt, and the "continual burnt offering" was the daily offering that was burned completely, while the "drink offering" was the wine poured out along with it.

God speaks through Moses to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He repeats the order of the offerings so that their life as a people would revolve around worship. Notice that sin was dealt with in a special way each month, even in the midst of a celebration.

For today: Christians believe that Christ offered the final sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10:12). That is why we can begin each day and each season by acknowledging our faults with sincerity and receiving his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.25:61:
This verse says that the Levites were counted, and there were 23,000 males from one month old and upward. They were not included in the general count of the children of Israel, because they were not going to receive an inheritance, that is, a share of the promised land. The phrase "inheritance" refers to the portion of land that each tribe would receive as its possession.

The narrator is recording the second census, taken on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. The Levites are counted separately because their task was to serve in the sanctuary, and they would not have a territory of their own like the other tribes. God set them apart for that service.

For today: our security does not depend on how much we possess, but on belonging to God and serving him. We can trust that he cares for those who place their lives at his disposal, even when they have little in material goods.
exp.32:42:
They set out from Punon, and camped at Oboth. "Departed" here means "having set out," and "camped" is the word for what they did, not a sign that they stayed there forever. It was simply one more stop in the wilderness.

Moses, at God's command, wrote down the list of all the stages of the journey from Egypt to the border of Canaan (Numbers 33:1-2). This verse is near the end of the route, as Israel drew close to Moab. Scholars are not entirely certain of the exact location of Punon and Oboth, though they are usually placed to the south or southeast of the Dead Sea.

For today: God watches over every stage of the road, even the stops that seem ordinary. If you feel today that you are only passing through or waiting, trust that He records and guides every step and leads you forward.
exp.29:5:
It says that if a young unmarried woman made a vow to God and her father forbade it on the same day he learned of it, that vow lost its force. The word meaning to forbid or prevent is not used here; instead, the verse notes that she had bound herself to a solemn commitment. God would forgive her, because the vow was not carried out due to her father's opposition.

Moses gives these instructions to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. In that society, the father was the head of the household and was responsible for his house. This law brought order and protected the family from promises made without counsel. Scholars debate how to apply it today, since it reflects the culture of its time.

For today: before promising something to God, let us think carefully and seek wise counsel. A promise spoken in haste can weigh heavily later on. God takes our words seriously, but He is also merciful.
exp.23:12:
Balaam tells Balak that, even if he gave him his house full of silver and gold, he could not go against the word of the Lord. He would do nothing, neither good nor bad, on his own initiative. The phrases "to go beyond" the commandment, "of mine own mind," and "what the Lord saith" are explained in the verse itself: going beyond means disobeying, "what the Lord saith" is what God has said, and "of mine own mind" means by my own decision. He would speak only what the Lord spoke.

Balaam is a foreign prophet. Balak, king of Moab, had called him to curse Israel, promising him honor and riches. But three times God caused him to bless the people. Balak, angry, dismisses him, and Balaam reminds him that from the beginning he said he would speak only what God gave him. Even so, other biblical passages show that his heart was divided by greed.

For today: obedience to God must not be for sale. When money, prestige, or pressure tempt us to bend what is right, let us remember that faithfulness is worth more. Let us ask God for an upright heart, one that not only speaks well but also lives well.
exp.0:15:
This verse closes the list of the twelve men chosen to help with the census. It says they were the "renowned of the congregation," that is, those chosen from among the people. They were "princes," meaning leaders or heads of their tribes, and "heads of thousands," which means those in charge of large groups of families within Israel.

The book tells what God said to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. God commanded that the men of Israel who were able to go to war be counted, and to help Moses and Aaron he set apart one leader from each tribe. This verse summarizes who they were and what place they held. Afterward, they help gather the people and register each one by name.

For today: God cares about order and values service. If you have some responsibility, in your family, your church, or your work, carry it out faithfully, knowing that God sees you and counts on you.
exp.29:2:
This verse says that if a person makes a solemn promise to God, or swears to commit to something, they must not break their word. They must carry out everything they said with their mouth. A "vow" is a promise made to God, and "binding herself by a bond" means that the person made a serious commitment. "Violate" here means to break or leave unfulfilled.

Moses speaks to the leaders of the tribes of Israel and passes on what God commanded him. This is the introduction to a law about vows. Afterward, the chapter explains particular cases, such as that of a young woman living in her father's house.

For today: think before you promise. If you tell God or someone that you will do something, try to keep it. And if you are not sure you can, it is better to promise less and be faithful in what you do say.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that on the second day of the dedication of the tabernacle, it was the turn of Nethaneel, son of Zuar, to present his offering. He was the prince (that is, the chief or leader) of the tribe of Issachar. The word "did offer" means that he brought his gifts to God.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Moses. Each day, a leader of one of the tribes of Israel brought his offering to dedicate the altar and the tabernacle. The day before, Nahshon of Judah had done so. What follows shows that Nethaneel brought exactly the same thing, no more and no less.

For today: God cares for every name and every gift. No one is forgotten. We can serve faithfully without comparing ourselves or competing, knowing that God values our offering made with a sincere heart, even when others give something similar.
exp.15:41:
This verse says that the people gathered against Moses and Aaron to accuse them. Then they looked toward the tabernacle, the tent where God made himself present among them, and saw that the cloud covered it and the glory of the Lord appeared. The word "testimony" refers to the tablets of the law kept there. "Congregation" is the community of Israel.

The narrator tells what happened after Korah's rebellion. God had already judged Korah and his followers, but the next day the people blamed Moses and Aaron for those deaths. Just as the tension was rising, God revealed his presence. Immediately he speaks to Moses, and the text that follows shows that a new judgment is coming.

Today, when we get angry or blame others, it is wise to look first to God. Before continuing to argue, we can pray, acknowledge his authority, and ask him for humility to listen.
exp.13:8:
This verse says: do not rebel against the Lord, and do not be afraid of the people of that land. "They are bread for us" means that we will defeat them easily, the way one eats bread. "Their defence is departed from them" means that their protection no longer covers them. And the Lord is with Israel.

Joshua and Caleb are speaking, the two spies who trusted God. The other ten spies had given a report full of fear, and the people wept and wanted to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb ask them to believe God's promise. There are different views about exactly what was meant by the "defence" (literally, "shade"), but the general idea is that God was no longer protecting them.

For today: when fear tells you that the problem is too big, remember that God is with you. Trusting Him does not mean denying the difficulty, but looking at it in the light of His promise and moving forward in obedience.
exp.2:48:
Moses took the redemption money from the Israelites who were left over. These were the firstborn who were not covered by the exchange with the Levites. The phrase "over and above" means there were more firstborn than Levites, and "redeemed" means bought back through a payment or a substitute.

God had said that the firstborn of Israel belonged to him. So the Levites were set apart in their place. Because the firstborn numbered 273 more than the Levites, God commanded that five shekels be paid for each one. The text tells how Moses obeyed what the LORD had commanded, and that money was given to Aaron and his sons.

For today: God cares about the details and wants complete obedience, not half-hearted obedience. We can ask ourselves what commitment to God we have left "over" or unfulfilled, and do something about it with honesty and gratitude.
exp.9:20:
The Kohathites, descendants of Kohath, began to walk carrying the holy things of the sanctuary, such as the ark. While they were arriving, the other Levites, who were going ahead, set up the tabernacle. "Set up" means that they got it ready and raised it.

Moses recounts how Israel left Sinai, each tribe in its place. From verse 17, the "others" seem to be the Gershonites and Merarites, who carried the framework of the tent. So, when the holy objects arrived, the place was already ready. God wanted order and reverence in his presence.

Today we can learn to serve with order and to prepare the ground for others. In the church, the family, or at work, your task may not be seen much, but it helps everything be ready to honor God.
exp.17:1:
God tells Aaron to bring near his brothers, the tribe of Levi, who are the tribe of his father. They will be joined to him and will help him. Aaron and his sons, on the other hand, will serve directly before the tabernacle of the testimony, that is, the tent where the ark with the commandments was kept.

The LORD speaks, and he does so after the rebellion of Korah and the death of many who came near to the holy things improperly. God makes clear who has each responsibility: the priests take care of worship, and the Levites support them in the service.

For today: God distributes different tasks among his people, and all of them matter. Serve with joy in the place you have been given, without envying others or looking down on your own work, because we all work together to honor God.
exp.32:23:
They set out from Mount Shapher and camped at a place called Haradah. The sentence about "departed" meaning "having set out" and "settled" meaning "camped" should be removed or rewritten, since those words do not appear in the verse. It is one more stop on the journey through the wilderness.

Moses is writing, at God's command, the list of every place where Israel camped from Egypt until they came near the promised land. Numbers 33:2 says that Moses recorded their departures by the Lord's command. As for the exact location of Haradah and the other sites on the list, there is no certainty, and scholars do not agree.

For today: God remembers every stage of your journey, even the ones that seem long or unimportant. When you feel that you are only passing through, trust that He guides you step by step and that no stretch of the road is lost before His eyes.
exp.32:49:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses while the people were camped on the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho. The word "spoke" shows that God gave Moses a direct message. "Saying" announces that what God wanted to communicate comes right after.

The people of Israel had finished their long journey through the wilderness and were about to cross the Jordan into the promised land. God is the one who speaks, and Moses is the one who receives and passes on his words to the people. What follows are instructions for this new stage, especially so that Israel would not be defiled by the idolatry of the peoples of Canaan.

For today: before beginning a new stage, it is good to pause and listen to God. Reading his Word and praying help us enter changes with clear direction and not only with our own ideas.
exp.6:46:
He says that Eliasaph, son of Deuel, brought his offering. For the peace offering (a fellowship offering, which was shared as a sign of friendship with God) he gave two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of the first year. Before this, the burnt offering and the sin offering are mentioned.

The account is in Numbers 7, where the leaders of the twelve tribes present offerings for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Eliasaph represented the tribe of Gad. Each leader brought the same thing, one day after another. The text does not explain why it repeats everything, but it shows that God values each tribe equally.

Today we can learn to give without comparing ourselves to others. Your service or help may look like that of many others, but God does not see it as something repeated. Offer him what is yours with sincerity and faithfulness, without seeking applause.
exp.0:19:
This verse begins the census list of the tribes. It speaks of the descendants of Reuben, the eldest son of Jacob, who was also called Israel. They were counted by their generations, their families, and their fathers' houses, recording the name of each male twenty years old and upward, that is, those who were able to go out to war.

The account is set in the wilderness of Sinai. God commanded Moses to count the people, and the writer of Numbers records the census tribe by tribe. The count organized the people for marching, camping, and defending themselves. Reuben appears first because he was the oldest, though other passages show that he lost certain privileges.

For today: God knows his people by name, not as an anonymous crowd. You can trust that He sees you and counts you as part of his family, and this invites you to serve faithfully in your own place, whether great or small.
exp.27:5:
It is a daily sacrifice of lambs, which this explanation calls a continual burnt offering: an offering that was entirely burned and was repeated without stopping. It was established at Mount Sinai. The phrase about a sweet savour means that God was pleased with this offering. The phrase about an offering made by fire means an offering burned in the fire on the altar. The words about the evening period most likely refer to twilight, though they have been understood in several ways.

God speaks through Moses to the new generation of Israel, near the time they are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of the offerings commanded at Sinai, so that their lives would revolve around worshiping him every day, morning and evening.

For today: God values constancy. We can set aside a moment at the start and at the end of the day to pray, give thanks, and offer our lives to him, not only when we feel inspired.
exp.4:19:
It says that if the woman suspected of unfaithfulness truly had turned aside from her husband, become defiled, and lain with another man, then the curse would come upon her.

Here the priest speaks, addressing the woman during the ritual of jealousy, which God gave to Israel when a husband suspected unfaithfulness without having any witnesses. It was a procedure before God, not before men. Scholars discuss how the ritual should be understood, but the text presents it as a way of leaving the judgment in God's hands and protecting the innocent woman.

For today: when there are suspicions or doubts in a marriage, one should not accuse or destroy with rumors. It is wise to seek the truth honestly, through dialogue and prayer, and to trust that God knows all things and judges with justice.
exp.17:31:
It says that when the Levites offer God the best of what they receive (the tithe of the tithes), they will no longer bear guilt for it. It warns them not to treat as common what is holy, because that could bring death. The phrase in the source for "bear guilt" means carrying the blame; the other term means treating what is set apart with contempt.

God speaks to Moses and tells him what to say to the Levites. They did not receive land as an inheritance; they lived from the tithes of the people. Now God orders them in turn to set apart a portion, the best of it, for Him. In this way they too learned to give, and what remained they could eat freely with their families.

For today: let us give God our best, not the leftovers, of our time, money and talents. And those of us who serve in the church should remember that what we have received comes from God and deserves respect and gratitude.
exp.2:45:
This verse speaks of a small surplus. There were 273 firstborn sons of Israel who had no Levite to take their place. The verse's wording about "exceeding" or "being more than" refers to that gap in numbers, so the verse itself shows it clearly. A "redemption" is the payment made to free someone who belongs to God.

God speaks to Moses during the census in the wilderness. He said that every firstborn was his, and so he accepted the Levites in their place to serve in the sanctuary. They were counted one by one: each Levite covered one firstborn. The 273 who were left without a replacement were redeemed at five shekels each, and the money went to Aaron and his sons.

For today: nothing God claims is left to chance, and every claim has a price that has been covered. This reminds us that we belong to God and that he himself provides the redemption. We can live thankfully and offer him what we are and what we have.
exp.25:42:
It says that the whole family of the Shuhamites, who were the tribe of Dan, had 64,400 men counted. The word "counted" refers to those who were registered in the census, that is, the men from twenty years old and up who were fit for war. Dan had only one family, that of Shuham.

Moses and the priest Eleazar take this second census by God's command, on the plains of Moab, after a plague and before entering the promised land. It served to prepare the army and to divide the land according to the size of each tribe. Shuham seems to be the same son of Dan whom Genesis calls Husim, though not everyone is sure.

For today: God keeps track of his people and does not see numbers without faces. Even a family that seems small has its place and its share in God's plan.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that if a foreigner living among the Israelites wants to keep the Passover to the Lord, he must do it following the same rules and laws. The word "sojourner" refers to a foreigner who lives among the people as a resident. "Native of the land" refers to someone born in Israel. There is one rule for both.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, and Moses passes it on to the people. He has just explained that whoever neglects the Passover without a valid reason will be cut off from his people. Now he makes clear that a foreigner who wishes to take part may do so, but in the same order. The invitation is real, and the rule is the same for everyone.

For today: God opens the door to anyone who wants to draw near to Him, regardless of origin. We can imitate Him by giving sincere welcome to newcomers in our church or community, and treating them as equals.
exp.25:32:
This verse says that Zelophehad, son of Hepher, had no sons, but only five daughters. Their names are listed: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.

Here the narrator of Numbers is recording Israel's second census. They were close to entering the promised land, and families were counted by tribe so the inheritance could be divided. Zelophehad belonged to the tribe of Manasseh. Mentioning his daughters is striking, because the lists almost always name only men. Later, in Numbers 27, they ask to receive their father's inheritance, and it is granted to them.

For today: God sees and remembers those whom society overlooks. He values people who seem to have no place, and He calls us to defend what is just with respect.
exp.33:25:
The verse names the leader of the tribe of Issachar: Paltiel, son of Azzan. The word "prince" here does not speak of royalty, but of a leader or representative of his tribe.

God speaks to Moses when Israel is about to enter the promised land. He commands that each tribe provide a leader to help the priest Eleazar and Joshua divide the land. Outside this passage, the Bible gives no further details about Paltiel.

For today: God counts on people who serve faithfully, even though almost no one knows them. Today you can ask Him to help you carry out with responsibility a simple task in your family, your church, or your work, knowing that He sees it.
exp.13:1:
It says that the whole people of Israel complained against Moses and Aaron, their leaders. With great bitterness they cried out that it would have been better to die in Egypt or right there in the desert. The words "they complained" and "we had died" here are rendered simply as the people's own complaint, the wish that they had already died.

They speak after ten of the twelve spies returned from exploring Canaan. They had given a fearful report about the inhabitants of the land. The people became frightened, wept all night, and stopped trusting God's promise. Their complaint in fact was also against God, who had brought them out of Egypt.

When fear takes hold of us, we tend to exaggerate and forget what God has already done for us. Instead of complaining and wishing to turn back, we can bring our fear to God in prayer and remember his faithful promises.
exp.14:39:
God wants his people to remember his commandments, obey them, and live set apart for him. The word for "remember" in the verse is one the reader will see as "remember." "Be holy" means that they belong to him and live according to his character.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to instruct Israel to put tassels with a blue cord on the edges of their clothing. They were a visible reminder, so that they would not keep following only their own desires and what their eyes saw. At the end, God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt to be their God.

For today: we can create simple reminders of God, such as a verse on our phone or a prayer at the start of the day. Obedience is not a burden, but a response to the one who rescued us and loves us.
exp.19:23:
God says that Aaron is going to die soon. The phrase "gathered to his people" is an old way of saying that he will die and join his ancestors. Aaron will not be able to enter the promised land because he and Moses rebelled against God's command at the waters of Meribah, which means "the waters of quarreling" (Meribah).

God speaks to Moses and Aaron on Mount Hor, near Edom. Shortly before, at Kadesh, the people complained about having no water, and Moses and Aaron did not honor God in front of everyone (Numbers 20:12). Now God fulfills what he had said: Aaron will die, and his son Eleazar will take his place as priest.

God is merciful, but he is also serious about obedience, even with his closest leaders. Today we can learn to obey him carefully, especially when we are tired or upset, and to trust that he continues to guide his work from one generation to the next.
exp.6:79:
Ahira, leader of the tribe of Naphtali, presented one golden spoon weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned before God. A shekel was a unit of weight, and the spoon was more like a small dish or cup for carrying the incense.

This is the twelfth and final day of the offerings for dedicating the tabernacle. The passage records what Moses wrote down: each tribal leader brought the same offering, day after day, with the same items and the same weights. In this way the whole nation shared equally in consecrating the place where God dwelt among them.

For today: God values each person contributing their part, even when it seems repetitive or hardly noticeable. No offering was left unmentioned. Today you can serve with steadiness and joy in what falls to you, without comparing yourself to others, knowing that God sees and remembers every act of sincere giving.
exp.23:1:
This verse tells that Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw the people of Israel camped in order, tribe by tribe. Then the Spirit of God came upon him. "Camped" here means settled in their tents, and the word "saw" is the same as in the verse above.

The narrator describes Balaam, a foreign prophet whom King Balak hired to curse Israel. He had already tried twice, seeking omens (signs or portents), but God did not allow it. Now, seeing that God wanted to bless Israel, Balaam gave up those practices and looked out toward the wilderness. What follows is his third message, and it will be a blessing, not a curse.

For today: God fulfills his purposes even when others oppose them. If you trust in him, no curse can cancel his blessing over your life. Also, strive to listen to God with sincerity and not to seek your own advantage.
exp.34:24:
This verse says that if someone killed another person without intending to, the community will protect them from the relative who seeks to avenge the death. It will return them to the city of refuge where they had taken shelter. There they were to live until the high priest died, the one who had been anointed with holy oil. The one who caused the death is the slayer, and the phrase "had fled" means that they had sought refuge.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. These laws separated accidental death from murder. In this way life was protected and unjust revenge was prevented, but the value of shed blood was also taken seriously. How exactly the death of the priest connects with the end of the exile is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when someone fails us without ill intent, let us seek justice with mercy, not revenge. God cares for both truth and compassion.
exp.6:45:
It says that Eliasaf, leader of the tribe of Gad, brought a male goat as an offering "for a sin offering." That is, an animal presented to cover sin and cleanse guilt. A "male goat" is a billy goat, the adult male of the goat.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, repeating in detail the offerings of each tribal leader for the dedication of the tabernacle. Each leader brought the same thing, day after day, for twelve days. This repetition shows that all the tribes took part equally. The sin offering reminded the people that, even when dedicating something to God, they still needed forgiveness.

For today: before serving God or giving something to him, acknowledge with humility that you need his forgiveness. Christians believe that Jesus made the definitive atonement for us, so we can approach with confidence and gratitude.
exp.6:76:
This verse ends the list of what Pagiel, son of Ocran, brought to the altar. Here the animals for the peace offering are named. That offering was a fellowship offering, in which a shared meal was eaten before God. Goats are the male goats, and the lambs are young lambs in their first year. Pagiel was the leader of the tribe of Asher.

Moses, as the biblical account records, tells how each tribal leader brought his offering over twelve days, when the tabernacle was dedicated. Each tribe gave the same, without competing or standing out. In this way it was shown that the whole people worshiped together, with equal worth before God.

Today we can learn to give to God with steadiness and without comparing ourselves to others. What He looks at is a grateful heart, and worship is more beautiful when we live it in unity with other believers.
exp.21:3:
Moab spoke with the elders of Midian, that is, the leaders of that neighboring people. He told them that Israel was going to strip everything around them clean, the way an ox eats the grass of the field until it is bare. The words here refer to the land that lies near them and to the pasture, the green ground where the animals feed.

It also makes clear that Balak, the son of Zippor, was king of Moab at that time.

Israel had just defeated the Amorites, and Moab was afraid because of the great number of people. The Moabites speak with Midian looking for allies, and afterward Balak will send for Balaam to curse Israel. The one speaking sees Israel as a threat that will consume everything.

For today: fear makes us see threats where God is at work, and it pushes us toward crooked solutions. Instead of acting out of fear, we can pray and trust that God cares for his people.
exp.25:33:
This verse closes the list of the families of the tribe of Manasseh. "Those that were numbered" refers to the people registered in the census, in this case the men of fighting age. According to this count, Manasseh had 52,700 men.

God told Moses and the priest Eleazar to take this census at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. It served to organize the army and divide the land according to the size of each family. It is notable that the five daughters of Zelophehad are mentioned: later God recognizes their right to inherit. The figures are the ones the text gives, and nothing needs to be added to them.

For today: God knows and counts each person, and each one has a place among his people. Today you can value those others overlook, and remember that you too count for Him.
exp.33:2:
This verse marks the southern limit of the land that God would give to Israel. That border would run from the wilderness of Zin, along the coast of Edom, to the edge of the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea, toward the east.

God himself speaks to Moses, when the people are about to finish their journey through the wilderness and are near to entering Canaan. He gives clear instructions about the boundaries of the inheritance, so that each tribe would know where to live and there would be no confusion. Some exact details of these places are debated among scholars.

For today: God is a God of order and of concrete promises. You can trust that He keeps what He says and provides what you need. Give thanks for what He has already given you, and live with order and gratitude within it.
exp.26:17:
God answers Moses and tells him to take Joshua, son of Nun, a man in whom there is spirit. He is to lay his hand on him. The phrase about the spirit can refer to the Spirit of God or to a special character and disposition for leading; scholars understand it in both ways.

Moses knows that he will soon die, and he asks God to set a leader over the people, so that they will not be like sheep without a shepherd. God answers by pointing to Joshua, who had already served Moses faithfully. Laying on the hand was a gesture of blessing and of handing over authority before the people.

God cares for the people and prepares their leaders in advance. If you serve others today, be faithful in small things, and help prepare those who come after you.
exp.21:12:
Balaam got up early and gave his answer to Balak's messengers. He told them to go back to their own land, because the Lord would not let him go with them.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and wanted Balaam to curse them. God had already told Balaam not to go and not to curse Israel, because they were a blessed people. Balaam repeats that answer, though he does not tell the whole of what God said. Some think this left a door open for later, but that is an interpretation.

When God has spoken clearly, we do not need to keep bargaining. Obeying at once and with firmness protects us from temptations, pressures, and offers that look attractive.
exp.20:12:
From there they moved on and camped on the other side of the Arnon River, in the wilderness. That river marked the boundary between two territories: Moab and the Amorites. The word for "camped" here means they settled down for a time, and "boundary" means a border or dividing line.

The one who recorded the book, traditionally Moses, notes Israel's stops in the wilderness one by one, as they were drawing near to the promised land. The verses that follow refer to the "Book of the Wars of the LORD," a work we do not have today. For that reason we know nothing more about it.

For today: God leads His people step by step, even through stages that seem to be only part of the journey. Trust Him at every stopping place, and remember with gratitude the places He has brought you through.
exp.13:19:
God answers Moses' prayer by saying that he does pardon the people, just as Moses asked. The words "according to thy word" in the King James Version are what Moses asked for. The pardon is real, though the verses that follow will show that it does not erase all the consequences.

Here the Lord is speaking. Israel had rebelled at Kadesh by believing the evil report of the spies, and God intended to destroy them. Moses interceded and appealed to God's character: patient, merciful, and just. God pardons, but the verses that follow show that that generation would not enter the promised land.

For today: we can pray with confidence for others, relying on who God is. We also learn that being forgiven does not always remove the consequences of our actions, but it keeps us in relationship with God.
exp.25:3:
It says that Moses and Eleazar were to count the Israelites from twenty years old and upward. The phrase "you shall count" means "you will count," and "twenty years old and upward" means "from twenty years old and onward." The verse adds that this followed what God had already commanded Moses and the people who came out of Egypt.

Moses and the priest Eleazar speak in the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan, just before entering the promised land. It is a second census. The first was taken at Sinai, and the earlier generation had died in the wilderness. This count serves to organize the people, prepare them for war, and later divide the land.

For today: God numbers his people and forgets no one. Each generation must obey him for itself, not live off the faith of its parents. Today you can ask yourself how you will faithfully follow God in your own place.
exp.5:13:
This verse describes what the Nazirite was to bring to God at the end of his period of dedication: a one-year-old male lamb without blemish for the burnt offering (an offering burned up completely), a one-year-old female lamb without blemish as a sin offering, and a ram without blemish as a peace offering, which expressed fellowship and thanksgiving.

God speaks to Moses to give the law of the Nazirite, the person who set himself apart voluntarily for the Lord for a time. When that period was completed, he came to the entrance of the tent of meeting with these offerings. They showed total surrender, the need for forgiveness, and joy in being at peace with God.

For today: when you finish a season of devotion or service, do not trust in your own effort. Give thanks to God, acknowledge your need for forgiveness, and offer him your best, resting in Christ, the perfect Lamb.
exp.5:10:
This verse says the priest will offer one of the birds as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, which was burned whole for God. In this way he would make atonement, that is, cover the Nazirite's wrong for having become unclean near a dead body. On that same day, he will hallow his head, that is, his hair was set apart for God again.

God speaks to Moses about the rules for the Nazirite, a person who voluntarily committed to living set apart for the Lord. If someone died suddenly beside him, without his seeking it, his vow was stained. That is why he needed to be purified and begin again. Scholars debate why something unintentional was called a "sin," but the text shows that the uncleanness had to be dealt with seriously.

For today: when you fail or feel stained, do not stay far from God. He offers a way to be cleansed and to start again. Christians see this fulfilled in Christ, and we can draw near with sincerity.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that Israel was to sound the trumpets on days of gladness, at their solemn feasts and at the beginning of each month, while the burnt offerings and the peace offerings were being offered. "Peace offerings" refers to the offerings of peace or fellowship. "For a memorial" means that the sound would serve to keep them in God's mind. At the end, God declares: "I am the Lord your God."

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, when the people are getting ready to set out on their journey. The silver trumpets served to call the people together, to direct their travels, to summon them to battle, and also for worship. Here they are shown in their use for joy and thanksgiving.

For today: let us not wait only for hard moments to cry out to God. When you receive a joy or begin a new stage, take a moment to give thanks to him aloud or with a song.
exp.6:57:
This verse says that Gamaliel brought a male goat as an offering for sin. The word "atonement" in the older wording refers to covering or repairing a wrong before God, and it is only one part of the complete offering he presented.

Here the narrator of Numbers carefully records what each tribal leader brought to dedicate the tabernacle. Gamaliel was the prince of the tribe of Manasseh. Each tribe brought the same offering, day after day, and the text repeats the complete list. In this way it showed that no tribe was more important than another.

For today: God invites us to acknowledge our wrongs honestly and not overlook them. Christians believe that Jesus is the final atonement for our sin. Today we can draw near to God with humility and confidence, asking for forgiveness and giving thanks for his grace.
exp.21:22:
This verse tells how Balaam's donkey saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road, with a sword drawn in his hand. The word "drawn" means taken out of its sheath. The animal left the road and went out into the field. Balaam, who could not see the angel, struck the donkey to make her return to the road.

The text does not present a voice speaking here; it narrates the story. Balaam was traveling with the leaders of Moab, although God had become angry about his journey. The angel took the position of an opponent, that is, someone standing against him. While Balaam was blind to what was spiritual, the animal sensed the danger.

Today we can learn not to become angry at once when something gets in the way of our plans. Sometimes God uses obstacles to protect us or to correct us. Before we insist, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask whether we are going the right way.
exp.32:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel left a place called Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at another called Hazeroth. The word "departed" means "setting out," and "encamped" means "camped." It is just one more stop in the list of the journey.

Moses writes this record of all the stops Israel made from Egypt to near the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). Kibroth-hattaavah means "graves of craving," because people died there after giving in to the desire for meat (Numbers 11:34). Hazeroth is where Miriam and Aaron later spoke against Moses (Numbers 11:35; 12). The exact location of these places is uncertain.

For today: God remembers every step of our journey, even the difficult ones. Let us not hide our stumbles; let us learn from them and move forward, trusting that God is still guiding us.
exp.9:0:
This verse is a simple introduction: God speaks to Moses. The word "Lord" is the name of God in this translation, and "saying" announces that a specific instruction is coming. The word "spake" reminds us that God communicates with his people.

It is God who speaks, and he speaks to Moses, the leader of Israel. The people are in the desert, camped near Sinai, and are getting ready to set out. God is going to give instructions about two silver trumpets, which would serve to gather the people together and signal when to advance. In this way, the march would not be disorderly, but guided by God.

Today we can learn that God wants to guide us with clarity and order. Before making decisions or starting a new path, it is good to stop and listen to his voice in the Bible and in prayer.
exp.6:54:
This verse describes the offering of Gamaliel, leader of the tribe of Manasseh, on the eighth day. He brought one silver dish weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, both filled with the finest flour mixed with oil. The word "offering" here refers to a grain offering. "Fine flour" is flour of the highest quality. The shekel was a unit of weight, and the phrase "after the shekel of the sanctuary" points to the official standard used in worship.

Moses records how each tribal leader, one each day, presented offerings for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. The offerings of all twelve are nearly identical. The text repeats them one by one, showing that each tribe was honored equally and took part with complete devotion.

God values the sincere giving of each person, without comparison. Today we can offer God our best in time, talents, and resources, with steadiness and without competing with others, trusting that he sees every offering made from the heart.
exp.28:10:
This verse commands offering one male goat as a sin offering to cleanse the sin of the people. This offering was added to others already presented: the sin offering of atonement (the one made once a year, on the Day of Atonement), the continual burnt offering (the daily sacrifice that was burned whole), and their grain offerings and drink offerings (the wine poured out).

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel about the feasts of the seventh month. This passage refers to the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of that month. It was a solemn day when the people acknowledged their sin and their need for forgiveness. The sacrifices were to be made just as God had directed.

For today: our sin is serious and needs forgiveness. Christians believe that Christ offered the complete sacrifice for us once for all. Today we can come near to God with sincerity and gratitude, confessing our faults and resting in his forgiveness.
exp.0:23:
This verse begins the record of the tribe of Gad. The men counted are those from twenty years old and upward, that is, those who were able to go to war. They are listed by their generations, by their families, and by the houses of their fathers, that is, according to their lineage.

God himself spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commanded him to take this census. Israel was preparing to organize itself as a people and to advance toward the promised land. Each tribe was counted, and the men of Gad numbered 45,650, according to the next verse.

For today: God knows and takes into account every person, and no one is a mere number to Him. Ask yourself how you can serve with your place and your gifts within your family and your church, knowing that your contribution matters.
exp.15:4:
Moses says to Korah and to all his followers that tomorrow the Lord will show who belongs to Him. The word "company" in the verse means the group of followers, so Korah's supporters are the people Moses is addressing.

Moses speaks. Korah, together with others, accused him and Aaron of thinking themselves superior, since they said that the whole congregation is holy. Moses fell on his face to the ground, probably in humility and prayer, and then leaves the decision to God himself. It will be God, not the opinion of men, who confirms whom He has chosen to draw near to Him with the incense.

For today: when you feel envy or a desire to occupy a place that God has not given you, stop and humble yourself. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, and trust that He is the one who calls and brings people near to Himself.
exp.6:59:
This verse announces the turn of the ninth day for presenting offerings to the Lord. It belongs to Abidan, son of Gideoni, who was the prince, that is, the leader of the tribe of Benjamin. This is only the beginning of his entry; the offering itself is described in the verses that follow.

Here the account tells how, at the dedication of the tabernacle, each tribe brought its offering on a different day. Moses records the list in order, and the text repeats almost the same wording for each leader. That repetition shows that each tribe was taken into account, with none placed above another. Earlier, Gamaliel of the tribe of Manasseh was mentioned, and now Benjamin follows.

For today: God values every person and every offering given with sincerity. You do not need to be the best known for your service to matter. Today you can give your time, your talents, or your resources with gratitude, knowing that God sees your devotion.
exp.4:16:
The priest was to take water that had been set apart for the service of God, called "holy water," and put it into an earthen vessel. Then he would take dust from the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water.

God gives this instruction to Moses for a difficult case: a husband suspects that his wife has been unfaithful, but there are no witnesses. The matter was brought before God and was not settled by revenge. What the dust means exactly is not made clear in the text. Some think it connects the water with the holy presence of God, and others think it speaks of humility.

Today we can learn that suspicions should not become violence or gossip. What is hidden is brought to God in prayer, seeking the truth with humility and justice.
exp.2:0:
This verse opens a list of families. The word "generations" means descendants or family history. Aaron and Moses are named, and everything is placed in the time when God spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai. Interestingly, only the sons of Aaron are listed, not the sons of Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, which tradition attributes to Moses. Israel was camped near Sinai, and God was organizing the people. Before assigning tasks to the Levites, the text presents the priestly family. Some understand that Moses is mentioned because of his authority, though the text does not explain why his sons do not appear here.
