For today: God works through concrete people and families, and their names matter to him. Think of those who passed on your faith, and give thanks for them. And ask yourself whom you can teach today what you have learned from God.
exp.13:11:
God says he will strike the people with a plague and destroy them. Then he promises Moses that he will make from him a nation greater and stronger than Israel.

God speaks, with grief and anger. The ten spies had given a bad report about the promised land, and the people, full of fear, wanted to go back to Egypt and even stone Joshua and Caleb. After seeing so many signs, they still did not trust. Moses does not accept the offer; instead he pleads for them, appealing to the honor of God.

For today: unbelief is no small matter; it grieves God, who has been faithful. When we doubt, let us remember what he has already done for us. And like Moses, let us pray for others instead of only judging them.
exp.2:37:
This verse says that Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons would camp on the east side of the tabernacle, directly in front of the entrance. They had the watch over the sanctuary, that is, the care and guarding of the holy place, instead of all the people of Israel. The word "toward" in the verse means the direction where the sun rises, the east. "The stranger" was someone who did not belong to the priestly family, and if such a person came near the holy things, he was to die.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and organizes the camp around his dwelling. Each group of Levites had a task and a place. Moses and Aaron's family received the most important place, the entrance. The severe warning showed that God is holy and that no one may approach him in any way they please.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude. Today believers have access through Christ, but we still take his holiness seriously, praying and obeying with reverence.
exp.9:27:
This verse closes the list of how the people of Israel traveled through the desert. "Departures" means the setting out or the movements of the camp, and the "armies" refers to the tribes organized in order, like a great army. In other words, this is how they set out when God gave the signal.

The narrator of the book sums up what he has just described: the order of march of each tribe with its leader. Shortly before, the people had left Mount Sinai after nearly a year. Right away Moses asks Hobab, his brother-in-law or father-in-law (the ancient text allows both readings), to come along with them.

God takes care of the order and does not act at random. If you are beginning a new stage, do not move ahead in haste or disorder. Seek God's guidance, arrange your steps with calm, and walk alongside other believers who support you.
exp.9:21:
The verse says that the standard of the camp of Ephraim, that is, the group of three tribes that camped under its banner, began to march in order, by divisions or companies. Elishama, son of Ammihud, was the leader of the tribe. Here "army" refers to the troops of that tribe.

This is part of the account of Israel's departure from Mount Sinai. Moses, as the people's guide, records the order of march that God had indicated. The Kohathites carried the sacred objects, and others had already set up the tabernacle by the time they arrived.

For today: God is a God of order, and he notices every person and every task. Do your part faithfully, even when it seems small or goes unnoticed.
exp.32:48:
This verse says that the people of Israel camped, for the last time in this list of journeys, on the banks of the Jordan River. The camp stretched from Beth-jesimoth to Abel-shittim, in the plains of Moab. "Pitched" means they set up their camp. "Finally" marks that they had reached the last place before entering the promised land.

Chapter 33 is a summary of the stages of the journey from Egypt, which the Bible says Moses put in writing at the command of the LORD. This verse closes the list. Right after this, God speaks to Moses to give instructions on how to take possession of Canaan. The places are named because the people were to remember the path they had traveled. We do not know exactly where each site was, but they are located east of the Jordan.

For today: before taking a new step, it is worth looking back and remembering how God has sustained you in each stage. That memory strengthens confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.6:27:
The verse says that part of the offering was one male goat, that is, a mature billy goat, for a sin offering. To atone means to cover over or remove the guilt of sin through a sacrifice. This was the sin offering, different from the burnt offering and the peace offering mentioned around it.

We are in the chapter where, at the completion of setting up the tabernacle, each tribe brought its offering for the dedication of the altar, one day per tribe. Here it is the turn of the prince Eliab, of the tribe of Zebulun. All the princes brought exactly the same thing, with no one wanting to outdo another.

For today: before we give our offering or serve God, it is good to recognize that we need forgiveness. Christians understand that Christ fulfilled what these sacrifices pointed toward. We can come near with humility and gratitude, not with pride.
exp.14:16:
This verse is a transitional phrase. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses, and with that a new instruction begins. The word "saying" tells us that a message is coming, one that Moses is to pass on to the people.

Here God is speaking, and Moses is the one who receives the word to bring to Israel. Earlier, God had said that the foreigner who lived among them would have the same law as they did. Now God gives instructions about the offerings they would present when they entered the promised land. This shows that God gave them hope: although they were still wandering in the desert, he promised them a land.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before we act, let us take time to listen to him in the Bible, and be willing to obey what he shows us, even when he speaks of a future we cannot yet see.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and to Aaron. "Lord" is the name of God, and the old spelling of the word "to" is not something your reader needs to know; the verse simply reads "unto." It is only an introductory phrase, but it reminds us that what follows is not human idea but instruction from God.

We are in the book of Numbers, when Israel is in the wilderness, arranged around the tabernacle. God speaks to the two leaders, Moses and Aaron, so that they will organize the service of the Levites. Right away he asks that the sons of Kohath, a family of Levi, be counted, since they would care for the most sacred things of the tabernacle.

For today: God still speaks to his people through his Word. Before serving, it is good to listen. Let your service in the church or in your family come from seeking first what God says, and not only from your own desires.
exp.33:6:
God indicates the northern boundary of the promised land. It was to begin at the great sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea, and reach as far as mount Hor. The word "border" means edge or limit, and the word "point out" means to mark out or draw. This mount Hor is not the same one where Aaron died, and it is not known for certain where it was.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people of Israel. They are close to entering Canaan, after years in the wilderness. God gives them clear boundaries so they know what territory they will receive and can divide it among the tribes in an orderly way.

For today: God is a God of order and of specific promises. You can trust your plans to Him and set healthy limits in your life, knowing that He keeps what He promises.
exp.6:30:
This verse describes the offering of Elizur, leader of the tribe of Reuben, on the fourth day. He brought one silver dish weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The shekel of the sanctuary was the official unit of weight. The word "offering" here refers to the grain offering. Fine flour is flour of the highest quality.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording in detail the offerings of Israel's leaders when the tabernacle was dedicated. Each leader, day after day, presented the same offering. Moses wrote it down so that each tribe would be remembered and none would go without recognition.

For today: God cares about every gift, even when it looks like the gifts of others. What we offer, whether our time, talents, or resources, has value when we give it sincerely. It does not need to be original, but it should come from the heart and be the best we have.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and to Aaron. It is only the introduction to what God is about to say next. "Lord" is the name of God, and the phrase "spake unto" means "spoke to."

Here Korah had gathered all the people in front of the tabernacle to oppose Moses and Aaron. Then the glory of God appeared, that is, his visible and powerful presence. In that tense moment, God himself takes the word. He does not wait for people to settle the dispute; he intervenes and speaks to those he had set in place as leaders.

For today: when there are conflicts or divisions, do not rush to defend yourself with your own words. Draw near to God and listen to him first. He sees what is happening and knows how to speak in the middle of the confusion.
exp.26:11:
God tells Moses to go up to Mount Abarim, a range of mountains east of the Jordan River. From there he will be able to see the promised land that God had already given to the people of Israel. The verse of the old spelling of words is not needed here, since the verse itself uses modern wording. The phrase "has given" speaks of a promise that God considers certain.

The Lord, the God of Israel, speaks to Moses near the end of his life. Shortly before, the laws about the inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad had been settled. Now God reminds him that he will not enter the land, because of what happened at Kadesh, when he did not honor God before the people. Even so, God allows him to see it.

For today: even when we do not see everything we long for fulfilled, we can trust that God remains faithful. Serve with dedication, and leave the results in his hands.
exp.27:10:
This verse commands that, at the beginning of each month (the new moon), the people offer to God a burnt offering: two young bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven lambs a year old. All of them had to be "without spot," that is, without any physical flaw. The burnt offering was an offering that was burned completely on the altar.

God speaks through Moses, toward the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Before entering the promised land, the people receive instructions about daily, weekly and monthly offerings. In this way their whole life revolved around worshiping God.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. We can begin each month, or each week, by setting aside time to pray, to thank him, and to hand him our plans once again.
exp.32:25:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Makheloth and camped at another place called Tahath. The phrase "having departed" simply describes that they had set out from the first place, and "camped" means that they pitched their camp. It is one more stop on their journey through the wilderness.

Moses writes this list at God's command, as is explained at the beginning of the chapter. He goes over each place where Israel camped from Egypt until they came near the promised land. Today it is not known for certain where many of these places were, including Makheloth and Tahath, and scholars do not agree on where to locate them.

God cares for every stage of our journey, even the ones that seem dull or unimportant. One more name in a list reminds us that He walked with His people step by step. Today you can remember the stages of your own life with gratitude and trust that God is also present in your now.
exp.7:12:
This verse commands that the Levites be presented before Aaron and his sons, the priests. Then Moses is to offer them as an offering to the LORD. The phrase about making them stand is explained here: the verb can be understood as having them stand before the priests. "Offering" here does not mean a sacrifice of death, but a giving over: the Levites are dedicated to God.

God speaks to Moses. The Levites will be set apart from among the people to help in the service of the tabernacle. They are presented in place of the firstborn of Israel. Before they begin, they are purified, and sacrifices are offered for them. This shows that serving God requires being cleansed and set apart.

For today: God does not use us on the basis of our own merit, but because he cleanses us and sets us apart. Before serving in your church or family, offer yourself to God with humility and give thanks for his forgiveness.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that the tribe of Reuben had its own banner, or standard, and camped on the south side, which is what "at midday" means. It was organized in divisions, that is, ordered groups. Its leader was Elizur the son of Shedeur. "Army" here refers to the group of tribes that camped together under one banner.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai. He gives them instructions for arranging Israel's camp in order around the tabernacle. Each tribe had its place, its leader, and its banner. After Judah, which went to the east, the southern group is described: Reuben, Simeon, and Gad. Numbers are given to organize the march.

For today: God cares about order and responsibility. In your family, your church, or your work, gladly fill the place that belongs to you, knowing that your service, though it may seem small, is important within God's plan.
exp.28:0:
It says that on the first day of the seventh month, the people were to gather for a holy assembly, that is, a gathering set apart for God. They could not do any hard labor, meaning the heavy everyday work. That day was called a day of blowing the trumpets: trumpets were sounded to mark the date as special.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, now close to entering the promised land. He repeats to them how to keep their feasts and offerings. This day later came to be associated with the Feast of Trumpets. The verses that follow explain the sacrifices they were to present.

For today: God invites us to stop. Set aside a fixed time each week to rest, pray, and meet with other believers, and let God order your heart before your busyness does.
exp.25:49:
This verse closes the list for the tribe of Naphtali. It says that their families, descended from Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem, added up to 45,400 men who were counted. "Counted" means registered in the census.

Moses and the priest Eleazar carry out this second census by God's command, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The earlier generation had died, and now the new one was counted before entering the promised land. The numbers would also serve to divide the land, according to the same chapter. The names and figures show that God kept his promises and knew his people.

For today: God does not see anonymous crowds but families with names. You can trust that He knows you personally, and also value every person in your community, even the one who goes unnoticed.
exp.30:19:
God commands that, after the war, everything the soldiers brought back from the battlefield be purified: the clothing, the objects made of leather, the fabrics woven from goats' hair, and the utensils made of wood. A "vessel" here means any container or utensil.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel after the war against Midian. According to the law, touching a dead body made a person unclean, and that uncleanness also extended to their belongings. For this reason the soldiers were to remain outside the camp for seven days and purify themselves. The passage deals with hard themes, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God is interested in everyday life. We can ask ourselves what things of the world we carry in our minds and hearts, and bring them before God with humility. Christians trust that Christ cleanses us completely.
exp.3:17:
This verse says: "Cut ye not off," that is, do not let the family of the Kohathites within the tribe of Levi be destroyed or disappear. "Kohath" is Kohath, one of the sons of Levi, and this group of families came from him.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron. The Kohathites were assigned to carry the most sacred things of the tabernacle, and approaching them in the wrong way was dangerous. That is why God gives clear instructions to protect them: that Aaron and his sons prepare and arrange everything beforehand. Some understand that the warning is meant to keep the Kohathites from dying through carelessness.

For today: God cares for those who serve, but he also expects reverence. If we have a service or responsibility in the church, let us take it seriously and with humility, and accept the guidance and order that help us serve well.
exp.13:9:
This verse tells that the whole people, furious, wanted to stone Joshua and Caleb to death. They had just urged the people to trust God. At that moment, the glory of the LORD, that is, his bright and powerful presence, appeared in the tabernacle (the sacred tent) before all the children of Israel.

Joshua and Caleb had explored Canaan and were encouraging the people to go in. The other ten spies had caused fear, and the people wept and rebelled. When they heard the truth, they reacted with violence. God intervened by showing his glory.

Today, we sometimes resent the person who calls us to trust God when we are afraid. Before rejecting a hard piece of advice, let us ask God for calm and check whether that word agrees with the Bible. He remains present, even when we react badly.
exp.12:10:
This verse names one of the twelve men chosen to explore the promised land: Gaddiel, son of Sodi, a representative of the tribe of Zebulun. It is part of a list of names, and the Bible tells us nothing more about him.

God told Moses to send a leader from each tribe to survey the land of Canaan, which He had already promised to Israel. Moses chose them, and Scripture preserves their names. Afterward, most of them returned full of fear and doubted God, while Caleb and Joshua trusted Him.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. When He entrusts you with something, do not stare only at the obstacles. Ask Him for courage to trust His promise and to act in faith, even when others are afraid.
exp.11:11:
Aaron pleads with Moses that Miriam not be left like a stillborn baby, with her body half destroyed. He uses a very strong image to express his anguish at seeing how the disease was harming her.

Aaron speaks after God corrected Miriam and him for criticizing Moses. Seeing his sister afflicted, he repents and acknowledges his wrong. He asks Moses for help, the same Moses he had earlier looked down on. Scholars do not say with certainty exactly what illness this was; the Hebrew word covered several skin conditions.

For today: when we are wrong and hurt others, the best thing is to acknowledge the mistake with humility. We can also ask forgiveness and pray for those who suffer the consequences, even for those we once criticized.
exp.6:74:
This verse says that Pagiel, leader of the tribe of Asher, presented for the burnt offering one young bullock, one ram, and one lamb of the first year. A "burnt offering" was an offering that was wholly burned upon the altar, given completely to God. A "bullock" is a young bull. The animals were males and without blemish, according to the law.

The book of Numbers tells that, when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering over twelve days. Here the narrator describes the offering of the eleventh day. It is almost identical to the others, and it is repeated in detail, perhaps to show that God values each tribe equally. Moses receives these offerings by God's command.

For today: God does not measure our devotion by how striking it is, but by how sincere it is. You can offer him your time, your work, and your care with steadiness and without comparing yourself to others, knowing that God looks at the heart of each person.
exp.15:1:
This verse tells of a group who rose up against Moses. There were two hundred and fifty men of Israel, and they were not just anyone: the "princes of the assembly" were the leaders of the people, "those of the council" were the ones who took part in the decisions, and "men of renown" were men who were well known and respected. To "rose up" means they rebelled openly.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Korah, Dathan, Abiram and On led this rebellion during the journey through the wilderness. According to what follows, they said that the whole people was holy and that Moses and Aaron considered themselves superior. Moses answered with humility, falling on his face.

For today: having prestige or a position does not protect us from pride. Before criticizing those who lead, it is wise to examine our own hearts and to pray. God looks at intentions, not at titles.
exp.22:3:
This verse says that God met Balaam. Then Balaam reminded him that he had prepared seven altars and had offered on each one a bullock (a young bull) and a ram. The word "ordered" here means that he had set them out ready and in order, so I will rewrite that comment: the verse itself says "I have prepared," which means he had got everything ready.

Balaam is speaking, a diviner whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. Balaam presents his offerings as if they could impress God. But God does not respond to the sacrifices as if they were a payment; instead, he puts his own word into Balaam's mouth. Some interpreters see here an attempt to win God's favor; the text says nothing more about his motives.

For today: God cannot be managed with our offerings or with our religiousness. Rather than showing him how much we do, let us come near with humility and ready to listen to what he says.
exp.6:70:
This verse describes the peace offering brought by Ahiezer. The word "fue," which today is written "fue," is simply the past tense of "to be."

This passage is a narrative, written in the tradition of Moses. Each day, a tribal leader brought his offering for the dedication of the tabernacle. Ahiezer represented the tribe of Dan. Although the offerings repeat with the same amounts, the text names each leader, and so it shows that each tribe was taken into account.

For today: God values the sincere devotion of each person, even when others give the same or more. Ask yourself what you can give today with steadiness and gratitude, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.10:6:
This verse describes what the manna looked like, the food God gave Israel in the wilderness. It was small and round, like coriander seed. Its color was like that of bdellium, a pale aromatic resin; it is not known for certain what substance this was, and scholars understand it in several ways.

The narrator explains this right after the people complained. They longed for the food of Egypt and grew tired of the manna. In describing it, the text shows it as real food, varied in how it was prepared and good, even though they looked down on it.

For today: sometimes we focus so much on what we lack that we stop valuing what God already gives us. Today you can write down three simple things you have received, and thank God for them in prayer before asking for anything more.
exp.6:50:
He says that Elishama brought for the burnt offering one young bullock, one ram, and one lamb of the first year. "Burnt offering" was an offering burned whole on the altar, with nothing kept back for the one who brought it. "Young bullock" is a young bull, and "lamb of the first year" is a young animal without blemish.

Here the narrator of Numbers speaks. When the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribe brought its offering on a different day, and the text repeats almost the same wording twelve times. Elishama was the leader of the tribe of Ephraim. The repetition shows that each tribe had the same worth before God and took part equally in his worship.

For today: the burnt offering expresses total surrender. We can ask ourselves what part of our life we keep for ourselves. God does not seek only things, but a heart that is devoted, steady, and thankful, in the great things and in the everyday.
exp.2:24:
This verse says that the sons of Gershon were to take care of and carry the softer parts of the tabernacle: the curtains that formed the dwelling, the tent, its covering, and the screen or curtain at the entrance. The word "hanging" here refers to a curtain that closed the doorway. The "tent of meeting" is the tent where God dwelt among his people.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, after counting the Levites. Each Levite family received a task and a place to camp. The Gershonites camped to the west, behind the tabernacle, under the direction of Eliasaph. In this way, the service to God was orderly and nothing was neglected.

For today: do not despise the task God gives you, even if it seems small or little noticed. Caring for curtains was not glamorous, but it was necessary for worship. Serve faithfully wherever you are, in your church, your home, or your work.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that the Moabites were very much afraid when they saw the Israelites. The word "afraid" tells us they felt fear, and the phrase "distressed" means they were filled with anxiety and worry. The reason was that the people of Israel were very numerous.

Here it is not a character who speaks; the narrator tells us what Moab felt. Israel had camped nearby, in the fields of Moab, and Balak, its king, had heard how Israel defeated the Amorites. For that reason he feared he would be the next. Later on, that fear leads him to seek out Balaam to curse Israel.

For today: fear can lead us to make wrong decisions, even to fight against what God is blessing. When something troubles us, it is better to pray and trust God before acting out of fear.
exp.6:61:
It says that Ahiezer, of the tribe of Dan, brought a golden dish weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned in the sanctuary. The "dish" was a small container, like a cup or bowl, used to carry the incense.

The passage is part of the account where each tribal leader brings his offering for the dedication of the altar and the tabernacle. The narrator is the author of the book, who repeats almost the same offering for each prince, day after day. This shows that every tribe took part equally in the worship of God.

Today we can learn that God values the giving of everyone, without comparison. Ask yourself what you can offer him sincerely: your time, your talents, or your prayer, which the Bible compares to incense.
exp.6:63:
This verse says that the prince Abidan, of the tribe of Benjamin, brought a male goat as an offering "for a sin offering." In today's language, this word means a sacrifice to cover sin and restore the relationship with God. The male goat was a young, healthy animal that was presented at the altar.

Here the account of Moses speaks. When the tabernacle was finished and dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering over twelve days. All of them brought the same thing, and the list is repeated on purpose. This showed that each tribe had the same worth before God and took part in his worship.

For today: before we give thanks or serve God, we need to recognize our need for forgiveness. Christians believe that Jesus is the complete sacrifice for our sins. We can come to God with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.7:18:
God says that he has given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons, the priests. They will serve in the tabernacle in place of the people and will make atonement for Israel, that is, they will do what is needed so that the people can draw near to God. In this way they will keep any plague from falling on the Israelites when they come near the sanctuary.

God speaks to Moses. When he freed Israel from Egypt, the firstborn of the Israelites were spared and belonged to him. Now God takes the Levites in place of them. The Levites are set apart, purified, and offered to God. This reminds us that approaching a holy God is a serious matter.

For today: God reminds us that coming near to him is not something to take lightly. As Christians, we believe that Jesus opens the way for us. We can respond with gratitude, reverence, and devotion, serving God and others with humility.
exp.23:16:
Balaam says he sees something of the future, but not for now, and that he sees it from far away. He announces that a star will come out of Jacob and a scepter will rise out of Israel, that is, a king with authority. That ruler will defeat Moab.

The word "corners" means the edges or borders of a land, and "Sheth" here is understood in different ways: some connect it with the descendants of Seth, others with a neighboring people.

Balaam speaks as a foreign prophet. Balak, the king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God put blessings in his mouth. Jews and many Christians have seen here a king like David and, beyond him, the Messiah. Christians relate it to Jesus.

For today: God keeps his promises even when they take a long time. If you are waiting for something you do not see close at hand, trust that God is still at work, and wait with patience and faith.
exp.2:47:
This verse says that Moses was to give the money for the redemption to Aaron and his sons. It was the payment for those firstborn of Israel who were left over, that is, those who had no Levite to take their place. The word "redemption money" here refers to payments made to free or redeem someone, and "left over" means that the firstborn exceeded the number of Levites.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness. The Levites were set apart to serve him in place of the firstborn of Israel. There were 273 more firstborn than Levites, so each of them was redeemed with five shekels. The money was given to the priests, who attended the sanctuary. The verses that follow show that Moses carried out what he had been commanded.

For today: God attends to the details and leaves nothing unattended. This reminds us that we belong to him and that redemption has a price. We can also support, with generosity, those who serve in the church.
exp.15:48:
This verse tells how many people died in the plague that fell on Israel: fourteen thousand seven hundred, not counting those who had already died in the rebellion of Korah. The word "plague" names a sudden, widespread death, and "the matter of Korah" refers to the affair of Korah and his group.

The narrator relates what happened after the people blamed Moses and Aaron for the death of the rebels. God sent a plague, and Aaron, with the censer, stood between the dead and the living to make atonement, and the plague was stopped. The number shows the seriousness of the judgment and also the mercy of God, who accepted a mediator. Some see here a foreshadowing of Christ, although the text does not say so.

Today we can learn that grumbling and rebelling against God have serious consequences. But we can also give thanks that God provides a mediator, Jesus, and pray for others with humility.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that the tribe of Dan was to camp on the north side of the tabernacle, under its own banner. The word "north" here is the direction the verse itself names, and "armies" refers to their groups or divisions in good order. Their leader was Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron as the people of Israel prepare to march through the wilderness. Each tribe received a fixed place around the tabernacle, which stood at the center. Dan was on the north side, and their group would close the march. This order shows that God is a God of order, and that His presence was the center of the people's life.

For today: God has given you a place and a task within His people. Serve faithfully where you are, without envying other places, and keep God at the center of your life, your family, and your church.
exp.22:2:
Balaam asks Balak to stay beside the burnt offering, that is, the offering burned completely on the altar. He goes off alone, hoping that the Lord will meet him, that is, that God will show himself to him. Whatever God shows him, he will report back to Balak.

Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam prepares altars and sacrifices, but he does not control what God will say. Some think he was looking for a sign or a message from God, while others see in him a questionable motive. The text does not make this entirely clear. What is clear is that God takes the initiative and puts His word in his mouth.

For today: we can prepare our offerings and plans, but what matters most is listening to God with humility, without trying to use Him for our own purposes.
exp.6:26:
This verse lists three animals for the burnt offering: a young bullock (a young bull), a ram, and a lamb of the first year. The burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar, leaving nothing for the one who brought it.

These words are part of Moses' account of the dedication of the tabernacle. Each tribal leader brought his offering on a different day. Here it is the turn of Eliab, leader of the tribe of Zebulun. All of them presented the same things, which shows that no tribe was more important than another before God.

Today we can learn to give God a complete surrender, not just the leftovers of our time or of our heart. And since each tribe offered the same thing with the same seriousness, we can serve him with joy, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.7:15:
God says that the Levites belong to him completely. He took them from among the people so that they would take the place of every firstborn, that is, the first male child born in each family. The phrase that would be rendered "I have taken them" simply means that God has taken them. In this way the Levites stand in place of the firstborn of Israel.

God speaks to Moses while the service of the tabernacle is being prepared. When God struck the firstborn of Egypt, the firstborn of Israel were spared, and God claimed them as his own. Now he chooses the tribe of Levi to serve him in their place, and so they are set apart and presented as an offering.

For today: what God has saved belongs to him, and not just a part of it. Today we can ask what place God has in our time, our work, and our gifts. Giving him our lives each day, with gratitude for his deliverance, is a simple way of serving him.
exp.6:12:
This verse describes the offering of Nahshon, the first leader to bring his gifts. He brought a silver dish weighing 130 shekels and a silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, both full of fine flour mixed with oil, for a grain offering. The "shekel of the sanctuary" was the official unit of weight used in worship. The fine flour is flour of the highest quality. The grain offering here is the offering of flour, which is what the verse calls the offering.

God spoke to Moses when the tabernacle and the altar were ready. Each tribal leader would bring his offering on a different day, to dedicate the altar. Nahshon represented Judah. Everyone would give the same things, which shows order and unity among the tribes.

For today: God values that we give Him our best, not what is left over. Ask yourself what part of your time, your talents, or your resources you are offering to Him with order, consistency, and a grateful heart.
exp.13:16:
Moses asks God to show his power, but not through punishment; rather, in the way God himself had made himself known. The word "magnified" in the verse above conveys the idea of being made great or shown to be great. Where the verse says "power," that is the force and strength of God being displayed. The phrase "according as thou hast spoken, saying" signals that Moses is about to quote the words with which God had described himself earlier.

Moses speaks after the people rebelled by believing the fearful report of the spies. God threatened to destroy them, and Moses intercedes. First he mentions God's reputation before the nations, and then he relies on God's character: slow to anger and great in mercy.

For today: when you pray, do not rely on your own merits, but on what God has said about himself. You can approach him with confidence to ask for forgiveness and help, remembering his mercy, and also intercede for others with humility.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that sometimes the cloud stayed over the tabernacle only one night, from evening until morning. When it lifted in the morning, the people set out. Other times the cloud stayed for the whole day, and if it lifted at night, they also set out.

The book tells how God guided Israel through the desert after leaving Egypt. The narrator describes how the cloud showed when to camp and when to move on. God had given those instructions through Moses, and the people were to obey them.

For today: trust God even when His timing changes. Sometimes He asks us to stay in one place for a long time, and other times He moves us suddenly. We can pray, listen to His Word, and be willing to follow Him, even when we do not understand the whole plan.
exp.8:5:
Here the verse says that some men could not keep the Passover on the appointed day because they were "defiled by the dead body of a man," that is, ritually unclean from having touched or cared for a corpse. For that reason they came before Moses and Aaron on that same day. "Passover" was the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Israel had just kept the Passover in the wilderness of Sinai, just as God had commanded. According to the law, touching a dead body brought uncleanness for several days, and that condition kept these men from taking part. These men did not ignore the problem or let it pass; they took it to the leaders.

For today: when something keeps us from fulfilling what God asks, let us not ignore it or be content to stay on the sidelines. Like these men, let us seek God's direction with humility and sincere desire, for He knows how to answer.
exp.13:44:
It says that the Amalekites and the Canaanites, who lived in that mountain region, came down and attacked the Israelites. They struck them and overcame them, and pursued them as far as a place called Hormah.

The words "smote them" and "discomfited them" are old ways of saying "struck them" and "defeated them."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier, the people refused to enter the promised land out of fear, and God said he would not go with them. Moses warned them not to go up. Even so, they went up on their own, without the ark of the covenant or Moses. This verse tells the result of that decision.

For today: obeying God at the right time matters. After disobeying, trying to fix things our own way, without his direction, does not work. It is better to return to him in humility and ask for his guidance.
exp.2:8:
God tells Moses to hand the tribe of Levi over to Aaron and his sons, who were the priests. The phrase "wholly given" means the Levites are a complete gift, placed entirely at the service of the priests. "You shall" is a command, and "from among the children of Israel" means they were set apart from the rest of the people.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The tabernacle needed care: setting it up, guarding it, and looking after its furnishings. The Levites would help the priests with that work, but without being priests themselves. Later the text explains that God took them in place of the firstborn of Israel (Numbers 3:12-13).

For today: serving God often means helping with simple, unseen tasks. Ask God where you can support your church with faithfulness and steady commitment, without seeking recognition.
exp.32:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the camp at Mithcah and settled their tents in a place called Hashmonah. The verb is rendered as "went from" in the verse your reader sees, and the verse's second sentence is replaced accordingly: "went from" means to set out, and "pitched" means to set up camp. It is one more stop on the long journey through the desert.

Moses is the one who records this list, at God's command (Numbers 33:2). He goes through each place where Israel camped from Egypt until they came near the promised land. It is not known for certain where Hashmonah was; scholars do not agree on its location. Even so, the text records it, as part of the remembrance of how God guided his people step by step.

For today: there are seasons of life that seem to be nothing more than stops along the way, with nothing special about them. But God sees them and remembers them. Trust that He is with you in the simple and slow times too, and keep walking faithfully.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that only the priests, descendants of Aaron, could blow the silver trumpets that God commanded to be made. And that command was not temporary: it was a lasting ordinance, something to be kept forever, throughout the generations. The word "shall blow" is rendered in this verse as "shall blow with the trumpets," and it simply means to sound them.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, as Israel was preparing to leave Sinai. The trumpets served to call the people together, to signal when to set out on the march, and later for war and for feasts. That the priests were the ones who sounded them showed that every movement of the people depended on the direction of God.

Today we can learn to listen for his voice before taking important steps. Before deciding something, pause, pray, and seek his guidance in the Bible, so that we move forward with order and confidence.
exp.30:32:
This verse is part of a list. It says that, among the spoils taken in the war against Midian, there were seventy-two thousand oxen. Oxen were strong animals, used to work the land and carry loads.

Here no character is speaking; it is the account of Moses. God had commanded a war against Midian, and afterward Moses and the priest Eleazar divided the plunder according to the Lord's instructions. The text gives exact figures to show that everything was counted in an orderly way and that nothing was divided at random. It is a difficult passage, and scholars understand it in different ways.

For today: God cares about order and honesty in the handling of goods. We can learn to be transparent and fair with the money and the things entrusted to us.
exp.32:4:
This verse tells that the people of Israel left Rameses, a city in Egypt, and camped at Succoth, their first stop. "Pitched" means they set up their camp to rest.

Moses writes this record of the stages of the journey, by God's command (Numbers 33:1-2). He reviews the road from Egypt to the promised land. The departure happened after the Passover and the death of the firstborn of Egypt. The text says that God also judged the gods of Egypt, and that Israel went out boldly, that is, openly and with God's victory.

God delivers, but he also guides step by step. Perhaps today you cannot see the whole road, but you can trust God to provide the next step. Give thanks for what he has already brought you out of, and move forward in faith.
exp.17:3:
God tells Aaron that the Levites will be joined to him and will take charge of the care of the tabernacle and all its service. The word "charge" in the verse means a responsibility or task assigned to someone. The word "stranger" refers to someone who did not belong to the tribe of Levi, that is, a person not authorized for that work.

God speaks to Aaron, the high priest, after the people had feared to draw near to the tabernacle and die. He gives the assignment: the priests serve in the most holy place, and the Levites help them. In this way the people were protected and what was holy was cared for.

For today: God orders service with distinct responsibilities, and all of them matter. We can serve with humility in the task that falls to us, without envying or looking down on the work of others, and taking seriously what God has entrusted to us.
exp.6:49:
This verse says that part of the offering of the prince was a golden dish weighing ten shekels and full of incense. The word "dish" here refers to a small cup or bowl for incense. The "incense" was a fragrant substance that was burned in worship. A shekel was a unit of weight, so this was a piece of gold of considerable value.

We are in the account of the offerings that the twelve princes of the tribes brought, one each day, to dedicate the altar of the tabernacle. Here it is the seventh day, and the turn belongs to Elishama, of the tribe of Ephraim. Each prince presented exactly the same thing, and Moses records it in detail, as if each gift deserved to be remembered separately.

For today: God values every offering given with sincerity, even when it looks like the offerings of others. You do not have to be original or stand out; what matters is giving your best with a willing heart.
exp.25:47:
This verse begins the list of the families of the tribe of Naphtali, one of the sons of Jacob. Two of its clans are named: the Jahzeelites, who come from Jahzeel, and the Gunites, who come from Guni. The family names in this verse are formed by adding a suffix that simply means "descendants of." The list continues in the next verse with two more families.

God himself commands this census through Moses, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The previous generation had died, and the people were about to enter the promised land. Counting each tribe and family served to divide the land fairly. The text says that Naphtali's total came to 45,400 people.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but family by family, name by name. Even the little-known names matter to him. You can rest in the knowledge that God knows you personally, and that encourages you to value and care for the small or overlooked people around you.
exp.25:50:
This verse gives the total of Israel's second census: 601,730 men who were counted. "Counted" means those who were recorded in the list. It refers to the men twenty years old and up, fit for war, according to the command at the start of the chapter.

The census was taken on the plains of Moab, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God had spoken to Moses and Eleazar to count the people. The previous generation had died because of their unbelief, and this new generation was getting ready to enter the promised land. The number is close to that of the first census, which shows that God sustained his people. Furthermore, the count would serve to divide the land as an inheritance.

For today: God knows his people and does not forget them. You can rest in the fact that you too count for him, and that God keeps his promises even when the road is long.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not decide on their own when to travel or when to stop. When the Lord commanded it, they broke camp; when the Lord commanded it, they set up camp again. "Pitched" means they set up their tents and camped, and "rested" means they stayed still, without moving, for as long as the cloud remained over the tabernacle.

The book of Numbers recounts Israel's journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. Here the narrator (tradition attributes it to Moses) explains how God guided the people with a cloud by day and a appearance of fire by night. It was a visible sign of his presence and direction.

For today: learn to wait and to move forward according to God's guidance, not only according to your hurry or your plans. Before an important decision, pray, seek his Word, and ask for wise counsel. If it is time to wait, wait with confidence; if it is time to move, move with obedience.
exp.13:32:
It says that the children of that people would have to wander like shepherds in the desert for forty years. They would bear the consequences of their parents' unfaithfulness to God. This would last until the last of the adults of that generation died in the desert. The phrase about bearing the consequences of their parents' unfaithfulness is what the verse conveys, and it means that the penalty for the parents' sin would fall on the children for a time.

God speaks through Moses. The spies had returned from Canaan, and the people, full of fear, rebelled and wanted to go back to Egypt. God judged them for not trusting Him, although He promised that their little ones would indeed enter the land.

For today: our decisions affect those around us, above all our family. Trusting God when we feel afraid is a valuable legacy. And even when there are consequences, God continues to care for and guide the next generation.
exp.13:35:
This verse recalls the twelve men Moses sent to explore the promised land. When they returned, they caused the whole congregation to complain against Moses, because they spoke badly about that land. "Searching" in this verse means exploring the land, and "discrediting" it means speaking badly about it in order to take away its worth.

Here the narrator summarizes what happened after God announced his judgment: the people, who would not trust, would spend forty years in the wilderness. Ten of the spies gave a report full of fear, and the people believed them. The next verse says that they died by a plague, while Joshua and Caleb survived.

For today: our words influence others. If we speak with fear or distrust, we can extinguish the faith of those around us. Let us strive to say what we see with honesty, but remembering that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.13:17:
He is slow to anger and great in mercy. He forgives wickedness and rebellion, but he does not leave the guilty unpunished who refuse to repent. The phrase "forgiving iniquity and transgression" means that he forgives, but he does not overlook sin as if it did not matter. The phrase "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" means that the consequences of sin reach the children and grandchildren.

Moses is speaking. The people, frightened by the report of the spies, rebelled and wanted to return to Egypt. God threatened to destroy them. Moses intercedes and reminds God of how he has made himself known, using words God himself spoke in Exodus 34:6-7. Many understand that the children suffer the consequences of their parents' mistakes, not that they are punished for the guilt of others.

For today: we can come to God with confidence to ask for forgiveness, but without taking sin lightly. Also, our decisions affect our family, so it is wise to live with responsibility.
exp.10:10:
Moses speaks to God with candor and complains. He asks why God has treated him badly, why he has not found favor in God's sight, and why God has laid on him the burden of all these people.

Moses leads Israel in the wilderness. The people weep and complain because they are tired of the manna and want meat. God becomes angry, and Moses also feels overwhelmed. He feels alone with a responsibility that is too great, and he tells God about it, not the people.

When you feel overwhelmed, you can bring your weariness to God honestly. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Praying this way is trusting him. And if the burden is too heavy, it is also wise to ask others for help, as God himself will do with Moses later.
exp.14:40:
This verse says that the LORD introduces himself by his name and by what he did: he brought Israel out of Egypt. His purpose was to be their God. He repeats "I am the LORD your God" at the beginning and at the end, like a seal that gives weight to what came before. In the older wording, the phrase "to be your God" means belonging to one another in a covenant relationship.

God speaks through Moses to the people in the desert. He has just commanded them to put tassels on the corners of their garments, with a blue cord, to remember his commandments and not be led astray by what they see and desire. He closes the command by reminding them who he is and what he has already done for them. His authority springs from his love and his rescue.

For today: before obeying, remember that God has already rescued you and calls you his own. Find a simple reminder, such as a verse on your phone or a prayer at the start of the day, so that you obey him out of gratitude and not out of fear.
exp.32:20:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the camp at Libnah and camped at a place called Rissah.

Moses writes this long record of Israel's stopping places during their journey through the wilderness, from Egypt to the promised land. He does so by God's command, as seen at the beginning of the chapter. It is not known for certain where Rissah was, and scholars do not agree. The list serves to remind us that God guided every stage of the way.

For today: sometimes our life seems like a series of unimportant stopping places. But God sees and remembers every stage. Trust that He is with you also in the times of waiting and of the journey, even when you do not yet understand where you are going.
exp.10:3:
The verse tells how "the mixt multitude" that was among them, that is, a mixed group of people who had left Egypt along with Israel, began to crave other foods strongly. The craving spread, and the children of Israel also wept and said, "Who shall give us flesh to eat?" The words "Who shall give us" express a longing that complains.

The people had just been freed from Egypt and were eating manna every day. Shortly before, God had shown his anger with fire because of their complaints. Even so, the discontent returned. Many understand that the mixed group was the origin of the complaint, although the whole people joined in.

Today, we can ask ourselves what we are remembering with nostalgia and what we are forgetting of what God has already given us. When we give thanks for what we have, the heart is protected from the discontent that spreads.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that things set apart for God by a person, that is, what someone dedicated and brought to the sanctuary, belonged to the priest. The same applies to whatever anyone gave to him. "Hallowed" here means set apart for God. And "shall be his" means it belonged to the priest and his family.

God speaks to Moses to order the life of the people in the wilderness. He had been speaking about restitution when someone wronged another person: the guilt had to be acknowledged, what was owed returned, and a fifth part added. If there was no one to return it to, it was given to the priest. In this way those who served in worship were supported, since the priests had no inheritance of their own land.

For today: if we have harmed someone, it is not enough to feel regret; God calls us to acknowledge the wrong and repair what we can. It also reminds us to support with generosity those who serve in God's work.
exp.14:22:
This verse is part of a sentence that begins in the previous verse. It says that if the people go wrong and do not keep everything that God commanded through Moses, this applies to every commandment given from the day God gave it, and also in the generations to come. The phrase "throughout your generations" refers to all the generations that follow.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are traveling through the wilderness. God explains what to do when the community sins without realizing it, through error or ignorance. He shows that there is forgiveness and a way of restoration, through the sacrifice and the intercession of the priest.

For today: God takes even our unintentional failings seriously, but He also offers mercy. Let us ask Him to show us where we are failing without noticing, and let us come to Him with humility, trusting in His forgiveness through Christ.
exp.22:15:
This verse says that God met Balaam and gave him the message he was to deliver. "Met" means that God came to him in order to speak with him. "Put a word in his mouth" means that he gave him the exact words. "Go again to Balak" is "return to Balak," and "thus you shall say" means "this is what you must say."

Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam prepared altars and sacrifices and withdrew to seek God. Here God takes control: Balaam will not speak what Balak wants or what Balaam himself desires, but what God gives him. Thus the word of God about his people cannot be bought or changed.

For today: when we speak about God or counsel others, let us first seek to listen to what He says in His Word, rather than saying what pleases people.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that Moses took the count of the people just as God had commanded him. The word "numbered" in the verse is the one that matters here, meaning he counted them one by one.

This happened in the wilderness of Sinai, where Israel was camped after leaving Egypt.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who reports what Moses did. God had asked for a count of the men twenty years old and up, those who were able to go to war. The counting also helped organize the camp and the tribes. Many understand it as a preparation for the journey toward the promised land.

For today: Moses did things "as the Lord had commanded." We can ask God to help us obey him in what he has shown us, even in simple and orderly tasks, trusting that he knows what he is doing.
exp.8:6:
The men tell Moses that they are unclean because they have touched a dead body. But they do not want to be left out of the Passover, and they ask why they should be kept from bringing their offering to the Lord at its appointed time, along with the rest of the Israelites. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, and "at its appointed time" means on the set day.

Israel had just left Egypt and was in the wilderness of Sinai. These men had become defiled by caring for or touching a corpse, something the law of Moses treated as ritual impurity. They do not rebel; they come with respect before Moses and Aaron, because they wanted to obey God.

For today: notice the heart of these men. An obstacle did not lead them to give up or to ignore what God asks; they brought it before the leaders and waited for an answer. When something keeps you from serving God, bring your need before him with humility and trust, and do not turn away.
exp.15:34:
This verse tells us that God sent fire and destroyed the 250 men who were offering incense. Before this, the earth had swallowed Korah, Dathan, and Abiram along with their households.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Korah and these leaders rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and they wanted to exercise the priesthood that God had given only to Aaron's family. Offering incense was a sacred task, and they took it on without being called by God. The account shows that God takes seriously who approaches Him and how they do so.

For today: come near to God with humility and reverence, in His way and not in your own. For Christians, Jesus is the one who opens the way for us (Hebrews 4:16). We can approach with confidence, but without pride or self-driven ambition.
exp.2:29:
This verse says that Elizaphan, son of Uzziel, was the leader of the Kohathite families. In other words, he was the head or the one responsible for that group within the tribe of Levi. The "house of the father" refers to the family clan, and the "chief" is the one who leads it.

God speaks to Moses and organizes the camp of Israel. Each Levite family had a place and a task in the service of the tabernacle. The Kohathites camped to the south and cared for the most sacred objects: the ark, the table, the lampstand, and the altars. That is why they needed a leader who would answer for them.

For today: God cares about order and values those who lead with responsibility. If you have a task in your family, your church, or your work, do it with seriousness, as a service to God. And pray for those who guide you.
exp.5:22:
God tells Moses to speak with Aaron and with his sons, who were the priests. He gives them a clear instruction: this is the way they are to bless the people of Israel. The word "saying" introduces what comes next, the exact text of the blessing.

The Lord speaks, and Moses is the one who passes the message on. It comes after the laws about the Nazirite, people who set themselves apart for God for a period of time. Now God gives the priests fixed words to bless with. In this way the blessing did not depend on them, but came from God, who had given it.

For today: we can bless others with simple words full of faith, remembering that the blessing comes from God. Today, encourage someone with a kind word, and pray that God will watch over them.
exp.16:9:
God tells Moses to place Aaron's rod again before the testimony, that is, near the ark where the tablets of the law were kept. There it would be kept as a sign or reminder for the rebellious people, the Israelites who had resisted God. In this way their murmurings against God would come to an end, and they would not die because of them.

God is the one speaking. After the rebellions of Korah and of the people against Moses and Aaron, God showed by a miracle whom he had chosen as priest: only Aaron's rod budded and produced almonds. The rod kept in place would be a lasting reminder of that decision.

Today, when we doubt or complain about what God has arranged, we can remember the times he has shown his faithfulness. Keeping such signs in mind helps us to trust rather than to murmur.
exp.17:18:
This verse says that all the set-apart gifts the people brought to God as holy things, God gave to Aaron, to his sons and to his daughters. "Given" is the word for "I have given them." "Perpetual statute" refers to a rule that never expires. The phrase about a "covenant of salt" seems to point to a firm and lasting commitment, though scholars explain it in several ways.

God speaks to Aaron, the high priest. The priests would not receive land as an inheritance, so God assigns them part of the offerings as their provision. In this way they could devote themselves fully to the service of the tabernacle, and the people shared in supporting them.

Today we can generously support those who serve God and his people, so that they can devote themselves to their work without anxiety. And if we serve, we can trust that God cares for those who place their lives in his hands.
exp.18:4:
This verse says that the red heifer is burned completely in the sight of the priest Eleazar: her skin, her flesh, her blood, and even her dung. "Dung" is the animal's waste. The phrase about the burning means that the one in charge sees to it that she is burned entirely, leaving nothing behind.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. He gives a law for cleansing the person who became unclean by touching a dead body. The ashes of this heifer were used to prepare the water of separation. Interpreters explain in various ways why everything was burned; many see the idea of a total and serious purification. What is certain is that the text does not give all the reasons.

For today: the cleansing that God gives is complete, not half-done. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ's sacrifice, which cleanses us fully. We can come to Him with confidence, hiding nothing, and receive His forgiveness.
exp.16:11:
The Israelites tell Moses that they are about to die. They repeat the idea three times: "we die, we perish, we all perish." It is an outcry of fear and despair. The word "perish" here means doomed to be destroyed.

The people of Israel are speaking in the wilderness. Shortly before, Korah and his followers rebelled and died, and then a plague killed many who were complaining. God had confirmed Aaron as priest by making his staff blossom. Now the people realize how dangerous it is to approach a holy God without his permission, and they fear that everyone will die.

For today: recognizing God's holiness should not leave us alone with fear, but lead us to humility. Today Christians believe that Jesus Christ, our high priest, opens the way for us to approach God with confidence and reverence (Hebrews 4:16).
exp.9:8:
This verse says that when Israel had to fight in its own land against an enemy who attacked them, they were to sound the trumpets with an alarm. In this way God would remember his people and save them. The word "oppresseth" means to trouble or harm someone, and the phrase "ye shall be remembered" means that God would keep them in mind to act on their behalf.

God speaks to Moses and gives instructions for the people in the wilderness, after commanding that two trumpets be made of silver. Those trumpets were used to gather the people, to signal when to break camp, and also for war and for festivals. The priests, the sons of Aaron, were to blow them.

For today: when you face a difficulty, do not rely only on your own strength. Cry out to God in prayer, with humility, and trust that he hears you and sustains you.
exp.12:6:
This verse names one of the twelve men chosen to explore the land of Canaan: Caleb, of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as "son of Jephunneh." The Bible does not say much more about his father.

God spoke to Moses, and Moses sent one leader from each tribe to survey the promised land. The text gives only the list of names. Later, Caleb and Joshua would be the two who trusted that God would give them the victory, while the other ten spread fear among the people.

For today: Caleb appears here as just one more name in a list, but God already knew him and was shaping him. Perhaps today you feel little seen or unimportant. Stay faithful in small things, because God sees your trust and can use it at the right moment.
exp.25:6:
This verse closes the list of the families of the tribe of Reuben. It says that when the men of this tribe were counted, there were 43,730. "Counted" here means those who were registered in the census. The descendants of Reuben, the firstborn son of Jacob, are the Reubenites.

God commands Moses and Eleazar to take this census after the plague in the wilderness. The people are close to entering the promised land. The count focused mainly on men of fighting age, and the record would also serve to divide the land. Reuben was the firstborn, but the text immediately recalls Dathan and Abiram, who rebelled.

For today: God knows his people and counts each one. Your place does not depend on your position or your family's past, but on faithfully following God. Today you can choose to obey him with humility.
exp.25:62:
This verse sums up who took the census. Moses and Eleazar the priest numbered the children of Israel in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, near the city of Jericho. "Those that were numbered" refers to the people who were recorded on the list of the nation.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who closes the account of the second census. About forty years have passed since the first one, which was taken at Sinai with Moses and Aaron. Israel is about to enter the promised land. The verses that follow explain that the previous generation died in the wilderness because of their unbelief, except Caleb and Joshua.

For today: God keeps his promises even when years pass and people change. We can trust that he continues to work and remains faithful with each generation, and that our obedience and faith matter.
exp.32:54:
It says that if Israel did not drive out the peoples living in Canaan, the ones left behind would be like splinters in their eyes and thorns in their sides. In other words, they would be a constant pain and a danger. The verse's wording points to the image of sharp things that pierce, and it means they would cause suffering in the land.

God speaks through Moses to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. Those nations were deeply tied to idolatry, and God warned that their influence would lead the people astray. Some scholars stress the aspect of divine judgment on those peoples; others, the protection of Israel's faith. Afterward, the book of Judges shows how this came to pass.

For today: it is not wise to live alongside small sins or habits that pull us away from God, thinking they will do no harm. Ask God and trustworthy brothers and sisters to help you remove them in time, before they wound you.
exp.6:13:
He says that Nahshon also presented a small gold dish that weighed ten shekels and was full of incense. Here the word for the small container is a little dish or bowl for the incense, and the incense is fragrant incense. A shekel was a unit of weight, and ten shekels would come to roughly one hundred grams, though the exact calculation is uncertain.

The book of Numbers tells how, when the tabernacle had been finished, the leaders of the tribes brought offerings for its service. Nahshon, of the tribe of Judah, was the first. Moses writes in detail because each leader gave the same, and so it is shown that all the tribes had an equal share in the worship of God.

For today: God values it when we give to him with order, with generosity, and with a sincere heart, without comparing ourselves to others. Think of something concrete, such as your time, your talent, or your money, and offer it to God this week with joy.
exp.15:2:
This verse tells that a group of men gathered against Moses and Aaron. They said to them, "Ye take too much upon you," which means "you have gone too far." They claimed that the whole congregation is holy and that the Lord is among all of them, so they did not understand why Moses and Aaron lifted themselves above the others.

The ones speaking are Korah, Dathan, Abiram, On, and two hundred and fifty respected leaders. What they say sounds true, because God had indeed called Israel holy. But their underlying motive seems to be envy and a desire for more power, since they were questioning the place God himself had given to Moses and Aaron. For this reason Moses falls on his face and lets God decide.

For today: before criticizing those who lead, let us examine our own hearts. A true statement can be used with wrong intentions. Let us ask God for humility to serve in the place he gives us.
exp.7:1:
God asks Moses to tell Aaron what he must do when he lights the lamps of the lampstand. The seven lamps were to give light toward the front, that is, toward the space in front of the lampstand. The lampstand is a stand that holds the lamps, and the phrase about the light shining forward shows that the light was directed ahead.

The LORD speaks, and Moses passes on the message. This takes place in the wilderness, when Israel already had the tabernacle. Aaron, as priest, had the task of lighting the lamps in the holy place. Afterward it is said that Aaron obeyed just as God had commanded, and that the lampstand was made according to the pattern God had shown.

For today: God values faithful obedience, even in small and constant tasks. We can serve him with care in simple things, such as praying, helping others, and setting a good example, so that his light may reach others.
exp.11:6:
God says that Moses is not like the other prophets.

The Lord speaks. Miriam and Aaron had criticized Moses, their brother, and questioned his special place. God calls them to the door of the tent of meeting and makes clear that Moses has a unique closeness with him: he speaks with Moses directly, not only in dreams or visions.

For today: God values faithfulness more than prestige. Instead of criticizing or envying those who serve, we can guard our tongue, respect others, and be faithful in what God has entrusted to us, even if it seems small.
exp.20:34:
This verse says that the Israelites completely defeated Og, king of Bashan, together with his sons and all his army, and that no one was left alive. Afterward they took possession of his territory.

The narrator of the book tells what happened as Israel was heading toward the promised land. Og came out to fight at Edrei, and God had told Moses not to be afraid, because He had already given him the victory. This account is harsh, and many read it within the ancient context of war and of God's judgment on peoples of that time. Some scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God is faithful to his promises. His help does not depend on your strength, so you can move forward with confidence and prayer, instead of being paralyzed by fear.
exp.6:7:
This verse tells that Moses gave to the sons of Merari, one of the families of the Levites, four wagons and eight oxen. They would use them according to their work, and everything was under the supervision of Ithamar, son of the priest Aaron.

It is part of the account of the offerings of the leaders of Israel for the tabernacle. The leaders gave wagons and oxen, and Moses distributed them according to the burden of each family. The Merarites carried the heavy parts of the structure, which is why they received twice as much as the Gershonites. The Kohathites did not receive wagons because they carried the sacred objects on their shoulders.

For today: God gives each person what is needed according to the task he entrusts to them. Instead of comparing ourselves with others, we can serve faithfully in what is ours, accepting order and support.
exp.6:67:
It says that Ahiezer, leader of the tribe of Dan, brought a golden spoon weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned in the sanctuary. A shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven grams according to common calculations, though the exact value is debated.

The book of Numbers tells that, when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering, one day after another over twelve days. The one who narrates is the author of the book, who repeats the list almost word for word for each tribe. In this way he emphasizes that all were equally important before God, with no one placed above another.

For today: God values what we give him sincerely, even when others give the same or more. Offer your time, your gifts, and your possessions gladly, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.3:44:
This verse closes the count of the family of Merari, one of the three groups of the Levites. It says that Moses and Aaron numbered them, and that they did so just as God had commanded through Moses. "Those that were numbered" are those who were registered or counted, and "by the hand of Moses" means that Moses was God's messenger.

Here the narrator of the book is recording the census of the Levites. The men from thirty to fifty years old were counted, those who could serve in the tabernacle. The sons of Merari were responsible for caring for and carrying the structural parts of the tent. The verse emphasizes that everything was done by God's command.

God is concerned with the simple and orderly service of each person. Even if your task seems small or little seen, it has value before Him. Serve faithfully and obey carefully, knowing that God sees you and calls you.
exp.27:17:
On the first day, the people were to gather for a holy assembly, that is, a sacred gathering set apart for God. The phrase "ordinary work" refers to everyday labor, the work of every day. On that day they rested from their labors and dedicated the day to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, who is about to enter the promised land. After the Passover on the fourteenth day, a seven-day festival began. This passage gives instructions about the offerings for worship. It recalled the deliverance from Egypt and taught the people to live thankfully.

Today we too can set aside a fixed time for God: leaving work and hurry behind, meeting with other believers, and remembering what He has done for us. Resting is also an act of trust.
exp.21:16:
Here Balak, king of Moab, promises Balaam that he will honor him greatly and do whatever he asks. In return, he begs him to come and curse Israel. The phrase "curse me" means to pronounce a curse upon them, and "this people" refers to the Israelites.

The ones speaking are the princes sent by Balak. He was afraid of Israel, which was camped near his territory. He had already sent a first delegation, and now he sends more important men with a greater offer. Balaam answers that not even a house full of silver and gold would make him disobey God. Yet the account shows that his heart was tempted by the reward.

For today: when someone offers us money, prestige, or comfort in exchange for giving up what God has shown us, it is good to pause and pray before answering. It is also worth examining whether, deep down, we desire that gain.
exp.2:36:
This verse continues the list of what the descendants of Merari were responsible for: the pillars that surrounded the court (the courtyard of the tabernacle), their bases (the sockets where the pillars rested), their pegs (the stakes that held the curtains in place), and their cords. These were the pieces that kept the boundary of the sacred place firm.

God speaks to Moses and shows him how to arrange the Levites around the tabernacle. The family of Merari, who camped to the north, was given the heavy task of caring for and carrying these structures. The work was not showy, but it was necessary so that worship could continue.

For today: God values simple and hidden service. If your task seems small, such as helping, organizing, or holding things steady, do it faithfully, because it also supports the work of God.
exp.34:17:
This verse says that if someone strikes another person with a wooden stick or club, hard enough to kill, and the person dies, that man is a murderer and must be put to death. "Hand weapon of wood" is a piece of wood held in the hand. "Murderer" here means one who kills on purpose, not by accident.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He is setting out laws about the cities of refuge. First he distinguishes deliberate killing, with iron, stone, or wood, from accidental manslaughter. The avenger of blood, the one who carried out the sentence, was part of the justice of that time.

For today: human life is sacred, and we are responsible for what we do with our hands and our words. Let us ask God to help us manage anger before it harms someone.
exp.26:5:
This verse says that God answered Moses. Moses had brought to him the case of some women who were asking for an inheritance. The name of God is "the Lord," and the wording "spake unto" is an older way of saying "spoke to."

The context is as follows: the daughters of Zelophehad had no brothers, and their father had died. According to custom, without a male son their family would lose its share of the land. They respectfully asked that this inheritance be given to them. Moses did not decide on his own, but presented the case to God, and God gave the answer.

For today: when we face a difficult or unjust situation, we can do what Moses did: bring it to God in prayer before deciding. And if someone brings us a need with humility, it is wise to listen to it carefully.
exp.10:32:
It says the people still had the meat between their teeth, not yet chewed, when the anger of the Lord was kindled and He struck them with a very great plague.

The narrator tells what happened in the wilderness. The Israelites complained about eating only manna and asked for meat, weeping and craving it intensely.
