God sent them quail in abundance, but the text shows their attitude was one of greed rather than thankfulness. For this reason that place was called the graves of craving (Kibroth-hattaavah).

For today: Examine your desires. Giving thanks for what God has already given you guards you against wanting things with an anxious and ungrateful heart. Ask Him to teach you to trust Him before you demand.
exp.19:14:
This verse sums up the history of Israel in a few words. It says that their ancestors went down into Egypt, that the people lived there a long time, and that the Egyptians mistreated them, and their fathers as well. The word "á" is an old form of "a," and "maltrataron" means that they made them suffer harshly.

Moses speaks on behalf of Israel and sends messengers to the king of Edom from Kadesh. The Edomites were descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob, which is why he says "your brother." Recalling their suffering, he seeks to awaken compassion and to ask permission to pass through his land on the way to Canaan.

For today: when you need to ask for help, speaking honestly about what you have lived through, without exaggerating or attacking, can open doors. And remembering how God has sustained you in the past strengthens your trust for what lies ahead.
exp.2:42:
This verse says that Moses counted all the firstborn males of Israel, from one month old and upward, and that the total came to 22,273. The phrase "by the number of names" means they were counted one by one, by name.

God had commanded Moses to take this count. The firstborn belonged to God since He saved Israel from the last plague in Egypt. Now God decides to take the Levites to serve Him in their place. That is why the firstborn had to be counted. Some scholars note that the total does not seem to fit well with other censuses of Israel, and various explanations have been proposed, but the text does not clarify them.

For today: God knows each person by name, not as a number. You can trust that He sees you and cares for you. You can also ask yourself: how am I using my life to serve Him?
exp.34:8:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God, called here the Lord, spoke to Moses. With it a new instruction begins. The word "saying" announces that a message follows which Moses is to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. The people are about to enter the promised land, and God had already given them instructions about the cities of the Levites. Now he moves on to another subject: the cities of refuge, where a person who killed someone unintentionally could find protection. In this way God cared for justice and also for mercy.

For today: before acting, be still and listen to God in his Word. He is interested in the details of everyday life and in protecting the vulnerable, and we can imitate him by being just and compassionate.
exp.13:23:
God says that his servant Caleb had a different spirit, that is, an attitude different from that of the rest of the people. Caleb followed God wholeheartedly and fully. That is why God promises to bring him into the land he explored, and his descendants will receive it as an inheritance.

God speaks here after Israel refused to enter Canaan out of fear, despite everything they had seen. Ten of the twelve spies discouraged the people, but Caleb trusted God's promise. Because of their unbelief, that generation would not enter the land, and Caleb was the exception.

For today: faith shows when a person keeps following God even when most others doubt. Ask God for a steady spirit, and obey him today in something concrete, even if no one else does.
exp.14:24:
This verse says that the priest will make atonement, that is, cover the sin with the sacrifice, for the whole congregation of Israel. God will forgive them because it was a mistake made without intent, an error or ignorance. They were to bring their offering made by fire to the Lord, and their sin offering.

God speaks through Moses. He is giving rules for when the whole community sinned without realizing it. Before this, a bull and a male goat are required. This shows that God takes sin seriously, even unintentional sin, but also offers a way to forgiveness.

For today: do not minimize your mistakes or live buried in guilt. If you discover that you have failed, even without intending to, come to God with humility. Christians believe that Christ is the complete sacrifice who gives us forgiveness and access to God.
exp.3:47:
This verse gives the total of the Levites counted for service: 8,580 men. "Numbered" means they were counted or registered. These were the men between thirty and fifty years old who could work in the tabernacle, that is, in the tent where God dwelt among his people.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, summarizing the census that God commanded. Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of Israel counted the Levites from the families of Kohath, Gershon, and Merari. Each group had different tasks, such as carrying and caring for the parts of the tabernacle. The text stresses that everything was done as the LORD had commanded.

For today: God knows and values each person who serves, even when their task seems small. Faithfully do the work entrusted to you in your church, your family, or your community, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.34:23:
This verse says that when someone kills another person without meaning to, the community must act as judge between two parties: the one who caused the death and the relative who has the right to avenge the dead person. The "congregation" is the gathered people of Israel. And the judgment must be made "according to these laws," that is, according to the rules God has just given.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. He was establishing cities of refuge. There, a person who killed without intention could find protection, so that an angry relative would not kill him before he had a fair trial. The verses before this one describe cases of accident, without hostility or evil intent.

For today: before condemning or taking revenge, we should seek the truth and distinguish between a mistake and a wrong done on purpose. God values justice together with mercy and order.
exp.6:48:
This passage describes the offering of Elisama, a leader of the tribe of Ephraim, on the seventh day of the dedication of the tabernacle. He brought one silver dish and one silver bowl, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The weight was measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, the official standard of weight for the offerings. A grain offering is a gift of thanks to God.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Each tribal leader brought, one each day, exactly the same offering. The text repeats the full offering every time, without summarizing it, as if each leader mattered equally. In this way all of Israel took part in setting apart the place where God would dwell with them.

For today: God values the devotion of each person, not novelty or comparison. Today you can offer him, with steadiness and simplicity, what you have: your time, your work, and your gratitude, without competing with anyone.
exp.0:14:
This verse gives the name of the representative of the tribe of Naphtali: Ahira, son of Enan. He is the last of a list of twelve men. The words "Of Naphtali" refer to Naphtali, one of the sons of Jacob, from whom that tribe comes.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to count the people of Israel, man by man, to know who could go to war. To help him, each tribe provides a leader, called a "prince" or "captain of thousands," that is, a head over large families. This verse closes that list before Moses and Aaron gather them together.

God knows and names each person who serves, even when that person is hardly mentioned again. Today you can serve in simple ways, without applause, trusting that God sees your faithfulness and does not forget you.
exp.34:33:
This verse commands the people of Israel not to defile the land where they live. "Defile" means to make impure or to stain. The reason is that God himself dwells among them, and so the land was not an ordinary place.

God is speaking, giving Moses instructions for the people, who are now close to entering Canaan. Earlier, the text spoke of murder and of the cities of refuge. Innocent blood stained the land, and for that reason no payment could be accepted to avoid the punishment of a murderer, nor to let out early someone who was to remain in the city of refuge. The worth of human life was taken very seriously.

Today we can remember that God is concerned with how we live in our home, our work, and our community. If he is near us, it is fitting to care for justice, to respect life, and to avoid corruption in what we do each day.
exp.32:14:
The text says that the people of Israel left Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai. The words "departed" and "pitched" here carry the same meaning as the wording in the verse. This is only one more step in the list of places they passed through.

This chapter is a record of the stages of the journey from Egypt to the promised land. The Bible says that Moses wrote it at God's command. Rephidim was a hard place, where water was lacking. Sinai is where, according to the book of Exodus, God gave the law and made his covenant with Israel. Here, in a single line, is a summary of what other books cover in many chapters.

For today: God can lead us from a place of scarcity to a place of meeting with him. If you are in a difficult stage right now, remember that it is not the end of the road. Keep walking in faith, because God knows every stop along the way.
exp.32:12:
The verse says that the people of Israel set out from a place called Dophkah and camped at another called Alush. Setting out is what the verse describes; camped is the word used for each stop along the way. It is one more of the stops on the journey through the wilderness.

This chapter is a list of the stages of the road from Egypt to the plains of Moab. Moses wrote it at God's command (Numbers 33:2) to record each day's journey. About the exact location of Dophkah and Alush there is no certainty; scholars do not agree. What we do know is that God guided every step.

For today: even the stretches of the road that seem insignificant in our lives do not go unnoticed by God. He remembers every stage of your journey, even the ones you nearly forget, and he walks with you through them.
exp.19:10:
Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod. Abundant water came out of the rock, and all the people drank, along with their animals.

The people were thirsty in the desert, and they complained against Moses and Aaron. God had told Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock (v. 8), but Moses, angry, called the people rebels and struck the rock. God still gave the water, but then he told them that they had not trusted him or honored him in front of the people. Because of this, they would not enter the promised land.

God is generous and can act even when we fail. But he also calls us to obey him in faith and not to act out of anger. When you are tired or frustrated, stop and ask: what did God say to do?
exp.2:9:
God tells Moses to appoint Aaron and his sons as priests, so that they carry out that office. "Appoint" means "put in the position." "The stranger" is someone who does not belong to the priestly family or to the Levites. If he came near the holy things, he "shall be put to death," that is, he would receive the death penalty.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites would help the priests with the care of the tabernacle. God wanted to protect the holiness of his presence and the order of worship. The severity shows that God is holy and cannot be approached carelessly.

Today we do not have human priests as mediators, because the New Testament presents Christ as our high priest (Hebrews 4:14-16). Even so, we can draw near to God with confidence and with reverence, grateful for the way he opened.
exp.9:31:
Moses tells his brother-in-law Hobab that if he comes along with them, then when God gives them the good things he has promised, they will treat him well too.

Israel is about to leave Mount Sinai for the promised land. Hobab wanted to return to his own land and his family, but Moses begs him to stay, because he knows the desert well and could be like eyes for the people. Moses offers to share with him the blessings of God. The text does not say here what Hobab's final answer was.

God takes care of his people through people with different gifts. Learn to ask for help with humility, and to value those whom God places in your path, sharing generously what you receive.
exp.25:19:
This verse says that the descendants of Judah, son of Jacob, were organized into three main families, each named after its ancestor: the Shelanites (from Shelah), the Pharzites (from Pharez) and the Zarhites (from Zerah). "Counted" means registered in a census. The names "Pharez" and "Zerah" are also written Fares and Zera today.

God speaks through Moses at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. A second census is taken before entering the promised land, so that the land can be divided according to the size of each tribe. It is mentioned that Er and Onan died in Canaan, which is why their line does not appear. Pharez and Zerah were born to Judah and Tamar.

God knows his people by name and remembers each family. You are not a mere number to him. You can also give thanks and honor the heritage of faith that others have left you.
exp.10:19:
He says that God will give them meat not just for a few days but for a whole month, until it comes out of their nostrils and they are sickened by it. The word "loathing" means disgust. Saying they "despised" God means they treated him as if he were worth nothing. God brings this charge against them because they wept and said it would have been better to stay in Egypt.

Here God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel in the wilderness. They were complaining about the manna and wanted meat. Their complaint went beyond food: it was distrust of God, who was with them and had freed them from slavery.

For today: when we complain, let us ask what that complaint says about our trust in God. It is good to ask him sincerely, but also to give thanks for what he already gives us, before disordered desire fills us with dissatisfaction.
exp.2:34:
The verse says that Zuriel, son of Abihail, was the chief of the families of Merari, one of the three branches of the Levites. Their place was to camp on the north side of the tabernacle. The verse's "north" is the direction the reader sees in the King James wording, so no separate word needs explaining here.

God is speaking to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. He is organizing the Levites, who were set apart to care for the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people. Each family had a place and a task. The sons of Merari were given the heaviest work: the boards, bars, pillars, and bases.

God cares about order and values every service, even the work that is not noticed. Today you can serve faithfully in what has been entrusted to you, without comparing yourself to others, knowing that God sees and values what you do.
exp.3:30:
This verse says that the sons of Merari were responsible for carrying the structural parts of the tabernacle: the boards, the bars, the pillars, and the sockets. The sockets are the bases or stands on which the boards and pillars rested. The charge of their burden means the responsibility assigned to them.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while the people are traveling through the wilderness. He is organizing the work of the Levites, and the Merarites, men from thirty to fifty years old, were given the task of carrying the heavy framework of the sanctuary whenever the camp moved. They worked under the direction of Ithamar, son of Aaron.

For today: no service to God is small. The Merarites did not see the most holy place, but without their quiet work the tabernacle could not be set up. Serve faithfully in the simple and hidden tasks, trusting that God values your labor.
exp.14:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people and announce something that will happen when they enter the land he is giving them. The phrase "the land of your dwellings" means the land where they are going to live, their settled home. It is the beginning of instructions about how to offer sacrifices there.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness. That generation had failed and had not entered the land because of their unbelief (chapters 13 and 14). Even so, God repeats his promise: the land will be given to them. It is a word of hope addressed to their children, and it also reminds the people that life in the land was to include worship.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we stumble. We can trust him and, looking ahead, plan a life where giving thanks to him and worshiping him come first, not only in hard times but also when everything is settled.
exp.6:53:
This verse marks the beginning of the offering for the eighth day. It was the turn of the leader of the tribe of Manasseh, whose name was Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur. Here a "prince" means the chief or leader of his tribe. The verse only introduces the person; the details of his offering come right after.

It is part of the account of the dedication of the tabernacle. For twelve days, each tribal leader presented the same offering, one per day, in order. The text repeats the full offering for each one, perhaps to show that no tribe was less important before God. Moses is the one who receives these offerings, following the Lord's instructions.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to someone who seems to be standing in the middle of a list. Your service and your devotion, however simple they may seem, have value before Him. Give consistently and wholeheartedly, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, inside the tabernacle of the congregation, and that is the phrase used here for the place that held the tablets of the law. It was on the first day of the second month, in the second year after Israel came out of Egypt. The word "saying" announces that God is about to give an instruction.

The Lord speaks, and Moses listens. The people had been at Sinai for nearly a year, where they received the law and built the tabernacle. Now God commands that the men fit for war be counted, as they prepare to set out. The book begins by showing a people organized around the presence of God.

For today: God still speaks to those who seek him in his Word. Before taking an important step, it is good to stop and listen to him and let him order our lives.
exp.32:24:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Haradah and camped at another place called Makheloth. It is one more stop on the journey through the wilderness.

Moses writes this record at God's command, as Numbers 33:2 recalls. It is a list of the stages of the road from Egypt to near the promised land. For most of these places, such as Haradah and Makheloth, it is not known for certain where they were, and scholars have not been able to locate them with confidence. Even so, they were recorded.

God takes note of every step of your journey, even the stretches that seem routine or unimportant. You can trust that He walks with you through the long and quiet stages, and that none of them is lost before His eyes. Keep walking in faith and gratitude.
exp.30:50:
It says that Moses and the priest Eleazar received the gold that the commanders of the army brought. These were jewels already crafted: the word "jewels" refers to valuable objects, and "wrought" means they were already made, not raw gold.

The captains of Israel had counted their soldiers after the war against Midian, and not one was missing. Grateful, they offered to the LORD part of the spoil as an act of thanks for having been kept safe. Moses and Eleazar, as civil and religious leaders, received the offering. Afterward it was weighed: about sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels.

For today: when God delivers us or cares for us, a healthy response is concrete gratitude. We can give generously from what we have, and do so in an orderly and transparent way, as here, where everything was handed to the responsible leaders and was counted clearly.
exp.17:5:
God tells Aaron that he himself chose the Levites, his relatives, from among all Israel. He gave them as a gift to help Aaron and his sons. Their task was to serve in the tent of meeting, the tent where God dwelt among his people. The word "to" appears here with its modern spelling, meaning the same as the older form.

The Lord speaks to Aaron, the high priest, after the people feared death for coming near the tabernacle. God orders who must care for the sanctuary and who may not come near it. In this way he protects the people from his anger and makes clear that the service is an assignment from him, not something each person decides for himself.

For today: all service to God is a gift and an assignment, not a credit to oneself. If you help in your church, do it with humility and gratitude, seeing those who serve alongside you as a gift of God to you.
exp.23:2:
Balaam begins to speak with a special message, called a "parable" (a solemn saying, almost like a poem or prophecy). He introduces himself as the son of Beor and as the man whose eyes are open, meaning someone to whom God grants the ability to see what others cannot see. Some translators understand "open eyes" as also meaning "clear eyes" or "closed eyes"; the Hebrew is debated.

Balaam is a foreign diviner hired by King Balak to curse Israel. After two attempts, he no longer seeks omens or signs, because he sees that God wants to bless his people. The Spirit of God comes upon him, and what he says is not what Balak expected.

For today: God can speak the truth even through imperfect people, but what matters is that each of us listens to God with sincerity and does not use spiritual things for our own gain. Let us ask him for open eyes to see his work and to obey him.
exp.20:6:
Here the people of Israel acknowledge their wrong. They say "we have sinned," because they spoke against God and against Moses. They ask Moses to pray to the Lord to take away the serpents, and Moses prayed for the people, bearing them no grudge.

The Israelites were traveling through the wilderness, and they complained that God and Moses had brought them out of Egypt to die. They despised the manna, calling it "this light bread." God sent fiery serpents, probably because of their painful bite, and many died. Now the people speak with repentance and seek an intercessor.

For today: when we honestly acknowledge our sin, God hears us. Let us speak with Him without excuses, and also pray for those who have offended us, as Moses did.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that God gives Aaron and his sons, the priests, a share of the most holy offerings the people brought. It concerns what was not burned completely on the altar: the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. The phrase "reserved from the fire" means these were set apart from what was burned. The word "sin offering" refers to the sacrifice made to cover a wrong. "Most holy" means it could only be handled with great reverence.

Here the LORD speaks to Aaron, after the people had complained about the danger of approaching the sanctuary. God commands that the Levites care for the sanctuary and provides for the priests, who received no inheritance of land.

For today: God cares for those who serve others. We can generously support those who devote themselves to teaching and serving in the church, and treat with respect what is dedicated to God.
exp.34:21:
This verse speaks of someone who kills another person without meaning to. So the law makes a distinction: if someone pushed another person or threw an object at him without malice or any plan, he is not a murderer.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to Israel, before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge are established, where a person who killed without intention could flee. There the assembly examined the case, so that family vengeance would not fall on an innocent person as though he were a murderer.

Today we learn that God looks at the heart and the intentions, not only at the deeds. Before judging someone who has hurt us, let us ask, with justice and mercy, whether it was an accident or wickedness. And let us seek the truth before we condemn.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses. It is an opening phrase: what follows is not Moses' own idea, but an instruction he was to pass on to the people.

Here the one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. Israel was camped in the desert, and the tabernacle, where God dwelt in the midst of the people, stood at the center. The commands that follow about cleanliness and purity remind us that the presence of God is holy and that the people were to take care to honor it.

For today: before asking anything of God, prepare yourself to listen. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible carefully, ready to obey what it shows you, because God continues to speak to his people through his Word.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that the group from the tribe of Benjamin had 35,400 men counted. "Host" means army, and "those that were numbered" are the men who were recorded in the census. They were men twenty years old and up, fit for war.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for arranging the camp of Israel around the tabernacle. Benjamin camped beside Ephraim and Manasseh, on the west side. If we add the three figures together, they give the 108,100 of the next verse. God wanted order, and his presence to be at the center.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds, but people with a place and a purpose. Ask yourself what your place is in your family and in your church, and fulfill your part there faithfully and without comparing yourself to others.
exp.20:19:
This verse continues to list the stopping places of Israel in the wilderness. From Bamoth they came to the valley that lies in the country of Moab, and then to the top of Pisgah, a high mountain that looks out toward Jeshimon, that is, the desert region. The phrase "looks toward" means that it stands facing that place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, noting the route of the people, almost like a travel diary. It comes right after a song about the well that God gave them. This takes place toward the end of the years in the desert, as Israel draws near to the promised land. Some of the exact places cannot be located with certainty today.

For today: God accompanies every stage of the journey, including those that seem like ordinary transfers. Remember with gratitude where you have seen his care, and keep moving forward with confidence, one step at a time.
exp.32:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Tarah and camped at another place called Mithcah. "Removed" means "having set out," and "pitched" means "camped" or "settled for a time." It is one more of the stops in the desert.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, and Numbers 33 says that Moses wrote these stages by God's command. It is a summary of the journey from Egypt to the promised land. It is not known with certainty where Tarah and Mithcah were today, and scholars do not agree. The list serves to remind us that God guided his people step by step, over years.

Today: sometimes our life seems like a list of places we pass through, with not much to stand out. This verse reminds us that God sees and counts every stage. Trust that he accompanies you also in ordinary days and in long waits, and move forward faithfully one step at a time.
exp.21:33:
Balaam acknowledges before the angel of the Lord that he has sinned. He says he did not know that the angel was standing in the way against him. Then he offers to turn back home if it is displeasing to God that he continue. "If it displeases you" means "if you do not agree with my journey."

Balaam speaks as a diviner who was traveling with the princes of Moab to meet Balak. The angel had just told him that his path was perverse and that his donkey had saved his life. Balaam could not see the angel, but his donkey could. His confession sounds late, and some think it was more fear than sincere repentance. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

Today we can learn to listen to God before He corrects us harshly. Ask Him to show you whether your path pleases Him, and obey Him with a sincere heart, not only out of fear.
exp.24:16:
It says that God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies and to strike them. "Harass" means to trouble or treat as an adversary. The phrase "will strike" means "will beat" or "will defeat." It is an order addressed to the whole people.

The LORD speaks to Moses just after Israel fell into idolatry and immorality at Peor. According to the passage, women of Moab and Midian enticed them to worship Baal of Peor. Cozbi, a Midianite princess, died in that episode. God explains that the Midianites deceived Israel with their wiles, that is, with their traps or schemes. It is a command given in a specific moment of history.

For today: sin rarely comes head-on, but disguised as friendship or as something attractive. We can ask God for wisdom to recognize the influences that pull us away from Him and to set firm boundaries in time.
exp.17:23:
It says that God gave the Levites the tithes of Israel as their inheritance. The people brought those tithes to the Lord as an offering. That is why God told them they would not receive land among the other tribes. The word "inheritance" here means a share or possession. The word "offering" in this verse refers to something set apart for God.

The Lord is speaking to Moses. The Levites were in charge of the service of the tabernacle, and the people were not to come near its holy objects. Since they would have no land to farm, God provided for them through the tithes. In this way they could devote themselves fully to their work.

For today: We can support with generosity and good order those who serve the church full time. We can also trust that God cares for those who give themselves to his service, even when they have little.
exp.5:24:
This verse is part of the priestly blessing. It asks that the Lord "make his face shine upon thee," that is, that he look on you with favor and closeness, like someone smiling at a person they love. "Be gracious unto thee" means that God shows you compassion and favor, even though you do not deserve it.

God himself speaks to Moses and tells him to say to Aaron and his sons, the priests, how they are to bless the people. The words were not theirs; God placed them on their lips. In this way the people knew that the blessing came from the Lord, who declares that his name would be put upon Israel.

For today: when you feel guilty or far from God, remember that his desire is to look on you with kindness. You can draw near to him trusting in his mercy, and you can also bless others by asking that same grace for them.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that the tribe of Judah set out first. The "standard" was the banner that identified a group of tribes, and the "divisions" were its organized companies. Nahshon, son of Amminadab, was the leader of that whole army.

The people were leaving the Sinai desert for the first time, after almost a year there. This is not a speaking character: it is the narrator of the book, who tells how Israel advanced following the cloud and the command of the LORD given through Moses. The order stands out: each tribe had its place and its leader. Judah went at the front, though the Bible does not explain here any further reason.

For today: God is a God of order and of guidance. Before moving forward, he seeks his direction, and serve gladly in the place that is yours, whether at the front or at the back, because everyone is needed.
exp.20:5:
This verse tells that God sent serpents among the people of Israel. The bites were so severe that many people died. The word "fiery" probably describes the burning pain of the venom, though some think it refers to how the serpents looked.

The people were crossing the desert, tired and discouraged. They had spoken against God and against Moses, complaining that there was no bread and no water, and they despised the manna. The narrator presents the serpents as a response to that rebellion. Afterward the people acknowledge their sin, and God provides a way of healing.

When we are tired, it is easy to complain and forget what God has already given us. This passage invites us to be thankful, and to return quickly to God with humility when we go wrong, trusting that He offers forgiveness and a way out.
exp.6:43:
Eliasaf, the leader of the tribe of Gad, brought a golden dish weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to the fragrant offering that was burned in the sanctuary. A shekel was a unit of weight, and the "dish" was rather a small container or cup for the incense.

No one speaks in this verse; it is Moses' account of the offerings of each tribe for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Each leader presented exactly the same offering, one per day, over twelve days. This is the sixth day. The repetition shows that each tribe had the same value before God.

For today: God values each person's offering without comparison. Give joyfully what you have, whether much or little, and do not expect applause. What matters is a heart willing to honor him.
exp.5:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses. With this statement a new instruction begins, which is developed in the verses that follow. The phrase "spake unto Moses, saying" shows that what follows is not Moses' own idea, but a message he was to pass on to the people.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. Next, God gives rules about the vow of separation, a way of dedicating oneself to the Lord for a period of time, open to both men and women. The word for this vow comes from a Hebrew term connected with being set apart or consecrated. The text does not explain here why it begins this way; it simply introduces the law.

For today: before looking for ways to serve God, it is good to listen to what He says. Set aside a moment to read the Bible carefully and ask Him to show you how to live set apart for Him.
exp.17:15:
This verse says that when a firstborn son was one month old, his parents had to pay for his redemption. The price was five shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. A small unit of weight, called a gerah in Hebrew, was a light measure, and twenty of them made up one shekel. "Redeem" here means paying so that the child was freed from service to the sanctuary.

God speaks to Aaron, the priest, and explains which part of the offerings belongs to him and his family, because the Levites did not receive land. The firstborn belonged to God from the time Israel left Egypt, and the redemption payment was a reminder of that deliverance. The Levites were set apart to serve in their place. The money helped support the priests.

For today: everything we have is a gift from God. We can give him our first and best with gratitude, and generously support those who serve in the church.
exp.30:9:
This verse tells that the Israelites burned all the cities, villages and fortified places of the Midianites. "Burned" here means set completely on fire, and the destruction was total, leaving nothing of their settlements standing.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. God had commanded this action against Midian because their women had led Israel into idolatry and immorality at Peor (Numbers 25 and 31:1-3). It is a judgment that belongs to a unique moment in Israel's history. Christians interpret it in different ways, but almost all agree that it is not a model for justifying violence today.

For today: this passage reminds us how serious sin is and how one bad influence can pull many people along with it. Guard your friendships and your habits, and remove from your life whatever separates you from God.
exp.25:25:
This verse lists the clans of the tribe of Zebulun, one of the sons of Jacob. It names three families descended from his sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. The ending "-ites" simply marks each one as the descendants of that man. "Counted" refers to the men recorded in the census.

God speaks through Moses and the priest Eleazar. After the plague in the wilderness, a second census is taken to count the men fit for war and to divide the promised land according to the size of each tribe. The verses that follow give the total for Zebulun: sixty thousand five hundred.

For today: God knows people by name and does not see them as a faceless crowd. Remember that you are valuable to Him, and in the same way, learn to value those who go unnoticed around you, especially in your family and your church.
exp.9:32:
The people set out from Mount Sinai and traveled for three days. The ark of the covenant (the sacred chest that represented God's presence and his agreement with Israel) went ahead of them, searching out a place where they could rest. Here the verse reads simply "went before them."

The narrator describes how Israel moved forward. Just before this, Moses asked Hobab, a relative by marriage who knew the desert, to travel with them as a guide. Some think the ark literally led the way, while others take it as a way of saying that God was directing them, along with the cloud mentioned in the next verse.

Today we can learn that God not only commands us to walk, but goes before us. Even when you cannot see the whole road, you can take the next step, trusting that he is already preparing a place of rest for you.
exp.14:28:
This verse says that the same law applies to the native-born Israelite and to the foreigner who lives among them. If someone sins "through ignorance," meaning unintentionally or by mistake, the way to be forgiven is the same for everyone. The word "native" refers to someone born in the land, and the "stranger" is the foreigner who lives there.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people, who are now close to the promised land. He explains how to deal with sins committed without intention, through an offering and the priest's atonement. Then he contrasts this with sin committed "with a high hand," that is, with open rebellion and deliberate contempt toward God.

For today: God offers forgiveness to everyone equally, without favoritism. If you fail without meaning to, turn to Him quickly and with humility. And do not play with sin, because a rebellious heart turns away from His grace.
exp.22:19:
This verse says that Balaam received the command to bless Israel, and that God has already blessed. The phrase that means "I have received a blessing" is rendered in this verse as "I have received commandment to bless," so the comment is rewritten here to match that wording: Balaam was given a command to bless. The word that means to undo or take back is rendered in this verse as "reverse," meaning to cancel it or turn it back. Balaam admits that he cannot change what God has decided.

The speaker is Balaam, a foreign prophet. Balak, king of Moab, was paying him to curse Israel. But God allowed him to say only what God wanted. That is why Balaam pronounces a blessing instead of a curse. The words before this verse remind us that God does not lie or change his mind the way people do.

For today: if you are a child of God, no negative word, pressure, or threat can undo what he has promised. Trust his faithfulness, even when you feel weak or criticized, and live thankful and obedient.
exp.15:24:
Moses rose up and went personally to find Dathan and Abiram, two men who had rebelled against him. The elders of Israel, that is, the leaders of the people, went along with him.

Dathan and Abiram, together with Korah, had challenged the authority that God had given to Moses and Aaron. God had commanded Moses to warn the people to move away from them. Moses did not send others: he himself went to the rebels, and the leaders went with him. Earlier he had summoned them and they had refused to come (v. 12).

When there is conflict, it is not always healthy to avoid it or to speak behind people's backs. Moses faced the situation directly and acted with courage, and he sought the support of trustworthy leaders. Let us ask God for wisdom to face problems with truth, humility and good witness.
exp.0:21:
This verse begins to count the tribe of Simeon, one of the sons of Jacob. Each man is recorded by name, according to his family and his father's house. Only males from twenty years old and upward who were able to go to war are included, that is, those who could serve in the army. The phrase "by their polls" means one by one, person by person.

God speaks to Moses in the Sinai desert and commands him to take this census of all Israel, tribe by tribe. The people had just come out of Egypt and were preparing to organize themselves and advance toward the promised land. The result for Simeon appears in the following verse: 59,300 men.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass; he knows each one by name. You can trust that you also matter to him, and that you have a place and a service within his family, the church.
exp.7:10:
Aaron will present the Levites before the Lord as an offering from the children of Israel. The word "offer" here means "present" or "dedicate," like someone handing something over to God with open hands. The result is that the Levites will serve in the ministry of the Lord, that is, in the work of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for setting apart the tribe of Levi. They would be the ones to take the place of Israel's firstborn, who belonged to God. The people would lay their hands on them, and in this way the Levites would represent the people in the service of God. Some scholars see in this act an identification or a symbolic giving over.

Today we can remember that serving God is a giving of oneself, not just a task. There are people who serve in the church quietly, out of sight; we can pray for them, support them, and also offer our time and our abilities with joy.
exp.31:6:
Moses asks the tribes of Gad and Reuben why they are discouraging the rest of the Israelites.

Moses, the leader of Israel, is speaking. Gad and Reuben had a large number of livestock, and they liked the lands east of the Jordan, so they asked to settle there. Moses reminds them what happened at Kadesh-barnea: when the spies spread fear, the people refused to go in, and that whole generation suffered the consequences.

For today: our decisions also affect others. Before choosing what suits us, let us ask whether our example encourages others to keep trusting God or discourages them.
exp.28:9:
This verse gives a precise measure: for each of the seven lambs, one tenth, that is, one tenth of an ephah of fine flour (very fine flour) mixed with oil. It was the grain offering that accompanied the animal burned on the altar.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, in the final days of the wilderness. Here the offerings for the day of trumpets are detailed, the first day of the seventh month, a festival of rest and worship. Nothing was left to improvisation: God showed how to draw near to him with order and reverence.

For today: come to God with intention and not out of habit. Just as Israel offered its best, you can give him your time, your attention and your gratitude without offering leftovers. Today, in Christ, we no longer bring lambs, but we do bring a sincere heart.
exp.31:4:
What it says: The tribes of Reuben and Gad ask Moses to give them that land east of the Jordan as their own property. "If we have found grace in your sight" is a respectful way of saying "if it seems good to you." The phrase "your servants" here refers to themselves, speaking with humility. "Possession" means a permanent holding. They ask not to cross the Jordan River.

Context: The speakers are the sons of Reuben and Gad, who had large herds of livestock. They saw that the lands already conquered were good for pasture. Moses reacts with concern, since he feared their request would discourage the rest of Israel and make it seem they wanted to avoid the war for the promised land. Later an agreement is reached: they would help conquer Canaan.

For today: Before we pursue what suits us, let us think about how it affects others. Our decisions, even good ones, should consider the good of the community and our commitments to it.
exp.20:4:
The people of Israel spoke against God and against Moses. They complained that they had been brought up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness. They said there was no bread and no water, and that they were sick of this light bread. That phrase refers to the manna, the food God gave them each day. Their word for it describes disgust or weariness.

The speakers are the people, and they are discouraged. They had just received a victory from God over the Canaanites. However, the journey became long, they had to go around the land of Edom, and their spirits sank. Their complaint ended up being against God himself. Afterward they acknowledged their sin and asked for help.

For today: when we are tired or discouraged, let us not forget what God has already done for us. Instead of complaining, we can thank him for what he gives us and bring our need to him with humility and trust.
exp.33:17:
It says that God orders Moses to choose one leader from each tribe of Israel. A "prince" here is a chief or head of his tribe. These men would help divide the promised land among the families.

The Lord speaks to Moses near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering Canaan. He had already appointed Eleazar the priest and Joshua as the main officers. Now he adds one representative per tribe, so that the division would be orderly and fair, and no one would feel they had been overlooked.

For today: God cares about order and justice, and he often spreads responsibility among several people. If you lead in your family, church, or workplace, try to share important decisions and listen to others, so that you act with transparency.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel departed from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-parez. "Departed" means they broke camp and moved on, and "camped" means they set up their tents to stay for a while. It is one more of the stopping places in the wilderness.

Moses writes this record at God's command, as the beginning of the chapter says. It is a list of the stages of the journey from Egypt to the promised land. It is not known with certainty where each place was, and scholars do not agree on where Rithmah or Rimmon-parez was located. What matters is that the journey was remembered step by step.

For today: God takes note of every stage of your path, even those that seem ordinary or meaningless. If today you are in a time of waiting or routine, trust that he is with you and that no stopping place is forgotten by him.
exp.6:52:
This verse ends the list of what Elishama, leader of the tribe of Ephraim, brought to the altar. For the peace offering, which was a meal of thanksgiving and fellowship with God, he brought two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of the first year. The word "was" appears in the older spelling, and "offering" is what is given to God.

Moses is recording how each leader of Israel presented his gift, one day after another, when the tabernacle was dedicated. Each tribe had its own day and its turn, and all of them brought the same things. In this way it is shown that every tribe was important before God.

Today we can learn that God values sincere and steady giving. Ask yourself what you can offer him with gratitude: your time, your talents, or your resources. Do it with joy, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.18:11:
This verse speaks of a person who had become unclean by touching a dead body. They had to be sprinkled with the water of purification (made with the ashes of the red heifer) on the third day and again on the seventh day, and then they were clean. The word "if" in the verse marks the condition: if they skipped the third day, the seventh day no longer made them clean.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron so that they may instruct Israel. Death made a person unclean, and whoever touched it could not come near the tabernacle, where God dwelt with his people. This rite gave a clear way back into fellowship. Many see in it a picture of the cleansing God gives, though the text itself focuses on the law of purification.

For today: God offers a way to be clean, but he expects us to follow it with obedience. Let us not put off drawing near to him in repentance; let us do it sincerely and in time.
exp.5:2:
It says that whoever made the Nazirite vow had to separate himself completely from everything that comes from the vine: wine, cider (a fermented drink, not necessarily made from apples), vinegar made from them, grape juice, and also fresh grapes or raisins. "Liquor of grapes" refers to any drink prepared from grapes.

God speaks, giving Moses instructions for the people. Men and women could make this vow voluntarily and for a limited time, to dedicate themselves to the LORD. Giving up the vine was a visible sign of consecration. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact reason for such a broad prohibition; it is thought to have expressed a total separation from the ordinary and from normal pleasures.

For today: dedicating ourselves to God sometimes means willingly giving up something good so that we make more room for Him. We can ask ourselves what thing, even a legitimate one, distracts us, and set it aside for a time with prayer and sincerity, not out of pride.
exp.30:29:
From the half that fell to the people as their share of the spoil, Moses was to take one portion out of every fifty: persons, cattle, donkeys, sheep and goats, that is, every kind of animal. That portion was given to the Levites, who were appointed to care for the tabernacle, the holy tent where God was present among his people.

God speaks to Moses after the war against Midian. He had already commanded that an offering be given to Eleazar the priest, taken from the portion of the soldiers. Here a larger share is required from the rest of the people, and the Levites, who received no land as an inheritance, were supported in this way.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and invites us to share what we have received. We can give generously to support those who serve in our church.
exp.30:48:
The army's commanders tell Moses that they counted all the soldiers who were under their command, and not one of them was missing. Their report is that they took the count of the men. In other words, every one of them came back alive from the battle.

The commanders of thousands and of hundreds are speaking, that is, the officers of the Israelite army that had fought against Midian. After the war and the division of the plunder, they take a count and present the report to Moses. Noticing that not one had died, they respond with an offering of gold to the LORD. The interpreters do not fully agree on the exact meaning of that offering, but it is understood as an act of gratitude and recognition for the lives preserved.

For today: When we look back over our lives and see that God has cared for us, the healthiest response is concrete gratitude. Take a moment to acknowledge his care and give him something of what you have: your time, help to others, or an offering.
exp.22:4:
It says that God himself gave Balaam the message he was to speak. "The Lord put a word in Balaam's mouth" means that God told him what to say, and not what Balaam or the king wanted. Then God orders him to return to Balak.

Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam prepared seven altars and offerings, and went off by himself to wait for God. Here God takes control: although Balaam was a divided man, he could only say what God gave him. Afterward he returns and delivers his message, which will not be a curse.

For today: our words matter, and we cannot always manipulate what God has decided. We can ask him to guide what we say, so that we speak truthfully and bless, instead of saying what others want to hear because of pressure or convenience.
exp.25:15:
This verse names two sons of Gad, Ozni and Eri, and says that from each one came a family: the Oznites and the Erites. In Genesis 46:16, Ozni appears as "Ezbon," a variant of the name that is explained in several ways.

Here the narrator speaks, and Moses acts under God's command. Israel is on the plains of Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. A second census is taken, counting the men able to go to war, and it serves to divide the promised land among each tribe and family.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. He names each family, even the little-known ones. You can rest in the knowledge that your name and your life matter to him. You can also value those who go unnoticed in your church or family, and give them a place.
exp.22:25:
Balaam reminds Balak that he had already told him: he can only do what the Lord directs him to do. The old words "á" mean "to", and "tengo de hacer" means "must do" or "have to do". Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. But on two occasions God caused him to bless the people instead. Frustrated, Balak asked him to neither curse nor bless. Balaam answers that he has no control over his words, since they depend on what God puts in his mouth. Later the Bible shows that his heart was not entirely upright, but here he acknowledges God's authority.

For today: God can speak with clarity even when the pressure of others pushes us to say what they want to hear. We can ask him for courage to be faithful to his truth, without exchanging it to please people or for convenience.
exp.1:32:
This verse says that the Levites were not included in the census of the other Israelites, because God himself commanded it to Moses. "But" is the meaning of the quoted word, and "counted" means registered for the army. The Levites were one of the tribes of Israel, but they were set apart.

Here the narrator closes the census of the twelve tribes that camped around the tabernacle. There had been 603,550 men counted as fit for war. According to Numbers 1:49-53, God set the Levites apart to care for, take down, carry, and guard the tabernacle, and for that reason they were not part of the army. Their place was holy service.

For today: God does not give everyone the same task, but every task from him has value. Accept with joy the place where he has put you, without comparing yourself to others, and serve faithfully there.
exp.30:46:
This verse tells how Moses set aside a share of the spoils of war against Midian. From the half that went to the people, he took one portion out of every fifty, both of people and of animals, and gave them to the Levites, who were in charge of the tabernacle. Everything was done just as God had commanded him.

Here the narrator of the book is recounting what Moses did. Earlier, God had commanded that the spoils be divided between the soldiers and the rest of the people, and that a part be set apart for the priesthood and the Levites. This portion for the Levites, who did not receive land as an inheritance, ensured their support while they served God.

For today: to support with generosity and order those who serve in the church or in ministry, without neglecting them, and to do so with obedience and gratitude, recognizing that everything we have comes from God.
exp.29:6:
This verse begins to speak of another case: a woman who is already married and makes a vow, that is, a solemn promise to God. The verse's own wording for "but" and "and" and "or" is not needed here, and the phrase about binding her soul simply means committing herself seriously to what she has said.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the message on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. In that time, vows were taken very seriously. These rules explain how responsibility worked within the family, first with the father and then with the husband. Some scholars see here a protection of the order of the household; others note that it also shows care and forgiveness toward the woman.

For today: think carefully before promising something to God or to others, and when you have a family, talk with them about important decisions. That way your words will be sincere and wise.
exp.29:7:
It says that if a married woman made a vow, and her husband heard of it and said nothing, that vow stood firm. Keeping silent without objecting is what the wording describes, and the vow was made in earnest before God.

Moses passes on this instruction from God to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. At that time the household operated under the authority of the father or husband, and this law regulated the vows made to God. Its purpose was to keep order in the home and to take promises seriously. The verses that follow show that the husband could cancel the vow on the same day he learned of it.

Today we can learn that our promises to God are serious. Before promising something, it is wise to think it through and, if we are married, to talk it over with our spouse, so that there is unity and no one promises lightly.
exp.25:16:
This verse continues the list of the families of the tribe of Gad. Here two more sons of Gad appear: Arod (elsewhere called Arodi) and Areli. From each one came a clan that carries his name with an ending, so that the clans are called Arodites and Arelites, meaning "the descendants of" that man.

God, through Moses and the priest Eleazar, commands that a new count of the people be made. About forty years have passed in the desert, and the previous generation has died. The men able to go to war are counted, and the clans are also recorded, since they would serve to divide the promised land.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every name matters, even though almost no one today knows Arod or Areli. If you sometimes feel small or overlooked, remember that God knows you and keeps you in mind.
exp.10:12:
Moses asks God where he is supposed to get meat to give to all these people. The people weep before him and say: "Give us flesh, that we may eat." The comment on the wording of the older text about the old spelling and the phrase meaning is not needed for this reader, so it is left out.

Moses speaks here as a man worn out. The people of Israel were traveling through the desert and grew tired of eating only manna. Moses feels that God has placed a burden on him that is far too heavy. He compares himself to a mother who has to carry a baby, and he feels that he cannot bear everything. Soon after, he tells God that he cannot carry them alone.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by the needs of others, do not keep it to yourself. Moses was honest with God and spoke to him about his weariness. Bring your burden to him in prayer, and also seek help from other people, because we were not made to carry everything alone.
exp.27:24:
This verse says that on the seventh day of the feast, the people were to gather for a holy convocation, that is, a special assembly set apart for God. They were also not to do any servile work, which means the heavy labor of everyday life, the kind done to earn a living.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. Here the offerings and feasts of the year are explained. This verse closes the week of the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread, where the last day was a special day of rest and worship.

For today: set aside a time in your week to pause, rest from anxious striving, and gather with others to worship God. Let your rest be more than a pause; let it be a moment to remember that everything you have comes from Him.
exp.0:36:
This verse gives the result of the census of the tribe of Benjamin: 35,400 men twenty years old or more who were able to go to war. The phrase "those numbered of them" means "those who were registered." "According to the count of the names" means that each man was recorded by his name.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commanded him to count the people of Israel, tribe by tribe, with the help of one leader from each tribe. The census served to organize the camp and the army. This figure is one of those the book records one by one.

For today: God does not see anonymous crowds, but people with names. Each one counts for Him and has a place among his people. Today you can remember that you matter to God, and also value each person in your church or your family, leaving no one forgotten.
exp.12:17:
Moses sent the twelve men to explore the land of Canaan. He gave them directions: go up from the south, through the region of the Negev, and reach the mountainous area. To "spy out" means to explore and observe carefully. "The south" is the direction meant by the southern side.

Moses speaks here to the people of Israel, who were in the wilderness, near the land God had promised them. The scouts were to bring back information about the land and its inhabitants. The passage also notes that Moses changed the name of Hoshea to Joshua, a detail that highlights the man who would later lead the people.

Today we can learn that trusting God does not keep us from planning wisely. Before making an important decision, it is wise to observe, ask questions, and prepare well, but without letting fear overshadow God's promises.
exp.1:28:
This verse says that the tribe of Naphtali also camps in this group, and that its leader, or captain, is Ahira, son of Enan. The word "captain" refers to the prince or person in charge of the tribe. It is part of a list that names each leader.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and gives them instructions for arranging the camp of Israel. Each tribe had a place and a banner. Naphtali camped to the north, next to Dan and Asher. The numbers that follow count the men fit for the army. The order shows that God guided his people with care.

For today: God knows people by name and gives them a place. If you feel unimportant, remember that he values faithful service, even when it is quiet. Ask him where he wants you to serve today.
exp.18:18:
This verse says that a clean person was to sprinkle the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day. At the end of the seventh day, the person being purified would wash his clothes and bathe in water. That same evening he would be clean. To "sprinkle" means to splash water on someone, and "unclean" means ritually impure.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. Someone who had touched a dead body became impure and could not approach the tabernacle. To return to the community, water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer was used. It was an orderly process with set times, which showed the seriousness of death and the holiness of God.

For today: many Christians see in this a shadow of the cleansing God gives through Christ (Hebrews 9:13-14). If you carry guilt or moral stain, you do not have to cleanse yourself alone. Come to God with sincerity, confess, and receive his forgiveness.
exp.19:1:
This verse tells us that in the wilderness of Zin there was no water for the whole people. So the people gathered together against Moses and Aaron, that is, they came together to complain to them. The word "congregation" refers to the people of Israel assembled together.

The narrator reports that Israel was camped at Kadesh, where Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, had just died. The people had a real need: without water neither they nor their animals could survive. But their response was to complain against their leaders, and in the verses that follow they even wish they had died earlier. Moses and Aaron were in mourning and were also carrying this pressure.

For today: when something important is lacking, we can bring our need to God honestly before blaming others. Asking him with trust is better than letting complaint harden the heart.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that God's cloud was always over the tabernacle. By day it appeared as a cloud covering it, and by night it had the appearance of fire.

According to tradition, the author of the book recounts what Moses recorded about the people of Israel in the wilderness. After the tabernacle was set up, God showed his presence with this cloud and this fire. The passage that follows explains that when the cloud moved, the people walked, and when it stopped, they camped. In this way God guided them day and night.

God does not leave his people without direction. Today we do not see a cloud, but we can seek his guidance in prayer, in his Word, and in wise counsel. Let us learn to wait when he stops and to move forward when he opens the way.
exp.32:39:
This verse says that the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the south of the land of Canaan, learned that the Israelites were drawing near. The phrase "at noon" is an old way of saying "to the south." The phrase "heard of their coming" means that the news of their arrival reached him.

Here the narrator speaks, noting each stop on Israel's journey through the wilderness. This detail appears right after the death of Aaron, and it is similar to the account in Numbers 21:1-3, where Arad attacks Israel. Some scholars think it is a memory of the same episode; others believe it is only a brief mention. It cannot be said for certain which explanation is correct.

For today: moments of grief or change often come with new pressures. Even so, God did not abandon his people. When you face losses and challenges at the same time, trust that God continues to guide your steps.
exp.22:27:
Verse 28 tells us that Balak took Balaam up to the top of Peor, from where he could look out over the wilderness. The sentence about the word for "wilderness" or "desert" is dropped here, since the reader's verse does not use those words. "Top" is the highest part of a mountain, and the phrase "looketh toward" means that it faces that place directly.

Balak, king of Moab, wanted Balaam to curse Israel. He had already tried this in two places, and God had allowed only blessings. Balaam had just said that he would do only what the LORD told him. Balak, not giving up, looked for a third place, thinking that perhaps God would change his mind.

For today: the will of God cannot be changed by insistence or by changing the setting. Instead of seeking God's approval for what we have already decided, let us ask him to help us want what he wants.
exp.9:26:
This verse says that Ahira, son of Enan, was the leader of the company of the tribe of Naphtali. The word "host" here does not refer to a war, but to the tribe organized in order, like a great division of the people. Naphtali was the last tribe in the line of march.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, traditionally understood to be Moses. Israel was just leaving Sinai toward the promised land, and the text lists the order of march in detail. Each tribe had its place and a named leader. Naphtali went at the end, with Dan and Asher, guarding the rear of the people.

For today: God notices the service that seems small or hidden. Ahira does not hold a famous place, but his name was written down. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, even when no one applauds you.
exp.11:10:
Aaron speaks to Moses in great distress. He calls him "my lord," which is an important change, and he begs that God not count this sin against them. He admits that they acted foolishly, that is, without thinking clearly, and he confesses: "we have sinned."

Miriam and Aaron had criticized Moses, and God confronted them in anger. When the cloud lifted, Miriam was left with a serious skin disease, described in this translation as a leprosy, white as snow. Aaron, frightened, humbles himself before the brother he had earlier criticized and asks for mercy for both of them. Right away Moses intercedes for Miriam.

When we humbly admit that we were wrong, the door opens to forgiveness and restoration. If we have criticized or belittled someone, it is worth asking that person's forgiveness without excuses, and praying for them.
exp.32:10:
They left the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin. The words "separated" and "camped" in this passage are unusual, meaning they had set out and pitched their camp. This Sin is not the wilderness of Sinai, even though the two names look alike.

Moses writes here, at God's command, the list of the stages of the journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab (Numbers 33:1-2). It is like a travel record that remembers how God led them step by step. According to Exodus 16, in the wilderness of Sin the people complained about having no food, and God gave them manna.

For today: sometimes our life seems like a list of places we pass through, and some of them are hard. Remember that God is present in every stage. Note how He has cared for you along the way, and trust that He will also sustain you on the next stretch.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that the males of the Gershon family, counted from one month old and upward, totaled 7,500. The phrase that means "according to the count" is rendered here simply as "according to the number of," and the phrase meaning "from one month up" is rendered as "from a month old and upward."

Moses records this census at God's command (Numbers 3:14-15). The Levites were set apart to serve in the tabernacle, and so they were counted from the time they were born, not from age twenty as the men who would go to war were. Each family of Levi had its own place and its own task, and the Gershonites were assigned to camp behind the tabernacle, on the west.

For today: God knows and values each person, even the youngest. He also reminds us that no service is small in His eyes. Faithfully do the part that is yours, even when no one notices.
exp.0:7:
This verse is part of a list of leaders. It says that from the tribe of Issachar, Nethaneel, son of Zuar, was chosen to help Moses. He is one more name among the leaders of each tribe of Israel.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, at the beginning of the count of the people. He tells him to count the men fit for war and indicates that one leader from each tribe should accompany him. In this way the people were put in order, and each tribe had someone to represent it. The list continues with other tribes, and in it appear names that are not mentioned again very often.

For today: God knows by name those who serve, even when almost no one notices them. If your service is simple and little seen, it is no less valuable. Serve him faithfully where you are.
exp.0:1:
God tells Moses to take a census of all Israel. A list or count of the people is what is meant here. They were to count all the men, family by family, according to their fathers' households, writing down each name one by one. Counting them person by person is what is meant by the number of their names.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, one year after leaving Egypt. The people already had the law and the tabernacle, and now they were to be organized. According to the verses that follow, the men twenty years old and up who were fit for war were counted. Many understand that it was also preparation for the journey toward the promised land.

For today: God cares about each person, by name and by family. We can imitate him by paying real attention to others: remembering their names, praying for them, and not treating anyone as part of an anonymous crowd.
exp.35:12:
This verse closes the book of Numbers. It says that everything before it is the commandments (orders) and the judgments (fixed rules) that the Lord gave to Israel through Moses. They were given on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, opposite the city of Jericho.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. He sums up what the Lord commanded when the people were about to enter the promised land. The previous chapter tells how the daughters of Zelophehad married within their own tribe, so that the family inheritance would not pass to another tribe. In this way they obeyed what the Lord had commanded.

For today: God speaks to us in plain words, and obeying them matters more than only knowing them. Today you can choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice with faith and simplicity, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.3:45:
This verse begins the final summary of the census of the Levites. It says that all the Levites were counted by Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of Israel, organized by their families and by their fathers' households. "Counted" means registered or numbered. "Leaders" refers to the heads of the tribes.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers summarizes the work done with the three Levite families: Kohath, Gershon, and Merari. Only the men from thirty to fifty years old were counted, those who could serve in the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people. Everything was done according to the command of the LORD, with order and with several people in charge.

God knows each person and gives each one a place in his work. No service is small when it is done in obedience to him. Ask yourself today: what simple task has God placed near you, and how can you do it with faithfulness?
exp.11:1:
Here María and Aarón, brothers of Moisés, ask whether God has spoken only through him, or whether he also speaks through them. The phrase "And the Lord heard it" is the verse's own wording and needs no further explanation.

The passage begins with a complaint from María and Aarón against Moisés because of the Ethiopian woman he had married. Scholars do not agree on a single explanation of who she was. But in verse 2 it appears that the root of the problem is also envy: they wanted the same authority as Moisés. What they say is not entirely false, since both of them had spoken on God's behalf, but they use it to belittle their brother.

For today: before we criticize a leader or a brother, let us examine our hearts. God hears what we say, even in private.
exp.5:16:
At the end of the time of dedication, the Nazirite was to bring a ram as a peace offering to the Lord. Along with the ram came a basket of unleavened bread. The priest also offered the grain offering and the drink offering that were poured out. The peace offering was an offering of thanks and fellowship.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the Nazirite vow, a person who voluntarily set themselves apart for the Lord for a period of time. Here the sacrifices at the close of that vow are described. The peace offering was an offering of gratitude and fellowship, and part of it was shared in a meal before God.

For today: when you finish a season of devotion or service to God, do not close it with pride, but with gratitude. Give thanks to him, share with others what he has given you, and remember that every good thing comes from his hand.
exp.2:28:
The verse says that the families descended from Kohath were to pitch their tents beside the tabernacle, on the south side. The word "southward" in the verse is the direction they were to face, and the sentence that explains an older wording has been removed here because the reader's verse uses "southward" directly. "They shall pitch" means they would set up their camp in that place.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and gives an order for the camp of Israel. The Levites, the tribe set apart for sacred service, surrounded the tabernacle. Each Levite family had its place and its task. The Kohathites were responsible for caring for the most sacred objects: the ark, the table, the lampstand, and the altars.

God cares about order and values every task, whether great or small. Today we can ask ourselves what place and what service he has entrusted to us in our church or family. Carrying it out faithfully and humbly, without comparing ourselves to others, is a way of honoring God.
exp.15:43:
This verse is very brief: it says that God spoke to Moses. It is the introduction to what God will say next. "LORD" is the name of God, and the word "spake" is the old form of "spoke," which in this verse is simply the way the English reads.

The narrator tells us that the people had gathered against Moses and Aaron, accusing them after the rebellion of Korah. Then the glory of God appeared over the tabernacle. Moses and Aaron came before God, and He spoke to them. What follows is a serious announcement of judgment, and it also shows that Moses and Aaron interceded for the people.

For today: when there is conflict and tension, the wisest thing is to draw near to God and listen to Him before we react. He speaks with truth and also gives room for us to intercede for others.
exp.12:27:
The twelve men Moses sent to explore Canaan return and give their report. First they confirm that the land is good: it is a place of rich abundance, a way of saying that it is fruitful and plentiful. As proof, they show the fruit they brought back. Moses and the people would have read the phrase "given the land a good report" as meaning they told them the news, so "they told" the people what they had found.

The explorers speak before Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation, at Kadesh, after forty days of travelling through the land. God had already promised them this land. This first report is true and encouraging, but right after it comes a "but" that fills the people with fear.

For today: thank God gratefully for the good things he gives you, and do not let a fearful "but" erase your trust in his promises.
exp.33:18:
This verse begins the list of the men who would help divide the land of Canaan. The first one named is Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, of the tribe of Judah. He was the representative of his tribe.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. The land had to be divided with order and justice. Eleazar, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe would do that work. Caleb was already known: of the twelve spies, he and Joshua trusted that God would give them the land (Numbers 14).

For today: God often entrusts responsibilities to those who have been faithful over time. Serve God with faith in small things and in difficult ones, even when no one sees you. Your faithfulness today prepares your service tomorrow.
exp.32:3:
This verse says that, while the Israelites were leaving Egypt, the Egyptians were burying their firstborn sons, whom the Lord had struck dead. The old form "Á" is an older spelling of "a", and "judgments on their gods" means that God also showed his power over the Egyptian gods, leaving them without strength.

The author is Moses, who, at God's command, records the stops the people made in the desert. This is the beginning of that list of journeys. Before naming the places, he recalls how it all began: with the Passover and the departure from Egypt. Some scholars think the "gods" refer to the plagues that challenged the Egyptian deities, but the text does not give more details.

For today: God keeps what he promises, and no power can overcome him. If something has you tied down or afraid, remember how God delivered his people. Trust in him and take the next step, even when you cannot see the whole path.
exp.12:24:
