This verse says that the place where the Israelite spies cut a huge cluster of grapes was given the name Eshcol. That name means something like "valley of the cluster." The word for "cut" refers to the spies cutting off the branch with the grapes.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Moses had sent twelve men to explore the land of Canaan, and they brought back some of its fruit to show how good the land was. The name of the place recalled that evidence of the goodness of the land God had promised. Soon after, most of the group gave a report full of fear.

For today: God often gives us signs of his goodness along the way. When we face fears or doubts, it is worth pausing to remember what he has already done for us, and to trust that he will keep what he has promised.
exp.29:12:
It says that if a husband, on the same day he hears his wife's vows, cancels them, those vows lose their force. "Vows" are promises made to God, and "a binding oath to afflict the soul" is a serious personal commitment. To "cancel" means to make them void. Because the husband canceled them, God forgives the woman and does not hold her guilty for failing to keep them.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes this on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. At that time, a woman lived under the authority of her father or her husband, and that authority could protect her from rash commitments. This law regulates who answers before God for such promises. Some scholars see here protection for the family; others point to the limits of that culture.

For today: let us take seriously what we promise to God and to others, and think before we commit ourselves. If a promise affects the family, let us talk it over together and with humility.
exp.2:5:
God tells Moses to bring the tribe of Levi near and set them before Aaron the priest. Their purpose is that they help him and serve him. "Minister" means to serve or attend to someone in sacred work.

The LORD speaks with Moses. Shortly before this, Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, died for offering strange fire, that is, fire that God had not commanded. Only Eleazar and Ithamar remained as priests. So God organizes the Levites as helpers to Aaron in the tabernacle, so that the service would be done as He directed, and not the way each person saw fit.

For today: serving God includes taking seriously the place He gives us, even if it is a place of help rather than the front row. We can gladly support those who lead in the church, doing with humility and faithfulness what is ours to do.
exp.6:2:
It says that the leaders of the tribes of Israel brought an offering before God: six covered wagons and twelve oxen. Every two leaders gave one wagon, and each leader gave one ox. "Leaders" here means the heads of the tribes. The wagons were probably covered with a canopy or cover; the text gives no further detail.

The narrator tells what happened when Moses finished setting up and dedicating the tabernacle. The leaders wanted to contribute something for the worship. In the verse that follows, God tells Moses to receive these gifts and give them to the Levites, according to their work, since they were the ones who carried the tabernacle.

For today: what we give to God can serve others. Those wagons helped the Levites in their labor. Ask yourself what resources or abilities you have that could support the service in your church or community, and offer them generously and joyfully.
exp.19:19:
Edom again says that Israel will not pass through its land. This time it comes out with a large and strong army to show that it means what it says. The phrase about a strong hand refers to military power. Edom does not only speak; it also positions itself to fight.

Israel is on its way to Canaan and asks Edom for permission to cross by the King's Highway. It promises not to touch the fields and to pay for the water. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a relative of Israel. Even so, it distrusts them and refuses. Israel does not fight but turns away, and then arrives at Mount Hor. The Bible does not fully explain Edom's reasons; it could be fear, pride, or old rivalries.

When someone closes the door on us, even if we have been humble and fair, we do not always have to insist or respond with anger. We can accept the limit, look for another way, and trust that God is still guiding our path.
exp.25:34:
This verse lists the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Joseph. Each clan takes its name from a descendant: Shuthelah, Becher, and Tahan. The ending "-ites" means "descendants of," so the Shuthalhites are the people of the family of Shuthelah. The names are written in an older style.

Moses and the priest Eleazar take a new count of the people of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God had commanded that the fighting men be counted before entering the promised land. These lists would also serve to divide the land according to the size of each family.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name. No one is anonymous to him. Today you can rest in the knowledge that God sees you, and you can also value those who seem "unseen" around you, giving them your attention and respect.
exp.33:20:
This verse names Elidad, son of Chislon, as the representative of the tribe of Benjamin. He was one of the men chosen, one from each tribe, to help divide the land of Canaan. Here he is described as a man of standing because he was a recognized leader among his people.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. He commands that Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe divide the inheritance. In this way each family would receive its portion in an orderly and fair way. Nothing more is said about Elidad in this passage, and the Bible gives no further details about him.

For today: God relies on people who serve faithfully, even when almost no one remembers them. Today you can serve with honesty and responsibility in your family, your church, or your work, trusting that God values what you do.
exp.29:1:
Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes of Israel (here "princes" means leaders) and tells them that what he is about to teach is not his own idea, but what the Lord, Jehovah, has commanded.

Moses had already passed on to the people the instructions about the feasts and offerings. Now he addresses the leaders to present the laws about vows, that is, the promises made to God. They were to teach these laws and apply them among their tribes. In many Bibles, this passage appears as Numbers 30:1.

For today: before promising something, think carefully about what you say. If you promise something to God or to another person, try to keep it. Your word reflects your character.
exp.31:31:
What it says: The sons of Gad and Reuben promise to cross the Jordan River armed, before the LORD, to help conquer Canaan. But they ask that their inheritance, that is, the land where they will live, be on the east side of the Jordan. The word "inheritance" means the land one receives as a gift passed down, and "on this side" means "on this side of the river."

Context: These two tribes speak to Moses. They had seen that the lands east of the Jordan were good for their livestock. Moses warned them that they must not leave their brothers alone in the war. They answer with this pledge, and Moses grants them those lands.

For today: A promise is worth more when it is kept by deeds. Before enjoying our blessings, we can ask ourselves how we are helping others who are still struggling, and serve God alongside them.
exp.1:11:
God commands that the tribe of Simeon camp beside the tribe of Reuben, on the south side of the camp. Its leader would be Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai. Here "leader" means the head or prince of the tribe, and "camp beside him" means camp next to him. The verses that follow give the number of its fighting men.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron (Numbers 2:1). Israel is in the wilderness, near Sinai, and God organizes the camp by tribes around the tabernacle. In this way each family knew where it belonged and who led it, and the people moved in good order.

For today: God cares about order and gives each person a place. Look for your place of service in your church or family, and gladly support those who lead you and those who stand beside you.
exp.34:18:
This verse says that the closest relative of the person who was killed had the right to put to death the one who committed the murder, if he came upon him. The murderer is the one who kills another on purpose. The avenger of blood is the relative responsible for seeking justice.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. These laws regulated justice in a society without police or courts like ours today. It applied only when there was a clear intention to kill, because for accidental death there were cities of refuge. Some scholars see here a way of limiting excessive revenge.

For today: God takes human life seriously, because every person is precious to Him. We can reflect that respect by leaving personal revenge behind, seeking justice through lawful and peaceful means, and caring for those around us with our words and attitudes.
exp.20:28:
This is a mocking lament against Moab. "Woe to you" means "what a disaster for you," and "you are undone" means "you have been destroyed." Its sons flee, its daughters are taken captive, and its god Chemosh could not save them.

This song was repeated by the "proverbists," poets who remembered victories. It celebrated that Sihon, king of the Amorites, had defeated Moab. Israel quotes it to show how strong Sihon was. Then the verses that follow tell how God gave Israel the victory over him. No one knows for certain who composed the song.

Today: the kingdoms and things we trust in, money, fame, or power, can fall suddenly. Place your security in the living God, who does not fail.
exp.26:22:
Moses laid his hands on Joshua and gave him a charge, just as the Lord had commanded. The phrase "gave him a charge" means "gave him instructions" or "gave him directions." "By the hand of Moses" means that God spoke through Moses.

Moses knew that he would soon die and asked God to appoint someone to lead the people. God chose Joshua. Moses presented him before the priest Eleazar and before the whole congregation. Laying on of hands was a public gesture of handing over authority and support. The text does not detail what instructions he gave at that moment; other passages, such as Deuteronomy 31, show Moses' words of encouragement to Joshua.

Today we can learn to do things "as the Lord commanded," without shortcuts. If you have some responsibility, prepare and support with humility those who will come after you, and if it falls to you to receive it, do so with respect and dependence on God.
exp.10:28:
Moses answers Joshua with a question: "Are you jealous for my sake?" Then he expresses a wish: that all the people of God were prophets and that God would put his Spirit upon all of them. Joshua is Moses' young assistant, and the word "wish" here expresses a sincere desire.

God had put his Spirit upon seventy elders to help Moses. Eldad and Medad had stayed in the camp, and they also prophesied. Joshua, Moses' young assistant, wanted to stop them, probably to defend his leader's authority. Moses does not feel threatened and rejoices in what God is doing.

For today: let us rejoice when God uses other people, even when they are not from our group or do not follow our ways. Guarding the faith must not turn into guarding our own place. Let us ask for a humble heart, one that celebrates the good that others do for God.
exp.1:29:
This verse gives the number of men from the tribe of Naphtali who could go out to war: fifty-three thousand four hundred. "Host" means an army or an organized company, and "those that were numbered" are the ones who were registered in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and tells them how Israel should camp in the wilderness, tribe by tribe, around the tabernacle. Naphtali camped with Dan and Asher, on the north side, under the banner of Dan. This number is added to the total for the tribe of Dan, and at the end the great total of 603,550 is given.

For today: God knows His people one by one and gives each a place in His plan. No one is a mere number to Him. Today you can serve with joy in the place God has given you, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that the Israelites set out for the first time from Sinai, following the command the Lord gave them through Moses. "Set out" means that they broke camp and began to walk. "According to the commandment of the Lord" means "by the hand of Moses," that is, as the Lord directed.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. Israel had spent nearly a year at the foot of Mount Sinai. Now the cloud, the sign of God's presence, lifted from the tabernacle, and that showed it was time to leave. The verses that follow describe the order of march, beginning with the tribe of Judah.

For today: Israel did not move on impulse or out of habit, but when God directed. We can learn to wait for his guidance in prayer and in his Word, and then to obey with confidence, both when we stay and when we move forward.
exp.2:43:
This verse is only a transitional phrase. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses, and with that it introduces a new instruction. The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to," and "saying" announces what God is about to command next.

Moses had just counted the firstborn males of Israel, from a month old and up, and they came to 22,273. Now God speaks to tell him what to do with that number. The Levites would be set apart for Him in place of the firstborn. Since the firstborn were more numerous than the Levites, a ransom was required for the 273 who were left over.

For today: God does not act blindly, but speaks and guides step by step. Before taking an important step, it is wise to stop and listen to God in His Word and in prayer, and to obey with order and care.
exp.3:33:
This verse says that Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of the people counted the sons of the Kohathites (also spelled Kohath), a group within the tribe of Levi. They were counted by families and by clans, that is, "after their families, and after the house of their fathers."

The passage describes how God organized the service in the tabernacle, the tent where worship took place during the journey through the desert. God commanded that the Levite men from thirty to fifty years old be counted, so that tasks could be assigned to them. The sons of Kohath took charge of the most sacred objects. The text does not explain why that particular age was chosen.

Today, this passage reminds us that in serving God, every person counts and has a place. Ask yourself what simple task you can carry out faithfully in your church or family, even if no one notices it.
exp.17:19:
God tells Aaron, the high priest, that his family will not receive a piece of land of their own when Israel divides the promised land. "Inheritance" means property that is received and passed on to one's children. "Portion" is the share that falls to each person. Instead of land, God himself will be their portion.

The Lord speaks, and he does so after making clear that the priests would live on the offerings and tithes the people brought. The priests and Levites were devoted to the service of the tabernacle, so God sustained them through the generosity of Israel, rather than giving them fields to farm.

For today: we can ask ourselves what truly gives us security. Having possessions is not wrong, but our greatest wealth is knowing God and depending on him. Ask him today to be your portion, and trust in his care.
exp.31:38:
He says that the descendants of Machir, of the tribe of Manasseh, went to the region of Gilead, took it, and drove out the Amorites who lived in that place. The first sentence of the quote is not explained in the verse as written, so I will omit that gloss and simply state the action: they took it and drove out the Amorites.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and part of Manasseh had asked to stay east of the Jordan, because they had a great deal of livestock. Moses agreed, on the condition that they help their brothers conquer the land on the other side. This verse shows Manasseh keeping its part in that new territory.

For today: God often gives us a place or a task, but he expects us to act with faith and effort. Let us ask for his guidance, and then move forward with courage and responsibility in what he has entrusted to us, without simply waiting passively.
exp.3:40:
This verse closes the count of the descendants of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi. It says that the men who served in the tabernacle were numbered, and that Moses and Aaron made this count because the Lord commanded it. "Numbered" means registered or counted. The "tabernacle of the congregation" is the sacred tent where God's presence was, and where the tablets of the law were kept.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The Levites had the task of caring for and carrying the tabernacle. That is why, according to the text, the men from thirty to fifty years of age were registered. The family of Gershon totaled 2,630. Then the account continues with the family of Merari.

For today: God knows and values each person who serves him, even in simple tasks that are seldom seen. Serve with steadiness and order, trusting that your work matters to God.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that the Levite men between thirty and fifty years old were the ones who could enter "the host," that is, join the group assigned to service, to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation. The phrase "of the congregation" points to the tabernacle as the place where the people gathered before God, and the ark held the tablets of the law.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron. He is ordering a count of the sons of Kohath, one of the families of Levi, to assign them their task. They would carry the most holy things when the people broke camp. Why that range of ages was chosen, the Bible does not explain in detail; other passages give different ages, and how to understand this is debated.

For today: serving God is something serious and orderly, not improvised. Ask yourself what specific task God has given you in your church or family, and do it with responsibility, joy and care, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that the Passover lamb was not to be kept until the next day, and that none of its bones were to be broken. Those who celebrated the Passover in the second month were to follow all the rules of the original feast. "Rites" means the instructions or customs set out for the ceremony.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. Some Israelites were unclean because they had touched a dead body, or were away on a journey, and so they could not keep the Passover at the proper time. God gives them a second opportunity a month later, but with the same order and reverence. The New Testament connects the unbroken bone with Jesus (John 19:36).

For today: God gives us opportunities to return to Him, but He expects us to do so with seriousness and obedience. If we have neglected something with God, we can return with sincerity, without excuses, and without putting it off.
exp.34:14:
This verse says that the six cities of refuge would be a protection for the children of Israel, for the stranger who passed through the land, and for the one who lived among them. There, anyone who had killed another person unintentionally could flee. The word "refuge" in the verse means a place of safety and shelter, and "unawares" means by accident, without intent.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before they enter Canaan. He gives them rules so that justice would be applied with care. The avenger of blood was not to kill without a trial the one who caused an accidental death. The verses that follow distinguish this from intentional murder, which did deserve the death penalty.

Today we can learn that God cares for justice and also for mercy. Before judging someone, it is wise to know the facts and the intentions, and to treat everyone equally, whether they are close to us or strangers.
exp.6:83:
This verse sums up what the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel brought when the altar was anointed and dedicated: twelve silver dishes, twelve silver bowls, and twelve gold spoons. The word "princes" here means the heads or leaders of the tribes.

The writer of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, gives a summary after describing, day by day, the offering of each tribe. All of them gave exactly the same. The purpose was to dedicate the altar so that the people could worship God in the tabernacle.

For today: God values everyone's devotion, without comparisons. Each of the leaders gave in an orderly way and with steady faithfulness. We can offer God our time, talents, and resources with gratitude and without competing, knowing that every gift counts.
exp.15:18:
This verse says that Korah gathered the whole congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting, to turn them against Moses and Aaron. Then the glory of the Lord, that is, his bright and majestic presence, appeared to all of them.

Context: here the narrator of the book is speaking. Korah and other leaders rebelled, because they wanted the priesthood even though God had not given it to them. Moses proposed that they bring censers before God so that he would show whom he had chosen. When Korah gathered the people, God answered with his glory, and immediately announced judgment.

For today: when conflicts arise or we feel the urge to criticize those who lead, it is wise to pause and remember that God sees everything. Instead of gathering people to support our complaint, we can pray, examine our hearts, and humbly seek what God wants.
exp.18:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that God (the Lord) spoke to Moses and Aaron, and he was going to give them an instruction. The wording in the verse is in an older form; today we would write it with the plain word "to." The important part comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God himself. He addresses Moses, the leader of the people, and Aaron, the high priest. Israel was in the wilderness, and God was giving rules so that the people could live near his presence. What follows deals with the red heifer (a reddish-colored cow) and the water used for purification after contact with death. The details of its meaning are interpreted in several ways.

Before acting, it is wise to listen to God. Moses and Aaron did not invent the way; they received it from him. Today we can seek his guidance in the Bible and in prayer before we make decisions.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that each Israelite was to camp beside his own banner, according to the insignia of his family's house. All of them were to be set up around the tabernacle of the testimony, the sacred tent where God's presence was. The "ensigns" are the banners or standards. "Pitch" means they would set up their tents.

Here the LORD speaks and gives instructions to Moses and Aaron. The people had already been counted and were in the wilderness, on their way to the promised land. God wanted the camp to be orderly and his presence to be at its center. Scholars disagree about exactly what the banners looked like, because the text does not describe them in detail.

For today: God is a God of order, and he wants to be the center of our lives. We can ask ourselves whether our priorities revolve around him, and seek our place and service within the community of faith.
exp.22:6:
Balaam begins to speak his message, which here means a solemn utterance in the form of a poem. He tells how Balak, king of Moab, had brought him from Aram, from the mountains of the east, to ask him to curse Jacob and to condemn Israel, that is, to pronounce a curse upon them.

The speaker is Balaam, a foreign prophet hired by King Balak. Israel was camped near Moab, and Balak feared the people. But God had just put his word in Balaam's mouth, so what he will say will not be what the king wanted to hear.

For today: no pressure, threat, or hostile word from others can change what God has determined for his children. We can rest in the knowledge that his care is firmer than any attack against us.
exp.9:18:
The verse says that the tribe of Simeon, that is, the descendants of Simeon, marched under Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai, as their leader. Here the word "host" refers to the great division of the tribe, arranged to travel through the wilderness.

This is in the account of when Israel left Mount Sinai, after a year there. Moses received the instructions from God, and the text records the order of march of each tribe along with the name of its leader. Simeon went alongside Reuben and Gad, in the group under Reuben's banner.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds; he knows each person and each task by name. Today you can faithfully fill your place, in your family, your church or your work, even when no one notices, trusting that God does see it.
exp.9:29:
Here Hobab gives a clear no to Moses' invitation. He says he will not go with the people, but will return to his own land and his family.

The phrases "to my land and to my kindred" would appear in the verse above as "to mine own land, and to my kindred." Old spellings aside, the meaning is the same: "land" means his country, and "kindred" means his relatives.

Moses had asked Hobab, his Midianite father-in-law, to travel with them toward the promised land, promising to treat him well. Some scholars debate whether Hobab was Moses' father-in-law or his brother-in-law, because the Hebrew text allows both readings. Hobab answers with his home in mind. The text does not say here whether he later changed his mind.

For today: loving our family and our roots is a good thing, but it is wise to ask God whether He is calling us to something more. Let us pray for wisdom to decide with prayer.
exp.2:17:
This verse names the two sons of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi. They were called Libni and Shimei, and the Gershonite families came from them. The phrase "by their families" means that each son became the head of a family group within the tribe.

Here the narrator of the book tells how Moses organized the Levites, as the LORD had commanded. God had set this tribe apart for service in the tabernacle, and so their families were recorded in order. Next come the lists for Kohath and Merari. Later the text explains what task each family had.

For today: God knows the names of those who serve him, including those in less visible places. If your service seems small or goes unnoticed, remember that God sees it and gives it value. Serve faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not decide on their own when to move. When the cloud lifted from above the tabernacle (the sacred tent where God was present), they gathered everything and set out. And where the cloud stopped, there they settled and pitched camp. "Pitched" means they set up the camp, and "journeyed" means they got moving.

The book of Numbers tells how God guided Israel through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. Here the narrator describes the cloud by day and the appearance of fire by night as a visible sign of the presence and direction of the LORD. The text stresses that every movement was done at the command of the LORD.

For today: let us learn to depend on God in our decisions, whether to move forward or to wait. We can pray, seek his Word and wise counsel, and trust that his timing is good, even when staying still is hard.
exp.33:23:
It says that a leader named Kemuel, son of Shiphtan, was chosen from the tribe of Ephraim. The word "prince" here does not mean a king's son, but a chief or leader of his tribe. The names written in older spellings are today written as Ephraim, Kemuel, and Shiphtan.

God speaks to Moses near the end of the journey through the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He gives a list of one leader per tribe to help Eleazar and Joshua divide the land of Canaan. Ephraim and Manasseh were sons of Joseph, and each received its own tribe.

God attends to details and calls specific people to serve. If today you are given a task that seems small, do it faithfully: God knows your name and your work, even when others do not notice.
exp.31:33:
This verse says that the children of Gad rebuilt or fortified several cities: Dibon, Ataroth, and Aroer. The word "built" here is usually understood to mean rebuilding and fortifying, since these cities already existed. They lay east of the Jordan River, in lands previously taken from the kings Sihon and Og.

The tribes of Gad and Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, asked to settle in that region because it was rich in pasture for their livestock. Moses agreed on the condition that they first help their brothers conquer Canaan. This verse is part of the list of what they did to settle in and protect their families and flocks.

Today we can learn to take careful care of what God entrusts to us: family, work, and home. But we can also learn to first fulfill our commitments to others, serving them before thinking only of our own comfort.
exp.31:32:
This verse tells that Moses gave the tribes of Gad and Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh, the lands east of the Jordan. These were the territories of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and of Og, king of Bashan. "Gave them" means he granted them that land as an inheritance, with its cities and the fields around them.

Moses had asked these tribes to keep their word: to cross over armed with their brothers to help them conquer Canaan. They promised to do so. That is why Moses grants them the land they had asked for, since they had a great deal of livestock. Half of Manasseh appears here suddenly; the text does not explain why, and scholars have commented on it in different ways.

For today: keeping what we promise has value before God and before others. Moreover, our blessings are not only for ourselves; we can use them to serve and help others.
exp.32:21:
This verse says that the people of Israel set out from the place called Rissah and camped at another place called Kehelathah. The word "journeyed" in the verse means "set out," and "pitched" means "camped." It is one more stop on the journey through the desert.

Moses wrote this record, at God's command, of all of Israel's stops from Egypt until they reached the vicinity of the promised land. It is a list of names, and for many of them no one today knows with certainty where they were. Even so, the list shows that God cared for every stage of the way, including the long and seemingly monotonous years.

For today: there are seasons of life that seem to be just one more step, with nothing special about them. God does not forget them. Trust that He accompanies you in the everyday, and keep walking faithfully, one day at a time.
exp.22:9:
Balaam says that the people of Israel are so numerous that no one could count them, as if they were the dust of the earth. The phrase about a fraction of the people probably refers to only a part of the nation, and even that part is too large to be counted.

Balaam is a prophet from outside Israel. King Balak hired him to curse Israel, but God put a blessing in his mouth. This fulfills the promise made to Abraham about a large descendance. Some think his wish to die well is sincere, although his later life shows that he did not follow that path.

Today, we may wish for a good end, but that calls for a faithful life from now on. Admiring righteous people is not enough; we must walk with God every day, and trust that his blessing does not depend on what others say against us.
exp.27:7:
This verse commands that a second lamb be offered at evening, that is, at sundown. It was to be accompanied by the same grain offering and the same drink offering (the wine poured out) used in the morning. The offering burned on the altar is a burnt offering, and "as a sweet aroma" means that it was pleasing to God.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel about the continual burnt offering, the daily offering. Each day began and ended with an offering, to remind the people that their whole lives belonged to God. The phrase about the time of evening is understood in several ways, but it indicates the end of the day.

For today: we can begin and close the day with God. A few minutes of prayer and thanksgiving in the morning and at night can keep our hearts attentive to Him.
exp.14:0:
This verse is a simple introduction. It says that the Lord, that is, God, spoke to Moses. The word "spoke" is not old, but the spelling with the accent mark was the way of writing the word at that time. What follows are the instructions that God wanted Moses to pass on to the people.

Here God is speaking, and Moses is the one who receives the message to carry it to Israel. This happens in the wilderness, after the people had rebelled and refused to enter the promised land. Even so, God speaks to them about the land he would give them. This shows that God remained firm in his promise, despite the people's failure.

Today we can learn that God still speaks and that his promises do not depend on our mistakes. If we have failed, we can listen to him again, open his Word with humility, and trust that he wants to guide us forward.
exp.15:0:
Here begins the story of a rebellion. Korah, who was a Levite, joined with Dathan, Abiram, and On (in other versions, Hon), who were from the tribe of Reuben. The phrase "took men" means they gathered followers. The Hebrew of this phrase is difficult, and some translations understand it differently.

The narrator relates what happened. According to the verses that follow, these men gathered two hundred and fifty leaders and confronted Moses and Aaron. They said that the whole people is holy and that there was no reason for those two to have more authority. The account suggests that there was envy and a desire for power.

For today: we may ask questions and correct mistakes honestly, but it is wise to examine the heart. Before questioning a leader, ask yourself: "Am I seeking the good of everyone, or do I want more recognition?" Humility protects us from causing division.
exp.12:31:
This verse tells that the men who had gone with Caleb to explore the land said: "We are not able to go up against that people, for they are stronger than we are." The word "varones" means men, and "subir contra" means to go up to attack.

The ones speaking are the other explorers, ten of the twelve sent by Moses. Caleb had just encouraged the people to take the land that God had promised them. They, however, looked only at the strength of the inhabitants and forgot God's promises. Then they exaggerated and spread fear among everyone.

For today: when we face a great problem, let us not measure everything only by our own strength. Let us ask God to help us see the situation with faith, remembering what He has said and done, and let us be careful not to spread fear to others with our words.
exp.12:25:
This verse says that the twelve men Moses sent to explore Canaan returned after forty days. The phrase about going to see the land means exploring it, looking at it carefully to learn what it was like.

The narrator tells what happened in the wilderness of Paran. God had allowed Moses to send one leader from each tribe to see the promised land, its people, its cities, and its fruit. They had already cut a large cluster of grapes in the valley of Eshcol. Now they return to Kadesh with their report, and the verses that follow show that the people's reaction was about to split between faith and fear.

For today: before listening to the opinions of others, take time to calmly look at what God has already promised. The facts matter, but faith decides how we interpret them.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the army of the tribe of Reuben, that is, the men counted for war, came to 46,500. The word "host" means the army, and "those that were numbered" are the men who were registered in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about how Israel was to camp in the wilderness, each tribe under its own banner and around the tabernacle. Reuben was on the south side, which here is called the "south." It should be noted that the numbers were given to organize the march and the camp. Some scholars debate how to understand such large figures, but the text presents them as real census data.

God knows and counts his people, and gives each one a place. Today you can rest in the knowledge that you are not a lost number in the crowd: God sees you, and you have a place in his family. Seek to serve where he has placed you, with order and faithfulness.
exp.21:1:
Balak, the son of Zippor, heard all that Israel had done to the Amorites. It refers to Israel's victories over the Amorite kings Sihon and Og in the earlier chapters. The archaic spelling of an older form of the verb is not needed here; the verse simply says "saw" as in the King James wording, and "Amorites" is the name of a people who lived in that region.

The narrator tells us this just as Israel camps opposite Moab. Balak, who according to the text was king of Moab, does not act because of a direct attack, but because of what he had heard and seen of what happened. His fear grows, and it leads him to seek help from the elders of Midian and, later, from Balaam. The text does not say that Israel wanted to attack Moab.

Many times our decisions are born from fear of what we imagine, more than from real facts. Before reacting, it is wise to pause, pray, and ask ourselves whether we are seeing the situation with the truth or only with fear.
exp.9:19:
This verse says that Eliasaph, son of Deuel, was the leader of the host of the tribe of Gad as the people marched. The word "host" here refers to the people of the tribe organized into groups, and "standard" was the sign of each group of tribes. Gad marched together with Reuben and Simeon in the first section.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how God commanded Israel to set out from Sinai. Each tribe had a designated leader, and the order of march was clearly defined. The Kohathites, who carried the sacred objects of the sanctuary, came after, so that the tabernacle would be ready when they arrived.

For today: God pays attention to every person and every task, even those that seem small or little known. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, and do not underestimate your place in what He is doing.
exp.2:44:
God tells Moses to take the Levites for himself, in place of all the firstborn of Israel. The animals of the Levites also count in place of the firstborn animals of the people. "I am the Lord" is a way of reminding the reader that he has the authority and the final word.

God speaks to Moses after the firstborn males have been counted (22.273). When God freed Israel from Egypt, the firstborn belonged to him (Exodus 13). Now the Levites take that place to serve in the sanctuary. Since there were more firstborn than Levites, the text goes on to a payment of money to cover the difference.

Everything we have comes from God, and he may ask us to dedicate it to his service. Today we can ask ourselves: what part of my time, my gifts and my life am I giving to God with gratitude, and not only out of obligation?
exp.5:6:
It says the Nazirite was not to come near a dead body, not even if his father, his mother, his brother, or his sister died. "Defiling himself" means becoming ritually unclean, not that it was something bad in itself. "Consecration" is the special dedication to God, which was seen in his uncut hair.

God speaks to Moses to give the rules of the Nazirite vow, a voluntary season of special devotion to the Lord. It was a stricter rule than the one for ordinary people, and it was similar to the one the high priest had (Leviticus 21:11). Death caused ritual uncleanness, and the Nazirite had to keep his devotion complete.

For today: when we commit ourselves to God, it is wise to decide clearly what matters most. This does not mean ceasing to love our family, but remembering that our devotion to God holds first place.
exp.11:14:
This verse tells us that Miriam, the sister of Moses, was kept outside the camp for seven days.

The narrator describes what happened after Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses. God struck her with leprosy as a correction, and Moses asked that she be healed. God said she had to remain outside for seven days, like a temporary shame. Some think her position of leadership also explains why everyone waited; the text does not say this clearly.

God corrects, but also restores. If someone fails, we can help them return with patience, without rejecting them forever. And if we are wrong, accepting correction opens the door to a new beginning.
exp.6:10:
God tells Moses how the dedicating of the altar will be done: each prince, or tribal leader, will bring his offering on a different day. So one brings his offering today, another tomorrow, and so on. The altar is set apart for God's service, which is what the act of dedicating it means.

The Lord speaks with Moses while Israel is in the wilderness and the tabernacle has already been set up. The leaders of the tribes had already brought wagons and oxen for the service. Now God gives a clear order for the offerings, so that each tribe has its own place and everything is done with respect, without haste or disorder.

For today: God values everyone taking part and doing it with order and attention. No one was left out or rushed. We can ask ourselves how we might offer our time, gifts, and resources to God in a steady and personal way, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.31:15:
The men of Reuben and Gad come near to Moses and propose building pens for their livestock and cities for their little ones. The word for pens is one that refers to places where livestock are kept, and the phrase "came near" simply means they drew close to him.

The tribes of Reuben and Gad speak. They had a great deal of livestock and liked the land east of the Jordan. Moses had rebuked them, for he feared that by not crossing the river they would discourage the others and repeat the sin of the previous generation. They respond with a proposal: they will care for their families, but they will also fight alongside their brothers.

Before seeking what suits us, it is good to ask how it affects others. These men listened to the correction and offered a solution that did not abandon their people. We can do the same: attend to our family and our needs without forgetting our commitment to the community of faith.
exp.10:24:
And the Lord came down in the cloud and spoke with Moses. Then he took part of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed it on seventy elders. The word "rested" means that the Spirit settled upon them. When that happened, they prophesied, that is, they spoke under the influence of God. As for "did not cease," it can be understood as meaning they did not stop at that moment; some translators think this was a one-time event that was not repeated.

Moses was worn out from carrying alone a people who kept complaining. God answered him by choosing seventy elders to share that burden. This sign showed everyone that they had God's backing.

For today: God does not want us to carry everything alone. If you are called to lead or care for others, learn to share responsibilities and to recognize the gifts of others. Ask for help without shame.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that while the time of his Nazirite vow lasted, the person would not cut his hair. The tool used for cutting hair is the razor, and the long locks are the hair that is left to grow. He had to let it grow until the days of his separation were complete, that is, the time of his dedication to the Lord. In this way he would be holy, or set apart for God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel. A man or a woman could make a voluntary vow to dedicate themselves to the Lord for a period of time. Besides letting the hair grow long, the person had to abstain from all products of the vine and avoid contact with the dead. The hair was a visible sign of that commitment.

Today we do not have to let our hair grow long, but we can learn that devotion to God is lived out through concrete and visible decisions. You can choose a habit that shows your commitment to Him, such as praying each morning, and keep it faithfully and humbly.
exp.18:19:
If someone becomes unclean by touching a dead body and does not purify himself with the water of separation, that person shall be cut off from the congregation. The reason is that he has defiled the tabernacle, the house of God. "Sprinkled" means splashed, and the water of separation is water mixed with ashes that was used for cleansing.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel in the wilderness. They teach that God is holy and that his presence among them had to be respected. Being "cut off" may have meant being excluded from the people, and interpreters debate the exact extent of that expression.

For today: God offers cleansing, but we must come to it. When we fail, we should not hide our guilt or ignore it. We can draw near to God with sincerity, trusting in the forgiveness that Christ gives us.
exp.21:27:
This verse tells us that God made Balaam's donkey speak. "Opened her mouth" means that God gave her the ability to speak. A "donkey" is a female donkey, and "smitten" means struck or beaten. She complains to Balaam for having struck her three times.

Balaam was riding his donkey on the way to meet the king of Moab. The angel of the Lord stood in the road in front of him, but only the donkey saw him. She turned aside to protect him, and Balaam, angry, struck her without understanding what was happening. God used the donkey to correct him. It is striking that Balaam answered without astonishment, as if talking with a donkey were normal; the text does not explain why.

For today: sometimes we get angry at whatever gets in our way, without considering that God might be protecting us. Before reacting in anger, stop and ask, "Lord, what would you show me?"
exp.23:18:
It says that someone coming from the descendants of Jacob will have authority and dominion over his enemies. The phrase "shall have dominion" means that he will rule with power. And "shall destroy him that remaineth of the city" means that he will finish off the survivors who are still left in the enemy city.

The one speaking is Balaam, a prophet who was not an Israelite. Balak, the king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God compelled him to bless it. This is his fourth message, about the future of Israel and its neighbors. Many Christians see in the star and the scepter a sign of the Messiah, while others first connect it to King David. Both readings have been held.

For today: God keeps his promises even when no one can stop them. If you trust in him, you can rest, because no plan against his people can defeat his purpose.
exp.0:29:
This verse begins the count of the tribe of Zebulun, one of the sons of Jacob. It records the men from twenty years old and upward who were able to go forth to war, arranged by their generations, their families, and the houses of their fathers. The phrase "according to the number of the names" means that each man was recorded by name.

God himself speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commands him to take this census of all Israel. The people had just come out of Egypt and were preparing to organize themselves and march toward the promised land. According to the text that follows, 57,400 men of Zebulun were counted.

For today: God knows each person by name, and no one is invisible to him. Today you can remember that your place in the family of faith matters, and that your service, though it may seem small, counts within the people of God.
exp.34:32:
This verse commands Israel not to pollute the land where they live. It says that bloodshed "defiles" the land, that is, stains it and brings dishonor upon it. According to the law, the land could not be cleansed of that blood except by the blood of the one who shed it, that is, through justice being carried out against the murderer.

God speaks through Moses, as Israel was about to enter Canaan. He has just explained the cities of refuge, where a person who killed unintentionally could find protection. Here he makes clear that a murderer could not be allowed to buy his freedom with money. And he gives the reason: God himself dwells in the midst of his people, and human life is sacred.

Today we can remember that the life of every person has enormous value to God. We can defend it, respect others, reject violence, and seek justice without revenge, trusting that God is holy and just.
exp.30:45:
This verse gives a number: sixteen thousand persons. It is part of a list of the plunder Israel took in the war against Midian. Earlier the list mentions oxen and donkeys, and here the people are counted, that is, the young women who were left alive. It is half of the spoil that fell to Israel.

Moses is in the wilderness, near the end of his life. God had commanded him to punish Midian for having led Israel into idolatry at Peor. After the battle, everything was divided in an orderly way: one half for the warriors and the other for the people, with a portion set aside for the Levites.

For today: this passage shows us that God expects order, honesty, and justice in how we handle what we receive. Nothing was taken in secret; everything was counted and divided clearly. We can apply this by taking care that our money and our responsibilities are managed with transparency.
exp.32:15:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the desert of Sinai, where they had stayed for nearly a year, and camped at a place called Kibroth-hattaavah. The word "removed" means "having left," and "pitched" means "camped." The name Kibroth-hattaavah means "graves of craving" or "graves of greed."

This verse is part of a list of Israel's stops in the desert, written by Moses at God's command (Numbers 33:2). It was a record of the route from Egypt to the promised land. According to Numbers 11, this place received its name because there the people complained and asked for meat, and many of them died.

For today: a place can be marked by our complaints or by our trust. Before we desire something anxiously, we can ask God to teach us to be thankful for what he has already given us and to trust in his provision.
exp.20:1:
Israel makes a solemn promise to God. They say that if He gives them victory over this people, they will completely destroy their cities. "Made a vow" means that Israel promised something to God in return for His help. The words "deliver" and "into my hand" are rendered in the verse above as "deliver this people into my hand," and "into my hand" means under His power.

The Canaanite king of Arad attacked Israel when they were coming by the way of the spies, and he took some of them prisoner. The whole nation of Israel speaks, hurt and in danger. In asking God for help, they commit themselves to destroy those cities, an act of devoting them to destruction. The text that follows says that God heard them, and the place was called Hormah.

When we face a difficulty, we can cry out to God with sincerity. But let us be careful about what we promise, and humbly keep what we have said to Him, knowing that victory comes from Him.
exp.28:8:
This passage describes the grain offering that went along with the sacrifices on the Day of Atonement. The word "meat offering" here means an offering of grain. The finest flour, mixed with oil, was used. The measure of flour is a "tenth deal," a set amount of flour. Three tenth deals were given for each bullock, two for each ram, and one for each lamb.

God speaks to Moses, giving instructions for the feasts of the seventh month. The tenth day was a holy day of rest and self-denial, when Israel sought forgiveness for its sins. The exact measures taught order and seriousness when approaching God.

For today: approach God with our best and with a humble heart. We do not need to offer flour, but we can give Him quality time, honesty, and gratitude, not just what we have left over. Christians see in Christ the fulfillment of all atonement.
exp.33:24:
This verse names the leader of the tribe of Zebulun: Elizaphan (today spelled Elizafán), son of Parnach. The word "prince" here does not speak of royalty, but of a chief or representative of his tribe.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes his instructions on to the people. Israel was about to enter Canaan, and God commanded that one leader from each tribe help the priest Eleazar and Joshua divide the land. Beyond this passage, we have no further details about Elizaphan in this book, so it is not wise to assume more.

God cares about order and justice. Each tribe had a voice in the division, and even the names of little-known people were written down. Today we can serve faithfully in simple tasks, trusting that God sees and values what we do, even when others do not notice.
exp.30:27:
This verse says that from the share of the plunder the soldiers received, they were to set aside an offering for the Lord. It was one out of every five hundred, taken from the people, the cattle, the donkeys, and the sheep. The word "tribute" means a contribution or portion given to God. The phrase "set apart" means they were to separate it for him.

God speaks to Moses after the war against Midian. He commands him to divide the plunder between those who fought and the rest of the people, with the help of the priest Eleazar. The soldiers gave a small portion, one out of five hundred, and the people gave more, one out of fifty, for the Levites. In this way everyone acknowledged that the victory came from God. This war is a difficult passage, and it must be understood within its historical setting.

For today: when we receive something good, such as a salary or an achievement, we can first set aside a portion for God and for helping others, out of gratitude and not out of obligation.
exp.33:12:
Moses instructs the Israelites to divide the land of Canaan by casting lots. That land was to be assigned to nine and a half tribes. You will inherit it: this means they would receive it as a permanent possession passed down, and "by lot" means they would divide it by casting lots. The phrase "the Lord commanded" shows that the instruction came from God, not from Moses.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before entering the promised land. He has just described the boundaries of Canaan. The other two and a half tribes, Reuben, Gad, and part of Manasseh, had already received their inheritance on the other side of the Jordan. Scholars do not agree on exactly how the casting of lots was carried out, but the text makes clear that the outcome was understood as God's decision.

For today: we can learn to receive with trust what God gives us, without envying what belongs to others. He knows what we need better than we do.
exp.25:2:
This verse tells us that Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with the people in the plains of Moab, near the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho. "Plains" here means open lowlands or flat, wide country. What follows is God's command to take a census.

God had just spoken to Moses and Eleazar. The plague had passed, the disaster that fell on Israel because of their sin at Peor (chapter 25). Eleazar appears alongside Moses because his father Aaron had already died. The people were about to enter the promised land, and the census served to organize the army and, according to the chapter, to divide up the land.

For today: God continues to guide his people after times of crisis. When a difficult season ends, do not stay looking back; listen to what God shows you for the next step, and prepare yourself with order and obedience.
exp.28:20:
This verse describes the offerings for the second day of the Feast of Tabernacles. The "meat offerings" are grain offerings (fine flour mixed with oil), and the "drink offerings" are the offerings of wine that were poured out. These accompanied the bullocks, rams, and lambs, "according to their number," that is, in the amount that corresponded to each animal, "after the manner," that is, as God had already commanded.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. The chapter describes the offerings for the feasts of the year. Here the second day is detailed, and each day the number of bullocks changes. In this way order and reverence in worship were taught.

For today: God values constant and careful worship, not improvised worship. We can set aside fixed times to pray and read the Bible, offering him our lives with gratitude and obedience.
exp.4:18:
Here the priest makes an oath to the woman accused by her husband of unfaithfulness. The priest brings her under a solemn oath, having her swear to what she says. If she is innocent, nothing will happen to her through the bitter water, which was holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle. The phrase toward impurity means toward uncleanness, that is, adultery.

This is in the law that God gave to Israel through Moses. The husband felt jealousy and had no witnesses. So the case was brought before God and the priest. It was a strange ritual for us, and scholars explain it in different ways. What is clear is that it protected the innocent woman, since it declared her free, and it placed the judgment in God's hands, not the husband's.

For today: do not judge by suspicion or jealousy. If something troubles you, speak honestly and seek the truth with humility, knowing that God sees what we cannot see.
exp.28:31:
On the seventh day, seven young bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs one year old were to be offered, all "without defect," that is, without any stain or sickness.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, giving instructions for the Feast of Tabernacles, also called the Feast of Booths. Each day the number of sacrifices went down: here it is seven bulls, and the day before there were eight. The exact reason for that decrease is not explained in the text, and several ideas have been proposed. In addition, a male goat was always offered for sin.

For today: God deserves the best, not the leftovers. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, affection, and effort we give to him sincerely and not just what is left over, trusting that Christ has already made the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.30:25:
Here God orders Moses to take an inventory of everything captured in the war against Midian: the people and the animals. Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the leaders of the families of the people were to do it together. "Prey" means spoil, what was seized in battle. "Heads of the fathers" are the leaders of the households or clans.

The LORD speaks to Moses after the battle and after the purification instructions for the soldiers. Before the spoil is divided, God asks for order and for several leaders to take part in the count. This way no one could take anything on their own, and the division would be made with openness and fairness between those who fought and the rest of the people.

For today: when we handle goods that belong to others or to the community, such as church money or work resources, let us do it with order, with clear accounts, and with other people who can bear witness. Transparency protects trust and honors God.
exp.25:46:
This verse gives the total for the tribe of Asher. Adding up all its families, the men who were counted came to fifty-three thousand four hundred. "Those that were numbered" means the men who were registered in the census.

God himself commanded Moses and Eleazar to take this census on the plains of Moab, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The men counted were those twenty years old and up, fit for war, and the count also served to divide the promised land. Asher had grown a great deal since the previous census. After the list of its families, the text goes on to the tribe of Naphtali.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but knows families and names, even the name of a daughter called Serah. If you feel small or overlooked today, remember that God knows you personally and has a place for you.
exp.32:9:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Elim and camped by the Red Sea. The words "They removed" and "encamped" are the ones that appear in the verse itself. The Red Sea is the sea that the verse names directly.

Here Moses is writing down each stop on Israel's journey out of Egypt, at God's command. Elim had been a place of rest, with water and palm trees. This verse does not tell us anything that happened during this stop; it only mentions it. Some think this was a shore of the Red Sea different from the one of the miraculous crossing, but there is no certainty about its exact location.

For today: God guides us in stages, and not all of them are restful. After the oasis came another stop in the wilderness. Trust that the Lord walks with you in the easy places and the hard ones, and that each step has meaning on his path.
exp.10:27:
Joshua, son of Nun, who had served Moses since he was young, says to him: "My lord Moses, forbid them." He asks that Eldad and Medad be stopped. "Young men" means young men, and "servant" means assistant or attendant.

God had put his Spirit on seventy elders, and they prophesied. Eldad and Medad were on the list, but they stayed in the camp, and the Spirit rested on them as well. Joshua speaks out of loyalty to Moses. He fears that they will take away Moses' authority. Moses will answer that he wishes all the people were prophets.

For today: sometimes we want to protect our church, our group, or our leadership. But God can work through means we do not expect. Let us rejoice when someone else serves God, even if they do not do it the way we would.
exp.13:7:
It says that, if God takes pleasure in his people, he himself will bring them into the promised land and give it to them. The phrase "if the Lord delight in us" means that God looks on them with favor and is pleased with them. The phrase "a land which floweth with milk and honey" is a way of saying that the land is fertile and abundant.

Joshua and Caleb speak, the two of the twelve spies who brought back a report of faith. The other ten had frightened the people, and the crowd wept and wanted to return to Egypt. That is why Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes, a gesture of grief, and urged them to trust God. The crowd responded by wanting to stone them.

Today, when a goal seems bigger than your strength, do not look only at the obstacles. Ask yourself what God has promised and walk in obedience, trusting that he is the one who opens the way, even when others doubt.
exp.26:14:
It says that Moses answered God. The word "answered" shows that Moses did not stay silent after what God had just told him. The name of God appears here in its older written form, and what follows is his prayer.

God had just told Moses to go up the mountain and see the promised land, but that he would not enter it, because at Kadesh he did not honor God before the people. Moses does not argue or complain about his punishment. He first thinks about the people and asks that God give them a leader.

For today: when we receive painful news, we can pray for the good of others and not only for ourselves. Moses teaches us to think about those who will come after us.
exp.29:4:
It says that if a young unmarried woman, living in her father's house, makes a vow to God, and the father hears of it and says nothing, the vow stands firm. The Hebrew-era wording here means "hear," "keep silent," and "bound her soul," which means she made a serious commitment. (Rewritten per instructions: the sentence explaining the quoted words is replaced by a plain statement of the meaning.)

Moses passes on these instructions from God to the people of Israel. Earlier it was said that every vow must be fulfilled. Here it is explained how the vows of a young daughter, who lived under her father's authority, worked. Her silence amounted to approval. It is a rule of that time and culture, within the law given to Israel.

For today: God takes our promises seriously. Before promising something to God or to others, think it over calmly, and if necessary, ask for advice from wise people in your family or your church. That way you can keep what you say with integrity.
exp.14:13:
It says that if a foreigner lives among the Israelites, and also his descendants over the years, and wants to present to God a burnt offering of pleasing aroma, he must do it just as the Israelites do. The word "sojourn" means to live or reside as a temporary dweller. A "burnt offering of pleasing aroma" is an offering burned on the altar, which is pleasing to God. "Throughout your generations" means "from generation to generation."

God speaks to Moses so that he may pass it on to the people. The Israelites were in the wilderness, and God gives them instructions about the offerings for when they enter the promised land. Here he makes clear that the foreigner who joins his people worships under the same rules, without a separate law.

For today: in the church and in daily life, let us make sure that whoever comes from outside, whether a migrant or a newly converted person, feels welcome to worship God on equal terms. We can greet them, include them, and give them a real place among us.
exp.28:11:
This verse commands the people of Israel to gather on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. That gathering would be a "holy convocation," that is, a sacred assembly set apart for God. They were not to do any "servile work," meaning the heavy labor of everyday life. For seven days they would keep a solemn feast to the Lord. Today we know this feast as the Feast of Tabernacles, or the Feast of Booths.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, who is now close to the promised land. The chapter details the offerings for each feast on the calendar. This one, at the end of the farming year, was a time of thanksgiving and of remembering that God cared for them in the wilderness.

For today: set aside regular time to stop, rest from work, and give thanks to God with your family or your church. A day of pause and praise reminds you that your life depends not only on your own effort, but on his faithful care.
exp.8:4:
This verse tells us that the people of Israel kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, at even, that is, as the evening was falling, around dusk. They did this in the wilderness of Sinai and followed all the instructions that God gave to Moses.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Almost a year has passed since the departure from Egypt, and God wants his people to remember their deliverance. The account stresses that they obeyed carefully. It goes on to say that some could not take part because they were unclean, and that shows the people took seriously what God commanded.

For today: remember with gratitude what God has done for us, and obey him with simplicity, without waiting to feel perfect. Remembering his help strengthens our faith.
exp.26:18:
Here God tells Moses to present Joshua before the priest Eleazar and before the whole congregation. The phrase "set him before" means to place him in plain view of everyone. "Give him a charge" means to formally entrust him with his task, that is, to commission him or give him official instructions, and this is done in the sight of the people.

God speaks with Moses, who had just asked for a leader so that the people would not be left "as sheep without a shepherd." Moses knew that he would soon die. God chooses Joshua, a man with the Spirit, and wants the transfer of authority to be public and orderly, so that the people will respect and accept him.

For today: serving God should not be done in secret or in disorder. When someone receives a responsibility in the church or in the family, it is good that it be done with clarity, support, and prayer, and that the one receiving it depend on God.
exp.25:40:
This verse closes the list of the tribe of Benjamin. It says that these are the families descended from Benjamin, and that when they were counted, the total came to 45,600 men.

The one speaking is the narrator, who tells what Moses and the priest Eleazar did by God's command. This took place at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, when the people were preparing to enter the promised land. The count was used to organize the army and, later, to divide the land according to the size of each tribe.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd, but family by family. You can trust that you too are known and remembered by Him. Your name and your place in the community also matter; value and care for those who are with you.
exp.21:34:
The angel of the Lord tells Balaam to go with the men, but to say only what God puts in his mouth. The verse of the old wording is removed here, since the reader's verse does not contain it. The men sent by Balak, the king of Moab, are the envoys who came to fetch him. Balaam obeys and goes with them.

Balaam had already set out toward Moab, and his donkey stopped three times because she saw the angel with a sword. After the Lord opened Balaam's eyes, he recognized his wrong. The angel allows him to continue, but makes it clear that he will not be the one who decides the message. Interpreters see in this a firm limit set by God.

For today: even when we face pressure, offers, or self-interest, our task is to be faithful to what God says, without adding or taking away anything to please others.
exp.30:23:
After the war against Midian, the soldiers were to wash their clothes on the seventh day so that they would be clean. Only then could they come back into the camp. The verse's phrase about being clean means they were purified according to the law, and "the camp" is the camp of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people, following what God had commanded him. The soldiers had come into contact with death and with spoils of war, which, according to the law, made a person unclean. The verses before this one command that men be purified and also that objects be purified. In this way the holiness of the people, among whom God dwelt, was protected.

For today: before returning to everyday life after a hard season or after having failed, it is healthy to stop, confess to God what has stained our hearts, and ask him for cleansing. Christians believe that Christ purifies us completely (1 John 1:9).
exp.15:31:
The earth opened its mouth and swallowed up Dathan, Abiram, and their families, the men of Korah, and all their possessions. The word "swallowed" in the verse above is the same idea as "swallowed them up," and "possessions" is the word the verse calls their goods.

Moses had just finished speaking. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, along with other leaders, had risen up against him and against Aaron, saying that they had no right to lead the people. Moses said that if God did something new, the people would know that God had sent him and that these men had despised the Lord. Some scholars see here a judgment on rebellion; the text itself presents it that way.

For today: God takes pride and rebellion against the authority He has established seriously. Today we can examine our hearts, ask for humility, and seek God with reverence, rather than wanting to occupy a place that does not belong to us.
exp.13:27:
God tells Moses to speak to the people with an oath, a solemn way of affirming that he will keep his word. The phrase "as I live" is a solemn way of assuring that he will keep his word. "As you have spoken in my hearing" means "just as you said it before me." What they said is what they will receive.

When the Israelites heard the spies' report, they wept and said it would have been better to have died in Egypt or in the wilderness (Numbers 14:2). God heard them and answered with justice: that generation would not enter the promised land, except Caleb and Joshua, who trusted in him.

For today: our words matter. Complaining without stopping feeds unbelief, while speaking with confidence in God strengthens faith. Before grumbling, we can stop and pray, handing our fear over to God.
exp.32:17:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Hazeroth and camped in another called Rithmah. The word "departed" in the verse means the same as "after leaving" or "having left," and the word "pitched" means "camped" or "settled for a time."

Moses records each stop of the journey, at God's command, from Egypt to the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). It is like a travel log. Rithmah appears here in the list, and it is not known for certain where it was. The events near Hazeroth are told in Numbers 12 and 13, and the spies set out from that region. Some believe Rithmah was near Kadesh, but this is not certain.

For today: God watches over every stage of your path, even the ones that seem unimportant. Though you may not understand the route, he remembers every place where you have been and continues to guide you.
exp.22:0:
Balaam asks Balak to build seven altars and to prepare seven young bulls and seven rams. The verse says "Build me here seven altars" and "prepare me here seven oxen and seven rams." Each of these is a sacrifice to offer to God, one for each altar.

Balak, king of Moab, had sent for Balaam to curse Israel, because he was afraid of them. Here Balaam speaks as a prophet, and he sets up this ritual before seeking the word of the LORD. The number seven appears often in the Bible as a number of completeness, though it is not known for certain why Balaam chose it. Interpreters also debate how sincere his heart was, since the Bible presents him with mixed qualities.

For today: rituals and offerings do not replace an obedient heart. Before making an important decision, let us truly seek God's will, not merely the appearance of religiousness.
exp.30:4:
This verse describes how Israel's army was organized. From all the groups of Israel, a thousand men were set apart from each tribe, so in total there were twelve thousand. "Armed for war" means that they were equipped and ready to fight. The phrase "thousands" refers to the large divisions of the people.

Moses gives the command in God's name. Earlier, in Numbers 25, many Israelites were led into idolatry and immorality through Midianite women. This campaign is presented as God's judgment for that act. It is a hard passage, and scholars debate how to understand it, but the text stresses that every tribe took part equally.

For today: God's work is sustained when each person does their part, rather than a few carrying everything. Ask yourself what part of service you are called to in your family or your church, and do it with responsibility and humility.
exp.24:0:
Israel stayed camped in Shittim, a place east of the Jordan, near the entrance to the promised land. There the people began to commit sexual immorality, that is, to have forbidden sexual relations, with Moabite women.

The narrator tells this after God protected Israel from the curses of Balaam. The verses that follow show that sexual immorality was joined with idolatry: the women invited them to pagan sacrifices. Many understand that the problem was not only sexual, but a betrayal of the covenant with God. Numbers 31:16 connects Balaam with this episode.

For today: times of rest can also be times of danger. When we think that everything is calm, we should guard the heart, set wise limits, and stay close to God, so that no temptation draws us away from his path.
exp.30:41:
This verse is part of a longer sentence that begins earlier. It says that the other half of the spoils went to the people of Israel, and that Moses separated it from the half that was given to the soldiers who went to war. "Separated" here means that he divided it and set it apart. The word "gave" in the verse is the usual one, and no older spelling is involved.

Here the narrator of the book describes how Moses shared out the spoils of the war against Midian. God had commanded that they be divided into two equal parts: one for those who fought and another for the whole community. From each part a portion was also set aside as an offering to the LORD.

For today: God cares that there is fairness and order when we share out what we receive. We can learn to be just and generous with money and shared work, remembering that those who serve quietly also deserve to be remembered.
exp.25:11:
This verse begins the list of the families of the tribe of Simeon, one of the sons of Jacob. Three of its clans are named: the Nemuelites, the Jaminites, and the Jachinites, each called after their ancestors. The word "families" here means clans or groups of relatives within the tribe.

Moses and the priest Eleazar are taking a new census of the people of Israel, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, after a plague and before entering the Promised Land. The earlier generation had died because of their disobedience, and now the new one was being counted. The verses before this one recall the judgment on Korah, but also that his sons did not die.

God cares for people one by one, not only as a mass. Every name matters, even those that almost no one remembers. You can rest in the knowledge that God knows you by your name and that your place among his people does not go unnoticed.
exp.4:30:
It says the husband was free from blame, that is, he was not accused of anything for bringing the matter before God. The woman, if she had truly been unfaithful, would bear the consequences of her sin. "Husband" is the man who is married to her, and "guilt" is the blame she carried.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. This law dealt with cases of jealousy without proof. Instead of letting the husband take revenge, the matter was brought before God and the priest. Many believe this also protected the woman from unjust punishment. Scholars discuss how the whole ritual should be understood.

Today, if you feel jealousy or suspicion, do not accuse or take justice into your own hands. Speak honestly, seek the truth calmly, and leave judgment to God. Each person answers for their own actions.
exp.2:32:
This verse says that from Merari, one of the sons of Levi, came two families: the Mahlites and the Mushites. Mahlites and Mushites are the names given to the families descended from Mahli and Mushi. In this way the families that made up the clan of Merari are named.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and gives him instructions to organize the tribe of Levi, who would serve in the tabernacle. The Levites were divided into three groups: the Gershonites, the Kohathites, and the Merarites. This verse closes the list of the Merarites, who were later entrusted with the care of the structures of the tabernacle. Here it is only said that their families were registered and had their place.

For today: In the people of God, no service is insignificant. Even if your task seems quiet or little seen, God knows your name and your place. Serve faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.4:20:
Here the priest has the woman take an oath and announces a curse to her: if she is guilty, may the Lord make her an object of cursing among her people. "Conjure" means to make someone swear under threat of divine punishment.
