The phrases "thigh that falls" and "belly that swells" have an exact meaning that is not clear; many believe they describe harm to the ability to have children, but this is not known for certain.

Moses receives this law from God. It concerns the ritual for jealousy, when a husband suspected unfaithfulness without having witnesses. The woman was left in God's hands, not in the hands of people. It was a solemn test, and some scholars note that it protected the woman from hasty punishment by others.

For today: do not accuse or judge others on the basis of mere suspicion. Bring your doubts to God, seek the truth calmly, and leave the final judgment in his hands.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that Moses spoke to the people of Israel and reminded them that they were to keep the Passover. It is not a new command, but a reminder that they should do it at the appointed time.

God had already commanded the Passover in Egypt, to remember how He freed His people from slavery. Now Israel is in the wilderness of Sinai, almost a year after leaving Egypt. Moses passes on what the LORD had commanded him. The text that follows shows that the people obeyed, although some could not take part because they were unclean, and this troubled them.

For today: God invites us to regularly remember what He has done for us. We can set aside fixed times, such as prayer, Bible reading, or the Lord's Supper, to thank Him and to obey Him with a sincere heart.
exp.31:21:
It says that when the land of Canaan has been conquered before the Lord (that is, under his guidance and with his help), the men of Reuben and Gad may return home. "Subdued" means brought under control or made to submit. "Guiltless" means free of any fault before God and before the people. Then the land east of the Jordan would be theirs as an inheritance.

Moses is the one speaking. The tribes of Reuben and Gad, who had a great deal of livestock, asked to stay in the lands east of the Jordan. Moses feared that their brothers would be left alone in the war, so he set them a condition: to cross over armed and fight alongside the other tribes until the conquest was finished.

For today: keeping what we have promised is part of being faithful to God. Moreover, our blessings are not only for ourselves; we must also support our brothers and sisters in their struggles.
exp.3:29:
This verse orders the counting of the men of the family of Merari, one of the clans of the Levites. Only those between thirty and fifty years of age were included in the count. They were the ones who "entered into the service," that is, those who joined the work group to serve in the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent where God dwelt in the midst of his people.

God speaks to Moses, and to Aaron, in the wilderness of Sinai. He is organizing the moving of the tabernacle. Each Levite family had a precise task. The sons of Merari were to carry the boards, the bars, the pillars and the sockets. These were heavy but important jobs. The verse does not say why that age was chosen; some think it was because of the maturity and strength needed.

For today: no service to God is small. Even if your task seems quiet or unremarkable, God knows it and counts it. Serve faithfully where He has placed you.
exp.32:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel left Marah and came to Elim, a place with twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. There they camped.

This chapter is a record of Israel's stopping places in the wilderness, and Moses wrote it at God's command. Earlier, at Marah, the water was bitter (Exodus 15). Now they arrive at a place of good water and shade. The list reminds us that God guided them step by step. The numbers twelve and seventy may have some symbolic meaning, but the text does not explain it, so it is wise not to claim too much.

After a bitter season, God often allows us to rest. If you are in a difficult stage today, trust that He knows your path. And if you are in a time of rest, thank Him and regain your strength.
exp.33:1:
God tells Moses to instruct the people of Israel: when they enter the land of Canaan, that land will be their inheritance, with its boundaries clearly defined. The phrase "when ye come into the land" is what the verse says. The word "inheritance" refers to the land that would be given to them as their portion.

The LORD speaks to Moses at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is near the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. Before they enter, God marks out the boundaries so that the people know what He had promised them and can divide it up in an orderly way. The verses that follow begin to describe those borders.

God keeps His promises with clarity and order. You can trust that what He promises, He sustains. Today, write down a promise from the Bible and ask Him to help you wait with faith and prepare with responsibility.
exp.20:22:
This verse says that King Sihon did not allow the Israelites to pass through his land. Instead, he gathered all his people and went out into the wilderness to attack them. He came as far as a place called Jahaz and fought against Israel there. The word "border" means the edge or boundary of a territory, and the phrase "but" here means "on the contrary" or "rather."

The narrator of the book tells what happened after Israel asked peacefully for permission to pass along the king's road, promising not to touch fields, vineyards, or wells. Sihon answered with war, and according to the account that follows, Israel won and settled in those cities. The exact location of Jahaz is not known with certainty.

For today: we can act with respect and good faith even when others respond with hostility. Doing what is right does not guarantee that we will be treated well, but it allows us to face conflicts with a clear conscience and trusting in God.
exp.22:16:
This verse tells how Balaam returned to where Balak was and found him standing beside his burnt offering, the offering burned on the altar. With him were the princes of Moab, that is, the leaders or chiefs of the land. Balak, the king, asks him anxiously: "What hath the Lord spoken?"

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and had hired Balaam to curse the people. Balaam had gone off alone to seek God, and God put in his mouth the message he was to deliver. So Balak expects a curse, but Balaam can only say what God has given him, and it will be a blessing.

For today: before we ask God to say what we want to hear, let us learn to listen to what He really says. His word does not change according to our desires or fears, and in it we can trust.
exp.0:46:
This verse says that the Levites were not entered into the count along with the other tribes. When Moses counted the men of Israel who were able to go to war, the tribe of Levi was set apart. The word "counted" means registered or numbered, and "families of their fathers" refers to the households and clans.

The narrator of the book tells what happened in the wilderness of Sinai. God commanded that the military count be taken, but He told Moses that Levi was not to be numbered with the others. Later, the book explains that the Levites were put in charge of the tabernacle, its care, and its transport.

For today: God gives each person a different calling, and not everyone serves in the same way. We can gladly accept the place God gives us, without comparing ourselves to others, and serve faithfully where He has placed us.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that the group of the tribe of Simeon, that is, the men who were counted in the census, totaled 59,300. "Host" means army or organized company, and "counted" means numbered in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions on how Israel was to camp in the wilderness, each tribe under its banner and with its leader. According to Numbers 1, the census counted the men twenty years old and above who were able to go to war. Simeon camped next to Reuben, on the south side of the camp. The order showed that the people were to live organized and with God at the center.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass; each person and each tribe has a place. Ask yourself where God has placed you to serve, and do it with order and faithfulness.
exp.7:4:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses to give him a new instruction. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "spoke to Moses" means that he spoke to Moses. What God says comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who listens in order to pass the message on to the people. Just before this, Aaron lit the lamps of the lampstand, as God had commanded. Now God moves on to another matter: setting apart and preparing the Levites to serve in the sanctuary. The text shows that all service to God begins with his word, not with human ideas.

Before doing anything for God, it is wise to listen to him first. We can set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and pray before making decisions or beginning a service in the church. In this way, what we do responds to what God says, not only to our own plans.
exp.6:62:
This verse lists the animals Abidan offered for the burnt offering: one young bull, one ram, and one lamb in its first year. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar. A young bull is a young ox.

Here the narrator is Moses (according to tradition), and he records the offerings each tribal leader brought for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Abidan was the leader of the tribe of Benjamin. Each leader presented exactly the same thing, on different days. That repetition shows order, equality, and that no tribe was overlooked.

For today: God values complete devotion, not only what is impressive. Since the burnt offering was burned entirely, it reminds us to offer God our whole heart. It also reminds us that our service, even if it looks the same as others' or is simple, has value before Him.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that those who could not keep the Passover on its regular date were to keep it one month later, on the fourteenth day of the second month, at evening. They were to eat the lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

God speaks to Moses. Some Israelites were unclean because they had touched a dead body, or they were away on a journey, and so they could not keep the Passover on time. God gives them a second opportunity, without making light of the feast. The Passover recalled the deliverance from Egypt.

For today: God is merciful toward those who have a real hindrance, but He expects that we will not neglect what He has asked of us. Today we can avoid putting off the time of prayer, thanksgiving and fellowship with God, and return to Him with confidence when we have failed.
exp.6:24:
This verse describes the offering of Eliab, leader of the tribe of Zebulun, on the third day. He brought one silver dish weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl of 70 shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official standard. Both were full of fine flour mixed with oil, for a grain offering.

The book of Numbers tells how, at the dedication of the tabernacle, each tribal leader brought his offering, one day after another, for twelve days. Each one presented exactly the same thing, without favoritism. Moses records everything in detail, showing that God values every gift.

For today: God does not compare our offerings with those of others; he receives gladly what we give sincerely. Give what you have with joy, without competing or boasting.
exp.22:8:
Balaam says that from the top of the crags he sees the people of Israel. What he sees is a people who dwell in confidence, that is, safe and at peace. Furthermore, the people shall not be reckoned among the nations means that Israel is set apart, distinct from the other nations. The hills are the high ridges, and the rocks are great stones.

Balaam, a diviner hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel, speaks here. But each time he tries to speak, God permits him only to bless Israel. Some understand that Israel is set apart by the covenant with God; others, by the way it lives. The text does not fully explain this.

For today: no one can undo what God blesses. If you have placed your life in his hands, you can live with confidence and without fear of what others say or wish against you.
exp.6:33:
This verse mentions one part of the offering for the fourth day: a male goat, that is, a full-grown goat, for a sin offering. A sin offering was the sacrifice given to cover sin and to seek forgiveness.

Moses records how the leaders of the tribes brought offerings for the dedication of the altar. Here it is the turn of Elizur, prince of Reuben. Each leader brought nearly the same thing, and the Bible repeats it again and again, as if to show that every tribe was received with equal worth before God.

For today: before giving or serving God, it is good to honestly acknowledge our faults. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10). Today you can pray sincerely, ask for forgiveness, and then serve with gratitude.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that on the eighth day after his purification, the person must bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest. He must present them at the entrance of the tent where God met with his people. The "tabernacle of the congregation" was that meeting tent.

God speaks to Moses about the rules of the Nazarite, someone who set himself apart willingly for the Lord. If someone died suddenly beside him, he became unclean through no fault of his own. Even so, he had to be purified and offer sacrifices. This shows that God cared for the holiness of what was dedicated to him.

For today: when we fail, or when something leads us away from what we promised God, there is no need to hide. We can return to Him simply and humbly, trusting in His forgiveness and starting again.
exp.32:0:
This verse opens a summary of the whole journey of Israel from Egypt. The places where the people camped and stopped along the way are the "stations" of the trip, and the groups in which they traveled, arranged like an organized army, are the "companies." Moses and Aaron led them.

The narrator is the one who writes the book of Numbers, and the text says that Moses put these stages in writing at the command of the LORD. Israel is about to enter the promised land, so the whole route is reviewed: every stop reminds the reader that God was with them during the years in the desert, even in their stumbles.

For today: remember your own path. Write down the "stations" of your life, those places and seasons, hard or good, and look for how God guided you in each one. Recalling his faithfulness will give you confidence for the next step.
exp.18:3:
Here it says that the priest Eleazar, son of Aaron, would take a little of the blood of the red heifer with his finger and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives an ordinance for purifying anyone who had become unclean by touching a dead body. The heifer was sacrificed outside the camp, and its blood was directed toward the place where God dwelt. The number seven usually indicates something complete, although the text does not explain every detail of the rite.

For today: cleansing before God was never something casual, but something He Himself established. Today we can draw near to God with humility, trusting in the purification He offers, and not in our own efforts.
exp.34:9:
God tells Moses to speak with the people of Israel. He warns them that when they cross the Jordan River and enter the land of Canaan, they must follow an important instruction. The words "when ye be come over" are an old way of saying "when you have crossed."

Israel was on the plains of Moab, about to enter the promised land. The LORD speaks to Moses, and Moses must pass the message on. What follows is the command to set apart cities of refuge, where a person who killed someone unintentionally could find protection until they were judged fairly.

For today: God cares about justice and mercy at the same time. We can imitate him by avoiding hasty judgments of others, and by making sure every person is heard fairly before being condemned.
exp.21:13:
This verse says that the leaders of Moab returned to King Balak and reported to him: "Balaam refuseth to come with us." The word "leaders" here means heads or officials, and "rose up" simply means they got moving.

The ones speaking are Balak's messengers. He wanted Balaam to curse Israel, because he was afraid of them. Notice that they do not repeat what Balaam said: that the LORD would not let him go. They summarize his answer as if it were only his own refusal. Why they did this, the Bible does not explain.

For today: when God tells us no, it is wise to obey firmly, even when others do not understand our reasons or keep pressing us afterward. We can also take care that, when we retell something, we do not change the original message.
exp.33:21:
It says that the leader chosen from the tribe of Dan was Bukki, son of Jogli. The word "prince" here does not mean the son of a king, but a head or leader of a tribe. In the older English wording, the name appears as "Bukki" as well, and many Bibles today write it the same way.

God speaks to Moses near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering Canaan. He orders that one leader from each tribe help Eleazar and Joshua divide the promised land. This list names those men. About Bukki we know only what this verse says; the Bible tells us nothing more about him.

For today: God takes care to name ordinary people who serve in tasks that seem small. If you have a quiet job in your family or in your church today, do it faithfully. God sees and remembers those who serve with honesty, even when few people know them.
exp.30:14:
Moses asks in astonishment and anger: "Have you let all the women live?" The word "saved" in the verse, which is also rendered as "kept alive," refers to those who were allowed to remain alive. The officers were returning from the war against Midian, and they had brought back the women as captives.

Moses speaks as the leader of Israel, upset with the military commanders. In chapter 25, Midianite women, following Balaam's advice, had led many Israelites into the worship of Baal-peor, and a plague killed thousands. Moses points out that these same women were the cause of that sin. This passage is difficult, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: faith needs attention to the influences that pull us away from God. It is wise to examine honestly what leads us astray and not to take lightly whatever damages our relationship with him.
exp.32:2:
This verse tells that the Israelites left Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover. "With a high hand" means with power and without hiding, and "in the sight of all the Egyptians" means that everyone saw them leave. The words "stations" and "journeys" refer to the places where they camped along the way.

It is part of a record of the stages of Israel's journey. The text says that Moses wrote it at the command of the LORD. Here the narrator recalls the beginning: God brought them out of Egypt, while the Egyptians were burying their firstborn and saw that their gods had been judged.

For today: when you look back, remember how God has guided you step by step. Keeping a record of his care, even in simple things, strengthens gratitude and trust for the road ahead.
exp.4:4:
This verse is a transitional sentence. It says that God spoke again to Moses. The word "again" shows that a new message is coming, separate from the one before it. "And the Lord spake unto Moses" simply means "the Lord spoke to Moses."

The speaker is God, and Moses is the one who receives the message to pass on to the people. He had just commanded that the sick and the unclean be sent out of the camp, because God dwelt in the midst of Israel. Now the passage moves to another subject: sin against other people, which requires confession and restitution, as the following verses show.

God does not stay silent in the face of our wrongs; he speaks to us and gives us ways to make them right. If you have hurt or wronged someone, guilt alone is not enough: acknowledge your mistake, ask for forgiveness, and, if you can, repair the harm. In this way we honor God and take care of our relationships.
exp.19:24:
God tells Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up to the top of Mount Hor. The phrase "bring them up" means to make them go up, that is, to accompany them up to the top. It is the beginning of a solemn moment, for there Aaron will end his days.

The LORD speaks with Moses near the border of Edom, toward the end of Israel's years in the wilderness. Aaron, the high priest, would not enter the promised land, because both he and Moses acted in rebellion at the waters of Meribah. Now God prepares the handover: Eleazar will take over his father's priestly service.

For today: our responsibilities are not eternal, and God continues his work through new generations. We can serve faithfully and also prepare others, passing on what we have learned with humility and trust in God.
exp.12:26:
This verse tells that the twelve men sent to explore Canaan returned to the camp. They came before Moses, Aaron, and all the people, at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Paran. The verse of the old form "á" as "a" and the phrase "diéronles la respuesta" meaning "les dieron su informe" have been removed, since they do not apply to the wording of the verse you are reading. Furthermore, they showed the people the fruit they had brought from the land.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, and he speaks of the explorers whom Moses had sent by God's command. After forty days, they return with their report. That report begins well, showing real fruit from the promised land, but soon it will be filled with fear and doubts.

For today: when God gives us a promise, it is good to look at the facts with faith and not only with fear. Before speaking of the difficulties, let us remember what God has already said and done.
exp.34:12:
This verse says that, of the cities the Israelites would give to the Levites, six would be cities of refuge. "Refuge" means shelter or protection. There, a person who had killed someone without meaning to, that is, by accident, could flee.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. In those days, a relative of the victim could seek revenge. These cities protected the unintentional killer until the community judged him. In this way life was guarded and justice was sought, without hasty vengeance. They also protected the stranger.

Today we can learn not to act in anger or revenge. Before judging someone, let us listen, seek the truth, and offer mercy, as God does with us.
exp.14:15:
It says that in Israel there would be one rule for everyone. The Israelites and the foreigner who lived among them were to follow the same law and the same right. The "stranger" is the outsider who lived with them, and "sojourneth" means to live or dwell there.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people. He is giving instructions about the offerings they were to bring when they entered the promised land. If a foreigner wanted to worship the LORD and bring his offering, he had to do it in the same way as the Israelites. In this way he was received as part of the worshiping community, without being treated as less. Some scholars see here a sign of God's openness toward all peoples.

For today: treat everyone with equal respect and justice, regardless of their origin. In church, at work, or in your neighborhood, make room for the newcomer, without favoritism.
exp.22:18:
This verse says that God is not like people: he does not lie, and he does not change his mind out of regret, like someone who makes a mistake and takes it back. What he says, he does; what he promises, he fulfills. Here, "repent" means to turn back on a decision. "Carry out" means to bring something to completion.

The one speaking is Balaam, a prophet who was not an Israelite. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel. But God allowed him only to bless it. Balaam tells Balak that God does not change his mind according to a king's wishes, and that a blessing already given cannot be revoked.

For today: you can rest in God's promises, because he is faithful and does not change his word according to circumstances. When you doubt, return to what he has said.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that the army of the tribe of Gad, that is, the men of that tribe who were counted, totaled 45,650. The word "host" means the army, and "those that were numbered" refers to those who were registered in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for camping and marching in order around the tabernacle. Gad camped on the south side, next to Reuben and Simeon. The numbers from the census served to organize the people, and the following verses add up the three groups on that side: 151,450 men.

For today: God cares about order, and He also cares about each person. No tribe was left uncounted. You can serve with confidence in your place, whether it is great or small, because God sees you and needs you in the body of His people.
exp.22:24:
Balak tells Balaam that, if he cannot curse Israel, then he should not bless them either.

Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel, because he feared that people. But Balaam could only say what God put in his mouth, and instead of curses, blessings came out. When he heard the great description of Israel as a lion, Balak could bear no more and asked for silence.

For today: when God's truth is inconvenient for us, we may feel tempted to silence it or twist it. It is better to let God speak, even when his words change our plans. His blessing does not depend on the opinions or desires of others.
exp.35:2:
This verse says that if the daughters of Zelophehad marry men from other tribes of Israel, the land they received as an inheritance would stop belonging to their fathers' tribe. It would pass to the tribe of their husbands.

"Taken from" and "put to" describe the land being moved from one tribe's share to another's. The word "lot" in the verse refers to the portion of land given out.

The heads of the families of Gilead, from the tribe of Manasseh, speak here. Earlier, God had commanded that the daughters of Zelophehad should inherit, because their father had no sons. Now these leaders worry that if the daughters marry outside the tribe, Manasseh will lose part of its territory. They bring their concern to Moses, and he considers it just.

For today: take care of what God has entrusted to us, such as family, faith, or possessions, and think ahead about how today's decisions will affect those who come after us.
exp.15:25:
Moses tells the people to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, whom he calls "wicked men." He also orders them not to touch anything that belongs to them, so that they will not be swept away together with them in their sins.

Moses is the one speaking. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram had rebelled against his leadership and that of Aaron, and they had drawn others into their rebellion. Moses warns the people before God acts, giving them the chance to separate themselves and save their lives. The passage shows that God judges rebellion, but it also gives warning with mercy.

For today: when we know that something goes against the will of God, it is not enough simply to avoid doing it; it is also wise to step away from whatever is pulling us toward it. This can be a friendship, a habit, or an environment. Separating ourselves in time is an act of wisdom and obedience.
exp.32:46:
This verse says that the people of Israel departed from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, opposite Mount Nebo. "They removed" means that they left or set out on their way. "Pitched" means that they camped, not that they stayed there forever.

This chapter is a list of Israel's stops from Egypt to near the promised land. The account presents it as a record that Moses wrote at the Lord's command (33:2). We are almost at the end of the journey. Nebo is the place from which Moses would later see the land (Deuteronomy 34), although this passage only mentions the camp.

God knows not only the destination of your life, but also every stop along the way. Perhaps today you are in a season of waiting or passing through that you do not fully understand. Trust that no stage is overlooked by God, and keep walking faithfully.
exp.6:31:
It says that Elishur, leader of the tribe of Reuben, presented a golden spoon that weighed ten shekels and was full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned in the sanctuary. The "spoon" was really a small container or cup for carrying the incense.

The narrator of the book tells how each leader of the twelve tribes brought his offering for the dedication of the altar and the tabernacle. Each one brought the same thing, on different days. This shows that the whole people took part in worship of God, and that no tribe was more important than another.

For today: God values the offering we give with order, dedication, and sincerity, without comparing ourselves to others. We can ask ourselves what we are offering him: our time, our gifts, or our affection. May it be something given with joy and from the heart.
exp.10:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel left Kibroth-hattaavah and went to Hazeroth, and that they stayed there. The people set out on the journey, and then they camped and stopped at that place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He has just told how the people complained about having no meat, and how God judged them with a plague. Kibroth-hattaavah means "graves of craving." The verse serves as a bridge: it closes that sad scene and continues the journey through the desert. Scholars are not completely certain where Hazeroth was.

For today: after a failure or a correction, life goes on, and God does not leave us stuck there. We can learn from what happened, ask for forgiveness, and keep walking with more trust in Him, instead of letting the desire to have everything right now control us.
exp.11:9:
It says that the cloud of God's presence withdrew from the tent of meeting (the tabernacle), and at that moment Miriam became leprous, white as snow. Aaron turned, looked at her, and saw that she was truly leprous. Here "leprous" refers to a serious skin disease, and we do not know for certain exactly what it was.

The narrator tells what happened after God defended Moses. Miriam and Aaron had criticized him, and God reminded them that Moses had a very close relationship with Him. The cloud departing shows that God was displeased, and the leprosy was the consequence for Miriam, who seems to have been the main voice in the complaint.

For today: speaking badly of others, especially of those who serve, carries real weight before God. Before criticizing, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask ourselves whether we are doing it with humility and love.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that the people of Israel camped when the Lord commanded it, and set out on the journey when the Lord commanded it. "At the commandment of the Lord" means "by the word or command of the Lord." "Camped" means they stayed in a place. "Set out" means they went on their way. They carried out what God had commanded through Moses.

This verse closes a section of the book of Numbers where the narrator explains how God guided Israel in the wilderness with a cloud over the tabernacle. Sometimes the cloud stayed for a night, and other times for days, a month, or a year. The people did not decide when to move; they waited for God's signal.

For today: learn to wait for and obey God's direction, both when it is time to stay and when it is time to move forward. Before deciding, pray and seek his will in the Bible.
exp.13:4:
Moses and Aaron fell with their faces to the ground, in front of the whole gathered assembly. The phrase "fell on their faces" means that they bowed down until they were lying on the ground. In the Bible, this gesture usually expresses humility, grief, or prayer.

The people had just heard the report of the spies and were filled with fear. They wept, complained against God, and even talked about appointing a leader to take them back to Egypt. Moses and Aaron did not argue or defend themselves. The text does not say here that they prayed aloud, so we do not know their exact words. But the gesture shows that they depended on God.

When everything seems to be falling apart and others give in to fear, we do not always have to respond with harsh words. Sometimes the best thing is to humble ourselves before God and seek him first.
exp.17:21:
This verse says that the rest of the Israelites were no longer to come near the tabernacle, the place where God made his presence known among the people. The reason was that if they did, they would bear a sin that would bring death. The word "testimony" refers to the tablets of the law kept there.

God speaks to Aaron, the priest. After Korah's rebellion and the death of many people, God organizes the holy service. The Levites would attend the tabernacle and bear the responsibility. In exchange, they would receive the tithes as their support, because they would have no land of their own. In this way the people were protected from approaching what was holy without proper care.

Today we learn that God is holy and deserves reverence. Christians believe that Christ opened the way for us to draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). Even so, we can come to God with gratitude and respect, not with carelessness.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that Joshua and Caleb spoke to the whole company of the children of Israel. They declared that the land they had passed through to search it was an exceedingly good land. The word "search" means to explore or examine it closely.

The speakers are Joshua and Caleb, two of the twelve men sent to explore Canaan. Ten of the spies had given a report full of fear, and the people wanted to rebel and return to Egypt. Moses and Aaron had fallen on their faces, and Joshua and Caleb, with their clothes torn in grief, tried to encourage the people to trust God.

Today we can learn that seeing a situation with faith does not mean denying the problems, but remembering that God is with us. When everyone around you speaks of fear, you can be a voice of trust, calm and respectful.
exp.21:19:
This verse tells how God came to Balaam at night. He told him that if those men came to call him, he could get up and go with them, but he would have to do only what God said. The words "came" and "said" in the old wording are simply the ordinary words "came" and "said" as they appear in the verse above.

Balak, king of Moab, wanted Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam had already said that he could not go against the word of God, but he asked to wait for another answer. God allows the journey with one condition. However, the text that follows says that God's anger was kindled because Balaam was going. Many think his heart was not sincere, though the text does not fully explain this.

For today: it is not enough to seek God's permission for what we already want to do. It is wise to ask him humbly and to obey him from the heart, even when his answer does not match our desires.
exp.3:32:
This verse sums up the work of the sons of Merari, one of the three families of the Levites. Their service in the tabernacle, called "of the testimony" because it held the tablets of the law, was to carry and look after the structural parts. They did all of it under the direction of Ithamar, son of the priest Aaron. The "bases" were the sockets on which the pillars rested.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. He explains how to organize the moving of the tabernacle. Each Levite family receives a specific task, and the Merarites carry the heaviest things: boards, bars, pillars and pegs. They had a supervisor who gave direction and responsibility.

For today: not all service to God is visible or striking. There are simple tasks, such as tidying, cleaning or helping, that sustain the life of the church. Do yours faithfully, knowing that God values it.
exp.4:24:
This verse says the priest will receive the offering of jealousy (a grain offering) from the woman's hand. The priest will wave it, that is, lift it up and move it before God as a gesture of presenting it to Him, and then he will bring it to the altar.

God gives this instruction to Moses for Israel. It was a procedure for when a husband suspected unfaithfulness and there were no witnesses. In this way the case was not settled by revenge or gossip, but by placing it before God. Scholars explain this rite in different ways, and it is not a practice commanded for today.

For today: when you feel suspicion or jealousy, do not accuse or judge hastily. Bring your concern to God in prayer, and afterward seek an honest and fair conversation.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that first Aaron and his sons, the priests, were to cover the sanctuary and all its furnishings when the camp was about to move. Only after that could the sons of Kohath come in to carry those objects. But they were forbidden to touch the holy things, because they would die.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. At that moment he arranges the work of each Levite family. The priests prepared the holy things, and the Kohathites only carried them. In this way it was taught that God is holy and that he must be approached with respect and in the order he himself established.

For today: draw near to God with reverence, without taking lightly what belongs to him. And serve gladly in the place that is yours, without wanting to do something that does not correspond to you. Christ now opens the way to God for us, but respect remains important.
exp.19:12:
This verse is a comment from the narrator. It says that the place would be remembered as "the waters of contention," that is, the waters of dispute or quarrel, because the people complained against God. The word "strove" means that they argued or fought with him. The phrase about God being sanctified among them means that God showed himself to be holy, and that his authority was to be respected.

Israel had no water in the desert, and the people complained harshly against Moses and Aaron. God provided water from the rock, but Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it, and God said that they had not trusted him or honored him before the people. For this reason they would not enter the promised land. Some think the sin was disobedience; others, anger or unbelief.

When something is lacking, we can bring it to God with trust and honesty, without grumbling or acting in anger. He cares for us, and obeying him with humility honors his name before others.
exp.22:14:
Here Balaam asks Balak to stand still beside his burnt offering, the offering burned on the altar. Meanwhile, Balaam withdraws to meet the Lord, that is, to wait for God to speak to him. The word "yonder" refers to a place set apart, away from the altar.

Balaam is the speaker, the prophet whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. This is the second attempt, now on the top of Pisgah. Balak believes that by changing location and offering sacrifices he will get God to change His mind. But God Himself comes to meet Balaam and gives him the message he must carry.

For today: God is not managed by rituals or by changing the setting. Before we speak or decide, let us seek with humility to hear what He actually says, even when it is not what others want to hear.
exp.17:9:
This verse says that the most holy offerings were to be eaten "in the holy place," that is, in a place set apart for God. It says that "every male" of the priestly family could eat of them, and that they were "a holy thing," set apart for God and given to the priests. The word "shalt eat" is an older way of speaking to Aaron and his descendants.

God speaks to Aaron after a time of complaint and judgment among the people. He makes clear that the priests and the Levites would receive no inheritance of land, so they would live from the offerings of the people. That food was God's provision, but it also had to be treated with respect, because it came from what was dedicated to Him.

Today we can learn to receive with gratitude and reverence what God gives us. We can also support generously those who serve in the church, and take care that what is dedicated to God is used with honesty and respect.
exp.34:27:
This verse says that the person who killed someone without meaning to had to stay and live in his city of refuge until the high priest died. "High priest" is the chief priest, and "slayer" is the one who caused a death. When the high priest died, that person could return to his land and his possession.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected the one who killed without intention, so that the avenger of blood would not kill him without a trial. At the same time, they took the value of life seriously. Why the death of the high priest marked the end is explained in several ways, and the text does not fully clarify it.

For today: God joins justice with mercy. We can learn to respect limits, accept the consequences of our mistakes, and trust that God offers protection and a path of restoration.
exp.17:29:
It says that when the Levites set apart the best part of the tithes they received from the people, to give to God, that tithe will be counted to them as if it were their own harvest. "Threshingfloor" is the place where grain was beaten to separate it from the husk, and "winepress" is where the grapes were trodden to produce the wine. That is to say, their portion is worth as much as the produce of a farmer.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses must tell this to the Levites. They did not receive land as an inheritance; they lived on the tithes of the people. Even so, they too were to give God a tenth of what they received, and the best of it, for the priest Aaron.

For today: God expects us to give our best, not the leftovers, even when we live on what others give us. If today you receive a salary or some help, be thankful and give generously and willingly, knowing that God looks at the heart.
exp.11:7:
God says that he speaks with Moses "mouth to mouth," that is, directly and up close. "Plainly" means clearly, and "not in riddles" means without hard puzzles or hidden symbols. Moses will also "behold the form of the Lord," an expression that speaks of a special closeness, though the text does not explain in detail what he saw. God ends with a question: how was it that they were not afraid to speak against his servant?

God himself speaks. Miriam and Aaron had criticized Moses and compared themselves to him, saying that God also spoke through them. God calls them to the tent of meeting and makes clear that Moses has a unique place, since he is faithful in all his house. Shortly afterward, Miriam is left leprous.

For today: let us watch our words about those who serve God, and avoid envy. If something troubles us, it is better to raise it with humility and respect, and to lay the matter before God.
exp.14:36:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and it prepares what follows. The name "Lord" is God's name, and the phrase "spake unto" means "spoke to." Here God is going to give a new instruction.

God speaks, and Moses is the one who receives the message for the people. Just before this, a man had openly disobeyed the Sabbath and was punished. Then comes the command to put tassels with a blue cord on the edges of their clothing, so that Israel would remember the commandments and not be led astray by their own desires.

God speaks to us so that we will obey him. Today we can create simple reminders, such as a verse on a phone or a prayer at the start of the day, so that we do not live led only by what we feel or see.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that the people of Israel waited for the cloud to move. If the cloud stayed over the tabernacle for two days, a month, or a year, they remained camped and did not move on. But when the cloud was lifted up, they set out on their journey. The word "journeyed" in the verse means that they took down the camp and started moving.

The book of Numbers tells the story of Israel's journey through the wilderness. Here the narrator explains how God guided his people with the cloud, which was a sign of his presence. They did not decide when to advance or when to stop. The text wants to show their obedience to the word of the LORD, given through Moses.

For today: learn to wait and to move forward according to God's guidance, even when you do not understand his timing. You may be in a long season of waiting. Pray, seek his direction in the Bible, and trust that he knows when it is time to stay and when it is time to take the next step.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that the Israelite spies went toward the south of Canaan and came to Hebron. There lived Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, descendants of Anak, people of great stature and renown. It also clarifies that Hebron had been founded seven years before Zoan, a city in Egypt. The word "south" in the verse means the southern part of the land; the phrase about Hebron's founding is simply a note that it had been built seven years earlier.

The narrator is the writer of the book, who tells of the mission of the twelve spies sent by Moses to explore the promised land. They were to see whether the land was good and whether its inhabitants were strong. The detail about Zoan was a note for the readers, and it is not known with certainty why it is included; some believe it shows how ancient Hebron was.

For today: when God leads us toward a goal, we also see giants along the way. Looking honestly at obstacles is helpful, but it should not erase our confidence in God's promises.
exp.30:16:
Moses orders that all the male children be killed, along with the women who had known a man by lying with him. The phrase "known a man by lying with him" means they had already had sexual relations. The girls who had not would be left alive.

Moses is speaking, angry with the commanders of the Israelite army, after the war against Midian. According to the text, the Midianite women, on the advice of Balaam, led Israel into idolatry and immorality at Peor, and many people died. The passage presents this as God's judgment on Midian. It is a very harsh text, and Christians understand it in different ways.

For today: this passage does not authorize any violence in our time. It reminds us that sin has serious consequences, and that God is the judge. And Jesus teaches us to love our enemies and to pray for them.
exp.4:13:
It says that a husband may be overcome by a "spirit of jealousy," that is, a strong suspicion or distrust toward his wife. The phrase is repeated with two possibilities: that she has in fact been unfaithful, or that she has not. In both cases, the husband feels jealous and has no proof.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. There were no witnesses, and this law set up a process before the priest, rather than letting the husband act on his own. In this way the wife was protected from unjust accusations, and judgment was left in God's hands.

For today: jealousy can cloud our judgment even without proof. Instead of accusing or acting in anger, let us bring those suspicions to God in prayer and speak with honesty and patience.
exp.25:58:
This verse says that Amram's wife was named Jochebed, and that she was the daughter of Levi. She was born in Egypt. With Amram she had Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam. The word "bare" in the verse means "gave birth to."

This is not the account of a single character; it is the record in Numbers of the census of Israel before entering the promised land. The Levites and their lineage are mentioned to make clear who Aaron and Moses descended from. The phrase "daughter of Levi" can be understood as a descendant of Levi, not necessarily a direct daughter, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God uses ordinary families and little-mentioned people, like Jochebed, to accomplish great purposes. Your faithfulness at home, though no one notices, can shape those whom God uses in the future.
exp.31:14:
Moses says that if the sons of Reuben and Gad turn away from following the LORD, God will again leave all Israel in the wilderness. The phrase "turn away from after him" means to stop following him. And "destroy all this people" means that their decisions would bring ruin on everyone.

Moses speaks with anger and concern. These two tribes wanted to stay east of the Jordan because there was good pasture there for their livestock. Moses feared that, by not crossing over with the others, they would discourage the people, as happened with the previous generation, which died in the wilderness because of its unbelief.

For today: our personal decisions also affect others. Before choosing what suits us, let us ask whether we are helping or hindering those who walk with us in the faith.
exp.6:86:
This verse adds up the animal offerings that the twelve tribes brought for the dedication of the altar. For the burnt offering there were twelve bulls, twelve rams and twelve one-year-old lambs, along with their grain offering. In addition, there were twelve male goats for the sin offering, that is, for the forgiveness of sin. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole for God.

It is part of the account in Numbers 7, written in the third person. Each tribal leader brought the same offering over twelve days, and here the total is given. God does not complain about the repetition: each tribe is taken into account. Afterward, Moses hears the voice of God from above the mercy seat, which shows that God accepted the offering.

For today: everyone can give something to God, and no one is left out. Ask yourself what you can offer sincerely, whether your time, your service or your help to others, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.3:5:
This verse describes how the ark of the testimony was to be covered for transport. Over the veil that already covered it, they were to put a layer of skins (the word translated "badgers' skins" is of uncertain meaning; some think of skins of sea animals or fine leather). On top of that they spread a cloth wholly of blue, the color of deep blue or violet. Last, they put in the staves, which were used to carry it.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving instructions to the Kohathites, a family of Levites. When Israel broke camp in the wilderness, Aaron and his sons covered the holy things first. Afterward, the Kohathites carried them without touching them. Everything showed that God is holy and that he must be approached with respect and order.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude, and serve him carefully in what he has entrusted to you, never treating what is sacred lightly.
exp.6:32:
This verse lists the animals that Eliab offered for the burnt offering: a young bull, a ram, and a lamb of the first year. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar, as a sign of total surrender to God.

This is a term the reader will not see in the verse, so it is simply noted here as the name of that other kind of offering.

Here it is not God speaking, but the narrator of the book. When the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering on a different day. Eliab, leader of the tribe of Gad, brought his on the sixth day. The text repeats each offering almost word for word, which shows that every tribe was taken into account equally.

For today: God values the complete surrender of the heart, not merely fulfilling an obligation. We can ask ourselves which parts of our lives, such as our time, our work, or our plans, we have not yet placed in his hands, and offer them with gratitude.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that the priest presents before God the offerings of the Nazirite: first the sin offering, and then the burnt offering, an animal given up entirely on the altar. The sin offering means covering a guilt so that the relationship with God is restored. The burnt offering expresses total surrender.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people. They relate to the end of the Nazirite vow, a person who set themselves apart for God for a period of time. When that time ended, they did not go alone: the priest presented their offerings. Even a very devoted life needed forgiveness and did not come before God on its own merit.

For today: although we serve God sincerely, we still need his grace. Christians see in Christ the complete offering. We can serve with devotion, but resting in his forgiveness, not in our own effort.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that the group of men from the tribe of Issachar, ready for war, numbered 54,400. The word "host" means army, and "those that were numbered" are the men who were counted, that is, recorded one by one.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai. He commands how Israel was to camp: each tribe in its place, around the tabernacle, under its leader. Issachar camped beside Judah, and its leader was Nethaneel. The numbers show a people who were organized, and the Bible does not explain every detail of the count here.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Each person counts and has a place. Think about where God has placed you, in your church, your family or your work, and serve there faithfully without comparing yourself to others.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that Moses was a very meek man, that is, humble, patient, and without any desire to defend himself. The Bible compares him with all the people of his time. The word "man" in this verse refers to a male human being, and the woman described in the passage is from Ethiopia or Cush, though some think she might have been another woman.

Miriam and Aaron, Moses' siblings, criticized him because of his wife and questioned his authority. This comment about Moses is usually understood as a note from the narrator: while they were speaking against him, Moses did not defend himself. It was God who heard them and acted. Some believe that Moses himself or a later editor added the phrase; the text does not make this clear.

Today, when someone criticizes us or doubts us, we can learn not to respond with anger or pride. We can pray, keep silent, and trust that God knows the truth and defends his people.
exp.16:1:
God tells Moses to speak to the people and to take twelve staffs, or rods: one for each father's house, given by its prince, that is, the head or leader of each tribe. Each leader was to write his name on his rod. The verse's comment about the old form "á" and "a" is removed, and "father's house" is explained in plain terms as the family or tribe.

God speaks to Moses after the rebellion of Korah and the people's complaints against Aaron. Many were asking who had the right to approach God as priest. God wants to give a clear sign that ends the argument and shows whom he has chosen.

For today: when jealousy or disputes arise about who has authority or a place in serving God, we can stop competing and trust that God knows whom he calls. Our task is to obey with humility the place he gives us.
exp.30:44:
This verse continues the list of the plunder that fell to the congregation of Israel. It says that, of the donkeys, thirty thousand and five hundred were given to them. Donkeys were pack animals, very useful for carrying loads and traveling.

It is a narrative account, not a speech. After defeating Midian, Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the leaders divided the plunder into two halves, between the soldiers and the rest of the people, just as God had commanded. From the portion of the people, one out of every fifty was set apart for the Levites, who took care of the tabernacle.

For today: this detail shows us that God cares about order, justice, and honesty in how we share what we receive. We can apply it by being fair at work, in the family, and in the church, and by gratefully setting aside a part of what we have to support the service of God and to help others.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that the priest will bring the suspected woman and stand her up in the presence of God. "Bring her near" means bringing her close to the holy place, and "before the Lord" means in the tabernacle, where God dwelt among his people.

God gives these instructions to Moses for Israel. It was a procedure for when a husband felt jealous and suspected unfaithfulness, but there were no witnesses. The case was not settled by personal revenge, but by bringing it before God. Scholars discuss how the rite worked in detail, and it has to be read within that ancient culture.

For today: when there are suspicions, jealousy, or wounds in relationships, do not act on impulse or with violence. First bring it before God in prayer, and seek wise and fair counsel before accusing anyone.
exp.3:36:
This verse closes the count of the Kohathites, one of the families of the Levites. It says that all who served in the tabernacle were numbered, which here is called the tabernacle of the congregation because it held the tablets of the law. Moses and Aaron took the count just as the Lord commanded. "By the hand of Moses" means that God gave the command through Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, traditionally credited to Moses. God had asked that the Levites of working age, from thirty to fifty years old, be counted so that the duties of the sanctuary could be assigned. The Kohathites were responsible for the most sacred objects, and the passage shows an orderly service, not an improvised one.

For today: God values faithful service, even the kind that goes unnoticed. Every task counts before Him when it is done in obedience. Serve where you have been entrusted, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.13:13:
Moses continues speaking with God. He says that the Egyptians will tell it to the inhabitants of Canaan. Those peoples had already heard that the Lord was among Israel, that he was seen face to face, and that his cloud stood over them. They also knew that God led them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire.

Israel had rebelled, believing the bad report of the spies. God said he would strike them with pestilence and make of Moses a nation greater than they. Moses intercedes for the people and appeals to God's reputation among the nations. He is concerned that his name would be dishonored.

When we pray for others, we can imitate Moses: come to God with humility, remember what he has already done, and ask that his name be honored. Interceding is not arguing with God, but trusting in his faithful and merciful character.
exp.30:47:
This verse tells us that the leaders of Israel's army came near to Moses. They were the officers over thousands, meaning those who commanded groups of a thousand soldiers, and also the captains of hundreds, who led smaller groups of one hundred. The word "captains" here refers to high-ranking officers.

Here the narrator is speaking, and those who come forward are the officers who had just returned from the war against Midian. Moses had already divided the spoil. Now these leaders come to make a report: not one of their men had died, and they want to present an offering to God.

For today: the leaders did not claim the victory for themselves or treat it as a prize of their own. They returned to God with gratitude. When something goes well in your life, take a moment to thank him and share generously what you have received.
exp.0:2:
God commanded that all the men of Israel from twenty years old and upward, those able to go out to war, be counted. Moses and Aaron were to carry out that count. The word "companies" refers to organized groups or divisions of an army, that is, the divisions within each tribe. The phrase "thou and Aaron shall number them" means that the two of them would take the census.

The LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, a year after leaving Egypt. The people were already arranged around the tabernacle and would soon march toward the promised land. The census served to put the people in order, to know what forces they had, and to prepare the way. They were counted by families and tribes, and each tribe would have a leader to help.

For today: God is a God of order, and he cares for each person. We can carefully organize our lives, families, and church, and take up with responsibility the task that is ours, knowing that our place matters.
exp.25:41:
This verse lists the descendants of Dan, son of Jacob. It mentions only Shuham, from whom comes the family of the Shuhamites. The verse says "after their families" because the people were organized by clans. Shuham is the same name that appears as Husim in Genesis 46:23, although it is not known for certain why the form changes.

God commands Moses and Eleazar to take this census at the end of the forty years in the desert. The previous generation had died, and the people were about to enter the promised land. The census served to organize the people and to divide the land according to the size of each family.

For today: God knows each family and each person by name. Even when we sometimes feel small or little noticed, He does not forget us. Today you can thank Him for your family and pray for it by name.
exp.4:11:
God tells Moses to speak to the people of Israel about a specific case: when a married woman goes astray, becoming unfaithful and betraying her husband. This is the opening of a law that continues in the verses that follow.

The Lord speaks, and Moses is the messenger. This passage deals with what is called the law of jealousy, for situations where the husband suspects unfaithfulness but there are no witnesses. Scholars debate how to understand the ritual that comes after, but the context shows that God wanted the people to settle these doubts before Him and not through violence or revenge.

For today: faithfulness and trust are very precious in marriage. If there are doubts or wounds, it is wise to seek God and speak honestly, without hidden accusations or revenge.
exp.10:16:
God tells Moses that He Himself will come down to speak with him beside the tent of meeting. He will take some of the Spirit that is already on Moses and place it on the seventy elders. In this way they will share with him the weight of the people, and Moses will no longer be alone.

God is speaking, answering Moses. The people were complaining again, asking for meat and longing for Egypt. Moses, worn out, had said he could not carry everything and even asked to die. God does not rebuke him here, but gives him concrete help: companions who will share the work.

For today: no one is called to carry everything alone. If you are exhausted from serving, ask God for His help and let others walk alongside you. Sharing the load is not weakness; it is part of God's care.
exp.9:5:
When the silver trumpets sound a signal of alarm the second time, the tribes camped on the south side (the "midday" side) are to break camp and set out. "Alarm" here does not mean danger; it is a strong, broken blast that served as a signal. "Journeys" refers to the trips or departures.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and gives him instructions for guiding Israel by means of trumpets. First the tribes from the east set out, then those from the south. In this way the people, who were a very large company, moved in order and not in confusion. The priests, the sons of Aaron, sounded the trumpets.

For today: God is a God of order and of clear guidance. We can learn to be attentive to his voice, especially in times of change, and to move when he indicates, neither rushing ahead nor falling behind.
exp.4:12:
This verse describes a situation in which a married woman might have had sexual relations with another man in secret. Her husband did not see it, there are no witnesses, and she was not caught in the act. The phrase that refers to sexual relations is not repeated here, and the phrase meaning caught while it was happening is also left out, since the verse above already makes clear that no one saw it.

God speaks to Moses to give an instruction to the people of Israel. This law deals with the case of a husband who feels jealous and suspects unfaithfulness, but has no proof. What follows in the chapter is a procedure before the priest, rather than the man acting on his own. Scholars understand some details of this ritual in different ways.

For today: suspicions without proof can destroy a marriage. Instead of accusing or letting jealousy carry us away, it is wise to seek the truth calmly, speak honestly, and bring the matter before God.
exp.0:27:
This verse begins the count of the men of the tribe of Issachar. They are counted by their generations, their families, and their fathers' houses, that is, according to their lineage. Only men from twenty years old and upward who were able to go to war are included. The phrase "according to the number of the names" means that each man was recorded by his name.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commands him to take this census of Israel shortly after leaving Egypt. The count served to organize the people as an orderly army. After this verse the total for Issachar is given: 54,400 men. The figures are repeated tribe by tribe, and there are different views on how those numbers should be understood.

For today: God knows and counts each person. No one is a lost number before Him. Serve where God has placed you, trusting that your place matters.
exp.0:37:
This verse describes the counting of the tribe of Dan. The men twenty years old and upward who were able to go to war were counted, organized by their families and by their fathers' households. "According to the number of the names" means that each man was recorded by his name. According to the next verse, Dan's total was 62,700.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the departure from Egypt. He commands him to count Israel, tribe by tribe, so that the people could be arranged like an army on the march. Each tribe had its place, and Dan was the second most numerous.

For today: God knows and counts each person, not an anonymous crowd. You have a place among his people and something to contribute. Ask yourself today what you can do, with your family and your church, to serve faithfully where God has placed you.
exp.35:3:
It says that when the Year of Jubilee comes, the land of Zelophehad's daughters will pass to the tribe of their husbands, if they marry men from another tribe. In this way, that land would no longer return to their original tribe.

The leaders of the families of Gilead, from the tribe of Manasseh, speak here. Earlier, God had commanded that Zelophehad's daughters should inherit, because their father had no sons. Now these leaders fear that, if the daughters marry men from other tribes, the land of their tribe will become smaller. They are concerned to protect the portion God assigned to them. Moses later confirms that they are right.

For today: God calls us to take responsible care of what He has entrusted to us, whether family, work, or possessions. Before making a decision, it is wise to think about the consequences and to seek His guidance with humility.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that the tribes of Gad and Reuben came to Moses, to the priest Eleazar, and to the leaders of the people to present a request. The word "á" is an old form of writing "to," and "princes" refers to the heads or leaders of the tribes, while "congregation" refers to all the people of Israel.

Israel was camped east of the Jordan, before entering the promised land. Gad and Reuben had a great deal of livestock, and they saw that the lands of Jazer and Gilead were good for pasture. That is why they speak before all the gathered authority, not only to Moses. Later it will be seen that their request caused concern, because it seemed they did not want to cross over with their brothers.

For today: when you have a desire or a plan, present it openly and before wise people. In this way intentions are made clear and unity with others is protected.
exp.27:19:
This verse says that, along with the animals for the sacrifice, the people were to bring a grain offering: fine flour mixed with oil. For each bull, three tenth parts (a tenth was a measured portion of an ephah, about two liters, though estimates vary); for each ram, two tenth parts. The word translated here as "offering" refers to a grain offering, and the flour was to be mixed with oil.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, who were close to entering the promised land. The offerings for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which followed the Passover, are explained. Everything was to be done in order, as a sign of gratitude and of fellowship with God.

For today: God values our giving Him the best of what He has already given us, with order and gratitude. We can set apart time, talent, or money for Him consistently, rather than leaving it to chance or to whatever is left over.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that God commands Moses to speak to the people: if anyone was unclean because he had touched a dead person, or was on a journey far away, he could still keep the Passover later. "Unclean" means impure under the ceremonial law, and "descendants" shows that this rule would also apply to their children.

Some men, made unclean by caring for a corpse, were unable to keep the Passover on time and asked what they should do. Moses waited for God's answer instead of improvising. God responded with a second opportunity: to keep it one month later, with the same rites.

For today: God makes room for those who feel left out or arrive late. If you feel far away or at a disadvantage, do not stay silent; come to God with your question, as these men did, and also make room for others.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that Moses accepted the wagons and the oxen that the leaders of Israel offered, and gave them to the Levites.

God told Moses to receive this offering for the work of the tabernacle, and to distribute it according to the task of each group. The wagons were used to carry the parts of the sacred tent. The sons of Gershon and of Merari received wagons and oxen because their burden was heavier. Moses did not keep anything for himself, nor did he divide it out of favoritism, but according to the ministry of each one.

For today: God distributes resources according to the need of each task, not according to how important we consider it. If you manage something in your church or in your family, do it with honesty and fairness, giving each person what they need to fulfill their calling.
exp.19:16:
Moses, speaking on behalf of Israel, asks the king of Edom for permission to cross his land. He promises not to pass through the fields or the vineyards, nor to drink from the water of the wells. He says they will go by the king's highway, the main public road, and will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left, until they have passed beyond his borders.

Moses sends messengers from Kadesh. Israel was on its way to Canaan, and crossing Edom would shorten the journey. Edom descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, so Moses speaks of kinship and recalls what God had done in Egypt. Even so, Edom refused.

When we ask for something, it is good to do so with respect, clarity, and a commitment not to cause harm. And if we are told no, we can learn to accept it with patience, trusting that God still guides our path.
exp.15:44:
God tells Moses and Aaron to step away from the people, because he wants to destroy them in an instant. Moses and Aaron fall facedown on the ground, as a sign of humility and of pleading.

The LORD speaks. The people have just complained against Moses and Aaron after the rebellion of Korah, and God had already judged the ringleaders. Even so, the congregation accused them of killing the LORD's people. That is why this judgment comes. Moses and Aaron do not respond in anger but lie prostrate, and right away Aaron makes atonement with the censer.

For today: when others offend us or rebel, we can imitate Moses and Aaron. Instead of defending ourselves or wishing for their punishment, we can humble ourselves before God and pray for them.
exp.22:5:
It says that Balaam returned to Balak after receiving a word from God. He found him standing by his burnt sacrifice, which was the whole burnt offering placed on the altar. There stood Balak and all the princes of Moab, that is, the leaders or nobles of the land, waiting to hear what Balaam would say.

The speaker here is the narrator. Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel, because he was afraid of them. Balaam prepared altars and sacrifices, but God himself put into his mouth what he was to say. For that reason what follows will not be a curse but a blessing. Scholars debate how sincere Balaam was, but the Bible clearly shows that God directs the message.

For today: No one can change what God has blessed. When you feel threatened by harsh words or pressure from others, remember that God is faithful to his own. Rest in him and make it your practice to speak only what is true and good.
exp.21:35:
When King Balak heard that Balaam was coming, he went out in person to meet him. He received him in a city of Moab, beside the Arnon River, at the edge of his territory.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and wanted Balaam to curse them. He had already sent messengers to him twice. Earlier, God had told Balaam to go, but to say only what God told him. That the king went out to the border shows how much he wanted this favor. Some see here also an attempt to impress or pressure Balaam.

For today: when others try to pressure or flatter us into changing our course, let us remember that our loyalty is to God. Let us ask Him for firmness to say and do only what He approves.
exp.32:38:
This verse says that Aaron was one hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on mount Hor. The phrase "was of the age of" means "was," and his age is recorded as a precise detail at the end of his life.

Here the narrator speaks, reviewing the stages of Israel's journey through the wilderness. Aaron, the first high priest, died there by the command of the LORD, as the previous passage tells. Numbers 20 explains that he would not enter the promised land, and connects this with what happened at the waters of Meribah. His death took place in the fortieth year, when the new generation was already drawing near to Canaan.

For today: our years are numbered, and God continues his work even when his servants depart. Let us serve faithfully in the time we are given, and trust that God cares for what comes after us.
exp.13:39:
It says that the people rose up early and went up to the top of the mountain. There they said: "Here we are, ready to go up to the place God promised, because we have sinned." The words "lo, we be here" mean "here we are," and "top" is the highest part of the mountain.

The Israelites had refused to enter the land out of fear, and God said that that generation would not enter. When they heard it, they wept. Now, suddenly, they want to go in on their own. They admit their sin, but Moses warns them that God will not go with them. Their repentance seems more like an attempt to fix things their own way than a true submission to God. The text does not describe what was in their hearts, but their actions show that they still are not obeying.

For today: recognizing a mistake is not enough if we then follow our own plan. Obeying God includes doing it in his time and in his way, trusting his guidance and not only our own effort.
exp.6:37:
In the offering of Shelumiel, it says there was one golden dish weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" here refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned before God. The "dish" was a small container, like a cup or saucer, not a utensil for eating.

The book of Numbers tells that when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribe brought its offering on a different day. The fifth day belonged to Shelumiel, prince of Simeon. The account, traditionally attributed to Moses, repeats the same gifts for each tribe. In this way it shows that all of them were given equal honor before God.

God values the sincere devotion of each person, no matter whether it seems repeated or unremarkable. Today you can offer him your steady service, your time, and your prayer with faithfulness, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.26:9:
This verse is part of a list of rules about who receives an inheritance when someone dies. It says that if the one who died had no children, neither son nor daughter, and no brothers, the inheritance passes to the brothers of his father, that is, to his uncles. The word "give" in the verse means to hand over, and the "inheritance" is the property and land that belonged to the family.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell Israel. This follows the case of the daughters of Zelophehad, who asked to inherit because their father had no sons. God agreed with them and set out a clear order so that the land would remain within each family and tribe.

Today we can learn that order and justice also protect the family. One practical application is to make clear, with a simple will, what you want to happen with your property, to avoid disputes and to care for those you love.
exp.9:22:
This verse says that Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, was the leader of the group of the tribe of Manasseh when the people set out on the march. The word "host" here means the whole body of men from that tribe, organized for the journey.

Moses gives these instructions while Israel leaves Mount Sinai on the way to the promised land. Everything was put in order: first the Kohathites with the sanctuary, then the standard of Ephraim, with Manasseh and Benjamin in that same group. Each tribe had its leader by name, so that the march would be orderly and no one would be lost.

For today: God notices each person and each task, even those that seem small. Do faithfully what is yours to do, whether at home, at work, or in the church, and trust that God sees your service.
exp.6:68:
This verse lists part of the offering of one of Israel's leaders: a young bullock (a young bull), a ram, and a lamb of the first year, all for a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was entirely burned on the altar as a sign of total surrender to God.

The book of Numbers tells that, when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering on a different day. Here it is Ahiezer, of the tribe of Dan, who presents the same as the others, with the same objects and animals. The account is not hurried: it repeats each offering to show that God values each tribe equally and receives with care what each one gives him.

For today: God never tires of seeing the devotion of each person. Your service does not need to be different from or greater than that of others; it is enough that it is sincere and complete. Offer him today what is yours with all your heart.
exp.6:47:
This verse says that on the seventh day it was the turn of Elishama, son of Ammihud, to present his offering. He was the "prince," that is, the leader or head of the tribe of Ephraim. The name "Ephraim" is simply the tribe of Ephraim, spelled in an older form.
