Moses is recording how the tabernacle, Israel's place of worship, was dedicated. Each day a leader of one tribe brought the same offering, and the account repeats it in full each time. This showed that all the tribes took part equally, with no tribe placed above another. The text then goes on to list what Elishama brought.

For today: God cares about real, specific people, and here the name of each leader appears. Our service, even when it seems repetitive or simple, does not go unnoticed by Him. Today you can give faithfully what falls to you, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.15:7:
Moses speaks again to Korah and asks him to listen along with the other Levites. Moses's words here are a request for attention, and the verse opens with a direct call to listen. "Sons of Levi" refers to the descendants of Levi, the tribe that God had set apart to serve in the tabernacle. It is a call to attention before a serious rebuke.

Korah and his group had rebelled against Moses and Aaron, because they also wanted the priesthood. Moses proposes that God himself will decide the matter the next day with the censers. Then he firmly reminds them of the honor they already had as Levites.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we value the place God has given us. Sometimes, out of wanting more recognition, we stop being thankful for what we have already received. Serving with humility and gratitude pleases God more than seeking the first place.
exp.5:12:
This verse begins the instructions for the end of the Nazirite vow. A "Nazirite" was someone set apart for God for a period of time, and the vow is that time of dedication. When the days were fulfilled, the person was to be brought "unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation," that is, to the entrance of the tent where God dwelt among his people.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses must pass the rules on to Israel. The Nazirite lived apart: he did not drink wine, did not cut his hair, and avoided touching the dead. This verse marks the ordered close of the vow, with offerings before the priest, just after the rules about when the vow was made unclean.

For today: when we make a commitment to God, let us not leave it half-finished or in silence. Let us close that season by presenting ourselves before him with gratitude, recognizing that everything we did was by his grace.
exp.6:78:
Here the offering of Ahira is recorded: one silver dish weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, weighed by the measure of the sanctuary. Both were full of fine flour mixed with oil, as a grain offering. One shekel weighed about 11 grams, although estimates vary.

The account in Numbers tells how each tribal leader brought his offering to dedicate the altar of the tabernacle, one leader per day over twelve days. Ahira, of the tribe of Naphtali, was the last. Although each offering is repeated in the same way, the text does not shorten them: God takes note of each one.

For today: do not belittle what you give to God because others give the same or more. He values every offering, service, or prayer made with faithfulness. Offer him what is yours with care, without comparing yourself.
exp.18:21:
This verse says that if an unclean person touches something, that object also becomes unclean. And if another person touches that object, that person is unclean until evening. The word "unclean" in this sense means impure according to the law, that is, not fit to approach worship. It does not speak of physical dirt, but of a ceremonial condition.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about the rules of purification after contact with death, with the rite of the ashes of the red heifer mixed with water. These laws taught Israel that God is holy and that whatever is connected with death cannot come near his presence without being cleansed. Interpreters explain the exact symbolism of the rite in several different ways.

For today: our influences and contacts affect us. We can be careful about what we allow into our hearts and, when we fail, turn quickly to God to be cleansed, knowing that Christ offers complete forgiveness.
exp.20:17:
This verse is part of a song that Israel sang at the well of Beer. It says the well was dug by the princes and nobles of the people, together with the lawgiver, whom some understand to be the one who leads or rules. They did it "with their staves," that is, with their staffs or rods of office. Then it says the people continued their journey from the wilderness to Mattanah.

The people of Israel are traveling through the wilderness toward Canaan. God had promised water to Moses at Beer, and the people respond with a song of joy. We do not know for certain how the well was dug with staves; it may be a poetic image. What is clear is that the water comes as a provision from God.

Today we can remember that God cares for us, even in dry times. When He gives us something, it is good to stop and thank Him, perhaps with a prayer or a song, rather than moving on without noticing.
exp.21:30:
God allowed Balaam to see what he could not see before: the angel of the Lord standing in the road with his sword drawn. A drawn sword means a sword taken out of its sheath, ready for use. When he saw it, Balaam bowed low and fell with his face to the ground, a sign of respect and fear.

Balaam was a prophet hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel. He was on his way, even though God had already warned him. The donkey had seen the angel and kept turning aside, but Balaam, angry, kept beating her without understanding. Here the narrator shows that the problem was not the animal, but Balaam's blindness.

For today: when things get blocked for us, before we get angry at others, let us ask God to open our eyes. Perhaps He is stopping us in order to correct us.
exp.6:60:
This verse says that Abidan, a leader of the tribe of Benjamin, presented a silver dish weighing 130 shekels and a silver bowl of 70 shekels. Both were full of fine flour mixed with oil, as a grain offering. The "shekel of the sanctuary" was the official unit of weight used in worship. In this verse, the grain offering is the gift of flour and oil. Fine flour is flour of the best quality.

Here the narrator of the book, who records the dedication of the tabernacle, speaks. Each day, a leader of one tribe brought exactly the same offering. In this way, Israel was dedicating the place where God dwelt among them. The text repeats everything in detail, which shows that God values each gift equally.

For today: give God your best, with consistency and without comparing yourself to others. Your sincere offering, whether large or small, has value before Him.
exp.33:0:
This verse is only an introduction. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses. The Lord is the name of God, and "spake unto" means "spoke to." It is the beginning of a new instruction.

Here God speaks, and Moses is the one who receives the message for the people. The Israelites are close to entering the promised land, after years in the wilderness. God is going to explain the boundaries of that land, so that they know clearly what he has given them as their inheritance. The verses that follow begin to describe those borders.

For today: God does not act blindly, but speaks and gives clear direction. Before moving forward on an important decision, we can stop to listen to his voice in the Bible and in prayer. He keeps his promises, and he also helps us understand what he has entrusted to us.
exp.35:10:
This verse says that the five daughters of Zelophehad, named Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, married their first cousins on their father's side. The phrase "sons of their uncles" means cousins. The word "inheritance" refers to the land each family would receive.

The writer summarizes how what God commanded Moses was fulfilled. Zelophehad had no sons, and God allowed his daughters to inherit the land. The leaders of Manasseh feared that if they married men from another tribe, the land would pass to that tribe. For this reason they were asked to marry within their own tribe, and they obeyed.

For today: these women trusted in God's justice and also obeyed with a willing heart. We can learn to care for what God entrusts to us and to follow his guidance, even when it asks us to accept limits.
exp.10:21:
Moses asks whether the flocks and the herds could be slaughtered to satisfy so many people, or whether all the fish of the sea could be gathered together to provide enough. He sees the problem only with human arithmetic.

Moses speaks with God. The people were complaining about the manna and asking for meat, and God promised to give them meat for a whole month. Moses, burdened and discouraged, counts about six hundred thousand men on foot and cannot see how it could be possible. God answers: "Has the Lord's arm been shortened?"

When a need seems impossible to us, it is easy to look only at our own resources. We can be honest with God, as Moses was, but we can also remember that his power does not depend on our calculations. Let us trust that he knows how to fulfill what he promises.
exp.22:21:
It says that it was God himself who brought Israel out of Egypt, not they by their own strength. Furthermore, it compares God's power on behalf of his people to that of a wild ox. That old word translates the Hebrew "reem," which many today understand to be a wild bull or buffalo, a strong and fearsome animal.

The speaker is Balaam, a foreign prophet. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God allowed him only to bless it. Balaam acknowledges that he cannot revoke that blessing. There is debate about whether the "strength" refers to God or to Israel, but in either case the source of the power is God.

For today: when you feel weak or threatened, remember that your security does not depend on your strength, but on God, who rescued you and sustains you. Rest in his care and thank him for what he has already done for you.
exp.31:11:
This verse says that, of that whole generation that came out of Egypt, only Caleb and Joshua were spared from the punishment. "Wholly followed the Lord" means they followed God completely, with a whole heart and without holding back.

Here Moses is speaking. He reminds the tribes of Reuben and Gad of what happened when Israel refused to enter the promised land out of fear and lack of faith. Moses worries that they, by wanting to stay on the far side of the Jordan, will discourage the people and repeat that same sin.

For today: following God with all your heart matters more than following the majority. Ask Him to give you steady faithfulness, even when others doubt or turn back.
exp.12:29:
This verse lists the peoples the spies saw in Canaan. The Amalekites lived in the south. The Hittites, Jebusites and Amorites lived in the hill country. The Canaanites lived by the sea and along the banks of the Jordan River.

The twelve spies, sent by Moses to explore the land, return and report to the people. Here speak the ones who give the discouraging report. They say the land is good, but they focus on the peoples who live there and on how strong they are. Afterward Caleb will call for trusting God and moving forward.

For today: describing a problem honestly is not wrong, but be careful that your list of obstacles does not grow larger than your trust in God. Before giving up, remember what He has promised and ask Him for courage.
exp.21:7:
Balaam asks the messengers to lodge there that night. He promises to bring them back word of the answer, just as the Lord (Jehovah) speaks to him. "Lodge" means "stay the night," and "bring word" means "tell." The princes of Moab stay with him.

Balaam is a man known for his blessings and curses. Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and sent messengers with payment to have him curse them. Balaam says he will wait for God's word, and that sounds good. However, God had already shown His will toward Israel, and later the Bible shows that Balaam's heart was not so clean. Some see prudence here; others see hesitation.

Before deciding, let us seek the voice of God. But if we already know what He thinks, we should not keep asking in search of another answer that suits us.
exp.31:26:
This verse says that the men of Gad and Reuben, all ready to fight, will cross the Jordan River before the Lord to enter the war, just as Moses asked. "Servants" here means themselves, speaking respectfully. The phrase "to the war" is what the verse says, and "my lord" refers to Moses.

The sons of Gad and Reuben are speaking. They wanted to keep the lands of Gilead, east of the Jordan, because they were good for their livestock. Moses complained that they would leave their brothers alone, and they promised to help in the conquest before settling down.

For today: keeping what we promise and not seeking only our own comfort. If we receive blessings, we should also accompany and support others in their struggles.
exp.31:17:
The passage says that the men of Reuben and Gad will not return to their houses until every family of the other tribes of Israel has received its land. "Inheritance" means the portion of land that belonged to each family.

The tribes of Reuben and Gad speak. They had a great deal of livestock and liked the land east of the Jordan. Moses feared they would leave their brothers alone. So they promise to build shelters for their families, but to go armed before Israel until everyone has their place.

For today: it is not enough to look after what is mine while my brothers are still fighting. We can ask ourselves whom we can help before we rest. Keeping a promise and serving others, even when it costs us, shows a faithful heart.
exp.30:30:
It says that Moses and Eleazar the priest carried out exactly what God had commanded them. It refers to dividing the plunder taken in the war against Midian: one part for the priest as an offering to the Lord, and another part, taken from half of the people, for the Levites. The phrase about doing as the Lord commanded is an old-fashioned way of saying they obeyed to the letter.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator. He tells that Israel's leaders followed the instructions given earlier about the spoils. After the battle, what had been taken had to be divided in an orderly and fair way, recognizing that God was to receive his share and that the Levites, who cared for the tabernacle, were to be supported.

For today: obeying God in concrete matters, even practical ones such as money or resources. We can ask ourselves whether we are honestly and orderly carrying out what God has already told us in his Word.
exp.3:9:
God commands that the lampstand and all its utensils be wrapped in a covering of badgers' skins and placed on a carrying frame, a kind of litter with poles for carrying. The meaning of the word translated "badgers" is uncertain; some think of another animal or of fine leather.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about the service of the sons of Kohath, of the tribe of Levi. When the people moved through the desert, they were to carry the holy things of the tabernacle, but without touching them. Everything was covered with care, because it belonged to God.

For today: treat what belongs to God with respect and order, such as his Word, your time of prayer, and your service to others. Doing it with care and without carelessness shows that you value it.
exp.25:10:
This verse says that, although Korah died for rebelling against Moses and Aaron, his children did not die. The word that opens the sentence in the original means "but." It is a short phrase, yet it shows that the punishment did not reach everyone in that family.

We are at the second census of Israel, at the end of the forty years in the desert. The text is a kind of record that summarizes the story. It recalls the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, which ended in judgment (Numbers 16). The text does not explain why the children were spared. Perhaps they did not take part in the rebellion, but the text does not say so. Later on, descendants of Korah appear serving in worship and in the Psalms.

For today: our mistakes can affect others, but God does not judge us by what our family did. Each person can walk with God and begin again.
exp.12:23:
The explorers came to the valley, or brook, of Eshcol and cut down a branch of a vine with a cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it hanging from a pole. They also gathered pomegranates and figs. A vine's branch-and-grape stem is called here the shoot of the vine, and the word for exploring here means to scout out the land.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moses had sent twelve men, one from each tribe, to scout out Canaan, the land God promised to Israel. They were to see what the place was like and what its people were like. The cluster served as proof that the land was fertile, just as God had said. Afterward, however, most of the people doubted, for they saw the obstacles more than the promise.

For today: God keeps what He promises, and sometimes He gives us small signs of it. Be thankful for those signs, but do not let fear of problems make you forget the faithfulness of God.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that the offerings were to be made according to the number of animals. If someone brought more than one, each animal's offering had to be prepared with the same measures just stated. The drink offering was wine poured out as part of the worship.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people of Israel. They were still in the wilderness, and God was giving them instructions for when they would enter the promised land. These rules gave order to the worship, and the verses that follow say they applied equally to the Israelite and to the foreigner who lived among them.

For today: God values being served with order, sincerity, and without neglecting anything. We can also learn to treat everyone with justice and without favoritism. Drawing near to God does not depend on our position, but on an obedient heart.
exp.5:19:
This verse says the priest will take the offerings that the Nazirite placed in his hands and wave them, that is, lift them up and move them before God as a solemn presentation. That portion then belongs to the priest, along with the breast and the shoulder (the foreleg) that also correspond to him. When this is finished, the Nazirite may drink wine again.

God speaks through Moses. A Nazirite was someone who made a special vow of consecration for a period of time: he did not drink wine, did not cut his hair, and avoided touching the dead. This verse describes the ceremonial close of that vow, when the promised time was complete.

For today: when you commit yourself to God, follow through on what you promised until the end, and take a moment to thank him. Finishing a dedication well is also a way of worshiping.
exp.6:34:
Elizur, leader of the tribe of Reuben, finished his offering with a "peace offering": two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of the first year. The word "peace offering" refers to the offering of fellowship or thanksgiving, and the male goats are fully grown goats. The text closes by saying that this was the offering of Elizur, son of Shedeur.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers, traditionally attributed to Moses, tells how each tribal leader, one each day, brought his offering for the dedication of the tabernacle. They all brought the same things, and the text repeats this with each name so that none is forgotten.

For today: God values each person, even when their contribution looks like someone else's. Today you can give with gratitude what is yours to give, without comparing yourself, knowing that God sees and remembers your devotion.
exp.20:14:
This verse describes how the waters of the streams run down through the ravines until they reach the area near Ar, a city of Moab, and stop at the Moabite border. "Border" means boundary or limit, and the verse's word "lieth" simply describes the stream lying along that edge.

The text appears to be a quotation from an ancient song, taken from the book of the wars of the LORD. That book is not known from other sources. The verse does not say who wrote it, and its Hebrew is difficult, so some details are translated in different ways. Here it is used to point to the Arnon River, the boundary between Moab and the Amorites, as Israel moved through the wilderness.

For today: Israel remembered in songs what God had done for them, as at the Red Sea. Write down some occasions when God helped you, and review them when you face a difficult road. Remembering strengthens trust.
exp.32:40:
This verse says that the people of Israel left mount Hor, where Aaron had died, and camped at a place called Zalmonah. It was not a city where they would stay, but just one more stop on the journey.

This is part of a list of the stages of Israel's journey from Egypt to the promised land. Moses wrote this record at God's command (Numbers 33:2) so that the people would remember each step. Locating Zalmonah precisely today is difficult, and scholars do not fully agree. What matters is that God was guiding the people even after a great loss, such as the death of Aaron.

For today: even after painful farewells, life goes on and God continues to guide. Take the next step with confidence, knowing that He cares for every stop along your path, including the ones that seem small.
exp.34:13:
This verse commands Israel to set apart six cities in total: three east of the Jordan River and three in the land of Canaan, to the west. They are called "cities of refuge," meaning cities of safety. A refuge is a place of protection or shelter.

God himself speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before the people entered the promised land. These cities protected anyone who killed someone without meaning to. In this way, the victim's relative could not take revenge right away, and the accused had a trial before the assembly. They also served the foreigner who lived among them.

For today: God values justice and mercy together. We can avoid judging others in haste, listen before we condemn, and offer help to someone who has stumbled.
exp.2:31:
This verse says that Eleazar, son of the priest Aaron, would be the chief over all the leaders of the Levites. The word "overseer" in the verse above is the word the old text used for this role. Eleazar's task was to watch over those who took care of the sanctuary, that is, the tent where God dwelt among his people.

God himself gives these instructions to Moses in the wilderness. The Levites were set apart to care for and carry the tabernacle. Each family had a task, and the Kohathites took care of the holy objects. Eleazar was placed over them all so that everything would be done with order and reverence.

For today: God cares about order and responsibility in serving him. If you have a responsibility, in the church, at home, or at work, do it with seriousness and humility, and support those who oversee it faithfully.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells how the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the south, heard that the people of Israel were coming along the road of the spies. Some believe this was a known route, though its exact name is uncertain. Then he attacked Israel and took some of them away as prisoners.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Numbers, traditionally Moses. Israel was traveling through the desert, near the promised land, after the death of Aaron. The attack came suddenly and caught them by surprise. As the text that follows shows, the people did not remain paralyzed: they asked God for help by making a vow.

For today: when an unexpected blow comes, even if you have suffered a loss, do not stay in discouragement. Bring your need to God with sincerity and trust that he listens, as he listened to Israel.
exp.25:5:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Reuben. It names two of his sons, Hezron and Carmi, and says that from each of them came a "family," that is, a clan. The Hezronites and the Carmites are simply the descendants of those men.

God speaks to Moses and to Eleazar the priest, after the plague that fell on the people in the wilderness. A new count is taken of the men twenty years old and above, fit for war, before entering the promised land. The previous generation had died, and this list set out the division of the land by families. The names show that God kept track of every clan.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. He knows names, families and stories. If today you feel small or overlooked, remember that your place is real before him. And value your own family and your church as part of God's plan.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that the person who had made the Nazirite vow, and became defiled, must dedicate again to God the time of his vow. He must bring a lamb of one year as a trespass offering, to make amends for his fault. The days he had already completed shall be lost, that is, they do not count; he must start over. The "Nazirite" period is the time of special consecration of the Nazirite.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people. A Nazirite set himself apart for God for a time, and had to avoid contact with a dead body. If someone died suddenly beside him, he became unclean. That is why the law provided a way of cleansing and a fresh beginning.

For today: if you fail in a commitment to God, do not stay buried in guilt. God offers forgiveness and the chance to begin again with a sincere heart.
exp.3:27:
This verse sums up the work of the descendants of Gershon, one of the three Levite families. They took care of the cloth coverings of the tabernacle, the curtains of the courtyard, and the cords. "Charge" means an assigned responsibility, and the phrase "under the hand of Ithamar" means under his direction and supervision. Ithamar was a son of the priest Aaron.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for organizing the service of the Levites in the wilderness. Each family had a specific task, and the Gershonites had theirs under priestly supervision. In this way, the care of the holy place was carried out with order and reverence.

For today: God values simple and unseen work when it is done faithfully. Serve where you have been entrusted, accept the guidance of others, and remember that no task is small if it is done for the Lord.
exp.32:45:
This verse says that the people of Israel left a place called Dibon-gad and camped in another called Almon-diblathaim. The word "departed" in the source refers to leaving, and the word meaning "camped" is the same as the verse's "encamped." It is one more stop on the journey through the wilderness.

Moses writes this list of campsites at God's command (Numbers 33:2) to remember the road traveled from Egypt. Here the people are already near the promised land, at the end of the forty years. Some details about these places are not known with certainty, but what matters is the record of each stage.

For today: God takes note of every step of your journey, even in days that seem ordinary or repeated. If today you feel like you are passing through, remember that He guides and remembers every stage. Take a moment to thank Him for the places where He has sustained you.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses while the people were in the wilderness of Sinai. It was the first month of the second year after they came out of Egypt. The word "saying" introduces an instruction that is about to follow. The name "LORD" is God's name, and the spelling used in some older Bibles is simply an older form of the modern word.

God speaks, and gives the message to Moses so that he will pass it on to Israel. They were at Sinai, where they had received the law and built the tabernacle. One year after leaving Egypt, God asks them to keep the Passover, which commemorated their deliverance. Some scholars note that this month comes before the census of the second month that opens this book, although the book does not follow a strictly chronological order.

God speaks to us with purpose and invites us to remember what he has done for us. Today we can set aside regular times, such as prayer, Bible reading, or the Lord's Supper, so that we do not forget his faithfulness.
exp.28:39:
1) What it says: The verse text arrived empty. In the Reina-Valera 1909 it usually reads: "And Moses told the children of Israel all that the Lord had commanded him." That is, Moses passed on to everyone the instructions he had received.

Context: The narrator of the book is speaking. Moses has just received from God the rules for Israel's feasts and offerings (chapters 28 and 29). This verse closes that section. Moses does not keep the instructions to himself, but faithfully hands them on to the people, so that they know how to worship God.

For today: When you learn something from the Word of God, do not keep it to yourself. Share it faithfully and humbly, without adding or removing anything, with your family or your friends.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that Moses did exactly what God commanded him. Moses put Aaron's staff back before the testimony, that is, in front of the ark where the tablets of the law were kept. He neither added nor removed anything.

Here the narrator recounts what happened after Aaron's staff budded, a sign that God had chosen him for the priesthood. The people had complained greatly against Moses and Aaron. God commanded that the staff be kept as a reminder for the rebellious, so that they would stop complaining and not die. Immediately afterward, the people react with fear.

For today: simple and complete obedience is a way of trusting God. Today you can ask yourself what God has asked of you in his Word that you have not yet done, and take one concrete step, without arguing or delaying it.
exp.9:34:
Every time the ark set out, Moses would pray aloud. He asked God to rise up, to scatter his enemies, and to make those who hated him flee before him. The phrase "when the ark set forward" describes the moment the ark began to move. "Scattered" means dispersed and spread apart.

Moses, the leader of Israel, speaks as the people begin their march from Mount Sinai into the wilderness. The ark of the covenant went at the front, as a sign that God was leading them. Moses recognizes that the journey faced opposition and that victory depended on God, not on the strength of the people. This prayer is repeated at the end with another request, when the ark came to rest.

Before taking an important step, we can begin with a simple prayer. Asking God to go before us, to guard us from what opposes us, and to guide us reminds us that we do not walk alone or depend only on ourselves.
exp.20:2:
God heard the cry of Israel and gave them victory over the Canaanites. The Israelites completely destroyed their enemies and their cities, and they named the place Hormah.

The king of Arad had attacked Israel and taken some of the people captive. Then the people made a vow: if God gave them victory, they would destroy those cities. This verse tells how God answered. Soon after, however, the people complained again against God and Moses.

When we are in trouble, crying out to God is the best first step, and He listens. But we also learn not to forget His help: Israel received an answer and, shortly afterward, was grumbling again. Thank God today for a prayer He has already answered.
exp.15:17:
These verses tell us that the 250 men who followed Korah did what Moses had asked. Each one took his censer (a vessel for burning incense), put fire in it, and laid the sweet incense on top. Then they stood at the entrance of the tabernacle, together with Moses and Aaron.

Moses had spoken earlier, and here the narrator recounts what happened next. Korah and his group were questioning the authority of Moses and Aaron, and they wanted the priesthood as well. Moses proposed a test before the LORD so that God Himself would show whom He had chosen. The men agreed, and offering incense was something God had reserved for the priests.

For today: drawing near to God with humility, respecting the way He asks us to come to Him. Before claiming a place or a recognition, it is worth asking ourselves whether we are seeking to serve God or to be more important than others.
exp.6:21:
This verse mentions one male goat as a sin offering. The verse of the word "expiation" is an old word meaning to cover or cleanse guilt, and it is part of the list of gifts brought by Nathanael, son of Zuar, leader of the tribe of Issachar, along with the burnt offering and the peace offering.

Here the account of Moses speaks. When the tabernacle was finished, each tribal leader brought his offering, one day after another. The lists are almost identical for each tribe. This shows that everyone took part equally in worshiping God, and that they all recognized their need for forgiveness.

For today: do not come to God as though you did not need forgiveness. Christians believe that Jesus is the final offering for our sin. Confess your failings sincerely, receive his forgiveness with thankfulness, and live grateful, without comparing your giving to that of others.
exp.30:5:
Moses sent them to war, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand men in all. With them went Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, carrying the holy objects and the trumpets to give the signal.

The people of Israel were at the end of their journey through the desert, near Canaan. God had commanded Moses to punish Midian, because its women and Balaam had led Israel into idolatry at Peor. The account is told by the author, and Moses organizes the campaign. That a priest went, and not a general, shows that the act was understood as carried out under God's authority. Exactly what the holy objects were is not clear; some think of objects from the sanctuary, and others think of the trumpets themselves.

For today: before undertaking something difficult, first seek God's direction and surround yourself with people who remind you who is truly in charge. Let God go ahead of you, not only your own strength.
exp.2:38:
This verse says that Moses and Aaron counted the Levites by their families, just as God had commanded. They counted every male from one month old and upward, and the total was twenty-two thousand. "Numbered" here means recorded or registered in a count.

The book of Numbers tells how God organized Israel in the wilderness. The Levites were set apart to care for the tabernacle and to serve in it. Here the narrator reports the result of the count God ordered. Right after this, God asks that the Levites take the place of Israel's firstborn. Some scholars point out that the figures for the individual groups add up to a little more, and there are several possible explanations, but the Bible does not clarify it.

For today: God knows and counts each person, even a baby one month old. You can serve him with the assurance that your place matters and that he sees you, even when your task seems small.
exp.20:15:
The people of Israel continued on their journey through the wilderness and came to a place called Beer, which means "well." This is said to be the well that the Lord spoke about to Moses. There, God promised to give them water if Moses gathered the people together.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Numbers. Israel was already near Moab, after many years in the wilderness. God had cared for them in difficult places, and the text remembers that faithfulness. Right after this, the people sing a song of joy for the water they received.

For today: God knows what we need before we reach the place of testing. We can trust that He provides, and when He does, it is good to stop and thank and praise Him, as Israel did.
exp.5:26:
This verse says that the priests, when pronouncing the blessing over the people, would be putting God's name upon the Israelites. That is, they marked them as belonging to God. And God himself promises: "I will bless them." What matters is that the blessing does not come from the priests but from God. The word "put" here means "place" or "call upon."

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for Aaron and his sons, the priests. He teaches them the words with which they were to bless Israel: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee..." This verse closes that blessing and makes clear that God is the one who truly blesses. This takes place while the people are in the wilderness, on the way to the promised land.

If you belong to God, you bear his name and can trust his care. Today, when you bless someone, you can pray simply, remembering that God is the one who gives the blessing.
exp.5:14:
This verse describes part of the offering that the Nazirite had to bring when his time of dedication came to an end. It includes a basket with bread and cakes made of fine flour mixed with oil, all of them unleavened, that is, made without yeast. The verse also mentioned the grain offering, which was an offering of flour, and the drink offerings, which were offerings of liquid, usually wine, poured out before God.

God gives these instructions to Moses so that he may pass them on to Israel. The Nazirite was someone who made a special vow to devote himself to the Lord for a period of time. When that period was complete, he brought a full offering to the tabernacle. The unleavened bread expressed purity and gratitude for what had been received.

For today: when you finish a season of giving yourself to God or serving Him, do not let it pass by without notice. Take some time to thank Him, simply and sincerely, recognizing that every good thing comes from Him.
exp.15:42:
This verse tells that Moses and Aaron went to stand in front of the tabernacle, the tent where God made his presence known among his people.

The verse of the rebellion of Korah is what the narrator describes next. The following day, the people blamed Moses and Aaron for the death of the rebels. When the crowd gathered against them, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud. The two leaders approached the place where God revealed himself, and then God spoke to them about the judgment that was coming.

When we are accused or pressured, we can imitate Moses and Aaron: instead of defending ourselves in anger, let us first draw near to God in prayer, asking him for wisdom and calm before we respond.
exp.25:55:
It says that the land of Canaan would be divided by casting lots, and that this division would apply to everyone, to the large family as well as the small one. Here "lot" is not blind chance but a way of deciding. A "possession" is the portion of land that is received and passed on to the children. "Divided" means split up.

God speaks through Moses after the second count of the people in the wilderness. The new generation was about to enter the promised land. The size of each tribe would be used to give more or less territory, and the lot would decide which area each tribe would occupy. Many understand that this showed God himself assigning the inheritance.

For today: we can trust that God cares for each person, whether our life seems large or small. In this way we can be thankful for what he gives us, without envying what others receive.
exp.24:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel "joined themselves" to Baal-peor, that is, they united with or attached themselves to that false god of Moab. For this reason, the anger of the Lord, that is, his burning wrath, was kindled against Israel.

The narrator of the book tells what happened at Shittim, near the promised land. The Israelites mixed with Moabite women, who invited them to eat in sacrifices to their gods. What began as closeness ended in idolatry and immorality. God responded with judgment, and the following passage shows how serious it was. Baal-peor was a local god of Peor, and the details of his worship are not fully known.

Today we can ask ourselves what small things gradually draw us closer to what turns our hearts away from God. It is wise to guard our friendships and habits, and to return to Him quickly with humility.
exp.25:35:
This verse continues the list of the families of Ephraim. It says that Eran was the son of Shuthelah, and that from him came the family of the Eranites.

This appears in Israel's second census, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God, through Moses and Eleazar, commanded that the people be counted before entering the promised land. The records would serve to divide the inheritance among the families. It is not a speech but an official register, and that is why it names even small families.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name, even when no one else remembers them. You can trust that your life and your quiet work matter to him. And you can also value those who go unnoticed, giving them a place and recognizing them.
exp.24:3:
God tells Moses to take the leaders of the people and hang them up in the open, "in the face of the sun," that is, in broad daylight and publicly. In this way his anger would be turned away from Israel. The Hebrew verb for "hang" is unclear: it may mean hanging, impaling, or displaying in public.

God is speaking, and he is very angry. Israel, camped near Moab, had joined in idolatry and sexual immorality in the worship of Baal of Peor. Interpreters do not agree on whether the leaders were guilty or were responsible as leaders. The next verse shows that the judges were to punish the guilty.

For today: God takes idolatry and unfaithfulness seriously, and those who lead carry greater responsibility. Today we can ask what things compete with God in our hearts and return to him with humility.
exp.27:26:
This verse commands that a burnt offering be offered to God: two young bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven lambs in their first year. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar. The phrase "a sweet savour" means that the offering was pleasing to God.

Moses passes on to Israel God's instructions for their feasts. This passage refers to the day of firstfruits, also called the feast of weeks, when the people presented the first fruits of the harvest. It was a day of holy assembly, when they rested from work and worshiped God with thankfulness.

For today: God deserves the first and the best, not the leftovers. We can set apart time, attention, and resources to give thanks to Him with a devoted heart, remembering that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.28:18:
Each day of the feast a male goat was offered as a sin offering. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt. It was added to the continual burnt offering, the daily sacrifice that was burned up entirely. The "gift" was a grain offering with oil, and the "drink offering" was poured-out wine.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people, now close to the promised land. Here the offerings for the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month, are described. Each day had its own list, and the number of bulls went down. Even in a joyful feast, God reminded the people that they needed forgiveness.

For today: do not take sin lightly, but do not live under guilt either. Christians believe that Christ offered the complete sacrifice once for all (Hebrews 10:10). Today, thank Him sincerely, and return to Him when you fail.
exp.28:28:
This verse describes the offering for the sixth day of the Feast of Tabernacles: eight young bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs one year old, all without blemish. "Without blemish" means without any physical flaw. The animals here are young bulls.

God speaks to Moses, who passes the instructions on to Israel, giving directions for the feasts of the year. In this feast, which lasted seven days, the number of bulls went down each day: thirteen on the first, twelve on the second, and so on until seven. Scholars debate the exact meaning of that decrease, and the Bible does not explain it. What is clear is that everything was done in order, according to the law, and that it included a male goat for sin.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, care, and effort we give him sincerely and in an orderly way, trusting that Christ has already offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.23:6:
He says that Israel will be like someone carrying water in abundance: from his hands or his buckets water will flow, and his descendants will live in well-watered lands. "Seed" means descendants. He also says that his king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be raised high. "Exalted" means lifted up or set on high.

Balaam speaks, a prophet from another people. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God put blessings in his mouth. Agag seems to be a title of Amalekite kings; some scholars think he is mentioned as an example of a powerful king. Water speaks of life and abundance.

For today: God fulfills his plans even when others oppose them. Trust that his blessing on your life does not depend on the words or the pressures of people. Seek to live close to him, like a tree beside the water.
exp.14:6:
God says that, along with the sacrifice of a ram, wine must be offered as a drink offering, that is, wine poured out before God. The measure is a third of a hin (the hin was a unit for liquids; its exact equivalent today is debated).

The phrase in the verse "for a sweet savour unto the Lord" means an offering that pleases God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel, while they were still in the wilderness. He promises them a land where they will be able to offer these offerings. The measures increase according to the animal: lamb, ram, bullock. In this way it taught that worship was to be orderly and not improvised.

For today: God is interested in the details of our devotion. We can give our time, our work, and our hearts willingly and sincerely, not just what is left over. Paul speaks of offering our lives as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).
exp.10:4:
Here the people look back with longing on the food of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. "For nothing" means free, without paying. They complain that now all they see is manna.

The Israelites are speaking, stirred up by the rabble, a mixed crowd of people who left Egypt with them and let their craving carry them along. They are in the wilderness, after being freed from slavery. God gave them manna every day, but they grew tired of it. In remembering Egypt, they forget that there they were slaves; the "for nothing" was not entirely true, for the price was their freedom.

When we are weary, it is easy to idealize the past and forget its chains. Before you complain, give thanks for what God gives you today, and remember honestly where he brought you from.
exp.30:51:
This verse says that all the gold the army commanders offered to the Lord weighed 16,750 shekels. The captains of thousands and the captains of hundreds were the officers over those groups of soldiers. A shekel was a unit of weight; its exact equivalent in grams is calculated in different ways, but it is usually estimated at about 11 grams.

Israel had just fought against Midian. The officers reported that not one soldier had died, and so they brought this offering to make atonement for their souls. Moses and Eleazar received the gold and brought it into the tent of meeting as a memorial before the Lord. The text does not explain in detail why they felt that need; we see a grateful and reverent heart.

For today: when God delivers us or blesses us, we can respond with concrete gratitude. Giving generously, and not only saying thank you, is a way of acknowledging that everything comes from Him.
exp.3:31:
This verse lists what the descendants of Merari were to carry: the pillars of the court that surrounded the tabernacle, their bases, their pins and their cords, with all their vessels and tools. The bases are the foundations on which the pillars rested, and "vessels" here means equipment or objects in general. In addition, Moses was to assign to each of them by name each piece that would be under their care.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron as He organizes the service of the Levites during the journey through the wilderness. The Merarites, between the ages of 30 and 50, carried the heaviest parts of the structure. By distributing and naming each piece, every man knew exactly what he was responsible for. They were under the direction of Ithamar, son of Aaron.

For today: God values service that almost no one sees. Carrying pins and cords was not glamorous, but it was necessary so that worship could continue. Today we can serve faithfully in simple tasks within the church, knowing that God knows each one by name.
exp.0:16:
It says that Moses and Aaron took with them the men whom God had designated and who had already been named one by one. The word "men" means men, and "identified by their names" means they were identified by their own personal names. The "á" before "these" is only old spelling.

The narrator recounts how Israel was organized in the Sinai desert. God commanded Moses to take a census, and from each tribe he chose a leader, called a prince or captain. These men would help count the people and guide them. Moses and Aaron receive them to begin that task.

God works with concrete people, whom he knows by name. Today we can serve with confidence in our place, whether great or small, knowing that God sees us and calls us. We can also value teamwork and support those who lead with responsibility.
exp.13:0:
All the people of Israel began to cry out and weep aloud throughout the night. "Lifted up their voice" means they raised their voices loudly, like a cry of anguish and despair.

The Israelites had just heard the report of the twelve men whom Moses had sent to explore the promised land. Ten of them spoke out of fear, saying that the inhabitants were very strong. The people became frightened and stopped trusting God's promise. For this reason, their weeping was not an expression of repentance, but of fear and lack of faith.

When fear takes control of us, it is easy to forget what God has already done for us. Instead of letting anxiety carry us away, we can stop, remember his promises, and bring our fears to him in prayer before we make decisions.
exp.21:40:
This verse says that the next day Balak, king of Moab, took Balaam up to the high places of Baal, which were raised places where that god was worshiped. From there Balaam could see only the farthest part of Israel's camp. "Took" means he took him along with him, and "utmost part" means the edge or the most distant part.

Here the narrator speaks. Balak was afraid of Israel and had hired Balaam to curse them. After offering a feast, he takes him to a religious place with a good view, perhaps thinking that in this way the curse would have more force. But, as the story goes on, God allows Balaam only to bless.

For today: we cannot manipulate God by changing place, ritual or plan. His will is not bought or bargained for. Instead of seeking God's approval for what we want, let us humbly seek what he has already said.
exp.23:21:
It says the Kenites will be driven out or destroyed, and that Asshur will carry them away captive. "Kenite" is the Kenite people, and "Asshur" is Assyria, a northern power. Here "driven out" suggests "consumed" or "laid waste."

Balaam speaks, a pagan prophet whom Balak hired to curse Israel, but God compelled him to bless it. In his final messages he announces the fate of several nations. The Kenites lived in high places and believed themselves secure, "with their nest in the rock." Scholars do not agree on the historical details of this captivity.

No human security, neither a stronghold nor a good position, protects us if God decides otherwise. We can rest in Him, not in our defenses, and live with humility.
exp.3:16:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God (Jehovah) spoke to Moses and to Aaron, the two leaders of Israel. What follows is a new instruction from God.

The one speaking is God himself. He is giving orders about the care of the tabernacle. The sons of Kohath were to carry the holy things, but without touching them, because they could die. Now God speaks again to protect that family. Moses and Aaron were to organize the work well so that no one would approach the holy things carelessly.

God takes the time to give clear instructions to care for his people. Today we can approach him with reverence and listen to his Word with attention. If he guides us with such care, we can trust that his directions seek our good.
exp.30:13:
It says that Moses was filled with anger against the leaders of the Israelite army as they returned from the battle. "Captains" were the commanding generals; "tribunes" were leaders of a thousand soldiers, and "centurions" were leaders of a hundred. "Was wroth" means "was angry."

Here the narrator tells us Moses's reaction. Israel had fought against Midian, and the soldiers brought back captives and spoils. Moses became angry because they had let the women live, the same women who, on the advice of Balaam, had led the people into idolatry at Peor, where many people died. To him, the task was not complete or fully obeyed.

For today: obedience to God is not carried out halfway. If we have tolerated something that pulls us away from Him, it is wise to ask Him for courage and sincerity to correct it, and not to excuse it as something small.
exp.21:25:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord went forward and stood in a very narrow place, where there was no room left to get around him, neither to the right nor to the left. "Narrow place" is a tight passage, and the phrase "neither to the right nor to the left" means that there was no way to turn to either side.

Balaam, a prophet from another land, was riding his donkey toward Moab, called by King Balak to curse Israel. God did not agree with that journey. The angel, with a sword in hand, blocked the road, but only the donkey could see him. She had turned aside and had been struck twice. Here she can no longer get around him, and she lies down on the ground.

Today, God sometimes closes doors to stop us, and we get angry about what is happening without asking ourselves whether He may be speaking to us. Stop to pray and examine your direction before stubbornly insisting on your own way.
exp.4:10:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses. The name "Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament, and the word "saying" indicates that what follows are words Moses was to pass on to the people.

God speaks, and Moses is the messenger. Previously the text spoke of offerings for the priests, and now a new instruction begins about a case of suspected unfaithfulness in marriage, when there were no witnesses or proof. This law was given to Israel in the wilderness, and scholars explain it in different ways. What is clear is that the people were to bring this matter before God and not settle it through revenge.

For today: before acting out of suspicion or anger, let us bring our doubts to God in prayer and seek wise counsel. He sees what is hidden and He is just.
exp.30:20:
This verse says that the priest Eleazar spoke to the soldiers who were returning from the battle. He explained that what he was about to tell them was not his own idea, but the ordinance of the law, the command that God had given to Moses.

Israel had just fought against Midian. The soldiers had touched dead bodies, and according to the law they were considered unclean for worship. For that reason they had to stay outside the camp for seven days and purify themselves. Eleazar, the son of Aaron, taught how to do this, including with the objects and the spoil.

For today: before returning to normal life, it is good to stop, acknowledge what has worn us down or stained us, and return to God with humility. He cleanses us and helps us begin again.
exp.0:48:
It says God told Moses not to include the tribe of Levi in the count of the men of Israel. The words "you shall not number" and "neither take the sum" mean that they were not to be registered together with the other tribes. "Only" marks an exception: all the tribes were counted, except this one.

The LORD speaks and gives the instruction to Moses in the wilderness, at the time when the census of the men fit for war was being taken. The Levites were set apart for another task: to care for, carry, and set up the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people. For this reason they did not go to war with the other tribes. Their service was different, but just as necessary.

For today: God does not give everyone the same task, and all of them have value. If your service is quiet or not very visible, do not despise it. Do it with gratitude, because God has placed you there.
exp.2:1:
This verse gives the names of the four sons of Aaron: Nadab, who was the oldest, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar (today it is spelled Itamar). It is part of a family list. The word "firstborn" means the first son born.

The book of Numbers tells how God organized Israel in the wilderness. The narrator presents the family of Aaron and Moses, and explains that these men would serve as priests. The verses that follow say that Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire, that is, fire that God had not commanded. So Eleazar and Ithamar continued in the service.

God cares about the details and knows each person by name. This passage also reminds us that serving God is a serious matter, and that we need to do it with reverence and obedience, not in our own way. Today we can ask ourselves: am I seeking to please God according to his Word?
exp.21:37:
Balaam tells Balak that he has arrived, but that he does not have the freedom to say whatever he wants. The question "Have I now any power at all to say anything?" means: "Do I really have the power to say anything on my own?" He affirms that he will speak only the word that God puts in his mouth.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and had sent for Balaam so that he would curse them. Balak complains that Balaam took his time in coming, and he reminds him that he can honor him, that is, reward him. Balaam answers that his message depends on God. Scholars debate how sincere his intentions were, since other passages show him with doubtful motives.

For today: before speaking or deciding under pressure, remember that God's truth is worth more than flattery, money, or fear. Ask Him to guide your words.
exp.25:8:
This verse continues the census of the tribe of Reuben. It names the sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. It reminds us that Dathan and Abiram were among the well-known leaders of the people, men famous in the congregation. Their rebellion was an uprising against Moses and Aaron, and by joining Korah in opposing them, they rose up against God.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks as the people are reminded of their history before entering the promised land. The rebellion of Dathan and Abiram, which took place decades earlier (Numbers 16), is recalled as a solemn memory. The text goes on to say that the earth swallowed them, but the sons of Korah did not die.

For today: holding a position or having influence does not protect us from pride. If we are called to lead, or simply to speak our opinion, let us examine our hearts: do we criticize out of love for the truth, or out of a desire for power? Let us ask God for humility.
exp.15:46:
Aaron, the high priest, did what Moses had commanded him. He took the censer, a vessel in which incense is burned, and ran toward the people. The plague had already begun. He put the incense on the fire, and made atonement, that is, he sought to cover the people's guilt before God.

After the rebellion of Korah, the people blamed Moses and Aaron for the death of the rebels. God became angry and began to send a plague. Moses, aware of how serious it was, ordered Aaron to act at once. Aaron obeyed without hesitation, even though it put him at risk.

For today: when someone around you is in spiritual danger, do not just stand and watch. Pray for that person, intercede for them, and act with love and urgency, even when it costs you.
exp.6:55:
This verse mentions part of the offering of Gamaliel, leader of the tribe of Manasseh: one golden spoon weighing ten shekels, full of incense. The word "incense" refers to a fragrant mixture that was burned in the sanctuary. A shekel was a unit of weight, and here it is used to indicate the value of the offering.

It is part of an account in the book of Numbers. For twelve days, each tribal leader presented his offering for the dedication of the altar and the tabernacle. Moses records it in detail. The offerings of all the leaders were identical, and each one was noted with the same care, which shows that God values each tribe equally.

For today: God sees and remembers what we give sincerely, even when others give the same or more. Offer your time, your gifts, or your resources with a grateful heart, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that the Levites will be brought before the Lord, at the entrance of the tabernacle. Then the people of Israel will lay their hands on them. The phrase "thou shalt bring" means that the Levites are to be brought forward before the Lord.

God is speaking to Moses. The Levites were to be set apart to help in the service of the tabernacle. Laying hands on them was a gesture that many understand as a way of identifying with them and presenting them to God on behalf of the whole people. In this way, the Levites would serve on behalf of all the Israelites. The text does not explain the gesture in more detail.

For today: serving God is not only the task of a few. We can support those who serve in our church with prayer, offerings, and encouragement, and so take part in their work.
exp.9:14:
This verse tells us who led the tribe of Issachar when the people set out. His name was Nethaneel, and he was the son of Zuar. The word "host" here refers to the company or division of the tribe.

The book of Numbers tells how Israel left Mount Sinai for the first time, following God's command given through Moses. It is a narrative, not a speech. Each tribe had a leader, and the text names them one by one, in order. Judah went first, and Issachar came after, with its own leader.

For today: God notices each person and the place that belongs to them. Even a name that seems to be only part of a list counts for Him. Serve where you are, with order and faithfulness, even when no one else notices.
exp.26:20:
He says that Joshua will stand before the priest Eleazar, and that Eleazar will seek God's direction through the Urim. According to that answer, Joshua and all the people will decide when to go out to war and when to come back. The phrase that reads "ask counsel for him" means "will seek guidance for him"; "judgment" means decision or direction; "word" means a spoken word or instruction. "Go out and come in" refers to going into battle and returning, or to everyday life.

God speaks to Moses, who knows that he will soon die. God shows him who will be the new leader: Joshua. But He makes clear that Joshua will not decide alone; he will depend on God's direction. It is not known exactly how the Urim worked; it is generally understood as a sacred means of learning God's will.

For today: even when we are capable, we need to seek God's guidance before deciding. Pray, read the Bible, and ask for wise counsel before taking important steps.
exp.6:8:
Moses did not give carts or oxen to the sons of Kohath, because their task was to carry the holy things of the sanctuary on their own shoulders. The verse says they were to carry them upon their shoulders.

The people of Israel were in the wilderness, and the leaders of the tribes had brought carts and oxen as an offering. Moses distributed them according to the work of each Levite family. Gershon and Merari transported curtains, boards and pillars, and they needed carts. The Kohathites carried the most sacred objects, such as the ark, and were to carry them by hand, according to Numbers 4. The text says nothing more about the reason for this difference.

God gives each person a different task, and not all of them are done with the same tools. Today we can serve faithfully in what God has entrusted to us, without comparing ourselves to others or envying their resources.
exp.3:38:
This verse describes the men of the family of Gershon who were counted for service. They were between thirty and fifty years old, and "entereth into the service" means they joined the working group for the tabernacle. To minister means to serve, and "the tabernacle of the congregation" is the sacred tent where God's presence was.

The book of Numbers tells how God organized Israel in the wilderness. Moses and Aaron carried out this count by the command of the LORD. Each Levite family had specific tasks, such as carrying and caring for the tabernacle. Why that age was chosen, the text does not explain in detail.

For today: God cares about order and values every task, even one that seems small. Serve where He has placed you, with responsibility and joy, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.21:17:
Balaam tells Balak's messengers that, even if the king gave him his house full of silver and gold, he cannot go beyond what the Lord his God has told him, whether in something small or in something great.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel, which was camped nearby. So he asked Balaam, a diviner from another land, to curse the people. Balaam speaks firmly, but then asks them to wait another night so he can consult God again. That shows his heart was still drawn to the reward, and the Bible makes this clear later on.

Saying the right words is not enough; one must obey God even when temptation keeps knocking at the door. If you already know what God wants, do not bargain with Him again.
exp.25:48:
This verse names two more clans of the tribe of Naphtali: the descendants of Jezer, called the Jezerites, and those of Shillem, called the Shillemites. Here "family" means clan, and the ending "-ites" indicates that they are descendants of that ancestor.

God commanded Moses and the priest Eleazar to take this second census on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. They counted each tribe and each clan, and afterward the land would be divided according to those numbers. For the new generation, this list was also a way of remembering their roots.

For today: although these names may seem distant to us, God does not forget anyone. No one is merely a number to Him. This encourages us to value our family and our church, and to serve faithfully even when our work goes unnoticed.
exp.25:21:
This verse sums up the census of the tribe of Judah: its families, counted separately, added up to 76,500 men. The word "counted" refers to the people registered in the census, and "families" refers to the groups that descended from each son of Judah.

God told Moses and Eleazar to take this census at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, after the earlier generation had already died. Men twenty years old and up who were fit for war were counted, because they would soon enter the promised land and also divide it according to the size of each tribe. Judah was the most numerous tribe.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass; he keeps a record of every family and every name. You can trust that you too matter to him personally. And, like those Israelites, it is worth remembering that we are part of something larger than ourselves.
exp.27:4:
This verse speaks of the grain offering that accompanied the lamb of the daily burnt offering. A tenth of an ephah was a little over two liters of very fine flour. It was mixed with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, that is, pure olive oil, roughly one liter. The phrase "as an offering" is the sense intended here. The modern measures are approximate.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to instruct the people on how to offer each day, in the morning and in the evening, the continual sacrifice. This was given to the new generation of Israel, who were about to enter the promised land. The flour and the oil expressed gratitude and devotion in daily work.

For today: God values consistency. We can set aside a moment each morning and each evening to thank him and offer him what we are and what we do, not waiting only for special occasions.
exp.1:8:
This verse sums up the total of the men from the three tribes who camped on the east side: Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. Added together, they came to 186,400 men of war. They were to set out first, organized in ordered groups, and the phrase "those that were numbered" refers to the men who were registered in the census.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, shortly after leaving Egypt. He gives them instructions for camping and marching in order around the tabernacle, each tribe under its own banner. Judah went at the front. Some see in this a foreshadowing of its future importance, since David would come from that tribe, and according to the New Testament, Jesus. That is a possible reading, though the text does not state it directly.

For today: God cares about order and about each person having a place. In your family or in your church, serve where God has placed you, without competing, trusting that he guides the way.
exp.25:14:
This verse begins the list of the families of the tribe of Gad. Each son or descendant of Gad gave his name to a clan: the Zephonites, the Haggites, and the Shunites. The word "families" here means clans, large groups of relatives who descended from a common ancestor. In some old printed texts, certain names were spelled differently than we see them today, for example, "Zephon" was written with a different form, and "Haggi" appears in other spellings.

God speaks to Moses and to Eleazar the priest so that they will count the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This is the second count, after almost forty years in the wilderness. It served to organize the people, prepare for war, and divide the land according to the size of each tribe and clan.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name. No one goes unnoticed by him. You can rest in the knowledge that your life matters to him, and also value the people around you who are small or overlooked.
exp.28:16:
This verse describes the offerings for the second day of the Feast of Tabernacles: twelve young bulls from the herd, two rams, and fourteen lambs in their first year, all "without defect," that is, without any physical flaw. Each day of the feast had its own list of animals.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel, in the seventh month. They were organized, repeated sacrifices, which taught that worship was to be done with order and obedience. The number of bulls went down each day. Interpreters explain this detail in several ways, and the Bible does not clearly state its reason.

Today we no longer offer animals, since Christians believe that Christ offered himself once and for all. Even so, we can learn to give God our best, not our leftovers, and to worship him with consistency, not only when we feel like it. A daily practice of prayer and thanksgiving can be a good way to do this.
exp.13:15:
This verse repeats what the neighboring nations would say if God destroyed Israel. They would say that the Lord did not have the power to bring his people into the land he had promised them with an oath, and so he killed them in the wilderness. The word "bring" in the verse above is the key idea here: it means to lead or bring someone in, and "promised them with an oath" means pledged with a solemn vow.

Moses is speaking with God. The Israelites have just rebelled because they were afraid to enter Canaan, and God said he would punish them. Moses intercedes for the people. He is concerned that God's name will be damaged before the nations, and then he appeals to God's mercy and patience.

For today: when we pray for others, we can do so with humility, relying on the character of God and not on our own merits. It is also worth asking ourselves whether our lives honor God's name before those who observe us.
exp.28:33:
This verse says that on the seventh day of the feast, in addition to the many animals already mentioned, one male goat was also offered as a sin offering. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt. The "continual burnt offering" was the daily offering that was burned completely. The "meat offering" was an offering of grain, and the "drink offering" was wine poured out.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses instructs Israel about the feasts of the seventh month, the Feast of Tabernacles. Although it was a time of joy, the need for forgiveness was never forgotten. Each day included a male goat for sin. Then comes the eighth day, a special solemn assembly.

For today: even in moments of greatest joy, it is wise to humbly recognize that we need God's forgiveness. Christians believe that Christ offered the final sacrifice, so we can celebrate with gratitude and with a clean heart.
exp.13:37:
This verse says that, of all the men Moses sent to explore Canaan, only Joshua and Caleb were left alive. The other ten spies died from a plague sent by God.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel rebelled. Ten spies brought back a report full of fear, and the people grumbled against Moses. Only Joshua and Caleb had trusted that God would give them the land. For this reason God preserved them, while those who spread discouragement died.

For today: our words influence others. We can sow fear or faith. When everyone around us doubts, God honors the one who keeps trusting Him and remains faithful to Him, even if he is almost alone.
exp.34:30:
This verse says that no one could accept money or payment in exchange for the life of a murderer. The word "price" in the source refers to a ransom or compensation, so I'll note that the verse rules out buying one's way out of the penalty. "Without fail" means without exception. If someone killed another person on purpose, that person had to die.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. These laws protected the value of human life and kept the wealthy from buying their freedom. Witnesses were required, so that justice would be handled carefully. The verses that follow speak of the land being defiled by spilled blood.

For today: human life has a worth that money cannot erase. We can ask for fair justice for everyone, without favoritism, and trust that God loves justice and also offers forgiveness.
exp.34:19:
This verse describes a case of deliberate murder. If someone pushes another person out of hatred, or throws something at them from a hiding place (the word "ambush" means a planned trap), and that person dies, the one who did it is a murderer. What matters here is the hatred and the advance planning.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The law distinguishes between a crime committed with evil intent and an accidental death, for which the cities of refuge existed. The "avenger of blood" was the one who carried out justice, and only when the intent had been proven. It was a rule of that time and that society.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at actions. Hatred that is kept inside does harm and can grow. Ask God to heal any resentment you hold against someone, and seek reconciliation before anger hardens.
exp.30:49:
The army's commanders tell how they offered to God the gold and jewelry they collected in the war. They did it "to make an atonement for our souls." The bracelets are the wristlets, the earrings are the ear pendants, and the chains are the necklaces.

The commanders of thousands and of hundreds are speaking to Moses. They have just fought against Midian, and not one of their soldiers died. They recognize that this victory was a gift from God and respond with gratitude. Some think they also wanted to ask forgiveness for having come close to death and to what was unclean in battle. The text does not fully explain this.

Today we can learn that when God protects us or gives us something good, the right response is humble gratitude. Think of a recent blessing and thank God with an offering, an act of service, or a sincere prayer.
exp.12:4:
This verse begins the list of the twelve men whom Moses sent to explore Canaan. The first one named is Shammua, son of Zaccur, of the tribe of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob. "Scouting the land" means exploring it, and "leader" means the chief or head of his tribe.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Paran, near the southern edge of Canaan. He orders that a leader from each tribe be sent to examine the land he would give them. The text takes great care with the names because these were real people with responsibility before the people. Later, ten of them will bring back a report full of fear.

For today: being a leader or having influence is a great responsibility. God knows us by name and expects faithfulness and trust, not only that we do the task well, but that we believe what He has already promised.
exp.14:8:
Next, God asks that, along with the bullock offered as a sacrifice, a grain offering also be presented: three tenth parts of fine flour, mixed with half a measure of oil. The "hin" was an ancient measure for liquids; its exact equivalent is calculated in different ways.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell Israel. These are instructions for when the people live in the promised land. They come after that generation doubted and refused to enter. God reminds them that he will keep his promise and that he still wants to be worshiped with order and gratitude.

Today we do not offer animals, because Christ offered himself for us. But this verse teaches us that worshiping God is not something careless or left-over. We can give him the best of our time, affection, and resources, with gratitude and with our whole heart.
exp.17:2:
God tells Aaron that the Levites will help him and carry out what he directs them to do, caring for the whole tabernacle. But they have a clear limit: they must not come near the holy vessels (the sacred utensils of the sanctuary) or the altar. If they do, they will die, and the priests with them.

God speaks to Aaron after episodes of rebellion and of intruding into worship, such as Korah's. He divides the tasks: the priests serve in the most holy places, and the Levites help in the care of the tabernacle. The purpose, according to the following passage, is to protect Israel from God's wrath.

For today: God cares about order and reverence. Each person has a place in his service, and no task is small. Serve with humility where God has placed you, without wanting to take the place of others, and treat what is holy with respect.
exp.15:26:
They say the people moved away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, just as Moses had asked. Dathan and Abiram, however, came out and stood at the entrance of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little children. The verse of "little children" is that it means the youngest members of the family.

Moses had just warned the people to separate themselves from these men who had rebelled against his leadership and against the order God had established. This verse tells the response: the people obeyed, but Dathan and Abiram stayed defiant. That their families were with them shows what a stubborn decision can drag along with it. The next verse announces God's judgment.

For today: when God warns us, it is better to obey in time than to harden ourselves. Our decisions also affect those we love.
exp.3:37:
