This verse begins the count of the sons of Gershon, another of the Levite families. They are numbered "throughout their families" and "by the house of their fathers," that is, according to their lineage and their clans. The sentence is left incomplete here and continues in the next verse, where the age range and the result of the count are stated.

Moses and Aaron, by the command of the LORD, take this census in the wilderness. They had already counted the sons of Kohath (2,750). Now they count the Gershonites, men from thirty to fifty years old, fit to serve in the tabernacle. The purpose was to organize the work and the transport of the sanctuary.

For today: God knows who you are and gives you a place in his work. No service done faithfully is small. Ask yourself what concrete task you can take on in your church or community, and do it with steadiness and order.
exp.3:7:
God explains how to wrap the table of the sacred bread for the journey. First a cloth of bright red is placed over it, and on top of that a covering of strong skins. After that the poles are put in, which were the rods used to carry it. The word for the skins is uncertain: it has been translated in several ways, such as badger, another animal, or fine leather.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. Israel was in the wilderness, and the tabernacle moved from place to place. The priests covered the holy objects, and then the Kohathites carried them without touching them. This taught respect for the holiness of God.

For today: treat with reverence and care what belongs to God, such as his Word, prayer, and service to others. Do it with humility and order, without taking it lightly.
exp.21:14:
This verse says that King Balak sent messengers to Balaam again. This time there were more princes, and they were of higher rank than the first ones. The sentence about the phrase "sent again" and the word for those of greater standing has been removed, since the reader's verse does not contain those words.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of the people of Israel and wanted Balaam to curse them. Balaam had already said that God would not let him go. But Balak did not accept that answer and thought that with more prestige and the promise of honor he could persuade him. The text only tells us what Balak did; it does not explain everything that was in his heart.

When God has already spoken clearly, we do not need to ask again in the hope of a different answer. Pressure, offers, and the insistence of others do not change the will of God. Let us obey what He has already shown us.
exp.32:35:
This verse is part of the list of places where the people of Israel camped on their journey through the wilderness. It says that they left Ezion-geber and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Zin, a place that here is identified with Kadesh. The word "pitched" means that they set up their camp.

Moses wrote this record at the command of the LORD, to preserve the memory of each stage of the journey from Egypt. Some scholars think this Kadesh is the same Kadesh-barnea mentioned in other passages, although not all agree. It is the place where, later on, Miriam, the sister of Moses, died.

God does not forget any step of our road. Even the stages that seem long or unimportant are recorded before Him. Trust that He accompanies your journey, even in your times of wilderness.
exp.1:18:
This verse says that the army of the tribe of Ephraim, that is, the men who were counted in the census, added up to forty thousand five hundred. "Host" means an army or an organized group, and "those that were numbered" means those who were counted.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron (Numbers 2:1). He gives them instructions so that the people camp and march in order around the tabernacle. Each tribe had its place and its banner. Ephraim occupied the western side. The figures show that the people were organized with care, and that God himself was at the center.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and he knows how many we are and where we are. You have a place among his people, even though at times you may feel like just one more among many. Serve with joy where God has placed you, and keep Christ at the center of your life and of your church.
exp.34:6:
This verse says that the total number of cities Israel would give to the Levites would be forty-eight. Each city included its "suburbs," which were the pasturelands around it, where the Levites could keep their livestock.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own, because their inheritance was to serve God. For that reason the other tribes gave them cities from their own inheritance. Six of these would be places of refuge for someone who caused a death without intending it.

For today: God cares for those who serve in spiritual ministry, and his people share what they have. We can support pastors, teachers, and missionaries generously and in concrete ways, each according to what God has given them.
exp.16:6:
Moses takes the twelve staffs, one for each tribal leader, and places them inside the tabernacle, before the Lord. The "tabernacle of witness" is the sacred tent where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept. There God was present in a special way in the midst of his people.

Israel had come out of several rebellions against Moses and Aaron, and the people were complaining about who had the right to serve as priest. God himself proposes a clear test: the staff of the man he chooses will bud. Moses obeys and leaves the matter in God's hands, without defending himself or arguing.

When there are conflicts or doubts about who is right, we can learn from Moses: instead of fighting, bring the matter to God in prayer and wait patiently for his answer.
exp.2:50:
This verse says that Moses gave the money of the redemption to Aaron and his sons. It was the payment for the firstborn who were left over.

Here the narrator tells what Moses did. God had set apart the Levites to serve him in place of the firstborn of Israel. The firstborn and the Levites were counted, and 273 firstborn were left over with no Levite to take their place. For each of them five shekels were paid, and that money went to Aaron and his sons, who served as priests.

For today: obeying God in small and practical things, including money. Moses did not change anything or keep anything for himself; he acted with faithfulness and order. We can ask God to help us be honest and dependable in what is entrusted to us.
exp.24:7:
Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, followed an Israelite man into his tent and killed both him and the Midianite woman he had brought there, using a spear. With this, the deadly outbreak came to an end; that is, the plague that was killing the people stopped.

Israel was camped near Moab. Many of the people had joined in sexual immorality and in the worship of Baal of Peor, and God sent a plague as judgment. While the people were weeping at the entrance of the tabernacle, this man brought the woman in full view of everyone, as if it meant nothing. It is a violent and difficult act, and the text presents it as zeal for faithfulness to God at a critical moment.

Today we are not asked for violence, but to take sin seriously. We can ask ourselves whether we are tolerating something that God calls grave, and take a brave and humble step to turn away from it.
exp.3:15:
This verse says that Eleazar, son of the priest Aaron, was responsible for caring for four things: the oil for the lamps, the sweet incense, the daily grain offering (the regular offering of grain each day), and the anointing oil. He was also in charge of overseeing the whole tabernacle and everything in it, including its vessels. The lamps referred to here are the lampstand with its lamps.

God is speaking to Moses while Israel is in the wilderness. He gives instructions about how the tabernacle is to be moved. The Kohathites carried the holy objects, but they were not allowed to touch them. Eleazar, as a priest, took charge of the most sensitive matters and of what was used every day.

For today: God values faithful service in everyday things. Caring steadily for what He entrusts to us, even when it seems small, is a way of honoring Him. Today we can ask ourselves what responsibility He has given us and carry it out with reverence and care.
exp.22:26:
Balak asks Balaam to come with him to another place. He hopes that it will please God for Balaam to curse Israel from there.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of the people of Israel and had hired Balaam to curse them. Twice God allowed only blessings. Balak thinks that changing the location will change God's answer. Balaam had already said that he would do only what the LORD told him.

For today: we cannot manipulate God by changing circumstances or places to get what we want. Instead, let us seek his will with humility, accept his answer, and trust that his promises do not change.
exp.34:28:
This verse says that everything explained about the cities of refuge, the killers, and the avengers was to be a permanent legal rule. The phrase "a statute of judgment" means a binding rule of justice. The phrase "throughout your generations" means from one generation to the next, and "in all your dwellings" refers to the places where they lived.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to Israel, shortly before they entered the promised land. The earlier laws distinguished between killing without intent, which allowed a person to flee to a city of refuge, and murdering on purpose. This verse closes that section and makes clear that the law applied in the whole territory, without exceptions.

For today: God values human life and desires justice that is clear, even-handed, and free from personal revenge. We can learn not to act on impulse or resentment, and to always seek truth and justice.
exp.7:6:
God tells Moses how to prepare the Levites. They were to be sprinkled with water of purifying, that is, water used to cleanse from sin or uncleanness. Then they would shave their whole body with a razor and wash their clothes.

The LORD speaks to Moses when the Levites are about to be set apart to serve in the tabernacle in place of the firstborn of Israel. Before drawing near to holy things, they needed a visible cleansing. It is not known exactly what this water was like; some think it relates to the water of purification in Numbers 19, but this is not certain.

For today: serving God matters, but first we need his cleansing. We can come near with humility, asking him for forgiveness and a clean heart before we serve.
exp.25:7:
This verse is part of a list of families. It is a brief detail, but it connects the family of Reuben with what follows in the account.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks, recording Israel's second census. This takes place at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. The census served to organize the people and divide the land by families. By naming Eliab, the text prepares the mention of his sons Dathan and Abiram, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron along with Korah.

God pays attention to every person and every family, even to names that seem simple. But each generation decides how to live. A family with a history of rebellion can choose today to trust God and obey him.
exp.2:33:
This verse says that the males of the family of Merari, counting from one month old and upward, added up to 6,200. "Counted" means registered or recorded in a census, and "according to the count" means according to the record that was made.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites were not numbered like the other tribes for war, but for service in the sanctuary. Each Levite family received a task. The sons of Merari were assigned to care for the boards, bars, pillars, and bases of the tabernacle. It was heavy work, little seen, but necessary.

For today: God counts and values each person, even in simple or hidden tasks. If your service seems small or little noticed, remember that it supports something God himself considers important. Serve him faithfully, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.24:1:
The Moabite women invited the Israelites to the sacrifices offered to their gods. The people ate of that meal and bowed down before those gods.

The narrator, Moses according to tradition, tells what happened when Israel camped at Shittim, near Moab, at the end of the journey through the wilderness. What began with forbidden relationships ended in idolatry, and God was angered. Scholars debate the details of the worship of Baal of Peor, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: great failures almost never begin all at once, but with small concessions. Ask yourself which invitations, friendships, or habits are gradually pulling you away from God, and decide in prayer to set limits in time.
exp.21:29:
Here the donkey asks Balaam whether she has ever behaved this way with him. She reminds him that she has carried him for years, and that she had never failed him before. Balaam admits: "Nay."

The donkey speaks because the LORD opened her mouth. Balaam was on his way to meet Balak, king of Moab, and he was angry because the animal kept turning aside. He did not see the angel with the sword, but the donkey did. Her question shows that there was a cause Balaam did not know about.

For today: before we become angry with someone or with a situation, it is wise to stop and ask whether there is something we are not seeing. God sometimes uses obstacles to protect us or to correct us.
exp.16:12:
The Israelites say that anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the Lord will die. They ask in distress whether all of them are going to end up dying. "Comes near" and "draws near" both mean approaching; "perish" means dying; "shall we be consumed" means "will we be finished?"

The people of Israel are speaking, addressing Moses. Shortly before, God had shown that Aaron was the chosen priest by making his staff blossom, after the rebellion of Korah. With so many recent deaths, the people feel fear before the holiness of God. Their reaction is more fear than healthy reverence; the Bible does not present it as a prayer, but as a lament.

God is holy and deserves respect, but we should not live paralyzed by fear. Today Christians believe that Jesus, our great high priest, opens the way for us to draw near to God (Hebrews 4:16). Come near to Him today in prayer, with humility and confidence, without hiding.
exp.0:39:
This verse says that the men of the tribe of Asher were counted. They were recorded by their generations, their families, and their father's houses, according to the list of names. Only those from twenty years old and upward who were able to go out to war were included.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. He commands a census of each tribe to organize the people, probably in preparation for the march toward the promised land. Asher is one of the twelve tribes, and its result appears in the following verse: 41,500.

For today: God cares about each person and each family, not only the crowds. He knows you by name and calls you to take your place and serve in your community, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.3:24:
This verse says that the sons of Gershon were to carry the cloth and leather parts of the tabernacle when the people moved: the curtains, the main covering, the covering of badgers' skins (the exact material of those skins is debated; some translations say fine leather or dolphin skins), and the curtain for the entrance. The word "testimony" refers to God's law, kept in the ark.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The Levites from thirty to fifty years old are organized so that each family has a clear task in carrying the tabernacle. In this way everything was done with order and respect for what was holy.

Today we can learn that no service to God is small. Carrying cloth may have seemed unremarkable, but it was necessary. Ask yourself what simple task you can do faithfully in your church or family.
exp.28:5:
This verse ends the list of offerings for the first day of the seventh month. It says that these offerings were presented in addition to the regular ones: the burnt offering of the month (the one for the new moon), the continual burnt offering (the daily one), each with its grain offering and its drink offerings, which were liquids poured out. The grain offering was the one made of flour and oil. The offering burned on the altar was the one that went up in smoke, and the phrase about it being a sweet savour expresses that God received it with pleasure.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how they were to worship at the festivals, and that the day of the blowing of trumpets was to be holy. These offerings were added to the daily ones, without replacing them.

For today: special moments of faith should not take the place of daily faithfulness. We can set apart time each day to pray and read the Bible, and give God something extra on important occasions.
exp.9:4:
When ye blow an alarm, the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward. This verse says that when the priests sounded the trumpets with an alarm signal, the tribes camped on the east side of the tabernacle were to break camp and set out. "When ye blow" is the same as "when you sound," and "alarm" is a special signal, different from the one that only gathered the people. "Shall go forward" means they would be on the move.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to make two silver trumpets. With them, signals were given: some to gather the people or their leaders, and others to announce when to set out. Israel was a large crowd and needed order to advance through the desert, following the direction of God.

For today: God is a God of order, and he wants us to follow him with attention. Set aside time each day to listen to him through the Bible and prayer, so that you can recognize when it is time to wait and when it is time to move forward.
exp.22:20:
This verse says that God has not counted the wickedness of Jacob, nor seen evil in Israel, that is, in the Hebrew people. "Iniquity" and "perverseness" mean wickedness and twisting. God is with them, and among them is heard the shout of a king, a cry of joy, like someone celebrating that their king is present.

Balaam, a foreign prophet, is the one speaking. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God allowed him only to bless it. Some understand that God does not see sin because he forgives; others, that he does not allow anyone to accuse them. Israel did fail on other occasions, so this is not a description of a perfect people.

For today: if you trust in Christ, rest in the fact that God's forgiveness is firm. No accusation, whether from others or from your own conscience, cancels his blessing. Respond with gratitude and joy.
exp.28:15:
Along with the many animals offered that day, one male goat was also presented as a sin offering. This was added to the continual burnt offering, the daily sacrifice that was burned completely, together with its grain offering of flour mixed with oil and its drink offering of poured-out wine.

Moses passes on God's instructions for the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. The number of bulls changed each day, but the male goat was repeated. In this way Israel was reminded that, even in a festival of joy, they still needed forgiveness, and that everything had to be done as God commanded.

For today: in the midst of your celebrations and blessings, do not forget to give thanks for forgiveness. Christians believe that Christ is the final atonement, so we can rejoice with a clean and grateful heart.
exp.25:29:
This verse lists the sons of Gilead, grandson of Manasseh. From Jeezer came the family of the Jeezerites, and from Helek, the family of the Helekites. "Family" here means a clan, that is, a group of relatives who descended from a common ancestor.

God speaks through Moses and the priest Eleazar. After the plague, on the plains of Moab, a new census of the people is taken. Israel was about to enter the promised land, and this list served to divide the inheritance according to the size of each clan. Some names change in other passages, such as Jeezer, which appears as Abiezer in Joshua 17:2. This may be due to a shortened form of the name.

God knows each person and each family by name. No one was a mere number to Him. Today you can rest in the fact that God knows you and keeps you in mind, even if you feel small or little noticed. You can also value those who go unnoticed around you.
exp.12:20:
Moses asks the spies to examine what the land is like: whether it is rich and fertile or poor and dry, and whether it has trees. He also tells them to be strong and of good courage, and to bring back some of the fruit of the land. The text notes that it was the season of the first ripe grapes, that is, the beginning of the grape harvest.

Moses speaks to twelve men, one from each tribe, whom God commanded to explore Canaan before the people entered it. He wanted clear information about the land and its inhabitants. Asking for fruit served as a concrete proof of what God had promised. The passage does not say how long the journey lasted in this verse, but the following verses show that they traveled through the region as far as Hebron.

Before taking a great step, God invites us to observe carefully and with courage. But looking is not the same as distrusting: let us seek the reality, without forgetting that God has already promised to be with us.
exp.23:8:
Israel rests calmly and securely, like a lion or a lioness lying down. No one dares to disturb them, because they know how dangerous they are. Then the verse repeats a promise: God will bless those who bless this people, and those who curse them will receive a curse.

The phrase "lay down" in the verse means he lowers himself to rest. "Seed" means descendants.

Balaam speaks here, the prophet whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. But God put blessings in his mouth, and this is his third time. The words recall the promise made to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. Balak becomes angry right away.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that God takes care of his own, even when others despise them. And this invites us to treat with respect and kindness those whom God loves, instead of speaking badly about them.
exp.26:15:
Moses asks the Lord to appoint a man to lead the people. He calls him "the God of the spirits of all flesh," that is, the God who gives life and knows every human being. "Congregation" is the whole people of Israel, and "set" means to appoint or establish someone.

Moses speaks after God has told him that he would not enter the promised land, because at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, he did not honor God before the people. Instead of complaining, Moses is concerned about Israel's future. He wants the people not to be left "like sheep without a shepherd." God answers by choosing Joshua.

For today: when we face change or limits, we can pray for those who will guide others, in the church, the family, or the workplace. God knows hearts and knows whom to call.
exp.12:15:
This verse gives the name of one of the twelve men chosen to explore Canaan: Geuel, son of Machi, a representative of the tribe of Gad. The verse that follows uses the word "reconocer," which means to explore or inspect the land.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Numbers. God had told Moses to send a leader from each tribe to examine the promised land. The list names each man along with his father and his tribe. Nothing more is known about Geuel; the Bible mentions him only here. He was part of the group that later brought back a divided report.

God notices people the world forgets. Geuel appears only once, yet his name was written down. Your service, even if it seems small or little seen, matters to God. And as this group, which was put to the test, reminds us, what matters most is to respond with faith and faithfulness when God gives us a task.
exp.2:26:
This verse names the four family groups that descended from Kohath, one of the sons of Levi: the Amramites, the Izeharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites. The endings "-ite" and "-ites" only indicate that they belonged to that line, that is, that they were descendants of that person.

God speaks to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai, while he organizes the Levites for service in the tabernacle. Each branch of Levi had a different task. The Gershonites cared for the curtains and coverings, and the Kohathites, according to the text that follows, camped on the south side of the tabernacle and looked after the sanctuary. The names show that God knows and gives orders to his people family by family.

For today: God overlooks no one and no service. Ask yourself what simple task he has entrusted to you, in your church or in your home, and do it faithfully, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.14:4:
This verse says that, along with the lamb offered to God, the Israelite was also to bring wine to pour out as a drink offering. The amount was a quarter of a hin (a measure for liquids, a few liters; its exact volume is not known). A drink offering is a liquid poured out as an offering. A burnt offering is the sacrifice that was burned whole.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people, while they were still in the wilderness. He announces how they would worship once they entered the promised land. The freewill offerings, vow offerings, and festival offerings included flour, oil, and wine, not only the animal. It was a worship that was orderly and complete.

For today: God looks not only at the greatness of our devotion but also at the details. We can ask ourselves whether we worship with our whole heart or only fulfill the main things. Today, offer God something concrete: your time, your gratitude, and your obedience.
exp.16:4:
God says he will make clear whom he has chosen: the staff of that man will bud. In this way God will put an end to the complaints that the people of Israel raise against Moses and Aaron. It also notes that the rod was a staff representing each family.

The LORD speaks to Moses. After Korah's rebellion and the people's complaints, many were still questioning why Aaron and his family served as priests. God proposes a clear sign, with twelve staffs, one for each tribe, placed before him in the tabernacle.

For today: when we feel the urge to complain about what God has commanded or about the people he has placed in charge, we can stop and bring our doubts to him with humility. He is patient and does not ignore our questions, but he prefers that we trust him rather than grumble.
exp.35:11:
This verse says that the five daughters of Zelophehad married men from the family of Manasseh, son of Joseph. That is why the inheritance they received stayed within their father's tribe. The word "inheritance" here means the land that was received as a family inheritance.

The one telling the story is the author of Numbers, closing the account of these sisters. They had asked for land because their father had no sons (Numbers 27). God granted their request, and then commanded that they marry within their own tribe so that the land would not pass to another. Here we see that they carried it out.

For today: God honors those who ask for justice with respect, and also those who obey afterward. We can boldly ask for what is right, and then live faithfully in what God directs us to do, even when it costs us.
exp.11:8:
This verse says that God became very angry with Miriam and Aaron, and that afterward he left. "Fury" is strong anger, and "was kindled" shows that it was intense, like a fire. "Departed" means that God withdrew from that place.

Here the narrator tells what happened after God spoke. Miriam and Aaron had criticized Moses (Numbers 12:1-2), and God called them to the tent of meeting. He explained that Moses was his faithful servant, with whom he spoke directly. Then he asked them why they had not been afraid to speak against him. When he left, the cloud moved away, and Miriam was left with leprosy.

For today: before criticizing someone who serves God, stop and think. God sees the heart and cares about how we treat others. Instead, pray for that person or speak to them with respect.
exp.4:21:
These waters that bring a curse if there is guilt would enter the woman's body. They would make her belly swell and cause her thigh to fall away. The word "bowels" refers to the inside of the body. "Thigh" probably refers to the reproductive organs, though scholars explain it in several ways. She responds, "Amen, amen," meaning "so be it," accepting the oath.

The priest speaks to a woman suspected of adultery, when the husband is jealous but there are no witnesses. The case is left in God's hands, not in people's opinions. If she was innocent, she was set free (v. 28).

Today, do not accuse or condemn over mere suspicions. Place what is hidden in God's hands, who sees the truth, and seek sincerity and trust in your relationships.
exp.13:33:
God says the punishment will fit the offense: each of the forty days that the spies scouted Canaan will become a year of wandering in the desert. Explored, the spies searched the land. The sins are what the verse calls "iniquities," and bearing them means carrying the consequences. The phrase about knowing God's punishment can be understood as experiencing what it means for God to turn away from them or to fail his plan.

The Lord speaks to Moses and to Israel. After hearing the bad report from ten spies, the people wept, rebelled, and even wanted to go back to Egypt. God answers that this generation will not enter the promised land, though their children will.

For today: our decisions have real consequences, and distrust in God can cost us years of blessing. When he asks us to take a difficult step, it is better to trust his promise than to be carried along by fear.
exp.11:5:
God asks Aaron and Miriam to listen carefully. He explains that when there is a prophet of the Lord among his people, he makes himself known through visions and dreams.

Here the Lord himself is speaking. Miriam and Aaron had criticized their brother Moses and considered themselves just as important as he was for speaking on God's behalf. For this reason God calls them to the tent of meeting and corrects them. He reminds them that prophets receive their message in indirect ways, but that with Moses there is a special closeness.

Today we can learn to value the gifts and callings that God gives to others, without envy or criticism. Each person has his or her place, and God knows what he is doing. Rather than judging, we can serve with humility where he has placed us.
exp.31:39:
This verse says that Moses gave the region of Gilead to Machir, of the tribe of Manasseh, and that Machir settled there. The word "gave" is what the verse says, and "settled" means that he took up residence in that place.

The book of Numbers tells how Israel was preparing to enter the promised land. The tribes of Reuben and Gad asked to remain east of the Jordan, and Moses also gave territory to part of the tribe of Manasseh. The descendants of Machir had already conquered Gilead, driving out the Amorites who lived there. Moses, as the leader of Israel, confirms that possession with his authority.

God often gives us particular places and tasks where we can serve him. We can receive with gratitude what he entrusts to us, whether a home, a job, or a community, and care for it with responsibility and faithfulness, without always looking at what others have.
exp.26:13:
God reminds Moses why he will not enter the promised land. The verse says that they disobeyed his command, which means they did not follow what he had said. The people had argued and quarreled with Moses, and the verse says they failed to honor God as holy in front of the people. Kadesh is the place where this happened.

God speaks to Moses on Mount Abarim, shortly before Moses dies. According to Numbers 20, the people complained about having no water. God told Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses and Aaron struck the rock and did not honor God before everyone. Many understand that there was anger and unbelief in this. Others emphasize the disobedience, and the Bible does not give more detail.

For today: obey God as he says, even when we are tired or upset. The way we act can show others who God is. And when we fail, he remains good and faithful.
exp.0:24:
This verse says that in Israel's census, the tribe of Gad had 45,650 men twenty years old and up. These were the ones who could go out to war. The phrase "those that were numbered" means "those who were registered," and I have left out the rest of that sentence's gloss since the verse here reads "those that were numbered." "Generations" and "households of their fathers" refer to the families and lineages of each tribe.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the departure from Egypt, and commanded him to count the men fit for the army. Israel was organizing itself as a people on its way to the promised land. Some scholars debate how to understand such large figures, but the text presents them as an official and orderly record.

For today: God knows and counts each person; no one is a mere number to Him. Today we can serve with confidence in our place within the church and the family, knowing that each contribution matters.
exp.5:20:
This verse closes the instructions about the Nazarite. A "Nazarite" was a person who set himself apart for God for a period of time, under a special vow. The "offering" was what he gave when that time ended. The phrase "beside that that his hand shall get" means that he could give, beyond what was required, whatever his hand was able to provide. Each person had to keep what he had promised, according to the law of the Nazarite vow.

God speaks to Moses to give rules to Israel. Earlier, the final ritual was explained: the priest presented the offerings, and the Nazarite drank wine again. This verse sums up and reminds the reader that the vow was a serious matter. Next comes the priestly blessing.

For today: if you promise something to God or to others, keep it with sincerity. And give generously, without settling for the minimum, because God looks at the heart.
exp.25:22:
This verse begins to list the descendants of Issachar, one of the sons of Jacob. It mentions two of his sons, Tola and Pua, and says that from each one came a family bearing his name. The forms "the Tolaites" and "the Punites" simply mean "the descendants of Tola" and "the descendants of Pua." The older spelling (Thola, Pua, Issachar) corresponds to Tola, Pua and Issachar.

Moses and the priest Eleazar take this census on the plains of Moab, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God ordered it after the plague, to organize the people before they entered the Promised Land and to divide the land according to the size of each tribe. Issachar totals 64,300 men counted.

For today: God knows people by name and counts them one by one. You can trust that you are not a lost number, and also learn to value each person in your family and in your church.
exp.6:73:
This verse describes part of the offering of Pagiel, prince of the tribe of Asher: one golden spoon weighing ten shekels (a shekel was a unit of weight, roughly 11 grams by estimate). It was full of fragrant incense. In this version, the spoon refers to a small container or cup for burning incense.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks. He is telling how, when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribe brought its offering on a different day. Each prince brought the same thing, and the Bible repeats it without changing a word. It was a way of showing that all the tribes had the same value before God.

For today: God values the sincere giving of each person, without comparisons. Give what is yours with joy, and do not worry about what others do.
exp.15:45:
Moses tells Aaron to take the censer, put fire from the altar in it, add incense, and go quickly to where the people are to make atonement, that is, to cover their guilt before God. The word "quickly" appears in the verse itself, so no further explanation is needed. The wrath of God is described in the verse as wrath that has gone out from the Lord, and the plague is the sickness that is killing many people. It had already begun.

A day before, the people had accused Moses and Aaron of the deaths of Korah and his followers, who had rebelled. God wanted to consume the congregation, but Moses acts at once as an intercessor. Aaron, the high priest, runs among the dead and the living, and the plague is stopped.

For today: when someone around us is in danger because of their own wrongdoing, we can pray for that person without delay, instead of judging them. Intercession is an act of love that can make a difference.
exp.28:34:
It says that on the eighth day, after the seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles, the people were to hold a solemn gathering. A "solemn assembly" means a sacred meeting, a day set apart for God. "Servile work" refers to ordinary labor, the hard everyday work. That day, no such work was done.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. Chapter 29 describes the offerings for the feasts of the seventh month. This eighth day closed the feast with a special rest and with its own sacrifices. Some think it marked a special ending; the Bible here does not explain more.

For today: set aside time to rest and be with God, without rush or tasks. Even if your week is very busy, you can pause, give thanks, and listen to him.
exp.20:9:
The verse says that the people of Israel set out and stopped at a place called Oboth. "Set forward" means they started moving, and "pitched" means they set up their tents to rest. It is not known for certain where Oboth was.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just been healed by God when they looked at the bronze serpent set on the pole. After that difficult moment, the people continued on their way toward the promised land. The text shows that God did not leave them behind: he sustained them and guided them stage by stage.

For today: after a trial or a great help from God, do not remain stuck. Take the next step with confidence, remembering that the Lord who healed you or sustained you continues with you on the road, even when it is a simple stretch with nothing special about it.
exp.28:25:
This verse describes the offerings for the fifth day of the Feast of Tabernacles: nine young bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs one year old, all "without blemish", that is, with no physical flaw. The "drink offerings" were liquids, such as wine, that were poured out as an offering, and the "meal offering" was the grain offering.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Israel. Numbers 29 details the offerings for the feasts of the seventh month. During this feast, the number of bulls went down each day: thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, and so on. Scholars have proposed several reasons for this pattern, but the text does not explain it.

Today, this order reminds us that God deserves our best and that our worship should be sincere and careful. We can set aside a fixed moment each day to pray and thank him, without giving him what is left over.
exp.20:26:
This verse quotes a popular saying from those who composed and repeated songs or poems, the ones the verse calls "they that speak in proverbs." They invite people to come to Heshbon, the capital of Sihon, so that the city may be built up and prepared. The phrase "let the city be built and prepared" means that it should be rebuilt and set on its feet again.

The speakers here are these poets, and they quote an ancient song. Many scholars think the original song mocked Heshbon, recalling how Sihon took it from Moab, and that later Israel used it to celebrate its own victory. Not everyone agrees on how the song was originally read, so it is wise to speak with caution. What is clear is that the passage shows how human kingdoms fall.

For today: the powers of this world may seem firm, but they do not last. Trust in God more than in what appears great and secure, and remember that only what He sustains endures.
exp.17:22:
It says the Levites are in charge of doing the work of the tabernacle, which here is called "of the congregation" because it held the tablets of the law. "They shall bear their iniquity" means they will carry the responsibility for the faults connected with the sanctuary. This will be a statute forever, and the Levites will not receive a land inheritance of their own like the other tribes.

God speaks to Aaron through Moses. After certain judgments, God sets apart one tribe to take care of the holy things and to protect the people from approaching improperly. In return, instead of land, they live on the tithes.

For today: God cares for those who serve others, and he also reminds us that serving him is a serious responsibility. We can support with generosity those who serve in the church, and serve ourselves with reverence and humility.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, the sacred tent where God was present among his people. Then he anointed it, that is, he smeared it with special oil, and he sanctified it, or in other words, he set it apart for God's exclusive use. He did the same with the altar and with all its utensils (the "vessels").

Here the book's narrator is speaking, recounting what happened on the day the tabernacle was ready. According to the context that follows, the leaders of the tribes respond by bringing offerings: six carts and twelve oxen. Scholars usually place this moment close to events narrated at the end of Exodus, although the book tells it afterward. For that reason some see here an account that looks back a little.

For today: before serving God, it is good to set apart what we give to him. We can dedicate to God our home, our work, or our time, and respond with generosity, as these leaders did.
exp.23:22:
Balaam speaks another prophetic message, his "parable." He cries out in amazement and fear, asking who will survive when God carries out what he has just announced. Here "survive" means to remain standing, to endure.

The speaker is Balaam, the diviner whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. But God compelled him to bless and to declare the fate of several nations. This is his final message: great powers will fall and others will rise. Scholars debate who Cittim, Assur and Eber are, so it is wise not to claim too much.

For today: empires and human securities are not eternal, and only God governs history. Instead of living in fear, we can trust in him and seek refuge in his care, not in our own power.
exp.6:14:
It says that Nahshon brought as an offering a young bull (a young ox), a ram, and a lamb one year old, to be burned completely on the altar. That is a "burnt offering": a sacrifice given whole to God. The animals were young and without defect, the best of the flock.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers is recording the dedication of the tabernacle. Each tribal leader presented his offering on a different day. This is the first day, and Nahshon represented the tribe of Judah. Interestingly, all of them brought the same things. It is repeated in detail to show that God values each gift, without comparison.

For today: give God your best, not what is left over. Your offering does not need to be greater than someone else's, but sincere and complete. Today you can offer him your time, your work, or your prayer with your whole heart.
exp.15:16:
Each of the two hundred and fifty men was to take his censer, which was a vessel for burning incense. They were to put incense in it and present themselves before the Lord. Moses and Aaron were also to bring their own censer.

Moses speaks to Korah and his followers. They had risen up against Moses and Aaron, saying that the whole congregation was holy and that they did not need their leadership. Moses does not defend himself with arguments, but leaves the matter to God. He proposes an act of worship as the test, and the next day God would show whom He had chosen to draw near to Him with the incense.

Today we can learn that we should not approach God in our own way or out of pride. Before asking for a place or recognition, it is wise to examine the heart and to trust that God is the one who calls and puts each person in his place.
exp.25:9:
This verse recalls what happened in Korah's rebellion. The earth opened and swallowed Korah and the rebels, and the fire consumed two hundred and fifty men. "Men" here means the men who were burned, and "became a sign" means they served as a warning to everyone.

Here the writer of the book, traditionally Moses, reviews the census of Israel's families. Reaching Dathan and Abiram, he recalls how they rose up against Moses and Aaron, and in reality against the LORD. The next verse clarifies something important: the sons of Korah did not die, so the family continued.

For today: God takes humility and respect for his authority seriously. Before we criticize or rebel, it is wise to examine our hearts. And there is also hope: God distinguishes each person, and no one is condemned solely for the sin of their family.
exp.3:12:
Here the instructions are given for preparing the altar of burnt offering, the large bronze altar where the sacrifices were offered, so that it could be carried. First the ashes left over from the offerings are removed. Then the altar is covered with a purple cloth. The ashes are what remains of the sacrificial fire. Purple is a reddish-violet color, associated with royalty and dignity.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron during Israel's journey through the desert. He explains how the priests must cover the sacred objects before the Kohathites, a family of Levites, carry them. Everything had to be done with order and respect, because what was holy could not be handled carelessly.

For today: approaching God with reverence and order. We can prepare the heart before praying or reading the Bible, setting aside distractions or old habits, so that we give God a place of honor.
exp.25:1:
God commands Moses and Eleazar to take a count of the people. All the men from twenty years old and upward are to be counted, family by family, that is, those who were able to go to war. "Sum" means the count or total, and "congregation" refers to the whole people gathered together.

This takes place after the plague that fell on Israel in Numbers 25 because of the idolatry at Peor. Nearly the entire generation of the wilderness had already died, and now a new generation stood by the Jordan, ready to enter the promised land. The count served to organize the people and prepare for the conquest and the division of the land.

For today: God cares for his people with order and purpose, and he does not leave things to chance. We can ask what task he is entrusting to us now, and prepare ourselves responsibly, trusting that he guides each new stage.
exp.32:41:
This verse says that the Israelites left the camp at Zalmonah and camped at Punon. The sentence that explains the older wording must be rewritten for words that appear in the verse: the Israelites set out from Zalmonah and made camp at Punon. It is one more of the people's stops in the desert.

Moses keeps a record of the stages of Israel's journey from Egypt to the edge of the promised land. This list reminds us that God guided every stretch of the way. Some of these places are little known, and it is not certain exactly where they were. Here the people were already nearing Canaan, after years of walking.

For today: sometimes our life seems like a list of small steps with nothing special about them. But God also cares for the ordinary stages. Trust that He walks with you at every stop, and keep moving forward in faith, one day at a time.
exp.30:42:
This verse says that the half of the spoil that belonged to the whole community of Israel, in sheep, came to 337,500. The word "congregation" means the people gathered together, and the word "was" in this verse is the English form of the same statement.

Moses is leading the people after the war against Midian. According to the chapter, God commanded that the spoil be divided into two equal parts: one for the soldiers and another for the rest of the people. From each half, a portion was set apart for God. The exact numbers show that everything was counted with order and justice.

For today: God values justice and generosity. We can ask ourselves whether we recognize that what we have comes from Him, whether we set something aside for Him and for others, and whether we value those who serve on the front lines as much as those who support them.
exp.14:31:
This verse tells us that while Israel was in the wilderness, some men found someone gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. "Found" here means they came upon him or caught him in the act. The Sabbath was the day of rest that God had commanded.

The one telling the story is Moses, or whoever wrote the book, and he recounts a real case. Just before this, God had spoken of sin done with a defiant hand, that is, done on purpose and in open defiance. This account seems to be an example of that, although the text gives no details about the man's intentions. For this reason, the people did not yet know what to do with him.

For today: God invites us to take His word seriously and not to treat lightly what He has asked. We can set aside time for rest and trust in Him, and examine whether there is something we know God wants that we are letting slide.
exp.23:7:
God brought Israel out of Egypt, and it says Israel has a strength like that of a "unicorn." That old word most likely refers to a wild ox or buffalo, a very strong animal (some scholars debate the exact term). Israel will overcome its enemies: it will "devour" them, break their bones, and strike them down with its arrows.

The one speaking is Balaam, a prophet from outside Israel. King Balak had hired him to curse the people, but God put blessings in his mouth instead. That is why, in the next verse, Balak becomes so angry.

For today: Israel's strength did not come from themselves but from God, who brought them out of Egypt. If you feel weak or threatened today, remember that the one who rescued you in the past is still your strength. Trust in his care and not in your own power.
exp.6:41:
This verse says that on the sixth day Eliasaph, son of Deuel, was the one to bring his offering. He was the leader ("prince") of the tribe of Gad. The word "prince" here means a leader or head of a tribe, not the son of a king.

We are in Numbers 7, when the tabernacle was dedicated. The text is a narrative, not a speech. Each day, a leader of one tribe brought the same offering to God, in order. Moses had already received God's instruction to receive them. The details are repeated to show that each tribe was taken into account equally.

For today: God cares about every person, and no one is less than another when it comes to giving thanks to him. We can offer him sincerely what we have, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.28:13:
It says that, together with the burnt offering animals, a grain offering was to be brought: fine flour mixed with oil. There were three tenth parts of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, and two tenth parts for each ram. The grain offerings are the offerings of grain, and fine flour is the finest and purest flour.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, who were close to entering the promised land. Here he gives instructions for the Feast of Tabernacles, which began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. Each day had its own offerings, and these served to worship God with order, gratitude, and reverence.

For today: God values an offering given with care and with the best we have. We can ask ourselves whether we give our time, work, and resources with gratitude and sincerity, not with what we have left over.
exp.3:1:
God asks Moses to count the descendants of Kohath, one of the three families of the tribe of Levi. The request to take a count means carrying out a census or registration. It was to be done by their clans and by their family lines, that is, arranged according to their households and ancestral houses. The name of this family is spelled Kohath in the verse above.

The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron. Israel was in the wilderness, and the Levites were not counted together with the other tribes, because they had a special task: caring for and carrying the tabernacle. The Kohathites would receive the most sacred duty, connected with the objects of the most holy place. The census served to organize that service well.

For today: God cares about order and values each person in their place of service. In the church and in the family, serving with responsibility and in harmony is a way of honoring God, even when our task seems small.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that the priest makes the woman accused of unfaithfulness drink the bitter water, the water that causes the curse. The "bitter water" is water mixed with dust from the sanctuary and the ink of the written curses. "Causes the curse" means that, if she is guilty, the water will bring harm to her; "enter into her" speaks of real pain.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses gives instructions to Israel. It was a procedure for when a husband felt jealous without having witnesses. The case was placed before God and not in the hands of human revenge. Some think it protected the woman, because the outcome depended on God. We do not know for certain how this happened in practice, and the Bible does not mention that it was repeated.

For today: do not hold on to suspicions or use them to punish others. Bring them to God in prayer and seek the truth with humility, dialogue and honesty.
exp.31:27:
This verse says that Moses gave instructions to the leaders who would continue guiding the people: the priest Eleazar, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the tribes. "Entrusted them" means that he placed them in charge, as a matter they were to look after and see carried out. "Princes" here means chiefs or leaders.

The tribes of Gad and Reuben had asked to stay on the east side of the Jordan, because there was good pasture there for their livestock. They promised to leave their families in the cities of Gilead and to cross over armed to help their brothers. Moses puts their promise into the hands of the leaders, so that there would be witnesses and people held responsible.

For today: when you make a promise, do not leave it only in words. Try to keep it faithfully and, if necessary, let someone you trust help you be steadfast.
exp.6:39:
He says that Prince Shelumiel, of the tribe of Simeon, brought a male goat as an offering for sin. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt before God. A "male goat" is a full-grown goat, an animal the law allowed for this kind of offering.

Here the account of Moses speaks. When the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribal leader brought his offering over twelve days. They were all nearly the same, and Scripture repeats them one by one, as if to show that no tribe was less important. Before the offering of thanksgiving, the need for forgiveness was shown.

For today: before we come near to God with praise or service, it is good to humbly acknowledge our faults. Christians believe that Christ offered complete forgiveness, so we can come with confidence, without pride and without fear.
exp.1:23:
This verse gives the total of the men registered in the camp of Ephraim, which included the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin: 108,100. "Numbered" refers to the men of fighting age, recorded in the census. "Armies" refers to their divisions or organization. "Shall go forward in the third rank" means that when the people set out on the march, this group would go in third place.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai. He tells them how to camp around the tabernacle and in what order to travel. In this way the people journeyed with order, and the presence of God was at the center.

Today we can learn that God is a God of order and that each person has a place to fill. Not everyone goes first, but everyone is necessary. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, without envying others.
exp.18:10:
It says that anyone who touches the dead body of a human being is unclean for seven days. Here "unclean" does not mean dirty or sinful, but barred from coming near the worship of God until the process of purification is complete. The word translated "touch" simply means to touch.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, giving rules for the people. Death, the consequence of sin in the world, could not be mixed with the presence of God in the tabernacle. For that reason a purification was prescribed using the water of separation, made with the ashes of a red heifer. Interpreters see in this a teaching about the holiness of God and the seriousness of death.

For today: let us take seriously that God is holy and that only He can cleanse us. When we feel that guilt or pain are pulling us away from Him, let us return to Christ, who offers forgiveness and life.
exp.31:0:
This verse tells us that the tribes of Reuben and Gad had a great number of livestock. When they arrived at the lands of Jazer and Gilead, east of the Jordan River, they saw that they were very good for raising animals. "Multitude" means a large amount, and "seemed good to them" is what the phrase means in the original.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The people of Israel were near the promised land, after defeating kings of that region. These two tribes were already thinking about staying there. In the verses that follow, they ask Moses for permission to settle in that area and not cross the Jordan. Moses is at first worried, and then they reach an agreement.

For today: it is natural to see what suits us, but it is worth asking ourselves whether our desires agree with God's call and with the good of others. Before deciding, we should pray and seek counsel.
exp.15:39:
This verse says that the metal plates on the altar were a reminder for Israel: no one who was not a descendant of Aaron should come near to burn incense before God. If anyone did, they could end up like Korah and his followers.

Moses is speaking of what God commanded. Korah and other leaders had rebelled, wanting the priestly service that God had given only to the family of Aaron. After the judgment, Eleazar turned the censers into a covering for the altar, as a lasting sign. Yet the next day the people began to complain again.

For today: God deserves to be obeyed on his own terms. We can ask ourselves whether we approach him with humility or with pride, and whether we accept the place he has given us without envying the place of others. In Christ we now have access to God, but we still draw near with reverence.
exp.26:6:
God tells Moses that the daughters of Zelophehad are right. He is to give them a portion of the land, just as he gives to their father's brothers, and to hand over to them the inheritance that would have gone to their father. A "possession of an inheritance" means land received as a family property, and "pass" means to transfer or hand over to another person.

The LORD speaks, answering Moses. Zelophehad's five daughters had asked for an inheritance because their father died without sons, and they did not want his name to disappear from Israel. Moses brought the case before God, and God settled it. This gave rise to a general rule about inheritances, which appears in the verses that follow.

God listens to those who ask for justice with respect. If someone today is overlooked or at a disadvantage, we can bring their case to God in prayer and, when it is within our reach, defend what is right with humility and courage.
exp.32:32:
The verse says that the people of Israel left Hor-hagidgad and camped at Jotbathah. The word "having departed" is the same as "setting out," and "pitched" means "camped." It is one more of the stops in the desert.

Moses wrote this itinerary at God's command (Numbers 33:2), when Israel was already near the promised land. The list recalls each stage of the journey. Deuteronomy 10:7 describes Jotbathah as a land of flowing streams of water, so it was a place of refreshment. Many believe Hor-hagidgad is the same site as Gudgodah, but this is not completely certain.

God watches over every stretch of your journey, even on the days that seem routine or merely like passing through. He does not forget you between one stop and the next. Today you can trust that he guides you step by step, and thank him for the "streams" he places along your path.
exp.17:24:
This verse is a simple transitional phrase: "And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying." With it, God begins to give a new instruction. The word "saying" introduces what follows as words that Moses is to pass on.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. Just before this, God explained that the Levites would not receive land, because their inheritance would be the tithes of the people. Now he gives them an instruction of their own: they too were to set aside a tenth of what they received and present it to the Lord. In this way the Levites also gave, and did not only receive.

For today: God speaks with order and purpose, and asks us to listen before we act. Moreover, no one is exempt from being generous. Even someone who lives on the provision of others can learn to give to God with gratitude.
exp.23:23:
It says that ships will come from the coast of Chittim, probably Cyprus or the lands of the Mediterranean. Those forces will bring suffering on Asshur and on Eber, and in the end they too will be destroyed. It is not certain who Asshur and Eber are, nor whom "he" refers to. Some think of ancient empires, and others of Greece or Rome.

Balaam speaks, a prophet whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. But God put only blessings and warnings in his mouth. This is his final message: he announces that powerful nations will rise and fall, and so he cries out, "who shall live?"

For today: no human power lasts forever. When you see that governments or crises seem enormous, trust in God, who still guides history. Put your hope in Him, not in what is passing.
exp.14:21:
This verse begins to speak about what to do when the people fail without meaning to. The word "erred" means to go wrong or fail, and the phrase about not observing the commandments refers to not keeping all the commands that God gave to Moses. It is about failing by mistake, not about rebellion.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel, as they are close to life in the promised land. Earlier he had spoken about thank offerings. Now he explains that if the whole community fails through ignorance, there is a way to be forgiven through sacrifices. This shows that God takes sin seriously, even unintentional sin, and at the same time offers forgiveness.

For today: do not minimize your mistakes or hide them. When you discover that you have failed, even without realizing it, come to God with humility. Christians believe that Christ gives us that complete forgiveness.
exp.28:19:
On the third day of the feast, the verse says, eleven bullocks (young bulls), two rams, and fourteen lambs of the first year were offered, all without blemish, meaning without any physical flaw. The grain offering that accompanied them and the drink offering of poured-out wine are described in the surrounding verses, so the sentence here names only the animals.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the instructions on to Israel. This is the feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day the number of bullocks went down: thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, eleven on the third. Scholars explain that descending order in different ways. In addition, a male goat was offered each day as a sin offering.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. We can ask ourselves which part of our time, affection, and effort we give him sincerely. And we can remember that Christ, the Lamb without blemish, has already made the perfect offering for us.
exp.26:7:
God tells Moses to speak to the people with a new rule: if a man dies without sons, his inheritance will pass to his daughter. The verse says "ye shall cause his inheritance to pass," which means "they will pass on" or "they will hand over." The inheritance is the land and the family's possessions.

The Lord speaks, answering Moses. The five daughters of Zelophehad had come before Moses because their father died without sons, and they feared their family would lose its share of the promised land. God declares that they are right and makes their case a law for all Israel.

For today: God listens to those who ask for justice with respect, and he cares about those who might be left forgotten. We can imitate that attitude by defending the vulnerable with humility, and bringing our needs before God with confidence.
exp.31:35:
The tribe of Gad, it says, also built up, or rebuilt, Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran. They were fortified cities, that is, cities with walls, and they also had folds for sheep, which are pens where the sheep are shut in. In this way they protected both the people and the livestock.

Moses is on the plains of Moab, before Israel crosses the Jordan. Gad and Reuben asked to stay on the east side of the river because they had a great deal of livestock. Moses agreed on the condition that they help their brothers conquer the land on the other side. This verse shows that they had begun to prepare their new home.

For today: God calls us to care for what he entrusts to us, such as family and work, without forgetting our commitment to others. We can build security for our own and, at the same time, serve God's people.
exp.25:28:
This verse lists the descendants of Manasseh, the son of Joseph. From his son Machir came the family of the Machirites. Machir was the father or ancestor of Gilead, and from Gilead came the family of the Gileadites.

This is not the speech of a single character but a record in the book of Numbers, where God directs Moses and Eleazar to count Israel by families. This second census takes place at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the Promised Land. It served to divide the land according to the size of each family.

For today: God knows our names and our family history, and no person is a mere number of little value to Him. We can thank Him for those who went before us in the faith, and think about what legacy of trust in God we will leave to those who come after us.
exp.27:11:
This verse gives instructions for the grain offering that accompanied the sacrifices offered at each new moon. With each bull, three tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil were offered, and with each ram, two tenth parts. The word for the grain offering means an offering, and an ephah tenth is roughly two liters, though ancient measures are difficult to pin down precisely.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, the new generation that was soon to enter the promised land. God reminds them how they were to worship him in an orderly way, including at the beginning of each month. The grain offerings expressed gratitude and devotion alongside the sacrifice.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. We can begin each week or each month by offering God, in prayer, our work, our time, and our provisions with gratitude.
exp.9:33:
This verse says that the cloud of the Lord covered or accompanied the people of Israel during the day, from the moment they left the camp. "Was above them" means it hung over them, as a visible sign of God's presence. "Camp" refers to the place where they had been gathered together.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting how Israel left Mount Sinai after nearly a year there. This is the people's first journey toward the promised land. The ark went ahead to search for a place to rest, and the cloud gave them shelter and direction. Later the text shows that the cloud also marked when to move and when to stop.

For today: God does not leave his people to walk alone. Even when we cannot see a cloud, we can ask him for direction each day and move forward confident that he goes with us.
exp.25:57:
This verse lists the families that descended from Levi: the Libnites, Hebronites, Mahlites, Mushites, and Korathites. Then it says that Kohath had Amram as his son. "Begat" means he was his father or ancestor. In the Bible, a "son" can sometimes mean a descendant, not only a direct child.

This appears in Israel's second census, taken in the wilderness before entering the promised land. The account is told by the narrator, and Moses had a part in that counting. The Levites were counted separately because they served in the tabernacle and would not receive land like the other tribes. Amram is mentioned because Aaron, Moses, and Miriam would come from him.

For today: God pays attention to families and to individual people, not only to the great names. Your life may seem like just one more line in a list, but God can use your faithfulness day by day to bless future generations. Serve him with steadiness.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that the tribe of Ephraim camped on the west side of the tabernacle, under its own standard and organized by companies, which were its divisions or groups. Its leader was Elishama, son of Ammihud. The standard was the banner that identified each group.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions for arranging the camp of Israel in the wilderness. Each tribe had a fixed place around the tabernacle, which stood at the center. In this way the people marched and camped in order, and God was in the midst of them. Scholars are not certain of exactly what the banners looked like.

For today: God cares about order and gives each person a place. You can serve joyfully where He has placed you, without comparing yourself to others, and keep God at the center of your home, your work, and your church.
exp.30:38:
It says that, from the spoils of war, there were thirty thousand five hundred donkeys, and of them sixty-one were set apart as the Lord's tribute. The tribute is a portion given as an offering. It was a small part, about one out of every five hundred, as with the other animals mentioned.

It is part of an account that Moses, the traditional author of the book, tells about the division of the spoils after the war against Midian. God had commanded that what was gained be divided between the warriors and the rest of the people, and that a portion be set apart for Him, which was handed over to the priest Eleazar. The numbers show order and care in carrying out what was commanded.

God deserves the first and the best, not the leftovers. We can set apart, with order and gratitude, a part of our time, money, and talents for Him, recognizing that all we have comes from His hand.
exp.34:31:
This verse says that no one could pay money to get a person who had killed unintentionally out of his city of refuge and back to his land. He had to stay there until the high priest died. The word "satisfaction" means a payment or ransom, and "fled" refers to the one who escaped to that city for protection.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected the unintentional killer from revenge by the victim's family. The text cares for human life and for justice: the killer's punishment was not bought off, and the one who had to remain in the refuge could not be freed for money. Some see in the death of the priest a symbolic closing of the time of penalty, but the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: justice and mercy cannot be bought. We can deal honestly with our mistakes, accept their consequences, and not use money or influence to escape them.
exp.11:12:
Moses cries out to God with a very short and sincere prayer: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." "Cried" means that he prayed aloud, with urgency. Here "beseech" means "ask earnestly," and "heal her" means heal her of her illness.

Miriam, the sister of Moses, had spoken against him and was left with leprosy, a disease of the skin. Aaron recognizes his error and asks for help. Moses, the one she had criticized, is the one who intercedes. God answers that she must spend seven days outside the camp, and the people wait until she returns.

Today, when someone has hurt us or spoken badly of us, we can pray for that person instead of holding on to resentment. God does not always remove every consequence, but he listens with mercy. This week, pray simply for someone who has offended you.
exp.23:14:
Here begins the fourth message of Balaam. "He took up his parable" means that he spoke a solemn message, in the form of a poem or prophecy. Balaam presents himself as the son of Beor and as the man whose eyes are open, meaning someone to whom God granted the ability to see what others do not see. The exact sense of this expression is debated, since other translations render it differently.

Balaam was a diviner hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel. But God put blessings in his mouth instead of curses. Now, before leaving, he announces what Israel will do in the latter days, that is, in the future.

For today: God keeps his word even when someone tries to oppose it. We can rest in the knowledge that his promises do not depend on people, and ask him to open our eyes to see his work.
exp.31:41:
This verse tells that a man named Nobah went out, conquered the town of Kenath together with the villages that depended on it, and gave it his own name: Nobah.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks. Israel was close to entering the promised land. The tribes of Reuben, Gad and part of Manasseh asked to stay east of the Jordan. This verse shows how some families of Manasseh conquered and occupied their territory. Beyond what the text says, it is not known with certainty who Nobah was.

For today: Nobah acted and left his mark, but what matters most is receiving what God gives and occupying it faithfully. Ask yourself what responsibility God has entrusted to you and how you can care for it with diligence and humility, seeking to honor his name more than your own.
exp.14:9:
It says that, along with the sacrifice of a young bull, the Israelite was also to bring wine for the drink offering, which was wine poured out as an offering. The measure was half a hin; the hin was a measure of liquids, and its exact equivalent today is debated, but it was roughly three or four liters. The phrase "offering made by fire, of a sweet savour" refers to a burnt offering that pleased God.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people while they were still in the wilderness. He gives them rules for when they would enter the promised land. Each animal sacrifice was accompanied by flour, oil, and wine, in amounts according to the size of the animal. This taught order and gratitude.

For today: God does not want mere compliance for its own sake, but a grateful heart. We can come to Him with the best we have, with order and joy, and not halfheartedly.
exp.1:0:
God says to Moses and Aaron. The name "Jehovah" is the name of the God of Israel, and it is left out of this translation. The old spelling in the verse is set aside, so the reader sees the words "And the Lord spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying," which is an introductory phrase announcing that an instruction is coming from God.

The one speaking is God, and he is speaking to the two leaders of the people: Moses, the guide, and Aaron, the priest. They are in the wilderness, after having come out of Egypt. What follows is a command about how the tribes were to camp around the tabernacle, the tent where God made his presence known among them. In this way, God was bringing order to the people and showing that he was at the center.

For today: before we organize our life, family, or work, we can stop and listen to God. He still speaks through his Word, and putting his voice first helps everything else find its order.
exp.28:22:
This verse describes the offering for the fourth day of the Feast of Tabernacles: ten young bulls (bullocks), two rams, and fourteen lambs of one year old, all without fault, meaning healthy and without spots. The grain offerings that went with them and the wine poured out as drink offerings are part of the same offering system.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people, before they enter the promised land. Each day of the feast, the number of bulls went down by one: thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, eleven on the third, and so on. Interpreters explain the meaning of this countdown in different ways; the Bible itself does not make it clear.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can ask ourselves whether we give him our time, affection, and resources with order and generosity, and not only when we have something to spare.
exp.3:41:
This verse begins the count of the sons of Merari, the third group of the Levites. It says they were numbered by their families and by the houses of their fathers, that is, according to their lineage. The sentence is incomplete and is finished in the verses that follow. "Numbered" means registered or counted.

God commanded Moses and Aaron to count the Levites who were between thirty and fifty years old and able to serve in the tabernacle. The sons of Merari were responsible for carrying the structural parts: boards, bars, pillars and bases. The sons of Kohath and of Gershon had already been counted. The text is narrative and shows the order in which the service was organized.

For today: God values every person who serves, even in tasks that are not very visible. If your service seems small or hidden, remember that God sees it and counts it as important.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that on the third day of the feast, a male goat was also offered as a sin offering. "Expiation" means covering or cleansing the guilt, which is why the sentence about it has been rewritten. This was in addition to the continual burnt offering, the daily offering that was burned whole. The grain offering was the meal offering, and the wine that was poured out was the drink offering.

God himself gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. This is the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day had a different number of bulls, but the goat for sin was always repeated. Thus, even in a feast of joy, Israel remembered that it needed forgiveness.

For today: even in times of joy, it is good to make room for humility and to recognize our need for forgiveness. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10:10). We can celebrate with gratitude and draw near to God with sincerity.
exp.3:13:
This verse describes how the altar of burnt offering was to be covered for travel. On it they were to place all its utensils: the shovels for removing the ashes, the fleshhooks (large forks for handling the meat), the firepans (containers for carrying coals), and the basins (for catching the blood). Then a covering of strong skins was spread over it, and the poles used for carrying it were put in place.
