The skins in this verse are described in the King James Version as "badgers’ skins," and that translation is uncertain; some believe they were skins of another sea animal or of fine leather.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. He is arranging the work of the Kohathites, a family of Levites, to carry the tabernacle during the march through the desert. The priests were to cover everything first, because the Kohathites were not permitted to touch the holy things.

For today: God cares about order and reverence. We can serve him with care, respect, and good preparation, even in simple tasks.
exp.26:0:
This verse introduces five sisters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. Their ancestors are named back to Manasseh, son of Joseph, to show that they belonged to a well-known family in Israel. "Came" means that they drew near to make a request. The phrase "of the families of Manasseh" refers to their clan within the tribe.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers is speaking. Israel was about to enter the promised land, and the land would be divided by families. The father of these women had died without sons, and they feared that their family would be left without an inheritance. So they came forward before Moses and the leaders.

For today: when something seems unfair, we can bring it with respect and courage before those who can help, trusting that God cares about the people others overlook.
exp.34:20:
This verse says that if someone strikes another person with his hand out of hatred, and that person dies, he is a murderer and must be put to death. The one who struck is the killer, and the avenger of blood, a close relative charged with carrying out justice, is the one who puts him to death.

God is speaking to Moses for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. Rules are being given about the cities of refuge. A distinction had to be made between deliberate killing, driven by hatred, and accidental death, which is addressed in the verses that follow. The law aimed to protect life and prevent unjust revenge.

For today: God values human life, and the intentions of the heart matter to him. We can ask him to free us from resentment and enmity, and seek reconciliation before anger grows and leads us to do harm.
exp.15:37:
It says that the censers, that is, the metal containers in which incense is burned, which Korah and his followers used, were to be beaten out into broad, flat plates to cover the altar. Although those men sinned and paid with their lives, the censers had been presented before the Lord, and for that reason they were made holy, that is, set apart for God. They would serve as a sign for Israel.

The Lord speaks to Moses. Korah and other Levites rebelled and wanted to exercise the priesthood, which God had given to Aaron and his family. God judged them, and now he orders Eleazar, the priest, to gather up the censers to leave a lasting reminder.

For today: God takes humility and respect for his order seriously. We can serve him with gratitude in the place he has given us, without seeking a position that is not ours, and remember that drawing near to him is a gift, not a right.
exp.2:14:
God commands Moses to take a census of the tribe of Levi. He was to count them according to their fathers' households and their families, including every male from one month old and upward. The phrase "the houses of their fathers" means their clans or family lines.

The LORD speaks in the Wilderness of Sinai. The firstborn of Israel belonged to God from the time he delivered them in Egypt. The Levites would be set apart to serve him in place of them (Numbers 3:12-13). That is why they had to be counted, so that their service in the tabernacle could be organized. Counting from one month old suggests that every Levite male belonged to God from very early in life.

God cares for each person and each family has a place in his plan. Today you might ask yourself: what place of service has God given me in my home and in my church? Serve him there with gratitude, remembering that he redeemed you and that you belong to him.
exp.14:14:
This verse says that Israel and the foreigner who lives among them will have the same rule for presenting offerings to God. The word "ordinance" in the verse means a rule or law. The phrase "for ever in your generations" means it will last through all the generations to come. The "stranger" in the verse is the foreigner who lives in the midst of the people. Before the LORD, both are treated the same.

God speaks to Moses while Israel is in the wilderness, and explains how offerings are to be presented once they enter the promised land. If a foreigner wanted to worship the LORD with offerings, he was to do it in the same way as the Israelites. In this way the door was opened for him to take part, without making him a second-class person.

For today: in the church and in everyday life, treat with the same respect and dignity anyone who comes from another place or culture. Before God, all of us have the same door open.
exp.1:31:
This verse sums up the count of the tribes of Israel who were organized in the camp. It says they were counted by families, "by armies" (that is, the men fit for war) and "by companies" (organized groups). The total was 603,550 men. The Levites are not included in this count.

God speaks to Moses in the desert, shortly after the departure from Egypt. He orders that the men of war be counted and that the camp be arranged by tribes, with the tabernacle at the center. In this way the people could camp and march in order. The Levites were counted separately because they had the task of caring for the tabernacle.

For today: God cares for his people with order and counts each one. You too have a place and a task in the community of faith. Seek to serve where God has placed you, with responsibility and with your eyes fixed on him.
exp.3:20:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses, and with that a new instruction begins. The word "saying" introduces the words that God is about to give next.

God speaks, and Moses receives the message to pass on to the people. The verses before this one dealt with the sons of Kohath and the care of the holy things, with the warning not to look at them so that they would not die. Now God moves on to order that the sons of Gershon, another family of Levites, be counted, so that their service in the tabernacle can be assigned. God does not leave the sacred work to chance, but organizes it with clarity.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and he cares about the order and the service of his people. Before acting, take time to listen to him in the Bible and ask him what specific task is yours in your church or family.
exp.20:24:
This verse tells that Israel took the cities of the Amorites and settled in them, including Heshbon and the villages around it. The word "Amorites" names a people who lived in that region. The "villages" were the small towns that depended on the main city.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sihon, king of the Amorites, refused to let Israel pass through and attacked them. Israel won the battle and received that land east of the Jordan. The text that follows explains that Heshbon was Sihon's royal city, and that he had taken it earlier from Moab.

For today: God keeps what he promises, but in his own time and by his own way. If you are waiting for something God has promised you, keep moving forward with faith and thankfulness, and do not lose heart because of obstacles.
exp.5:8:
It says that if a Nazirite, without meaning to, is near someone who dies suddenly, his consecrated hair becomes defiled. For that reason, on the day of his cleansing, which is the seventh day, he must shave his head. The time of special consecration to God is the period of his vow, and shaving means cutting off the hair completely.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to those who made a voluntary vow to set themselves apart for Him. Long hair showed that dedication. Even though the defilement was accidental, it required purification and an offering, as the following verses show. Interpreters often see here the seriousness with which God cares for what is dedicated to Him.

For today: if at some point we fail without meaning to, we should not hide it or treat it as minor. We can return to God with humility, ask for forgiveness, and begin again, trusting in His mercy.
exp.20:29:
It says that Israel destroyed the Amorite kingdom: Heshbon was laid in ruins, and the destruction reached as far as Dibon, Nophah, and Medeba. The words "we have shot at them" and "Heshbon is perished" are rendered this way in the verse above. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and some of its words are translated in several different ways.

It is part of an ancient song, a victory poem that quoted a popular chant. First the voice of the victors speaks, recalling how Sihon had earlier defeated Moab, and then they celebrate Sihon's fall before Israel. It is said that Israel won after Sihon refused them passage and attacked them (Numbers 21:21-26). This explains how Israel came to settle that land.

For today: human kingdoms and powers that seem invincible also pass away. We can rest in God and place our security not in power, money, or success, but in the One who endures.
exp.30:31:
This verse begins the count of the spoils of war against Midian. It says that what remained of the plunder, what the soldiers took, was 675,000 sheep. The list continues in the next verse with cattle and donkeys.

The narrator of the book records in detail the outcome of the war that God commanded Moses to wage against Midian. Moses and the priest Eleazar divided the plunder: one half for the soldiers and the other half for the people. From the people's share, a portion was set apart for the Levites, who cared for the tabernacle. Such exact figures show that everything was counted with care. Some scholars think the numbers are literal and others think they have a special meaning, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: we can learn to be orderly and honest with what we receive, and to set aside a part for the service of God and his work.
exp.14:30:
This verse says that whoever despised the word of the Lord and treated his commandment as worthless will be "cut off," that is, separated from his people. "Looked down on" means he held it in contempt, and "treated as void" means he regarded it as if it had no value at all. "His iniquity shall be upon him" means he will bear his own guilt.

God speaks through Moses. Earlier it was explained that sins committed by mistake could be forgiven through sacrifice. But sin committed with a defiant hand, that is, deliberately and in open challenge, was an open rebellion. Interpreters debate exactly what "being cut off" involved: exclusion, or also judgment from God. The example of the Sabbath appears next.

Today, we can take the Word of God seriously and not treat it lightly. If you see that you have disobeyed on purpose, do not harden your heart: confess it and seek forgiveness in Christ.
exp.19:2:
Here the people argue with Moses. The word "chode" means they scolded him and quarreled with him in anger, so it is rewritten here: they rebuked him and fought with him in anger. They say it would have been better to die along with their brothers, when they "died before the Lord", meaning when God judged them in the wilderness for their rebellion.

The whole congregation of Israel speaks, now at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin. Miriam, the sister of Moses, had just died, and there was no water. Thirst and grief mix with the complaint. Instead of asking God for help, they blame Moses. Interpreters see here a repetition of their earlier complaints.

For today: when something is missing and the pain weighs heavily, do not vent your anger on others or wish to give up. Bring your need to God with sincerity, because He can sustain you even in your own wilderness.
exp.9:23:
This verse says that Abidan, son of Gideoni, was the leader of the tribe of Benjamin while the people marched through the wilderness. The word "host" refers to the organized group of men from that tribe, and the word "standard" was the sign that identified each group of tribes. Here Benjamin marches together with Ephraim and Manasseh.

The book of Numbers tells how Israel left Sinai for the first time, after God gave instructions about the order of the march. The account is not a speech but a list showing that each tribe had a designated leader. This Gideoni is not the judge who appears later in the Bible; the text does not say they are the same person.

God values order and the service of each person. Although Abidan appears only in a list, his task mattered. Today you can serve faithfully in your place, even when no one notices.
exp.16:3:
God tells Moses to place the twelve staffs inside the tabernacle, in front of the ark of the testimony, which held the tablets of the law. There, God says, "I will meet with you," that is, I will make myself known and present to speak with you.

God speaks to Moses after the rebellion of Korah and the complaints of the people against Moses and Aaron. Many questioned who had the right to the priesthood. God proposes a clear sign to settle the dispute: the staff of the chosen one would bud.

For today: when there are doubts or conflicts, instead of arguing and grumbling, we can bring the matter into God's presence and wait for Him to speak. His answer is usually clearer and more patient than our opinions.
exp.21:31:
What it says: The angel of the Lord rebukes Balaam for striking his donkey three times. He explains that he himself went out to stand in the way to stop him, because Balaam's path was twisted, that is, crooked or wrong before God. To oppose you, to block your way, is the sense of the word translated here as "withstand."

Context: Balak, king of Moab, wanted Balaam to curse Israel. God had already allowed him to go, but his heart seemed inclined toward gain. The donkey saw the angel with the sword, and so she turned aside. Balaam, blind to what was spiritual, only grew angry. Now God opens his eyes and speaks to him directly. Some scholars see here a warning about his attitude, not only about the journey.

For today: When something blocks our way, let us not react in anger right away. Let us ask whether God is slowing us down out of love, and ask him for open eyes to hear him with humility.
exp.9:28:
Moses says to Hobab, the son of Raguel the Midianite, that Israel is on its way to the land God promised to give them. He invites him: "come thou with us, and we will do thee good," because God has promised good things for Israel. "We are journeying" means "we are setting out on the road." Hobab is called here "father in law," though the Hebrew word can also refer to a relative by marriage; for this reason some believe he was Moses' brother-in-law.

Moses speaks just as the people are getting ready to leave Mount Sinai. He wants to share the promised blessing with his family and, as is seen later, he is also interested in his help, since Hobab knew the desert well. Hobab answers that he prefers to return to his own land.

Today, if God has given us hope and blessing, we can warmly invite family and friends to walk with us in faith, without pressuring them and with generosity.
exp.21:18:
Here Balaam asks the messengers of Balak to stay and rest that night. He wants to wait and learn what more the Lord will say to him.

Balaam is a prophet from outside Israel. The princes of Moab offer him honor and wealth if he curses the people of Israel. He had already said he could not go against God, yet he asks again. God had already told him not to go (v. 12), so many readers understand this as showing a heart tempted by the reward. Others see it only as caution. The text does not make this entirely clear.

When God has already spoken plainly, there is no need to keep asking in the hope that the answer will change. Let us seek God's will sincerely, not to justify what we already want.
exp.10:22:
He says that God answers Moses with a question: "Is the Lord's hand waxed short?" That is, has my power become small or limited? The phrase is rendered in the verse above as "Is the Lord's hand waxed short?" Then God adds that Moses will see whether what He said comes to pass or not. The "hand" stands for God's power to act.

God is speaking, answering Moses. The people were complaining because they were tired of the manna and wanted meat. Moses, burdened, doubted: there were about six hundred thousand men on foot, and he could not see how there could be enough meat for a month. God reminds him that his power does not depend on what seems possible to Moses.

For today: when a need seems too great, do not measure God by your resources or your logic. Bring your worry to Him honestly, as Moses did, and trust that He can do what He promised, even when you do not yet see how.
exp.24:14:
This verse tells us the name of the Midianite woman who died along with Zimri: her name was Cozbi. She was the daughter of Zur, who was a chief or leader of peoples, that is, the head of several families or tribes in Midian. The phrase "chief of peoples" refers to a leader over groups of families.

The narrator of the book of Numbers explains what happened at Peor, when many Israelites fell into immorality and idolatry with Moabite and Midianite women. Phinehas acted with zeal, and God stopped the plague. The two dead are named, an important man of Israel and an important woman of Midian, to show that the sin was serious and public. Afterward God commands that Midian be confronted.

For today: sin does not stay hidden, nor does it become lesser because of social standing. Let us guard our friendships and decisions, and seek to be faithful to God in the small things.
exp.28:14:
This verse says that along with each of the fourteen lambs, a tenth portion of fine flour mixed with oil was to be presented. The tenth portion was a measure of flour, one tenth of an ephah. The grain offering is the offering of grain, and the fine flour is the finest, most carefully ground flour.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the words on to Israel. This concerns the feasts of the seventh month, here the Feast of Tabernacles, which involved many sacrifices. Each offering was measured precisely, so that the people would worship with order and reverence. The sacrifices pointed to the need for forgiveness and to thankfulness.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We might ask ourselves what part of our time, care, and resources we give to him consistently and gratefully, not only when we happen to remember.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that when the men of the tribe of Reuben who were twenty years old or more and able to go to war were counted, the total was 46,500. The phrase "those that were numbered" refers to those who were registered in the census. Reuben was the eldest son of Jacob.

God himself commanded Moses to take this census in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after bringing Israel out of Egypt. It was a record of each tribe's army before the people set out toward the promised land. The text repeats the same formula for each tribe, so that every one of them was counted by name.

For today: God does not have extra people, and no one gets lost in the crowd to him. Each person counts for him. We can rest in the fact that God knows us, and we can also make sure that no one in our church or family is forgotten.
exp.12:8:
This verse names the representative of the tribe of Ephraim among the twelve men sent to explore the land of Canaan: Hoshea, son of Nun. Later, in verse 16, Moses changes his name to Hoshea and calls him Joshua.

Here the writer of the book presents the list of chosen leaders, one from each tribe. God had told Moses to send these men to look over the land he was going to give to the Israelites. Hoshea appears without much detail, but later he becomes Moses' successor.

For today: God can use people who are barely mentioned at the beginning. Serve faithfully in the small task entrusted to you today, because God may be preparing you for something greater.
exp.20:33:
God speaks to Moses just as Og, king of Bashan, comes out with his whole army to fight. He tells him not to be afraid, because he has already handed the king over to him, along with his people and his land. He orders Moses to deal with him the same way he dealt with Sihon, the king of the Amorites who lived in Heshbon.

The Lord speaks. Israel is on its way to the promised land, and it had already defeated Sihon. Moses could have felt fear, since Bashan was a strong region. God reminds him of a past victory to encourage him. The text that follows tells how Israel won and took the land.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, remember how God helped you before. That memory can strengthen your confidence, and you can pray asking him for courage to take the next step in faith.
exp.12:5:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat, son of Hori, was chosen to be one of the twelve men sent to explore the land. "Princes" means leaders or chiefs of their people.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Numbers. Moses sent these men out from the wilderness of Paran, following the command of the LORD, to survey the land of Canaan that God was promising to give them. One representative is named for each tribe. About Shaphat we know only what this text tells us: his name, his father, and his tribe.

For today: God knows and names even those who hardly appear in the story. This reminds us that our service, though it may seem small or little seen, matters to Him. It also invites us to be faithful in whatever we are entrusted with.
exp.20:31:
It says that Moses sent spies to observe the city of Jazer, which was in Amorite territory. Then the Israelites captured its villages (the small towns around it) and drove out the Amorites who lived in that place. The word "spy out" in the verse above means to explore or examine before acting.

It is part of the account in the book of Numbers, which tells the story of Israel. After defeating King Sihon, the people continue advancing through the land east of the Jordan. Moses does not attack blindly, but first investigates. Shortly afterward God will tell him not to fear King Og. These are passages about ancient warfare, and it is good to read them in their historical context.

For today: trusting God does not remove the need to plan wisely. Before taking an important step, inform yourself, seek counsel, and pray. Faith and prudence walk together.
exp.9:1:
God tells Moses to make two trumpets of silver, shaped by hammering, that is, beating the metal into form and not casting it. They would serve two purposes: to call the whole assembly together, and to give the signal for the camp to set out on the move.

Here the LORD speaks and gives instructions to Moses as Israel is about to leave Mount Sinai for the promised land. The people were very numerous, so they needed a clear signal that everyone could hear. God did not let them move blindly, but in good order.

For today: God is a God of order who guides with clarity. We can set aside time to listen to his voice in the Bible and in prayer before taking important steps, and not move on impulse.
exp.4:2:
God commands that both men and women who are ceremonially unclean (the one with leprosy, the one with a discharge, or the one who touched a dead body) be sent out of the camp. The verse uses a word meaning "send out," so the sense is that they must be sent outside. The reason is that they must not defile the camp, where God himself dwells among his people.

The Lord speaks to Moses while Israel is in the desert, organized around the tabernacle. These purity laws taught that God is holy and that his presence was to be respected. They were not about looking down on the sick; it was a ceremonial order, and the separation was temporary. The Israelites obeyed just as God commanded.

For today: God still desires to dwell among his people, and that invites us to take holiness seriously. We can ask ourselves what things we should keep out of our lives or our church in order to honor his presence, always with compassion and seeking to restore people.
exp.23:15:
Here Balaam says that he heard the words of God, that he knows the knowledge of the most High, and that he saw a vision of the Almighty. The word "fallen" does not necessarily speak of sin, but of lying prostrate on the ground, and "having his eyes open" means that, even so, he saw clearly what God was showing him. "Almighty" means the Almighty.

Balaam was a prophet from outside Israel. Balak, the king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God compelled him to bless them. In this third message, Balaam announces what would happen to Israel and its enemies in the "latter days", that is, in the future. Many believers see in the "star of Jacob" a promise that points to the Messiah, although it has also been connected with King David.

For today: God can speak truth even when the one who carries it is not an example of a good life. Let us ask him for open eyes to receive his word with humility and to obey it, not only to know it.
exp.10:13:
Moses tells God that he alone cannot carry the whole people of Israel. It seems to him a burden far too great. "Bear" means to carry or endure, and "too heavy for me" means it is far more weight than he can manage.

Moses speaks to God, discouraged. The people are in the wilderness, tired of the manna, and they weep and ask for meat. Moses feels as though he has been given the task of raising an entire nation, and he is so distressed that he asks to die. God does not rebuke him; He answers with a solution: gather seventy elders who will help him bear the load.

For today: when you feel worn out from carrying everything, speak to God honestly, as Moses did. And do not be ashamed to ask others for help; God often sustains us through the people who walk alongside us.
exp.12:16:
This verse closes the list of the twelve men whom Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan. "Men" simply means the men sent, and "to spy out" means to explore or examine the land. It also tells how Moses changed the name of Hoshea, son of Nun, and called him Joshua.

The narrator of the book explains who was chosen. According to the beginning of the chapter, God commanded Moses to send one leader from each tribe. Hoshea means "salvation," and Joshua is usually understood to mean "the Lord saves," although the text does not explain why Moses made the change.

For today: God knows by name those whom He calls and entrusts them with real tasks. Ask Him for a faithful outlook, so that you see your challenges honestly, yet trust that He saves.
exp.6:35:
This verse introduces the fifth leader who brings his offering for the sanctuary. His name is Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai, and he was a prince, that is, a chief or leader of the tribe of Simeon. The word "day" shows that each chief presented his offering on a different day.

Moses records here how the tabernacle was dedicated, the tent where God dwelt among his people. Twelve chiefs, one from each tribe, brought the same offering over twelve days. The text repeats the details for each one to give every tribe its place and to show that none was less important.

For today: God cares about every person, even when their name is not famous. Let us learn to give with generosity and steadiness, without comparing ourselves to others. What we offer with a sincere heart has value before God.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that, after the plague, God spoke to Moses and to Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest. The verse's note on old words is not needed here, since the verse uses plain wording: "came to pass" simply means "happened," and "plague" is a great number of deaths, here the plague that struck the people. God was about to give them an order.

The one speaking is the Lord. The plague is the one from Numbers 25, which came because of Israel's idolatry at Baal-peor. Eleazar appears alongside Moses because Aaron had already died. God commands a new census, since the generation from the desert had nearly disappeared. Israel was close to entering the promised land, in the plains of Moab.

For today: God continues to speak and to guide his people after painful moments. Even when there are failures or losses, he does not abandon us, but gives us new direction. If you are coming out of a difficult season, listen to his word and take the next step with confidence.
exp.18:8:
This verse says that a man who was ceremonially clean had to gather up the ashes of the red heifer after it was burned. He would place them outside the camp, in a clean place, and the community of Israel would keep them. These ashes were used to prepare the water of separation, a water for purification. The word "purification" here describes a means of cleansing or making clean.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and they pass these instructions on to the people. The chapter explains how a person who had touched a dead body became clean again, something that made them unclean under the law. Scholars explain the exact symbolism of the rite in several different ways, but all agree that it showed the seriousness of death and the need to be cleansed.

For today: God cares that we can come near to Him clean. When you feel guilt or defilement because of sin, remember that He Himself provides the way of cleansing, and confess your failing with humility.
exp.32:6:
1) What it says: Israel left Etham and "turned back" toward Pi-hahiroth, a place facing Baal-zephon, and camped in front of Migdol. "Camped" means they pitched their tents. "In front of" means they were facing that place.

2) Context: Moses is recording the stages of the journey out of Egypt in writing, like a travel log. This change of direction brought them to a difficult place, with the sea ahead of them. Exodus 14 explains that God himself told them to turn back there. The exact location of these places is not known for certain, and scholars debate it.

3) For today: Sometimes God leads us down a road that seems like a mistake or a dead end. Even so, He knows where we are going. Trust His guidance, because at the end of the road He opened the sea.
exp.23:3:
This verse describes how Balaam presents his message. He says that he heard the words of God and saw a vision of the Almighty. Falling down to the ground means lying flat on the ground, as someone does when overcome before something great. Even so, his eyes were open, meaning he saw clearly what God showed him.

Balaam, son of Beor, was a diviner whom King Balak called to curse Israel. But the Spirit of God came upon him, and instead of cursing, he blessed the people. Some scholars think the falling down describes a prophetic trance; others see it as simple reverence. The Bible does not fully explain this.

For today: God can speak truth even through imperfect people, but what matters is listening to his word with humility. Before we give our opinions or make decisions, we can bow down before God in prayer and ask him for open eyes to see as he sees.
exp.31:22:
If the tribes of Gad and Reuben do not keep what they promised, Moses says, they will have sinned against God himself. He adds a warning: their sin will find them out, sooner or later, and its consequences will catch up with them even if they try to hide it. The phrase "ye have sinned against the Lord" means that they will have failed before God.

Moses is speaking to Gad and Reuben. They wanted to stay east of the Jordan because that land was good for their livestock. Moses grants them this on one condition: they must cross over armed with their brothers and help them conquer Canaan before they return home. In this way they would not leave the other tribes alone.

For today: when we make a promise, God takes it seriously. Keep the commitments you have made, even when no one is watching, and do not put your own comfort ahead of helping others.
exp.28:1:
It says that the people were to present to God a burnt offering, that is, an offering burned completely on the altar. It was "a sweet savour," a way of saying that it pleased God. They were to bring one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year, all without blemish, that is, healthy and free of any flaw. A bullock is a young bull, which refers to the cattle.

God speaks to Moses, and he passes it on to Israel. It was the first day of the seventh month, a holy day of rest and of the blowing of trumpets. Later it came to be known as the feast of trumpets. The offerings marked that day as special and set it apart for God.

Today we can learn to give God our best, not what we have left over. You can begin by setting aside quality time for him each day, with attention and gratitude, instead of giving him only the leftovers of your weariness.
exp.13:30:
God says that the little children of Israel, whom the people claimed would be plunder of war, will indeed enter the promised land. They will know that land and enjoy it, the very land their parents rejected.

God speaks to Israel in the desert, after ten spies gave a bad report and the people rebelled, grumbling that their children would die or be taken captive. God responds with judgment on that generation, but he shows faithfulness: he will fulfill his promise through the next generation.

For today: our doubts and complaints have consequences, but God does not abandon his plans. Trust that he cares for your children and for the youngest, and avoid saying that God failed you before you have seen how he works.
exp.31:23:
This verse says that the tribes of Gad and Reuben may build cities for their little ones and pens for their sheep. But they must keep what they promised. Folds are enclosed places where livestock is kept. "What has gone out of your mouth" refers to their given word.

Moses speaks to Gad and Reuben. They had a great deal of livestock and asked to stay in the lands east of the Jordan. Moses feared they would leave the rest of the Israelites alone in the war. So he allows them to stay, on the condition that they first help their brothers conquer Canaan.

For today: caring for family and work is good, but it must not serve as an excuse for forgetting our commitments. If we have promised something to God or to others, let us keep our word, even when it costs effort.
exp.24:5:
It tells that an Israelite man brought a Midianite woman to his brothers, in the sight of Moses and of the whole people. He did this while they were weeping at the entrance of the tent of meeting, the tent where God made His presence known among Israel.

The people had already fallen into idolatry and sexual immorality with the women of Moab and Midian, worshiping Baal of Peor. God had sent a plague as judgment, and Moses and the judges were ordering that the guilty be punished. While the people wept in repentance, this man acted with brazenness, as if sin did not matter. Scholars agree that the act was an open mockery against God.

Today it reminds us that sin is never a light matter. When others weep and seek God, we must not be indifferent or presume to do what He rejects. Let us ask Him for a tender heart.
exp.12:28:
This verse says that, although the land is good, the people who live there are strong, their cities are large and well protected, and that the spies saw the descendants of Anak. The word "but" introduces the contrast. The descendants of Anak were a group of men known for their great height and strength, according to the biblical account.

The twelve spies whom Moses sent to explore Canaan are speaking. First they confirm that the land is fertile, and then they present the difficulty. This "but" sets up the disagreement: Caleb responds with confidence, while the other spies will spread fear. The text does not say that they lied about what they saw, but that they interpreted it without taking God's promise into account.

For today: when you face a big problem, acknowledge what you see without denying it, but do not let it be the only thing that counts. Also ask what God has said, and trust Him.
exp.32:1:
This verse says that Moses wrote down the places the people went through, one after another, on their way out of Egypt. He did it because God commanded him. The words "goings out" and "journeys" refer to each time they broke camp and set out. Each stage of the road is a journey. The places where they stopped and camped are the stopping points.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and he says that Moses kept this record by the Lord's command. It comes after almost forty years of wandering in the desert, when Israel is about to enter the promised land. The list reminds the people that God guided them step by step. Some of the places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not agree on everything.

For today: remember your own journey. Writing down how God has cared for you at each stage, even the hard ones, strengthens your trust for what lies ahead.
exp.8:8:
This verse is very brief: it says that the Lord spoke to Moses. The name "Lord" stands for God, and the phrase "spake unto" means "spoke to." It is the introduction to a divine answer.

Some men were unclean because they had touched a dead body, and they could not keep the Passover with the others. They asked Moses whether they would really be left out. Moses did not invent an answer, but told them to wait. Now God responds and opens a second opportunity: to keep the Passover one month later.

When you face a hard question or feel left out, do not rush to decide on your own. Bring the matter to God in prayer and in his Word, and wait with humility. He listens and often shows a way you had not seen.
exp.17:4:
This verse says that Aaron and his sons, the priests, would have the responsibility of caring for the sanctuary and the altar. The word "keep" means to take care of something and watch over it carefully. The purpose was that the anger of God would not fall upon the people again.

God speaks to Aaron after Israel, at various moments, suffered judgments for drawing near to what is holy in the wrong way. That is why he divides the tasks: the Levites help, the priests take care of what is most sacred, and no outsider should come near. In this way everyone is protected.

For today: God takes reverence seriously, but he also cares for his people with order and responsibility. We can ask ourselves what task he has entrusted to us, in the church or in the family, and carry it out with respect, humility, and faithfulness, without neglecting what is holy.
exp.35:0:
This verse tells how the leaders of the family of Gilead, a descendant of Manasseh and Joseph, came before Moses and the other leaders of Israel to raise a matter. "Chief fathers" refers to the heads of the clans.

The ones speaking are the leaders of the Gilead clan, of the tribe of Manasseh. They are in the wilderness, near the end of the journey to the promised land. They come about a matter of inheritance: God had given land to the daughters of Zelophehad (Salphaad), and the leaders fear that if they marry men from another tribe, the land would pass to that tribe and their clan would lose it.

For today: when a problem arises, bring it with order and respect before those who have the responsibility to guide, and rely on what God has already said. Seeking wisdom and counsel before acting prevents conflict and protects what God has entrusted to us.
exp.2:30:
This verse says that the descendants of Kohath were responsible for caring for and carrying the most sacred objects of the sanctuary: the ark of the covenant, the table for the bread, the lampstand (the lamp with seven branches), the altars, and the vessels the priests used. They also took care of the veil, which separated the holy place from the most holy place. "In their charge" means that they were accountable for those things.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. He is organizing the Levites by family around the tabernacle, so that worship would be carried out with order and reverence. Each family received a specific task. The Kohathites camped to the south, and their work was the closest to what was holy.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is quiet. Ask yourself what small or specific responsibility you have been entrusted with, in your church or your family, and look after it with respect and consistency.
exp.25:13:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Simeon and says that, adding up all their families, there were 22,200 men. "Simeonites" means the descendants of Simeon, one of the sons of Jacob. Here the men of fighting age are counted.

God himself commands Moses and Eleazar to take this census near the end of the forty years in the desert. The new generation was about to enter the promised land, and the people had to be organized. It is notable that Simeon had been one of the most numerous tribes in the first census, with 59,300 men, and now it was greatly reduced. The Bible does not explain the cause here in detail; some connect it with the plague in Numbers 25, but that is an interpretation.

God knows and counts every family; no one goes unnoticed by him. Today, you can trust that you also matter to him. Value the people in your community, not as numbers, but as part of the people of God.
exp.33:14:
It says that two and a half tribes, that is, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, have already received their share of the land on the other side of the Jordan, toward the east, where the sun rises. The word for that share of land means the land a person receives as their own property, and the phrase about the sunrise means the east.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He explains how the land west of the Jordan will be divided among the remaining nine and a half tribes. Those three tribes had asked to stay on the eastern side (Numbers 32), and Moses makes this clear so that no one doubts who already has their portion. Then God names Eleazar and Joshua to lead the division.

For today: God makes sure things are done with order and clarity. We can follow his example by being clear about the agreements and commitments we have with others, so that confusion and conflict are avoided.
exp.13:38:
It says that Moses told all the children of Israel what God had said, and that the people felt deep sorrow. The phrase "mourned greatly" means they were filled with grief and sorrow, as when someone weeps over a loss. The old form of the word "to" is not needed here, so that comment is left out.

The Israelites had believed the bad report of ten spies and did not want to enter the promised land. So God said that that generation would not enter. Moses passed on that judgment, and the unbelieving spies died. Only Joshua and Caleb were spared. The people's weeping shows sorrow, although the text that follows reveals that it was not a complete repentance, since they soon acted on their own.

Feeling sorry for the mistake is not enough. We need to truly repent: to return to God, trust his word, and obey him today, without taking shortcuts or trying to fix things our own way.
exp.31:20:
This verse says that the men of the tribes of Reuben and Gad were to cross the Jordan River armed, in the sight of the Lord, and keep fighting until the Lord had driven out Israel's enemies. The word "armed" means "ready for battle," and the phrase "until he hath driven out his enemies" means "until he has driven out his enemies."

Moses is speaking. The tribes of Reuben and Gad had a great deal of livestock and wanted to stay in the lands east of the Jordan, which had already been conquered. Moses feared that their brothers would be left alone in the war, so he set them a condition: they had to help conquer the land on the other side of the river before returning to their families and their possessions.

For today: it is not enough to look after what we already have; we are also responsible for helping others. Keeping our promises and supporting the community of faith, even when we are already comfortable, is a way of being faithful to God.
exp.12:7:
He is not the patriarch Joseph of Egypt, but another man with the same name. He is part of a list of twelve leaders, one for each tribe.

God told Moses to send these men to explore the land of Canaan, which He was going to give to Israel. Moses chose them and sent them out from the wilderness of Paran. Later, ten of them would give a report full of fear, and this led the people to doubt God. The Bible says nothing more about Igal.

God takes note of each person by name, even though almost no one remembers them. Your faithfulness in small things matters. Today, when you have a task that seems insignificant, do it with trust in God and without being carried along by the fear of the majority.
exp.33:4:
This verse continues describing the southern border of the promised land. It says the boundary turned at Azmon and continued to the "river of Egypt," which was a watercourse that filled only in the rainy season. Its "goings out," meaning its ends, finished in the west, at the Mediterranean Sea, called "the great sea." Scholars do not agree on exactly where the river of Egypt was; many connect it with the Wadi el-Arish, in the Sinai.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. He wanted Israel to know clearly the land they would receive and how to divide it among the tribes.

For today: God is a God of order and of concrete promises. Just as He set clear boundaries for His people, we can trust that He keeps what He says. Today we can thank Him for what He has given us and live at peace within the limits He sets for us.
exp.25:36:
This verse gives the total of the men counted from the tribe of Ephraim: 32,500. "Counted" refers to those who were registered in the census. It then says that Ephraim and Manasseh are "the sons of Joseph," that is, the two tribes that descended from him.

God commanded Moses and the priest Eleazar to take this census on the plains of Moab, close to entering the promised land. The men counted were those twenty years old and older, fit for war, and the register would serve to divide the land according to the size of each family. Ephraim had dropped from 40,500 in the first census, something the text records only without explaining it.

For today: God does not forget anyone or any family. Each one has their place and their name before Him.
exp.9:24:
The tribe of Dan set out with its banner, arranged in divisions or ordered groups. Dan went at the very end of the whole procession, "gathering up all the camps," that is, closing the march as the rear guard of the other tribes. Its leader was Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai.

The book of Numbers tells how Israel left Mount Sinai, heading toward the promised land, in an order set by God through Moses. Each tribe had its place and its leader. Dan, the largest tribe of the northern group of four, guarded the back of the people. Why this position was assigned to it is not explained, so it is better not to invent reasons.

For today: in God's people there are visible places and quiet ones, like guarding the rear. All of them matter. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, without envying those who go ahead.
exp.31:40:
Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, went out and took some small towns and gave them a new name, "Havoth-jair," which means something like "the villages of Jair."

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers is speaking. He tells how some families of the tribe of Manasseh settled east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead, after Moses had given them permission. Giving a place a name was a way of claiming it as an inheritance. The exact details of where these villages were are explained in different ways, and it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God gives us tasks and specific places in which to serve. We can take on what has been entrusted to us with courage, remembering that everything we receive is a gift of God and that we should care for it with gratitude.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that the men of the family of Merari, counted by their families, totaled 3,200. They were the males from thirty to fifty years old who could serve in the tabernacle. "Counted" here means registered or enrolled in a census. The "tabernacle of the testimony" is the holy tent where God dwelt among his people.

The book of Numbers is a narrative, and here no particular person is speaking. God had commanded Moses and Aaron to take this count of the Levites. Merari was one of the three Levite groups, and his family was assigned to carry the boards, pillars, and bases of the tabernacle. It was humble and heavy work, but it was necessary.

For today: God counts and values each person, even those who carry out tasks that are rarely seen. If your service in the church or at home goes unnoticed, remember that God sees it and considers it important. Serve faithfully, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.15:21:
Moses and Aaron fall facedown and cry out to God. They call him "the God of the spirits of all flesh," that is, the God who gives life to every human being. They ask whether it is right for God to be angry with the whole people when only one man has sinned. The old wording "shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth" means "will you be angry?"

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram had rebelled against the leadership of Moses and Aaron, and many Israelites were following them. God said he would destroy the congregation. Moses and Aaron step in as intercessors, even though they had been attacked by these men. God responds by commanding the people to separate themselves from the rebels. Some think that "one man" refers to Korah as the leader.

Today we can pray for those who hurt us or who go wrong, without repaying evil with evil. Intercession asks for mercy, even when there is guilt.
exp.34:15:
This verse says that if a person strikes another with an iron object and the person dies, that man is a murderer, that is, a killer. The law requires that the murderer must die. "Murderer" means someone who kills another on purpose.

God is speaking to Moses, before Israel enters the promised land. He has just ordered six cities of refuge for the one who kills without meaning to. Now he marks the difference: an iron object, capable of killing, showed intent to do harm, so this was not an accident. In this way justice protected both the innocent and the victim.

For today: God values human life and takes justice seriously. We can be people who guard our words and actions, avoid violence, and ask for forgiveness in time, remembering that God sees the heart.
exp.20:32:
This verse tells how the Israelites turned and went up along the road that led to Bashan, a region to the north. Then Og, the king of that place, came out with all his people and his army to fight against them at Edrei, a city in that area.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Numbers, traditionally attributed to Moses. Israel had just defeated the Amorites and was moving toward the promised land. Now a new enemy appears and attacks first. What follows shows that God had already promised victory and had told Moses not to be afraid.

For today: when you face a big, new problem, remember how God helped you before. His past faithfulness encourages you to trust Him and not to live in fear.
exp.4:8:
It says that everything the Israelites set apart as a holy offering and brought to the priest belonged to the priest. The verse's wording "bring" corresponds to the idea of presenting or bringing the offerings. "Shall be his" means "belongs to him." In other words, these offerings became the support of the one who served God.

God speaks to Moses within the laws about how to deal with sin against another person. First the person confessed, then the harm was repaired and a fifth more was added. If there was no one to pay, the compensation went to God, that is, to the priest. The priests had no land of their own, so they lived from these offerings. Some details about how this was applied in practice are not explained here.

For today: when we have done harm, God calls us to acknowledge it and to make real amends, not only to ask forgiveness. We can also generously support those who serve in the church.
exp.35:9:
This verse says that the daughters of Zelophehad did exactly what the Lord commanded Moses. The instructions God gave about how they could marry are the ones the verse refers to. Zelophehad is the name this verse gives for their father.

The narrator records that they obeyed. Earlier they had asked to receive their father's inheritance, since he had no sons. God granted their request, but with a condition: they were to marry within their own tribe, so that the land would not pass to another tribe. This verse shows that they accepted that condition with confidence.

For today: when God grants us something, He may also ask for responsibility and obedience. The daughters of Zelophehad had asked boldly and then faithfully kept their commitment. We can learn to do the same: pray with confidence and obey with humility, even when that limits our choices.
exp.15:40:
This verse says that on the day after the judgment on Korah and his followers, the whole people complained against Moses and Aaron. The Hebrew-based wording here describes a complaint made quietly or openly, in anger. They accused the two leaders of being responsible for the death of those who had been punished.

The narrator tells what happened after God judged the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. God had shown his decision about who could offer incense, and even the altar was covered as a reminder. Still, the people blamed the leaders instead of recognizing that the judgment came from God. It shows how hardened their hearts were.

For today: when God corrects us or things hurt, it is easy to blame others. Before we complain, we can stop, pray, and humbly ask what God wants to teach us.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that God gave the Levites all the tenth in Israel as their inheritance, that is, as their provision. They received it in exchange for their work in the tabernacle.

God himself speaks to Aaron and the Levites. They would not receive land like the other tribes, since their portion would be serving God. Also, the common people were not to come near the tabernacle, and the Levites bore that responsibility. That is why God provides for them in this way.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his work. We can support with generosity and gratitude those who teach, care for, and serve in our church. And if we serve, we can trust that God is our true provision.
exp.29:9:
This verse says that if a widow or a divorced woman makes a vow, that is, a solemn promise to God, that vow stands. "Divorced" means a woman who has been put away by her husband. "Bound her soul" means to commit herself seriously. "Firm" means that it binds her and must be kept.

God gives these instructions to Moses, and Moses passes them on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. At that time, the vows of a daughter or of a wife could be reviewed and cancelled by her father or her husband. But a widow or a divorced woman had no one to cancel them, so she answered for them herself before God.

For today: when you promise something to God or to others, think carefully before you speak. God takes our word seriously, and we should keep what we promise with honesty and responsibility.
exp.2:35:
The verse says that the descendants of Merari had the responsibility of caring for the structural parts of the tabernacle: the boards (the frames that formed the walls), the bars that held them together, the pillars, the sockets (the bases where they rested), and all its vessels and accessories. The word "custody" means care and watchfulness.

God speaks through Moses during the census of the Levites in the wilderness. Each Levite family received a different task, and Merari had the heaviest: transporting and caring for the large pieces. They camped on the north side, beside the tabernacle. The Bible gives no further detail here, but the text shows a clear order.

For today: not all service to God is visible or brilliant. Some people care for what is basic, what holds everything else up. If your task seems small, remember that God sees it and values it. Do it faithfully.
exp.13:29:
God declares that the adult generation of Israel will not enter the promised land. The phrase about raising a hand is an old way of saying someone makes a solemn oath, and it is not in the verse you are reading, so it can be left aside. Caleb, son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, son of Nun, are the only exceptions.

God speaks through Moses. The spies had returned from Canaan, and the people, full of fear, complained against God and wanted to go back to Egypt. God judges them for their unbelief. Caleb and Joshua did trust that God would keep his promise. The little children, whom the people said would be taken as prey, would enter later.

For today: constant unbelief and complaining can rob us of blessings God already wanted to give us. When you face a challenge, remember what God has promised and do as Caleb and Joshua did: trust in him, even when most people are afraid.
exp.0:28:
This verse says that the men counted from the tribe of Issachar came to 54,400. Being counted means being listed or numbered. These were the men twenty years old and up, fit to go out to war.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the departure from Egypt, and commanded him to take this census. Each tribe was counted by its families and fathers' houses. In this way the people were organized to march and to camp in order. Some scholars understand these figures in a literal way, and others think the word translated "thousand" may have had another meaning. But the purpose of the census is clear: to organize the people.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Each family and each person had their place. You too have a place and a service in your church and in your family. Today, ask God how you can help.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that the place was called Taberah, a name that in Hebrew sounds like "burning" or "scorching," because fire from God fell on the people there. "The fire of the Lord burnt among them" means that the fire reached them. The verse's commentary on the old spelling is omitted here, since that word does not appear in the verse.

The narrator of the book explains the origin of the name. The people of Israel, in the wilderness, had complained within the hearing of God, and He answered with judgment. The fire consumed one edge of the camp. When the people cried out to Moses, he prayed and the fire went out. Even so, the complaints about food soon return.

For today: constant complaining can harden the heart. When you feel the urge to protest, bring your weariness to God in prayer, with sincerity and humility, and remember the good things He has already given you.
exp.30:8:
This verse says that Israel's army took the women of Midian captive, along with their little ones. It also took all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods. The verse itself makes the same point: the children of Israel took the women, the little ones, the cattle, the flocks, and the goods.

The account describes a campaign commanded to Moses shortly after the episode at Baal-peor (chapter 25), where Midian led Israel into idolatry. The text presents it as a judgment commanded by God. It is a hard passage, and scholars interpret it in different ways. Here the narrator only reports what happened; afterward Moses rebukes the officers for letting the women live (vv. 14-18).

This passage reminds us that sin and its influences have serious consequences, and that God takes the faithfulness of his people seriously. Today we do not use violence, for Christ calls us to overcome evil with good. Ask God to help you uproot whatever draws you away from him.
exp.3:10:
When the camp was on the move, the Levites were to cover the golden altar, that is, the altar of incense. First they wrapped it in a cloth of dark blue, which is the color the verse calls blue. On top of that they placed a covering of tough skins; the exact animal named in the verse is uncertain, and some believe it refers to another sea creature or to a fine leather. Then they put in the staves, the poles used to carry it.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. The sons of Kohath were to carry the holy objects of the tabernacle, but only after Aaron and his sons had covered them. In this way what was holy was protected, and no one was allowed to touch or look at it without permission.

Today we can learn to treat with respect and care what God calls holy. Before we pray, read the Bible, or gather with others, we can pause to remember in whose presence we stand.
exp.16:7:
He says that the next day Moses entered the tabernacle of witness and found that Aaron's rod, which belonged to the tribe of Levi, had sprouted. It did not only put out leaves: it had blossoms, shoots, and even ripe almonds. The phrase "had put out shoots" means that new growth had come out of it. Something like this does not happen naturally to a dry rod.

The people had rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and God wanted to make clear whom he had chosen for holy service. Each tribe placed a rod before the LORD, and God answered with a visible sign. Afterward the rod was kept as a reminder for the rebels, so that they would stop complaining.

For today: God can bring life where there seems to be nothing, and he invites us to trust his calling instead of arguing with it. We can hand him what feels dry or fruitless, and wait with humility.
exp.13:22:
God says that the generation that came out of Egypt will not enter the promised land given to their forefathers. None of those who provoked him and despised him will see it.

God speaks to Moses after the people believed the frightened report of ten spies and wanted to return to Egypt. Although they had seen God's signs, they repeatedly lost trust in him. Caleb, on the other hand, followed God faithfully.

For today: faith is not only remembering what God has done, but trusting him when the road is frightening. When you doubt, remember his past faithfulness and take the next step of obedience, knowing that God keeps what he promises.
exp.15:28:
Moses says that if these men die an ordinary death, the way all people do, then God has not sent him. The word "visited" here, in the verse above, means that God reaches them or judges them; in this case it refers to a common death, with nothing extraordinary about it.

Moses speaks against Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who rebelled against his leadership and Aaron's. They were saying that Moses had set himself above the people. Moses does not defend himself with arguments, but lets God himself show who sent him. The words that follow announce that the earth would open up, and so it happened.

For today: When someone questions your service or your calling, you do not need to defend yourself with pride or anger. Act with humility and sincerity, and trust that God will reveal the truth in his time.
exp.10:31:
Verse 32 says that the people stayed up all that day, all that night, and all the next day, gathering quails without stopping. Even the one who gathered the least gathered ten heaps (a "homer" each, a large measure; the text does not give the exact amount). They spread them out to dry, and "all around the camp" means all around the campground.

The narrator tells what happened in the desert. The people complained about eating only manna and kept demanding meat. God gave them what they asked for, but the account shows that they acted out of greed, and that is why the place was given a name that remembers that sin.

For today: before insisting on a desire, ask yourself whether you are asking for it with gratitude and trust in God, or with anxiety and greed. Sometimes receiving everything we want does not do us good if the heart is not healthy.
exp.6:4:
God tells Moses to receive the offerings from the leaders: the wagons and the oxen. Those things will be used in the service of the tabernacle, which here is called the tabernacle of the congregation because it housed the tablets of the law. Moses is to give them to the Levites, assigning to each group what it needs according to its work.

The LORD speaks to Moses. The twelve princes of the tribes had brought wagons and oxen as an offering, but before they are put to use, Moses waits for God's direction. The Levites carried the tabernacle on the journey. Afterward, Moses distributes the wagons according to the task of each Levite family, as the following verse shows.

God receives our offerings and uses them with order and wisdom. We can give generously of what we have, whether time, money, or abilities, and trust that God directs it to where it is needed. It also reminds us to respect the different gifts and tasks within the church.
exp.17:0:
God speaks to Aaron and tells him that he, his sons, and his father's household will "bear the iniquity of the sanctuary" and "the iniquity of your priesthood." This means they will be responsible for any fault or neglect in the service of the holy place. The sentence about "Á" being simply "a," and "llevaréis" being "llevarán," has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The Lord speaks after serious events such as the rebellion of Korah and the sign of Aaron's rod that budded. The people feared drawing near to the sanctuary and dying. God makes clear who is responsible for caring for what is holy and sets up order, with the Levites as helpers to the priests.

For today: if God entrusts you with a service, even a small one, take it seriously and with humility. Do it with care, recognizing that what is holy is not treated lightly, and trusting in God's grace to fulfill it.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the person who gathers the ashes of the red cow must wash his clothes and will be unclean until evening. This rule applies to the Israelites and also to the foreigner who lives among them, and it is a lasting ordinance, meaning a rule that was to last forever. "Unclean" here means ceremonially impure, not necessarily sinful.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron. The ashes were kept to prepare the water of purification, which cleansed the person who had become contaminated by touching a dead body. Curiously, the one who helped purify others also became unclean for a time. Interpreters explain this in several ways, and the text does not fully clarify it.

For today: serving others in their difficult needs can cost us something. Let us serve with humility, and remember that God provides the way to be cleansed, which Christians see fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 9:13-14).
exp.6:58:
Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, a leader of the tribe of Manasseh, brought his offering for the peace offering: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of the first year. The peace offering was a sacrifice of thanksgiving and fellowship, of which the people ate a portion before the Lord. A male goat is a full-grown goat.

The narrator of the book records, day after day, the offerings of the twelve tribal leaders when the altar of the tabernacle was dedicated. Each leader brought the same things, and the text repeats this with care. In this way it shows that God values each tribe equally, without comparing or competing.

Today we can give to God with gratitude and without comparing ourselves to others. What we offer, whether time, money, or service, has value when it comes from a thankful heart, even if others do something similar or different.
exp.6:64:
The verse tells what Abidan, leader of the tribe of Benjamin, brought for the peace offering: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of one year old. A peace offering was a fellowship offering, part of which was eaten in a shared meal before God.

Moses records here, one by one, the gifts that the twelve tribal leaders brought over twelve days for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Each leader presented exactly the same thing, with none standing out above another. The text seems to repeat itself on purpose, to honor each tribe equally.

God takes note of every offering, even those that seem small or repeated. What we give to God sincerely never goes unnoticed, and serving him alongside others, without competing or comparing ourselves, honors everyone equally.
exp.28:32:
This verse speaks of the offerings for the sixth day of the Feast of Tabernacles. Besides the animals, the grain offerings and the drink offerings (wine poured out before God) were to be presented. Everything was to be offered in the amount that corresponded to each animal, and according to what God had commanded, that is, as God had ordered it.

God spoke to Moses, and Moses to Israel, during the time in the wilderness. God wanted the people to celebrate their yearly feasts with order, gratitude and reverence. The repeated details show that worship was not left to each person's whim, but followed what God had indicated.

For today: God values worship that is sincere and also consistent. We can set aside regular times to pray, read the Bible and give thanks, not only when we feel like it. Faith grows stronger through habits that put God first.
exp.27:6:
This verse says that along with each lamb of the daily sacrifice, a drink offering was also to be presented, that is, a drink that was poured out as an offering. The measure was a fourth part of a hin, which was a measure of liquid (roughly a liter, although scholars are not entirely certain). It was to be wine of the best quality, poured out "unto the Lord in the holy place." The phrase "strong wine" means wine that is potent or choice.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, who were now close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of the continual burnt offering, the offering of every morning and every evening, which expressed their daily devotion to God.

For today: God deserves our best and not merely what is left over. We can ask ourselves how to give God our best each day, in our time, attention, and affection, with consistency and from the heart.
exp.25:17:
This verse closes the list of the families of the tribe of Gad. The word "numbered" means counted, that is, the men who were registered. In total there were forty thousand five hundred.

God commanded Moses and the priest Eleazar to take this census on the plains of Moab, after the plague in the wilderness. The Israelites were about to enter the promised land. According to the same chapter, the numbers would serve to divide the land among the tribes. Each family listed by name showed that God was still keeping his promise, even after years of hardship.

For today: God does not see you as a lost number in the crowd. He knows your name and your family, and he has a place for you among his people. Give thanks for your community of faith and commit yourself to serving in it faithfully.
exp.13:40:
Moses asks the Israelites why they are once again disobeying the Lord's command. Breaking the word of God means going against or ignoring what God has commanded. He warns them that this will not work out for them either; it will not succeed.

God had already said that, because of their lack of faith, the people would not enter the land and must return to the desert. Now, early in the morning, they say they have sinned and want to go up the mountain to fight. But they do this without God going with them. Moses warns them that without the presence of the Lord they will be defeated by the Amalekites and Canaanites.

Truly repenting is not just feeling sorry or doing something on our own to fix the mistake. It means listening to God and obeying him, even when his direction is not what we expected. Before acting, ask him: "Lord, what do you want me to do?"
exp.2:7:
It says the Levites were to take care of all the utensils and furnishings of the tabernacle, which here is described as the tabernacle that kept the tablets of the law. The sacred objects and articles are meant, not jewels. They were also to take charge of what the Israelites entrusted to them, that is, the tasks that belonged to the people in worship, and to serve in the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites are set apart to help Aaron and his sons, the priests. They did not offer the sacrifices, but they did the daily work that kept in order the place where God dwelt with his people. They served on behalf of the whole congregation.

For today: humble and constant service is also valuable to God. Caring for, organizing, cleaning, or helping in your church, without seeking applause, is a real way of worshiping him.
exp.4:17:
This verse describes a moment in the ritual. The priest stands the woman before God, uncovers her head (or lets her hair down; scholars understand this in different ways), and places in her hands the offering of memorial, which is the jealousy offering. Meanwhile he holds the bitter water that brings the curse, meaning that it would bring serious consequences if she were guilty.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the case of a husband who suspects unfaithfulness but has no witnesses. It was a solemn process that placed the matter in God's hands and not in human revenge. Today it is understood as a law belonging to that time, and the Bible does not say that we should repeat it.

For today: when there are suspicions or conflicts, let us not act with rumors or violence. Let us seek the truth with humility, trusting that God sees everything and is just.
exp.6:85:
This verse closes the account of the offerings from the twelve leaders of Israel. Each one gave a golden spoon full of incense. Each spoon weighed ten shekels, and the total came to one hundred and twenty shekels of gold.

Here the one speaking is not a character but the narrator of the book, who records in detail what each tribe brought for the dedication of the altar. The offerings of the twelve leaders are identical, so no tribe stands above another. The record shows that God took note of every gift.

For today: God values sincere and steady giving, even when it seems repetitive or small. We can serve him faithfully in everyday life, without seeking to stand out above others, trusting that he sees every act of love.
exp.7:25:
It says that the Levites over fifty years old would no longer do the heavy work of the tabernacle, but could still help their brothers. "Keeping watch" means taking care of and guarding what is holy. "Service" here refers to the heavy tasks, such as setting up, taking down, and carrying. "Duties" are their assigned responsibilities.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, when the service of the Levites is being organized. He gives them a time of active service, from twenty-five to fifty years of age. After that there is a change, not an abandonment: they kept accompanying and caring for the holy things. Some think this protected the older men from physical wear; the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: serving God changes with the stages of life, but it never ends. If you can no longer do what you once did, you can counsel, pray, encourage, and care for others. All sincere service has value before God.
exp.21:15:
This verse tells how Balak's second group of messengers came to Balaam. They repeated the king's request to him: "Let nothing, I pray thee, hinder thee from coming unto me." The old wording is easy to follow: "came unto" means "came to," "said to him" means "told him," and "I pray thee" means "please" or "I beg you."

Balak was king of Moab and feared the people of Israel, who were camped nearby. He had already sent a first delegation, and Balaam refused to go. Now Balak insists with officials of higher rank, to press and persuade him. Balaam already knew that God did not want him to curse Israel, so the insistence put his obedience to the test.

For today: when God has already spoken clearly, pressure or tempting offers should not change our decision. It is wise to return to God's Word and remain firm, without going around in circles about the matter.
exp.10:8:
This verse tells how the manna came. At night, when the dew fell on the camp, the manna fell along with it.

The narrator describes the life of Israel in the wilderness, after leaving Egypt. God gave them manna every day, and the people prepared it in various ways. But in the verses that follow, the people complain and weep because they want another food. Moses feels overwhelmed, and God becomes angry.

For today: God cares for us with daily provision, often simple and quiet, like the dew. Today we can pause to give thanks for what we have already received, instead of focusing only on what we lack.
exp.28:4:
It says that, in addition to the other sacrifices of the day, a male goat was to be offered as a sin offering. The word "atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt, and "reconcile" means to have peace with God again. It was an offering so that the people would be forgiven.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. This takes place on the first day of the seventh month, the feast of trumpets. There the people began a solemn season, which led up to the Day of Atonement ten days later. Amid so many offerings of praise, God made it clear that sin needed to be dealt with.

Today, Christians believe that Christ is the final sacrifice who reconciles us to God. We can come to Him with sincerity, acknowledge our failures, and receive His forgiveness with gratitude, without hiding anything or trying to pay for it on our own.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that when the whole people had to be gathered, the priests blew the trumpets, but with a different sound from the alarm. "But" is the word for "but", and "ye shall blow" means "you shall blow". The "congregation" is the community of Israel. The "alarm" was a sharper, broken blast, used to signal that the people had to set out.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, after commanding him to make two silver trumpets. With them clear signals were given: one blast to gather the people and another to break camp. In this way everyone knew what to do, and the journey was kept in order.

For today: God is a God of order and clarity. We can learn to recognize his voice, to respond when he calls us to gather with his people, and not to mistake an invitation to rest and worship for a signal of haste or alarm.
exp.14:10:
This verse says that the same rules for the offerings of flour, oil, and wine apply to every animal that is presented: whether it is a bullock, a ram, or a lamb, and whether it is from the sheep or from the goats. The word "or" appears throughout the verse as the link between each choice. No one was left outside the instruction.

God speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people of Israel. They were still in the wilderness, but God gives them rules for when they enter the promised land. He wants his worship to be orderly and wants everyone, without exception, to know how to come near to him with gratitude.

For today: God cares about the details of our worship and shows no favorites. We can come to him with sincerity, knowing that the same grace is for everyone. Ask yourself: is my worship steady and sincere, or do I only offer it when it suits me?
exp.6:25:
Eliab also brought one golden spoon of ten shekels, full of incense. The word "spoon" here refers to a small container or bowl, and the incense was burned as an offering of a pleasing aroma.
