Moses records how the leaders of the tribes of Israel brought offerings to dedicate the altar of the tabernacle. Each leader did so on a different day, and all of them presented the same things. This day belonged to Eliab, of the tribe of Zebulun. God wanted each tribe to be recorded by name.

God values every offering, even when others give something similar and no one singles it out. You can give your time, your talents, or your resources with a sincere heart, without comparing yourself to others. What you do out of love for God does not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.30:24:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and what follows are his instructions. "Lord" is the name of God, and the word "spake unto" simply means "spoke to."

The author narrates, and the one speaking is God. Israel has just defeated Midian, and the earlier passage has already explained how to purify the soldiers and the objects they brought back from the war. Now God gives instructions for dividing the spoil in an orderly way among the fighting men and the whole congregation. Moses was to do this together with the priest Eleazar and the heads of the families.

God attends not only to the great moments but also to practical details and to justice. Before deciding how to divide resources, organize a project, or settle a family matter, we can pause and ask him for direction. He guides with wisdom and order.
exp.23:9:
Balak's anger burned against Balaam. Striking the hands together was a gesture of anger and frustration. Balak complains to him that he called him to curse his enemies, but Balaam blessed them three times over.

Balak was king of Moab and was afraid of Israel, which was camped nearby. He hired Balaam, a prophet from outside Israel, to curse the people. But God allowed him to say only what God put in his mouth, and each time a blessing came out. So Balak, who had promised to honor Balaam, now dismisses him in irritation.

For today: no one can curse what God has blessed. If you trust in Him, do not fear the words, threats, or evil wishes of others. And when God directs you, seek to be faithful to His word even when that does not please everyone.
exp.32:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the wilderness of Sin and camped at a place called Dophkah. The sentence about "departed" means they had set out, and "camped" is what the verse says of them settling down there. No one knows for certain where Dophkah was.

Moses wrote this list of places at God's command (Numbers 33:2), to keep a record of the people's journey from Egypt. Dophkah does not appear in the account in Exodus, so it was a brief stop, with no event recorded there. Even so, it was written down. Afterward came Rephidim, where the water ran out.

Today we can remember that God also walks with us through the ordinary stages of life, the ones where it seems nothing important is happening. If you are in such a time today, keep trusting and moving forward. God guides you step by step, and nothing on your path escapes his notice.
exp.6:66:
Ahiezer, leader of the tribe of Dan, presented a silver dish weighing 130 shekels and a silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, that is, the official weight of the holy place. Both were full of fine flour mixed with oil, for a grain offering. The word "offering" here means a gift brought to God.

The narrator of the book describes the dedication of the tabernacle. Over twelve days, each tribal leader brought the same offering, and this is the tenth day, Dan's turn. The text repeats the details one by one, which shows that each tribe was valued equally, without any difference.

For today: God pays attention to every person and every gift, without comparing them. Offer Him sincerely what you have, without competing or looking down on what others give. Your service, large or small, has value before Him when it comes from a grateful heart.
exp.13:20:
God declares with an oath, "as I live": as surely as He Himself lives. He says that His glory, that is, His greatness and His power, will fill the whole earth. The word that the older text uses for "fill" is an old form of the modern word, so the verse reads plainly as "filled" here.

Yet even if the people fail, God's purpose will not be stopped.

The Lord speaks after Israel, frightened by the report of the spies, wanted to return to Egypt. Moses had pleaded for the people's forgiveness. God forgives, but makes clear there will be consequences: that generation, which saw His signs and still refused to trust Him, would not enter the promised land.

For today: God can forgive us and still allow us to face the consequences of our unbelief. Trust Him today, for His plans will be fulfilled, and it is better to walk with Him than against Him.
exp.1:33:
This verse says that the people of Israel obeyed everything God commanded Moses. Each tribe camped beside its own standard (its banner or sign), and when they set out, each person went with their family and their father's house, that is, their lineage.

The narrator of the book summarizes the order of the camp in the wilderness, after the census. God had shown Moses where each tribe was to be placed around the tabernacle, and the Levites were set apart for the sacred service. This verse closes the section and shows that the people carried out what had been commanded.

For today: their obedience was orderly and concrete. We can ask ourselves what clear instruction from God in his Word we have put off, and take a simple step today to carry it out, knowing that he cares for and guides his own.
exp.31:28:
Moses tells the children of Gad and the children of Reuben that if they cross the Jordan with the other Israelites, every man armed for battle and committed before the Lord, then they will receive the land of Gilead as their possession. "Subdued" means conquered or brought under control. "Ye shall give" is addressed to the leaders who will receive the order to hand over that land.

Moses speaks after these two tribes asked to stay east of the Jordan, because there was good pasture there for their livestock. Moses feared they would leave their brothers alone in the fight. So he sets a clear condition for them, and gives the instructions to Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy the blessings God gives us. He calls us to keep what we have promised and to help others in their struggle, without seeking only our own comfort.
exp.11:0:
The verse says that Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married; it repeats that he had taken her as his wife. The name "Cushite" refers in the Bible to Cush, a region south of Egypt.

Miriam and Aaron are the brothers of Moses. They speak against him, but what follows shows that their real complaint is something else: they resented that Moses had a special place as God's spokesman. It is not known for certain who this woman was. Some believe she was a second wife of Moses; others believe she was Zipporah, and that she was called this because she came from another region. The Bible does not make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our criticisms of others hide envy or a desire to be more important. Before speaking badly of someone, it is good to examine the heart and remember that God hears what we say.
exp.23:17:
This verse says that Edom, also called Seir, will be conquered by its enemies. "Will be taken" means that it will be occupied or brought under control. And that Israel "will act valiantly," that is, it will act with courage and strength. Seir is the mountain region where Edom lived.

Balaam speaks here, a foreign prophet whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. But God compelled him to bless them. In this fourth message he announces the future of several neighboring peoples. Many Christians see in the "star of Jacob" a promise that points to the Messiah; others connect it first to David. Both readings have been held.

For today: God fulfills his purposes even though no one can stop him, not even someone who wants to harm us. We can live with courage, trusting that he sustains his people and that his promises do not depend on our strength.
exp.23:5:
The verse compares the people of Israel to things full of life and beauty: streams that stretch out, gardens beside a river, aloes (fragrant trees) planted by God, and cedars beside the water. All are images of abundance, fruit, and strength. "Aloes" is an old word, and its exact identification is uncertain.

The speaker is Balaam, a foreign prophet. King Balak hired him to curse Israel, but God put a blessing in his mouth. Seeing Israel's tents pitched in good order, Balaam describes how God cares for his people and makes them prosper.

For today: just as trees beside the water bear fruit, our lives grow when they remain close to God. We can set aside a time each day to pray and read the Bible, trusting that He sustains us even when others speak badly of us.
exp.5:18:
This verse says the priest takes three things: the shoulder (the front leg) of the ram, already cooked, one unleavened cake, and one thin, flaky unleavened wafer. He places all of these in the hands of the Nazarite, right after the man has shaved his head at the end of his time of dedication. "Nazarite" means someone set apart for God by a vow.

Moses gives these instructions on God's behalf. The Nazarite had promised to be set apart for the Lord for a period of time, and when he completed it, a closing ceremony was held. Placing the offerings in his hands shows that he himself was presenting them, with the priest's help.

For today: when we make a promise to God, it is worth keeping it and finishing it with gratitude, offering to him with open hands what we have lived through and accomplished.
exp.6:40:
This verse ends the list of what Shelumiel, leader of the tribe of Simeon, brought. It speaks of the "peace offering," a sacrifice of fellowship and thanksgiving to God, which was shared in a meal. He offered two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of the first year. The male goat is a kid goat, and the word "was" appears spelled differently in this older version.

God speaks through Moses, and the account is written down. When the tabernacle had been set up, each tribal leader brought his offering, one day for each tribe. The offerings are almost identical. This shows that all the tribes were equally valued and that each took part willingly in worship.

For today: God values each person giving him their thanksgiving, even when others give the same thing or it seems repetitive. We can give thanks to him consistently and without comparing ourselves, knowing that our sincere offering counts before him.
exp.3:25:
This verse describes part of the work of the Gershonites. They were to carry the hangings of the court (the courtyard that surrounded the tabernacle), the hanging for the gate of the court, the cords, and all the equipment needed for their use. The "hanging" here is the curtain of the gate. The "instruments" are the tools and equipment. "So shall they serve" means that this would be their assigned work.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives instructions for organizing the Levites in the wilderness. Each Levite family had a specific task for carrying the tabernacle when the people moved. The Gershonites carried the cloths and curtains, under the supervision of Ithamar, son of Aaron. In this way everything was done with order and reverence.

For today: God values simple and unseen service. Carrying curtains and cords did not seem glorious, but it was sacred work. Faithfully do the task that has been entrusted to you, even when no one notices it.
exp.25:39:
This verse says that Bela, son of Benjamin, had two sons: Ard and Naaman. From each of them came a large family, named after him: the Ardites and the Naamites.

We are at Israel's second census, taken by Moses and the priest Eleazar at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God commanded them to count the men and record each family so that the promised land could be divided. The names of Ard and Naaman appear here alongside other lists in the Bible that differ a little, and it is not known for certain why; there are several possible explanations.

For today: God knows and remembers even the people almost no one mentions. Your name and your story matter to him. You can live with the assurance that you are not just a number, and also value those who go unnoticed around you.
exp.33:16:
This verse says that God names the men who will divide the land of Canaan among the people. The main officials are Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun.

The Lord speaks to Moses near the end of the journey through the desert. Israel is about to enter the promised land, and God gives instructions so that the division will be fair. Moses would not enter, so Joshua would take his place. Later, a leader from each tribe would also be appointed alongside them.

For today: God cares about order and justice when responsibilities or possessions are shared out. If you lead in your family, your church, or your work, try to act with openness, work as a team, and not decide alone, always seeking God's direction.
exp.35:4:
Moses gives the people an order on God's behalf. He tells them that the leaders of the tribe of Joseph were right in what they raised. Their request is just and fair, and Moses spoke according to the word of the Lord.

The leaders of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, feared that the land of Zelophehad's daughters would pass to another tribe if they married outside their tribe. That would leave their tribe with less territory. Moses consulted God and confirmed that their claim was correct. The solution comes in the following verses: the daughters could marry whoever they wanted, but within their own tribe.

Today we can learn to listen with humility. Moses did not dismiss a concern simply because it came from others; he took it seriously and sought God's guidance. A good leader, or a good parent or friend, recognizes when someone is right.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that throughout the whole time of his vow, the nazirite belongs to God in a special way. The "nazirite" period is the time of the nazirite's dedication, and "holy" here means set apart for the Lord.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel. A man or a woman could make this vow for a period of time, and had to keep certain rules, such as not going near a dead body, not even that of a family member. The verse sums up the reason: that person wore on his head a sign of devotion to God. Scholars do not agree on every detail of how this vow was lived out in practice.

For today: although we may not make a vow like that, we can ask ourselves what place we give God in our daily decisions. A sincere devotion shows in concrete and steady habits, not only in good intentions.
exp.15:35:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses. After the rebellion of Korah and his followers, God gives a new instruction. The phrase "spake unto" is an older way of saying "spoke to."

God speaks here right after a very frightening moment: the earth swallowed up the rebels, and fire came out and consumed the 250 men who were offering incense without authorization. The people fled in fear. Now God gives Moses a command about what was left behind: the censers, which had been used in God's presence and were therefore considered holy.

For today: God keeps speaking after times of crisis and guides us in what comes next. After a difficult moment, do not stay stuck in fear or disorder. Seek his direction in his Word and take the next step with reverence and obedience.
exp.28:17:
This verse describes the offerings for the second day of the Feast of Tabernacles. The "meat offerings," which are grain offerings mixed with oil, and the "drink offerings," which are wine poured out before God, were to be offered in the exact quantity for the bullocks, rams, and lambs, "according to their number," that is, as commanded.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, now close to entering the promised land. This chapter details the offerings for the feasts of the seventh month. Each day of the feast the number of bullocks went down, and this shows a careful order. Scholars explain the meaning of that descending count in several ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God deserves our worship with order, attention, and sincerity. We can set aside a regular time to pray and give thanks to him, not out of empty habit.
exp.0:6:
This verse names the leader of the tribe of Judah: Nahshon, son of Amminadab. It is part of a list of leaders, one for each tribe.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to count the people of Israel, especially the men fit for war. For this task, each tribe provides a representative. Judah appears third in this list. Later, Nahshon also appears in the genealogy that leads to David (Ruth 4:20-22) and, according to Matthew 1:4, to Jesus.

For today: God works through people with real names and real responsibilities. Even if your service seems small or little seen, God knows it. Serve faithfully where you are, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.20:8:
Moses obeyed God and made a serpent of bronze, or metal, and set it on a pole, which is called here a "banner." From then on, if a snake bit someone, that person would look at the metal serpent and be kept alive.

The people were in the desert and had complained against God and against Moses. Venomous snakes came among them, and the people recognized their sin and asked for prayer. Moses interceded, and God himself pointed out the remedy. The one speaking and acting was Moses, following God's instruction.

For today: when we recognize our wrong, God invites us to trust in Him and obey, even when His way seems simple or strange. The healing did not come from the metal figure, but from faith in God's promise. Today, look to God with trust.
exp.3:26:
This verse says that all the work of the sons of Gershon, that is, their burdens and their service, was to be carried out under the direction of Aaron and his sons. The words "burdens" and "service" are the ones that appear in the verse above, so we can say that "burdens" refers to the loads or responsibilities they carried, and "service" means the work they did. The Gershonites were to be given, as a task under their care, everything they had to carry.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. The Levites were divided into families, and the Gershonites took care of and transported the curtains, coverings, and cords of the tabernacle. God commanded that the work be organized and that Ithamar, son of Aaron, oversee this group.

For today: serving God is best when there is order and clear responsibility. Even tasks that seem small matter. We can ask ourselves what our task is in the church or the family, carry it out faithfully, and humbly accept the guidance and help of others.
exp.2:12:
It says that every firstborn belongs to God. When God struck down the firstborn of Egypt, he set apart for himself the firstborn of Israel, both of people and of animals. The verse of the word "hallowed" is "set apart as his own." "Smote" refers to the tenth plague. At the end God affirms his authority: "I am the Lord."

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, while he is organizing the people. The firstborn of Israel had been saved at the Passover, and that is why they belonged to God. Now he takes the Levites to serve him in their place, as seen in the previous verse.

For today: what we have and what we are was a gift from God, and it is not only ours. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, talents, or resources we are giving back to him with gratitude, remembering that he redeemed us.
exp.20:23:
It says that Israel defeated King Sihon "with the edge of the sword," that is, in battle with weapons. Afterward Israel took possession of his land, from the Arnon River to the Jabbok River, which reached as far as the border of the Ammonites. The text explies that they did not advance any further because that border was "strong," meaning it was well defended. The phrase "smote him" means "struck him down" or "defeated him."

The narrator recounts what happened near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel had asked for peaceful passage along the king's highway, without touching fields or wells. Sihon refused and attacked first. The account presents the conquest as a response to that aggression. This is a passage about ancient war, and it should not be used to justify violence today.

For today: Israel asked for peaceful passage before fighting. We can seek dialogue and respect first in conflicts. We should also notice that God sets limits, and we should learn to accept the limits He places in our lives.
exp.1:30:
This verse says that when all the men counted in the camp of Dan are added together, the total is 157,600. Dan was the tribe that marched at the rear, and so it says they would go "hindmost", that is, last, "with their standards", meaning following the banners of their group.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and explains how Israel was to camp and travel in the wilderness. Each tribe had its place, and Dan closed the march together with Asher and Naphtali, on the north side. This order showed that God is a God of order and that he cared for his people.

For today: not everyone takes the first place, and that does not make them any less important. If God places you in an inconspicuous spot, serve faithfully. He counts and values each person.
exp.7:16:
God says that every firstborn of Israel, both people and animals, belongs to him. The reason is that when God struck down the firstborn of Egypt, he set apart for himself the firstborn of Israel. Here "set apart" means dedicated to God, and the last plague in Egypt is the one being referred to.

God is speaking to Moses. The Levites have just been presented to serve in the tabernacle. God explains that they take the place of the firstborn of all Israel, who belonged to him because they had been spared during the Passover. In this way, the tribe of Levi serves on behalf of the whole people.

For today: what God has redeemed belongs to him. We can ask what place God holds in our lives, since he rescued us and calls us to live grateful, giving our time, talents and affection to his service, not only what we have left over.
exp.21:39:
Balak prepared a sacrifice or feast: he killed oxen and sheep. Then he sent some of that meat to Balaam and to the princes who had come with him. The word "sent" here means that he had the food delivered to them, as a sign of honor and welcome.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and had sent for Balaam to curse the people. Balaam had just said that he would speak only what God put in his mouth. Balak responds with honors and feasting, perhaps to win his favor. The text does not explain all of his motives, but the next step will be to take Balaam to a high place to see Israel.

We may be tempted to be swayed by flattery, gifts, or social pressure. This scene invites us to keep our loyalty to God firm, and to decide according to his word, not according to who honors us.
exp.1:13:
This verse introduces the tribe of Gad and names its leader: Eliasaph, son of Reuel. "Leader" here means the head or prince of the tribe. Gad appears alongside Reuben and Simeon, camping on the south side of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions on how Israel was to camp in the wilderness. Each tribe had its place, its banner, and its leader, and all of them surrounded the tabernacle, where God's presence was. The order helped the people move and live with reverence toward God.

For today: God knows each person by name and gives them a place among his people. Even if your service seems small or little seen, it is valuable. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, and keep God at the center of your life and your church.
exp.25:38:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Benjamin. It names Shupham and Hupham, and says that from each one came a family, with a name ending in "-itas," which means "descendants of." These names appear with variations in other lists in the Bible, which is normal in ancient genealogies.

After a plague, God told Moses and the priest Eleazar to count the people of Israel by tribe and family. The account records the result. This census served to prepare the division of the promised land, according to the size of each family.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds; he knows his people by name and by family. Even if you feel small or little noticed, you have a place in his story. Today you can thank him for that, and remember with appreciation someone whom almost no one mentions.
exp.14:23:
This verse speaks of what the whole people of Israel had to do if, without realizing it, the entire community failed to obey a command of God. They were to offer a young bull as a burnt offering, a sacrifice burned up completely, with a pleasing aroma to God, along with its grain offering and its drink offering of poured-out wine. In addition, they were to offer a male goat as a sin offering. "Error" means a mistake, and "atonement" means covering or repairing guilt.

God speaks to Moses to instruct Israel before they enter the promised land. He shows them that He provides forgiveness even for sins committed without intention, and that this forgiveness also extended to the foreigner who lived among them.

For today: God takes even our unintentional failures seriously, but He also offers forgiveness. We can ask Him to show us our hidden mistakes and come to Christ with confidence, who cleanses us.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that while a person was set apart for the Lord by a Nazirite vow, they were not to come near a dead body. The word "set apart" here is the verse's own word, and "dead body" refers to a lifeless corpse.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the Israelites. A man or a woman could make this special vow for a period of time. It had three signs: not drinking anything from the vine, not cutting the hair, and not touching a dead body. Touching a body made a person ritually unclean under the law, and this affected their dedication. Care was even required regarding the closest relatives, as the following verse shows.

For today: God values a sincere devotion, not a half-hearted one. We can ask ourselves what things we should set aside in order to serve him with greater clarity and faithfulness in this season of life.
exp.0:34:
This verse gives the result of the count of the tribe of Manasseh: 32,200 men. These were the men twenty years old and up who were able to go out to war. "Those that were numbered" means "those who were registered," which in this verse is the phrase "Those that were numbered of them."

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and orders this census, with the help of one leader for each tribe. The men fit for the army of Israel were counted, a people who had just been freed from Egypt. Manasseh and Ephraim were sons of Joseph, and here each one counts as a tribe. Scholars discuss how to understand numbers this large, but the text presents them as an actual, orderly record.

For today: God knows and records his people one by one. No one is a meaningless number. You can trust that God sees you, knows you, and has a place in his family.
exp.32:26:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Tahath and camped at another place called Tarah.

Moses is writing, at God's command, the list of Israel's stops in the wilderness, from Egypt to near the promised land. It is like a travel diary. Places like Tarah are not known with certainty today, and we do not know exactly where they were. The list shows that God guided every stage of the journey.

For today: there are seasons of life that seem like mere stops with no importance, but God sees them and remembers them. Trust that He walks with you also in times of waiting and routine, and keep moving forward step by step with faithfulness.
exp.28:36:
This verse says that on the eighth day of the feast, along with the bullock, the ram and the lambs, their meat offerings (offerings of flour and oil) and their drink offerings (wine poured out before God) were also to be brought. Everything was to be "according to their number," that is, in the amount that corresponded to each animal, "after the manner," that is, as God had already commanded.

God speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel about the feasts of the year. The eighth day, at the close of the Feast of Tabernacles, was a solemn assembly of rest. God wanted his people to worship him with order and not as they pleased.

For today: God values that we worship him with seriousness and with an obedient heart. We can set aside a fixed time each day to pray and read his Word, rather than leaving it to chance.
exp.13:34:
God says he will do what he has declared. For all those people who joined together in rebellion against him, the wilderness awaits them. There they will be consumed, that is, they will die off little by little until they are gone.

God himself is speaking, addressing Moses and Aaron. The spies had explored Canaan, and most of them gave a fearful report. The people rebelled, wanted to return to Egypt, and doubted that God could keep his promise. Because of this, that generation would not enter the land. Their children would enter after forty years.

For today: unbelief is not a simple mistake, because it pulls us away from what God wants to give us. When you feel fear before what he calls you to do, remember his past promises, pray, and trust him instead of being carried along by the complaints or fears of others.
exp.28:2:
This verse speaks of the grain offering that went along with the burnt offering. "Offering" is the word for the gift presented to God. "Fine flour mixed with oil" is fine, choice flour blended with oil. A "tenth deal" was one tenth of an ephah, a measure of flour. Three tenths were asked for each bullock and two for each ram.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel. This is the first day of the seventh month, a holy day of gathering and of the sounding of trumpets. It was a day of rest and worship, with special sacrifices. The flour and oil accompanied the animal, and the amount grew according to the value of the offering. Many see here the people's thankfulness for their daily bread, although the text does not explain it in those words.

For today: God cares about the details of our worship. We can give him our best, not what is left over. Today, before you begin the day, thank him for your bread and offer him your work with a sincere heart.
exp.33:10:
This verse continues describing the eastern border of the promised land. The line runs down from Shepham to Riblah, east of Ain, and then descends until it reaches the east shore of the sea of Chinnereth, which was later called the sea of Galilee. The word "border" here means the boundary or edge, and "shore" means the edge of the water. It is not known for certain where Shepham and Riblah were located today, and scholars debate this.

God speaks through Moses as Israel is about to enter Canaan. Before the land is divided, the Lord marks its boundaries clearly, so that each tribe would know what it would receive and there would be no confusion or quarreling.

For today: God is a God of order and of concrete promises. You can trust that He keeps what He says, and also learn to live thankful within the limits He has given you, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.25:54:
This verse says that the land of Canaan was to be divided by casting lots, and that each tribe would receive its inheritance according to the names of its ancestors. The word "Notwithstanding" means "nevertheless," and "inherit" means to receive as a possession, and "lot" was a method for deciding, something like drawing names from a jar.

God speaks to Moses after the people have been counted on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He gives the command to divide the territory fairly: more land for the larger tribes and less for the smaller ones. The verse joins the lot with the size of each tribe, and scholars explain in several ways how the two worked together.

For today: God cares for each person and gives each one a place. We can trust what He has given us, without envying what belongs to others, and manage with gratitude what we receive.
exp.13:18:
Moses asks God to pardon the wickedness of the people of Israel. He does not appeal to whether they deserve it, but to the greatness of God's mercy. He reminds God that he has already forgiven them many times, "from Egypt even until now."

Moses speaks after the people, out of fear, wanted to go back to Egypt and refused to enter the promised land. God threatened to destroy them. Moses intercedes and recalls what God himself had said about his own character: slow to anger and abounding in mercy. God answers that he pardons them, although later consequences come upon that generation.

For today: when you fail, come to God trusting in his character and not in your merits. And like Moses, pray also for others who go wrong, asking for mercy on their behalf. Forgiveness does not always mean that the consequences disappear, but it does mean that God remains with us.
exp.5:1:
God tells Moses to speak with the people of Israel. Any person, man or woman, could make a special vow of the kind called a Nazirite vow. The word means being set apart or dedicated. It was a voluntary decision to devote oneself to the Lord for a period of time.

Here the Lord speaks, and Moses is the one who passes on the message. It is an instruction within the law given in the wilderness. It is striking that a woman could also make this vow, something notable for that time. The following verses explain the signs of this dedication, such as abstaining from the fruit of the vine.

For today: devoting oneself to God springs from a sincere desire, not from pressure. We can ask ourselves what specific thing, such as a habit or a time of prayer, we could set apart for Him with joy and steadiness.
exp.15:14:
Moses becomes very angry and asks God not to accept the offering of his accusers. The phrase "Respect not thou their offering" in the King James Version carries the same meaning as the source's "no aceptes su ofrenda." Moses declares that he has never taken so much as a donkey from them, and he has never harmed any of them.

Dathan and Abiram accused Moses of bringing them out of Egypt, a land they describe as flowing with milk and honey, in order to let them die in the wilderness, and of ruling over them harshly. Moses responds with hurt, because his leadership was being attacked unjustly. He leaves the matter in God's hands so that God may judge.

When someone accuses us unjustly, we may feel anger, and that is human. Moses shows us what to do with it: bring it honestly before God and let Him be the judge, rather than taking revenge ourselves.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that if a person was clean and not on a journey, yet still chose not to keep the Passover, that person would be "cut off from his people." That means they would be separated from the community of Israel. Some understand that they could be driven out, and others that they would face judgment from God. "Shall bear his sin" means they would answer for their failure. "Offering of the Lord" refers to the Passover lamb.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. A few verses earlier, those who were unclean because they had touched a dead body, or who were away on a journey, could keep the Passover a month later. Here it is made clear that this second chance was no excuse for someone who simply neglected it.

For today: God is merciful toward someone with a real hindrance, but he calls us not to take lightly what reminds us of his salvation. Think of a practice, such as prayer, gathering with your church, or remembering the work of Christ, and do not let it slip through carelessness.
exp.23:19:
He says that Balaam, when he looked toward Amalek, spoke a prophetic message (the "parable" is a solemn saying or poem). Amalek was the first, that is, the leading one among the nations in its attack on Israel, or perhaps a powerful nation. But its "latter end," that is, its final fate, is that it will perish forever.

He is Balaam, a foreign prophet who was hired by Balak to curse Israel, but God compelled him to bless it. This is one of his last messages, in which he announces the fall of several enemy peoples. Amalek had attacked Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 17), and that is why its fate appears here as judgment.

For today: God sees all injustice and has the last word. We do not need to take revenge or despair before the power of those who do harm; we can trust that God acts with justice in his time, while we seek to live in peace and do good.
exp.13:43:
It says that the people of Israel, despite the warning, insisted on going up to the top of the hill to fight. But the ark of the covenant, which represented God's presence, and Moses stayed in the camp. The words "presumed to go up" mean that they were stubborn and refused to listen.

Moses had warned the people not to go up, because God was not going with them. Earlier, they had rebelled out of fear and refused to enter the promised land. Now, seeing the consequences, they wanted to obey on their own terms, but without God's guidance. The next verse shows that they were defeated.

For today: obeying God is not only doing what is right, but doing it in good time and with humility. If God corrects us, let us not press on out of pride or on our own. It is better to listen to him, ask forgiveness, and depend on him again.
exp.4:22:
What it says: The priest writes down the words of the oath's curse and then blots them out into the bitter water. In this way, the written words are mixed into the water the woman will drink.

Context: God speaks to Moses about the procedure for jealousy, a process for when a husband suspected unfaithfulness without proof or witnesses. The woman would present herself before the LORD, and the outcome was left in God's hands. Scholars debate exactly how the effect of the water was understood; the text does not fully explain it. It is worth noting that this rite protected the woman from arbitrary human punishment.

For today: When there are suspicions or conflicts without clear evidence, let us not take justice into our own hands or accuse lightly. Let us bring the truth before God, seek wise guidance, and act with honesty and respect.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that the western border of the promised land would be the great sea, that is, the Mediterranean Sea. So the coast would mark the western edge.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people of Israel, who are on the plains of Moab, close to entering Canaan. God describes the borders of the land he would give them as an inheritance: south, west, and north. With clear boundaries, the land could be divided among the tribes with order and fairness.

For today: God is a God of order and of specific promises. Just as he set clear limits on his people's inheritance, we can trust that he cares for the details of our lives. Give thanks for what he has given you and live with contentment within it.
exp.28:26:
It says that, in addition to the animals offered that day (young bulls, rams, and lambs), their grain offerings (offerings of flour and oil) and their drink offerings (wine poured out before God) were also to be presented. Everything was to be done "according to their number," that is, in the amount corresponding to each animal, "after the manner," that is, just as God had commanded.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel. This is the schedule of offerings for the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day had its own number of animals, and the numbers went down. This verse closes the instructions for the fifth day, and the offerings were repeated with order and precision.

For today: God values orderly and sincere devotion. We can ask ourselves whether we worship with consistency and with a willing heart, not only when it is easy for us.
exp.12:13:
The verse names Sethur, son of Michael, as the representative of the tribe of Asher. It is part of a list of twelve men, one for each tribe. A "tribe" refers to each of the family groups descended from the sons of Jacob.

Moses writes this list at God's command. The Israelites were in the wilderness of Paran, near Canaan, and Moses sent these leaders to explore the promised land. Afterward, ten of them gave a report full of fear, and only Joshua and Caleb trusted God. For that reason, Sethur was probably among the ten, although the text does not state this clearly.

God knows each person by name, and he also entrusts us with responsibilities. Today we can ask ourselves: when it is my turn to decide or to report, do I speak from fear or from trust in God's promises?
exp.7:20:
This verse says the Levites purified themselves and washed their clothes. Then Aaron presented them before the Lord as an offering, that is, as something given over to God for his service. He also made atonement for them, meaning an act to cover their faults and leave them clean to serve. The word "offered" here does not mean sacrificing them, but dedicating them.

This is a passage from the book of Numbers. God had already told Moses that the Levites would be a gift to Aaron and his sons, to help in the tabernacle in place of the firstborn of Israel. Here it is told that the people did what was commanded, and that the dedication began with cleansing.

For today: serving God does not begin with talent, but with a clean and surrendered heart. Before helping in your church or at home, you can ask God for forgiveness and offer him your day. Christians see in Christ the complete atonement that allows us to draw near.
exp.19:8:
It says that Moses went and took the rod that was kept before the Lord, that is, in the sanctuary, near the ark of the covenant. He did so as he had been commanded, that is, just as God had ordered him. A rod was a shepherd's staff, and this one represented God's authority and works among his people.

The people were in the wilderness of Zin, without water, and they were complaining against Moses and Aaron. God told Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock. The narrator notes that Moses obeyed by taking the rod, but shortly afterward he struck the rock instead of speaking to it, and that had consequences.

For today: obeying God in small things is not enough if we then change what matters most. Let us ask him to help us follow his complete instructions, even when we are tired or upset.
exp.14:27:
This verse says that when someone sins "by ignorance," meaning without meaning to or by mistake, the priest makes an atonement for that person before the Lord. "Atonement" means covering guilt through a sacrifice. In this way the person is reconciled to God and receives forgiveness.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel in the wilderness. He gives instructions about the offerings for sins committed unintentionally. The same law applies to the Israelite and to the stranger who lives among them. The text then contrasts this with sinning "with a high hand," that is, with deliberate rebellion, which was a defiance against God.

For today: God is compassionate toward our failings and offers forgiveness. If you recognize a mistake, do not run away or hide; come before God with sincerity, trusting in his mercy. And guard your heart so that you do not sin on purpose.
exp.22:12:
Balak asks Balaam to come with him to another place, from where he can see only a part of the people of Israel, not the whole camp. From there he wants Balaam to curse them. The phrase "I pray thee" means "please," and "utmost part" refers to the edge or the far end of the camp.

Balak is the king of Moab. He is afraid of Israel and has hired Balaam to curse them, but Balaam has just blessed them because God put those words in his mouth. Balak thinks the problem is the place or what can be seen, so he changes the setting, hoping for a different result. It is not certain why he believes that seeing only a part will help.

For today: we cannot change what God has decided, even if we change our location or our plans. It is better to stop resisting and trust that his will is good.
exp.7:24:
This verse says that the Levites, upon reaching fifty years of age, stopped doing the heavy work of the tabernacle. "Shall cease waiting upon the service" means they withdrew from that task, and "shall serve no more" refers to that active service, not to all help, as the following verse shows.

God speaks to Moses about the Levites, the tribe dedicated to the care of the tabernacle. They began to serve at twenty-five years of age. When they retired, they still accompanied their brothers in the watch, that is, in the vigilance and care of the place. Some think this prevented the wear of carrying and setting up the tabernacle; the text does not give the reason in detail.

For today: every stage of life has its own way of serving God. If we can no longer do what we once did, we can still advise, pray, and accompany others with joy.
exp.30:33:
This verse is part of a list of what Israel took as spoil. It says that, besides sheep and oxen, there were seventy-one thousand donkeys. Donkeys were beasts of burden and transport, very valuable in that time.

Moses and the priest Eleazar ordered everything captured after the war against Midian to be counted. The text is a record, not a speech. This count served to divide the plunder fairly among the soldiers, the community, and the sanctuary. This war and its commands are difficult, and readers interpret them in different ways.

For today: God cares about order and honesty in handling possessions. We can learn to be transparent and fair with money and with what others entrust to us, without keeping what does not belong to us.
exp.25:23:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Issachar. It names Jashub and Shimron, two of his descendants, and says that from each one came a family: the Jashubites and the Shimronites. Here "family" means a clan, a group of relatives descended from a common ancestor.

God speaks through Moses, and Eleazar the priest takes part in the census. This takes place at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, after the earlier generation had already died. The new generation is counted before entering the promised land, because the land would be divided according to the size of each family.

For today: God knows people by name and does not see them as a mass. Today you can remember that your life and your family matter to Him, even when others overlook them. Give thanks for those who went before you in the faith.
exp.0:32:
This verse says that in the tribe of Ephraim, son of Joseph, forty thousand five hundred men were counted. "Counted" here means registered or enrolled. They were men twenty years old and up, fit to go out to war, that is, to serve in the army of Israel.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commanded him to take this census, tribe by tribe and family by family. Israel had just left Egypt and was getting ready to march toward the promised land. The census showed order, organization, and the fulfillment of the promise that God would multiply his people.

For today: although this list may seem to be only numbers, it reminds us that God knows and takes account of his people, both as a group and each person. You have a place and a service within your faith community. Ask God today how you can serve faithfully where you are.
exp.20:25:
This verse explains why Heshbon was so important. It was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites. Earlier, Sihon had fought against a king of Moab and had taken all of his land, as far as the Arnon river.

The narrator gives this historical detail to help us understand what follows: a popular song that remembers the fall of Heshbon. Israel had just defeated Sihon and settled in his cities. The text shows that this land had already changed hands before, and that Sihon himself was a conqueror.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever. What seems strong today can fall tomorrow. That is why it is wise to trust God, not riches, positions, or our own strength, because only his kingdom remains.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that God asked that, when the people were counted, there be with Moses and Aaron one man from each tribe. Each one would be "head of the house of his fathers," that is, a leader or chief of his extended family. The word "you" in the verse refers to Moses and Aaron.

Here God is speaking, and he does so through Moses, in the Sinai desert. Israel was going to be organized for the census of the men twenty years old and up who could go to war. Rather than having two people do everything alone, God appointed a leader from each tribe to help. The verses that follow give their names.

For today: God cares about order and shares out responsibilities. If you lead something in your family, church, or work, do not carry everything by yourself; invite and trust others to help you serve.
exp.32:29:
This verse says that the Israelites left the place called Hashmonah and camped at another place called Moseroth. "Departed" means "set out from," and "encamped" means "pitched camp." It was one more stop on their journey through the wilderness.

Moses writes this chapter as a record of the stages of the road from Egypt until they arrived near the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). God commanded that each place be written down. Today it is not known for certain where many of these sites were, and scholars debate their locations. What matters is that the account shows that every step was remembered.

For today: even if your path seems full of pauses and movements you do not understand, God knows every stage. Remember how He has guided you until now, and move forward trusting that He is still with you at the next stop.
exp.14:2:
It says that when the people enter the promised land and want to present to God a burnt offering (something burned on the altar), they may do so in several ways: as a whole burnt offering (it was burned entirely) or as a sacrifice, for a special vow, by their own free will, or at the solemn feasts. It had to be from cattle or sheep, and its smoke was a pleasing aroma to the Lord, that is, something that pleased him.

God himself speaks to Moses so that he may instruct Israel. This is said to a generation that was still wandering in the wilderness, and it is a promise: they would reach the land. God gives them in advance the rules for worshiping him there.

Today we do not offer animals, since Christ offered himself for us. But God still values sincere worship, given out of love and not out of obligation. We may ask ourselves: what do I offer to God today from the heart, with gratitude and devotion?
exp.2:25:
It says that the sons of Gershon also took care of the curtains of the court, or enclosure, that surrounded the tabernacle and the altar. In addition, they took care of the curtain at the entrance of that court and the cords needed to use it. The curtain here is a hanging that served as the door.

God speaks to Moses and divides the work among the Levites. The Gershonites, one of their three families, were to be in charge of the fabrics, coverings, and cords of the tabernacle, which was the tent where Israel worshiped during the journey through the desert. When the people moved, they took them down, carried them, and looked after them.

For today: God values simple and unremarkable service, such as cords and curtains. If your task at church or in your family goes unnoticed, do it faithfully, because God sees it and gives it value.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that the sons of Aaron were priests who had been anointed, that is, set apart with oil for the service of God. The phrase "whose hands he filled" is an old expression, and it is the one that the verse above renders as "whom he consecrated." Filling the hands was a way of saying that they were consecrated, or given authority to carry out the priesthood.

The book of Numbers tells the story of Israel in the wilderness. Here the narrator presents the family of Aaron and Moses, and recalls that his sons were consecrated at Sinai. The verses that follow tell how Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire, something God had not commanded.

For today: serving God is both a privilege and a responsibility. We can draw near to Him with reverence, seeking to do things as He teaches and not only as seems right to us.
exp.27:13:
This verse speaks of the wine that was poured out together with the animals offered each month. A drink offering was an offering of liquid that was poured out before God. The instructions called for half a hin of wine for each bullock, a third of a hin for each ram, and a fourth of a hin for each lamb. A hin was a measure of liquid; its exact amount in liters is calculated in different ways. The verse ends by saying that this was the burnt offering of every month, that is, an offering burned up completely for God.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the words on to Israel, while the people prepare to enter the promised land. The instructions order their worship: every day, every week, every month and every feast. In this way Israel was reminded that their time and their lives belonged to God.

For today: God deserves orderly and constant worship, not only when we feel inspired. We can set aside regular moments to pray, read the Bible and give thanks, offering God our whole lives with simplicity and faithfulness.
exp.24:11:
God tells Moses to say to Phinehas: "I give unto him my covenant of peace." That is, God makes him a solemn promise of friendship and well-being. The word "covenant" means a firm commitment or agreement, and the phrase "say to him" means to pass on a message that must be communicated.

God speaks to Moses after Israel fell into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor. A plague fell on the people. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, acted with zeal for God, and the plague stopped. God acknowledges that act and rewards it with this promise. Some scholars debate how to apply this episode today, because it was a unique situation in Israel's history.

For today: God values those who take his holiness seriously. Let us ask him for a faithful heart that loves what he loves, and that always seeks peace with humility and not with violence.
exp.19:21:
This verse tells us that the whole people of Israel set out from Kadesh, a place in the desert where they had camped, and came to Mount Hor. The word "congregation" means the great gathered crowd of the people. "Journeyed" means that they set out and moved on from there.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just asked permission to pass through the land of Edom, but the king refused and came out against them with an army. Israel did not fight. They turned aside and kept on their way. At Hor, God would announce that Aaron was going to die there. The text does not say exactly where that mountain was, and that is a matter of discussion.

For today: sometimes a door closes and we must take another road, even when it hurts. Israel avoided conflict and kept moving forward. We can trust that God guides us even through the detours, and that every stage, whether hard or sad, is under his care.
exp.18:12:
It says that whoever touches a human corpse and does not purify himself defiles the tabernacle of the Lord. That person will be "cut off from Israel," that is, separated from the community (interpreters debate whether this means expulsion or a more severe punishment). The water of separation is the purifying water prepared with the ashes of the red cow. Touching a dead body means touching a corpse. "Unclean" means ritually impure, not necessarily sinful.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for the people in the wilderness. He wanted Israel to take seriously the holiness of his presence among them, and to see death as something foreign to God, who is life.

For today: God offers cleansing, but it must be received. Let us not ignore what separates us from him; let us come to Christ sincerely, for his blood purifies us (1 John 1:7).
exp.20:10:
This verse says that the people of Israel left Oboth and camped at Ije-abarim, a place in the wilderness that lay before Moab, toward the east. The phrase "toward the sunrising" means toward the direction where the sun rises. The verse's wording "pitched" means that they set up their camp.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording Israel's stops as they travel through the wilderness. He has just told how God healed those bitten by serpents when they looked at the bronze serpent. Now the people continue on, going around Moab, toward the promised land. It is not known for certain exactly where Ije-abarim was.

For today: God cares for his people not only in the great miracles but also at every stop along the way. Even if your present season seems only like a passing place in the wilderness, trust that he is still guiding you.
exp.25:37:
This verse begins the list of the families of the tribe of Benjamin. Three sons or descendants are named: Bela, Ashbel, and Ahiram. From each one came a family, and the family name ends in "-ites," which means "descendants of." So the Belaites are the descendants of Bela.

God speaks through Moses, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. A new count is taken before entering the Promised Land. The families of Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of Joseph, had already been counted, and now the list continues with Benjamin. The list would serve to divide the land according to the size of each family. Some Bible lists of Benjamin vary in the names, and it is not known for certain why.

For today: God knows and remembers each family by its name. You are not a number to Him. Today you can thank Him for your family and for your place among his people.
exp.0:11:
This verse names Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, as the leader of the tribe of Dan. It is part of a list of leaders, one for each tribe of Israel. The names may look strange because of how they are written in this translation; the same names are sometimes spelled differently in other Bibles.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to take a census of the men able to go to war. To help him, each tribe provides one man to represent it. That is why both a given name and a father's name are recorded. It makes each leader known and recognized by his people.

For today: God knows people by name, including those who serve without being famous. Your quiet work in the family, the church, or your job counts before Him. Serve faithfully, even when no one else notices.
exp.20:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel sang a song of joy over a well of water. "Spring up, O well" is like an invitation for the water to rise up, and "sing ye unto it" means "sing to it." The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to."

Israel was traveling through the desert, near Moab. At Beer, God had told Moses to gather the people so they could be given water. The ones singing are the Israelites, grateful for that provision. We do not know for certain where this song comes from, since the text quotes it without further detail, but it does show that the people remembered God's care through music.

For today: when God gives you something you needed, do not let it pass in silence. Stop, give thanks, and if you can, sing or tell others what He has done for you.
exp.25:20:
This verse says that from Pharez, son of Judah, two sons were born: Hezron and Hamul. From them came two families within the tribe of Judah: the Hezronites and the Hamulites. Here, "family" means a clan, that is, a group of descendants who carry the name of their ancestor.

This is part of Israel's second census, taken at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Moses and the priest Eleazar counted the men to organize the entry into the promised land and to divide the inheritance according to the size of each family. The lists remember that God was keeping his promise to multiply his people.

For today: God knows each family by name and forgets no one. You can trust that he also knows you and cares for your story. Give thanks for your family and pray for it.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that Moses did not settle the claim of Zelophehad's daughters on his own, but brought the matter before God. "Brought their cause" means that he laid out the case to ask for God's answer. "Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament.

Zelophehad's five daughters had no brothers, and their father had died in the wilderness. According to custom, only sons inherited the land. They asked that their father's name not be lost. Moses had no law for that situation, so he consulted God, and God gave the daughters their right.

For today: when you face a difficult or unjust situation and do not know what to do, first bring it to God in prayer. He listens and guides with wisdom.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that the descendants of Gershon, one of the three sons of Levi, were to camp behind the tabernacle, on the west side. The phrase "set up their tents" means they would make their camp there, and "behind" is the word used for the back of the tabernacle, which is the west side.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. The Lord arranges the camp so that the tabernacle sits in the center and the Levites surround it. The Gershonites were assigned to care for the curtains, the tent, and its coverings, as the following verses show.

For today: God cares about order and values every place of service, even the ones almost no one sees. Today you can serve faithfully in whatever you are given, without comparing yourself to others, trusting that God sees and appreciates what is done with love.
exp.0:22:
This verse says that when the men of the tribe of Simeon who were fit for war were counted, the total came to 59,300. "Those that were numbered" refers to the men who were recorded in the list. They were males twenty years old and above.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commands him to take a census of Israel, tribe by tribe, with Aaron as his helper. The purpose was to organize the people so they could march and, when the time came, enter the promised land. Simeon was one of the largest tribes at that time. Some scholars debate how to understand the large figures, but the text presents them as an actual count.

For today: God knows and counts each person; he does not see anyone as a valueless number. You can trust that you have a place among his people and something to contribute. Look for how to serve today where he has placed you.
exp.14:33:
This verse says that the man who was found gathering wood on the Sabbath was kept under custody. "They put him in ward" means that they held him in detention, and "it was not declared" means that it had not yet been settled what his punishment would be.

The narrator tells what happened in the wilderness. The Sabbath had already been commanded as a day of rest, but it still needed to be made clear what to do with someone who broke it on purpose. Moses and Aaron did not rush to decide; they waited for the word of God. Just before this, Numbers 15 speaks of sin committed with a high hand, that is, with deliberate defiance, and many understand that this case is presented as an example of that, although the text gives no further detail about the man's intention.

For today: when a decision is serious or delicate, let us not act on impulse or in anger. Let us pause, pray, and seek God's guidance in his Word before we judge or resolve.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that when the men of the tribe of Zebulun who were twenty years old or more and able to go to war were counted, the total was 57,400. "Those that were numbered" means those who were registered in the census.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commanded him to count the people of Israel by tribes, families and fathers' houses. Moses did this together with a leader from each tribe. The census organized the people for the march and, when needed, for their defense. Some scholars debate the exact meaning of these very large figures, but the text presents them as the actual count.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Every name and every family counted. You can trust that God knows you personally, and you can also help others in your church or family feel seen and valued.
exp.19:5:
Moses and Aaron withdraw from the people and go to the entrance of the tabernacle, which was the tent where God met with his people. There they fall facedown on the ground, and the glory of the Lord, that is, his bright and powerful presence, appears to them.

The people, with no water in the desert, complain bitterly against Moses and Aaron and even long for Egypt. The two leaders do not argue with them any further but seek God. He answers and gives them instructions for bringing water out of the rock.

When complaints and pressure surround us, we can do the same: step aside for a moment, humble ourselves before God, and ask him for direction before we respond. Praying first helps us avoid acting driven only by anger.
exp.29:8:
If a married woman made a vow and her husband, on hearing it, forbade her, that vow was cancelled. The word "forbade" here is the verse's own sense, so the verse keeps it. The phrase about binding her soul means that she had made a solemn commitment. She was not punished, because God forgave her.

Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes of Israel and passes on what God commanded about vows. In that society, the man was the head of the household and answered for his family. The law protected the order of the home and also the woman. Scholars explain in several ways how far this authority reached, but the text emphasizes divine forgiveness.

For today: before promising something to God, think carefully and speak with your family, because promises affect others. And if you cannot keep something for a just reason, God offers forgiveness to a sincere heart.
exp.0:42:
This verse says that when the men of the tribe of Naphtali who were twenty years old or more and able to go to war were counted, they came to 53,400. "Those that were numbered" means those who were recorded in the census. The phrases about the families and lineages of the tribe are rewritten here for the word "tribe" as it appears in the verse.

The narrator of the book speaks here. God had commanded Moses and Aaron to take this count in the wilderness of Sinai, with the help of a leader from each tribe. It served to organize the people, who would soon set out toward the promised land. Each tribe is named with its number, and none is left forgotten.

For today: God knows and counts his people one by one. You are not a lost number in the crowd. You can serve with confidence in the place God has given you, knowing that you count for Him.
exp.30:6:
It says that Israel went to war against Midian, just as God had commanded Moses, and that they killed all the men.

This happens right after God told Moses to punish Midian (Numbers 31:1-3). Earlier, the Midianite women, on the advice of Balaam, had led Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality at Peor (Numbers 25; 31:16). This was one of Moses' last acts. It is a hard passage, and scholars debate how to understand the language of "they slew all the males." Even so, the text presents it as God's judgment on a serious sin.

For today: God takes seriously the sin that drags others down. Let us ask Him to keep us away from whatever harms our faith, and let us humbly obey what He shows us.
exp.19:17:
Here the king of Edom gives a firm "no" to Israel's request. He says he will not let them cross through his land, and that if they try, he will come out against them with an armed force. "Armed" means with men of war, and the second phrase, the one that begins "lest," is simply the verse's own wording for "or else."

The speaker is the king of Edom, a descendant of Esau, the brother of Jacob. Moses had asked for passage along the King's Highway, promising not to harm crops or wells, and then offered to pay for any water they drank. Edom refused, perhaps out of fear or old rivalries; the text does not state the exact reason. Israel ended up going around his land.

For today: sometimes we receive a "no" even when we ask with humility and good intentions. Instead of responding with anger, we can accept the limit, look for another way, and keep trusting that God guides us.
exp.6:38:
This verse lists the animals offered for the burnt offering: a young bullock (a young bull), a ram, and a lamb of the first year. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar, as a sign of complete surrender to God.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks. He tells of the dedication of the tabernacle, when each tribal leader brought his offering over twelve days. This day belongs to Shelumiel, leader of the tribe of Simeon. The offerings of all the leaders were the same, and the text repeats them one by one, as if giving honor to each tribe.

For today: God values what we give him with our whole heart. We can ask ourselves what part of our life we are still holding back, and hand it over to him sincerely, trusting in Christ, who offered himself completely for us.
exp.25:59:
This verse says that Aaron had four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The words "á" and "é" are old spellings of "a" and "e." "Was born" here means that these sons were born to Aaron.

The narrator of the book (tradition says it was Moses) is taking the second census of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Here he goes through the family of the Levites, the tribe of the priests. He mentions Aaron's sons because the priesthood depended on them. The next verse recalls that Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire.

For today: God takes seriously the way we approach Him. Nadab and Abihu had a great privilege, but they treated it lightly. Come before God with reverence, gratitude, and obedience, and remember that spiritual privileges also bring responsibility.
exp.14:7:
This verse speaks of when someone offered a young bull, a young ox, to God. It could be a burnt offering, which was burned whole, a sacrifice to fulfill a special vow, or a peace offering, an offering of fellowship and thankfulness.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell Israel. They were still in the wilderness, and the Lord gives them instructions for when they would enter the promised land. Each animal sacrifice was to be accompanied by flour, oil and wine, and the amount depended on the size of the animal. The verses that follow give the measures for the bull.

For today: God cares about the details of our worship. We can ask ourselves whether we give God our best and with sincerity, and not merely out of habit. An offering of gratitude, time or service can be a way of saying to him: "Everything I have comes from you."
exp.19:20:
It says that the king of Edom refused to let the people of Israel pass through his land. The old words are "término," which means border or territory, and "apartóse," which means that Israel turned away and took another road.

The narrator then tells what happened after Moses asked permission to cross Edom by the King's Highway. Israel promised to pay for the water and to do no harm. Edom answered with a threat and came out with an army. Edom descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, so they were relatives. Israel did not fight, and the text does not explain in detail why it chose to withdraw. Later, Deuteronomy 2:4-5 mentions that God had told them not to attack Edom.

Today, when someone shuts the door on us, even a relative, we do not always have to respond with anger or fighting. Sometimes wisdom means respecting the boundary, looking for another way, and continuing to trust that God is guiding us.
exp.0:12:
This verse names Pagiel, son of Ocran, as the representative of the tribe of Asher. His name is the one that appears in the verse above. He was one of the leaders God appointed to help Moses count the people.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the departure from Egypt. He commands him to take a census of the men able to go to war, and he designates one leader for each tribe. This list of names shows that Israel was organized in an orderly way. The names of the fathers also indicate which family each leader came from. The exact meaning of the names we cannot be completely certain of.

For today: God knows and mentions by name people who may seem unimportant. If you serve quietly, in your family or in your church, remember that God sees your faithfulness and values it.
exp.26:21:
This verse tells us that Moses obeyed God. He took Joshua and presented him before the priest Eleazar and before all the people.

The word "congregation" that appears in the verse means the gathered community of Israel.

Moses knew that he would soon die and would not enter the promised land. He had asked God that the people would not be left like sheep without a shepherd. God chose Joshua, and Moses presented him publicly so that everyone would recognize him as the new leader. Joshua was to seek God's counsel through the priest, using the Urim, an object whose exact form we do not know.

For today: Moses prepared and supported the one who would follow him, without jealousy. We can do something similar: encourage others, teach them what we know, and support them in their service, trusting that God is the one who guides his people.
exp.30:12:
This verse says that Moses, the priest Eleazar, and all the leaders of the people went out to meet the Israelite army as it returned from war. They went out beyond the camp. "Princes" means leaders or heads of the tribes, and the word "unto" is the older form of "to," which we would now say as "to" in the phrase "went forth to meet them."

The text is narrative, and no character speaks here. Israel had just fought against Midian, and the soldiers were coming back with captives and spoil. That the leaders went out to receive them shows order and respect. It was also the custom to remain outside the camp until one was examined, because whoever had been in combat needed purification (v. 19). Soon after, Moses becomes angry about what the captains had done.

For today: When someone returns from a hard battle, whether a job, an illness, or a conflict, we go out to meet them with affection, but also with honesty. Standing with others includes listening to them and helping them give account before God with humility.
exp.10:17:
God tells Moses to speak to the people. "Sanctify yourselves" means to prepare oneself, to set oneself apart for God. The next day they would eat meat. They had wept and complained, saying that they were better off in Egypt. "In the ears of the Lord" means that God had heard them. God would give them meat, just as they had asked.

God is speaking, addressing Moses. Israel was wandering through the desert and had grown tired of the manna, the food God was giving them. They longed for the food of Egypt and forgot that there they had been slaves. Shortly before this, God had helped Moses with seventy elders, because the burden was too heavy for one man alone.

For today: when we complain, let us remember that God hears us. Before asking for more, let us give thanks for what He already gives us, and not idealize a past that once held us in chains.
exp.12:12:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that from the tribe of Dan the chosen man was Ammiel, the son of Gemalli. He was one of twelve men chosen, one from each tribe, to go and explore the land of Canaan. His name and his father's name are given to identify him clearly.

The narrator of the book speaks here, and everything happens by God's command to Moses. Israel was close to the promised land, and each tribe sent a leader to look over the territory. Later, ten of these men will give a report full of fear, and only Joshua and Caleb will trust God. Nothing more is told about Ammiel.

For today: God knows the name of every person, even of those who go almost unnoticed. He also reminds us that having an important responsibility calls for faith and courage. Let us ask God for the confidence to faithfully carry out whatever He entrusts to us.
exp.25:44:
The verse names the sons of Beriah, who was a grandson of Jacob through Asher. Two families came from Beriah: the Heberites, who descend from Heber, and the Malchielites, who descend from Malchiel. The word "counted" refers to the people recorded in the census.

God himself commands this census to Moses and to Eleazar the priest, when the people are about to enter the promised land. The previous generation had died in the wilderness. Now the new one is counted, so that the land can be divided according to the size of each family. That is why even the names of the smallest branches are written down.

For today: God cares about every person and every family, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your story also matter to him. Today you can give value to those who go unnoticed, greeting them by name and taking them into account.
exp.34:25:
This verse begins a condition: if the one who killed someone goes outside the limits of his city of refuge, where he had fled for protection. The killer is the person who took a life, and the word "border" means the boundary or edge. To "take shelter" there means he sought protection in that place. The verse is incomplete, and the consequence is stated in the next one.

God speaks to Moses, for the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected the one who had killed without intention, so that the avenger of blood would not put him to death without a trial. The protection came with a condition: he had to stay inside the city until the high priest died.

For today: God offers protection and also asks us to accept limits. If He gives us a path of grace, it is wise to remain in it with humility and not put ourselves in danger through impatience or carelessness.
exp.0:25:
This verse says that the men of the tribe of Judah were counted, arranged by their generations, families, and fathers' houses. Their names were recorded, one by one. Only those from twenty years old and upward were included, that is, those who were able to go forth to war.

God himself spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commanded him to take this census. Israel was preparing to march toward the promised land, and it was necessary to organize the people. The result for Judah, which continues in verse 27, was 74,600 men, the most numerous tribe.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but knows names and families. You also count for him. Ask yourself what your place and your service are within the community of faith, and offer it gladly.
exp.17:14:
This verse says that every firstborn or firstling, whether of people or animals, that is presented to the Lord belongs to Aaron and the priests. The phrase "opening the womb" means being the first to be born. But the firstborn of a man must be redeemed, that is, bought back by paying a price. The same is done with the young of an animal that was "unclean," meaning one that could not be offered in sacrifice.
