God is speaking to Aaron, the priest, after the Levites had been set apart to serve in the sanctuary. The priests received no land as an inheritance, so God assigned these offerings to provide for them. The redemption also served as a reminder that God delivered the firstborn of Israel in Egypt.

For today: God deserves the first and the best, not the leftovers. We can give him first place in our time, our money, and our decisions, and support with gratitude those who serve in teaching his Word.
exp.7:0:
This verse simply says that God spoke to Moses. "Lord" is the name of God in the Bible, and "saying" announces that a message is coming that Moses must pass on. It is a phrase that introduces what follows.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the messenger. We are in the wilderness, where the people of Israel are arranged around the tabernacle, the tent where they worshiped God. What follows is an instruction for Aaron, the priest, about the lamps of the lampstand. The text highlights that Aaron obeyed just as God commanded him.

God speaks, and his people are called to listen and to obey, even in tasks that seem small, such as lighting lamps. Today we can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible carefully, willing to do what God shows us, without putting it off for later.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that Moses counted the Levites just as God commanded him. The phrase "according to the word of the Lord" means "in agreement with what God said." The phrase "as he was commanded" means "as he had been instructed." He did not add anything or change anything.

God was speaking with Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. He asked him to count the sons of Levi, by their families, from the males one month old and upward. The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve in the tabernacle, which is why they were counted separately from the other tribes. The text shows that Moses carried out the instruction exactly as it was given.

For today: obedience to God also shows itself in the simple and ordinary things. Today you can ask yourself what God has asked of you in his Word, even if it seems small, and do it faithfully, without shortcuts or changes to suit your own preferences.
exp.20:13:
This verse quotes an ancient book called "the book of the wars of the Lord." It says that this book recorded what God did in the Red Sea and in the brooks of the Arnon. The phrase is incomplete and continues into the next verse.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Numbers, traditionally attributed to Moses. Israel was camped near the Arnon, the border between Moab and the Amorites. The author cites that work to support his account. We do not know what book it was, who wrote it, or whether it survived; it is not preserved apart from this mention. It is also not known with certainty what God did in the brooks of the Arnon, because the text is brief and difficult.

For today: to remember in writing what God has done for us. Recording his past help strengthens faith when we face new borders or trials.
exp.23:20:
Balaam looks at the Kenites, a people who lived in rocky country, and speaks a prophetic message. Here "parable" means a prophetic saying. He tells them that their place is strong and that their home is set in the rock, that is, in the stone, as a very secure place.

Balaam is a prophet who was called to curse Israel, but God compels him to bless them and to announce the future of several nations. The Kenites felt protected by the rocks, but the next verse says they will be carried away. The full historical detail of that prophecy is not known with certainty; what is clear is that no human stronghold is permanent.

For today: do not put your security only in what seems firm, such as money, work, or your position. All of that can change. Trust in God, the true rock that does not move.
exp.28:7:
This verse commands that, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the people present to God a burnt offering: one young bull from the herd, one ram, and seven lambs in their first year, all without blemish. A sweet savour is an expression meaning an offering that pleases God. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes the command on to Israel. That day was the Day of Atonement, when the people were to humble themselves (many understand this to mean through fasting and humility) and not do any work. The offerings reminded the people that they needed forgiveness and wanted to give themselves fully to God.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. Today we can give Him our time, our hearts, and our decisions with sincerity, trusting that Christ is the one who reconciles us to God.
exp.30:37:
This verse says that, from the spoil of cattle taken in the war against Midian, half belonged to the soldiers, and the number of oxen was thirty-six thousand. Of these, seventy-two were set apart as the Lord's tribute, that is, an offering or portion reserved for God. It was one out of every five hundred.

Moses is dividing the spoil by God's command (Numbers 31:25-30). One half was for the warriors and the other half for the people. From each half a portion was set aside for God: the portion from the soldiers went to the priest Eleazar, and the portion from the people went to the Levites. Such exact numbers show an orderly and fair distribution.

For today: God values order and honesty in how we handle what we receive. We can set apart, faithfully and gratefully, a part of our resources and our time for Him and for serving others, without keeping everything for ourselves.
exp.25:51:
God told Moses that he would soon give an instruction. "Jehovah" is the name of God in the Old Testament. The word "á" is an old way of spelling "a." It is a short phrase that introduces what comes next.

The people of Israel have just been counted for the second time, and the total was 601,730 men. They were already close to the promised land, nearly at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God speaks to explain how that land will be divided among the tribes, according to the size of each one. The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives the message and passes it on.

God does not leave his people without direction. Before each important step, he speaks. Today we can seek his guidance in the Bible and in prayer before we decide, trusting that he cares for every detail of our lives.
exp.18:14:
It says that any open container, or one whose lid was not tightly fitted, became impure if it was in a tent where someone had died.

The word "impure" here means ceremonially unclean, not dirty.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and gives the people of Israel in the wilderness rules about how to deal with the impurity caused by death. Death was seen as the opposite of God's holiness, and these rules taught that sin and death contaminate. A covered vessel was protected; an open one was not. Scholars also see a practical effect on hygiene, although the text emphasizes the ritual.

For today: what we leave open is easily contaminated. Let us guard what enters our minds and hearts, putting up covers such as prayer, the Word, and good friendships.
exp.24:10:
Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron the priest, turned away God's anger from Israel. "Fury" means strong anger, and "zeal" means a burning concern that God be honored. Because of Phinehas's action, God did not completely destroy the people. "Turn away" means to make someone turn back or stop, and "destroy" means to bring to an end or ruin.

The LORD speaks with Moses. At Baal-peor, many Israelites joined in idolatry and immorality with the women of Moab and Midian, and a plague killed twenty-four thousand people. Phinehas acted decisively against a flagrant case of that sin, and the plague stopped. God praises him and promises him a covenant of peace.

For today: we do not copy his violent act, but we can learn from his heart. We can love God so seriously that we do not take lightly what dishonors him, beginning with our own lives, and humbly seek the peace and good of others.
exp.6:16:
Here is described the last part of the offering of Nahshon, the first leader to present his gifts for the sanctuary. The "peace offering" was a fellowship offering, an expression of thankfulness and friendship with God. A "male goat" is a billy goat, and "a lamb of one year" is a young lamb. The word "was" is spelled with an older form in the source.

The book of Numbers tells how each tribe, through its prince, brought offerings when the tabernacle was dedicated. Moses is the one who receives God's instructions, and the account repeats in detail the offering of each leader, day after day. That repetition shows that each tribe had the same worth before God.

For today: give with gratitude and from the heart, without comparing yourself to others. God sees every offering, great or small, and receives it when it comes from a grateful heart.
exp.31:8:
This verse says that the spies of the earlier generation went up to the valley of Eshcol, looked at the land, and discouraged the people. With their words, they made the Israelites unwilling to enter the land that God was giving them. The phrase "discouraged the heart" means they took away their courage and confidence.

Here Moses is speaking. The tribes of Reuben and Gad had asked to stay east of the Jordan, and he fears that their decision will discourage the others, as happened at Kadesh-barnea. He reminds them that that fear brought God's anger and forty years of waiting. Moses uses the history as a warning.

For today: let us be careful with what we say, because our words can either encourage or drain courage from others. When others face a challenge, we can remind them of God's promises instead of spreading our own fears.
exp.7:3:
This verse says that the lampstand of the tabernacle was of gold beaten by hammer, made of one piece, from its base up to its decorative flowers. The word "candlestick" is what we would today call a lampstand or standing lamp. The word "work" in the verse refers to the way it was made. Moses made it exactly according to the pattern that God had shown him.

Context: God speaks to Moses about Aaron's work with the seven lamps, and the text makes clear that the lampstand followed the divine design. It comes just before God asks that the Levites be set apart and purified for service. The whole passage stresses a service carried out with order and obedience.

For today: God cares about the details of what we do for Him. Serve with faithfulness, without inventing shortcuts, and let His Word shape the way you serve, even in small tasks that few people see.
exp.18:6:
It says that the priest, after overseeing the burning of the red cow, had to wash his clothes and bathe his body with water. Only then could he come back into the camp of Israel. Even so, he remained unclean in the ceremonial sense until evening.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, giving them instructions for the rite of the red cow. Its ashes were to be used to prepare the water of purification, which cleansed those who had become contaminated through contact with death. It is striking that the one who helped purify others was also unclean for a time. Interpreters explain this in several ways, and the text does not give all the details.

For today: serving others in the midst of pain or sin can leave us weary or stained. Let us learn to pause, ask God for cleansing, and rest in his forgiveness before returning to the community.
exp.15:29:
Moses says that if the Lord does something new, never seen before, and the earth opens its mouth and swallows these men alive with everything that belongs to them, then everyone will know that they have despised the Lord.

Moses speaks. Korah, Dathan, Abiram and other leaders had rebelled against him and against Aaron, saying that they had no right to lead the people. Moses does not defend himself with arguments of his own, but lets God himself show who sent him. Afterward, the account says that the earth opened just as he had announced.

For today: when someone questions your work or your service, there is no need to fight for your reputation. Do what is right with humility and trust that God will make the truth clear. And examine your heart: do you respect the authority that God has placed, or do you grumble with pride?
exp.14:32:
This verse says that those who found the man gathering sticks brought him before Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation. They did not punish him on their own; they brought him before the leaders.

Earlier, God had spoken about sin committed with defiance, that is, deliberately rebelling against his word. The Sabbath was a sign of God's covenant with Israel. The narrator tells this case as an example of that deliberate disobedience. The details of the man's intention are not explained, but the text presents it as an act of defiance.

For today: when we see a fault, we can seek justice with order and humility, without taking revenge or judging carelessly. We can also examine our own hearts, so that we do not take lightly what God asks of us.
exp.6:81:
Ahira brought one male goat as a sin offering. "Atonement" is an old word meaning to cover over or cleanse guilt before God. It was an animal presented to acknowledge that sin needs to be forgiven.

Here the account of Moses is listing the offerings of each tribal leader when the altar of the tabernacle was dedicated. Ahira, of the tribe of Naphtali, was the last of twelve princes. Each one brought exactly the same thing, and the text repeats this to show that no tribe was worth more than another. All of them approached God in an orderly and united way.

Before offering anything to God, it is good to honestly recognize our faults. For Christians, Christ is the one who cleanses us completely. Today we can begin our prayer by asking for forgiveness sincerely and giving thanks for His sacrifice.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that the military group of the tribe of Dan, that is, "his host," numbered sixty-two thousand seven hundred men counted in the census. "Host" is an old word for army, and "those that were numbered" are the men who were registered in the count. Dan was the second most numerous tribe of Israel.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them instructions about how the people should camp in the wilderness. Each tribe had its place and its leader, arranged around the tabernacle. Dan was on the north side and led the group of three tribes together with Asher and Naphtali. The order showed that God cares for his people with purpose.

For today: God knows and counts each person, and gives each one a place. Today you can trust that your life and your service matter, even when they seem small, because they are part of something larger that God is doing.
exp.30:15:
Moses says that it was the Midianite women who, following Balaam's counsel, caused the Israelites to be unfaithful to God in the matter of Peor. The words "prevarication" and "mortality" are explained as follows: "prevarication" means betrayal or unfaithfulness, and "mortality" here means a great death toll: a plague that killed many.

Moses speaks to the commanders of the army, angry because they had spared the women. He is referring to what happened in Numbers 25, when Israel fell into idolatry and immorality with Moab and Midian, and a plague killed thousands. It is a hard passage; scholars interpret it in various ways, and it is best read within its historical context.

For today: our decisions and the influences we accept can draw us away from God. We must be careful about whom and what we surround ourselves with, and ask God for faithfulness.
exp.19:15:
It says that Israel cried out to God while they were suffering in Egypt, and that God heard their voice, sent an angel, and brought them out of there. Now they are in Kadesh, a town on the edge of the territory of Edom.

Moses speaks on behalf of all Israel and sends messengers to the king of Edom, whom he calls "brother," because the Edomites descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. Moses recalls what God had already done in order to ask permission to pass through that land. Despite his courtesy and his promises, Edom refused him. The "angel" can be understood as a messenger sent by God; some connect it with Moses himself, others with a real angel. It is not made clearer.

When we face a closed door, let us remember how God helped us before. That memory gives us humility, patience, and confidence to keep moving forward.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that, for each of the seven lambs, a tenth part was to be offered. A tenth is one tenth of an ephah, a measure for dry goods, and here it refers to fine flour mixed with oil. It was the grain offering that went with the animal. It is understood that the oil was also included, as in the earlier cases.

God gives these instructions to Moses, and he passes them on to the people of Israel. This concerns the Feast of Trumpets, on the first day of the seventh month. God wanted the people to worship him with order, gratitude, and reverence. In addition, the male goat offered for sin reminded them that they needed forgiveness in order to be reconciled with God.

For today: God values an orderly and sincere offering. We can set aside a fixed time each day to pray and thank him, not only when we have something left over, but as a constant offering of our heart.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that the standard of the camp of Reuben set out, with its groups or divisions. The standard here is the banner that identified that group of tribes. Elizur, son of Shedeur, was the leader of the tribe of Reuben.

The passage describes how Israel left Sinai on the way to the promised land. God had commanded the people to march in a precise order. First went Judah, then those who carried the tabernacle, and then Reuben. The narrator is the text of the Law, traditionally attributed to Moses, and it wants to show that God guided every step.

For today: God is a God of order, and He cares for each person, for even the names of the leaders were recorded. Ask yourself what your place is in your family or church, and serve it faithfully and without comparing yourself to others.
exp.29:3:
This verse begins to explain what happens when a young woman makes a vow to God. The word "youth" is a rendering of "mocedad," meaning youth, and "bound herself with an obligation" means that she committed herself to carry something out. She still lives in her father's house.

Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes and passes on what God commanded. First it is stated that every vow to the LORD must be kept. Then special cases are given. In that culture, the young woman depended on her father, and the law gave him a protective role: he could confirm or cancel the vow when he heard it. Some readers see here a safeguard against rash promises; others note the limits of that time.

For today: when you promise something to God, think carefully before you speak. And if you are a parent or a leader, use your authority to care for and guide, not to dominate.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that the children of Israel set forward and pitched camp on the plains of Moab, on this side of the Jordan, by Jericho. "Set forward" means they broke camp and started moving. "Pitched" means they settled down and camped.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had been in the wilderness for almost forty years and was now close to the promised land. This verse closes a long journey and opens a new scene: Balak, king of Moab, will be frightened when he sees the people, and that will lead him to seek Balaam to curse them.

For today: God keeps leading his people step by step, even when the road is long. Trust that he is bringing you toward his promises, and do not lose heart if you are still "camping" in a season of waiting.
exp.14:34:
God tells Moses that the man found gathering wood on the Sabbath must die. "Must surely be put to death" means he had to be executed without fail. The whole community was to stone him outside the camp, and that is what was done.

The Lord speaks, answering Moses. The people had put the man in custody because they did not know what punishment to give him. The Sabbath command was a sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:14-15). The preceding context speaks of sins committed with a high hand, that is, with deliberate defiance against God. Some scholars see here an open rebellion; others see an exemplary case within Israel's law.

For today: God takes obedience and holiness seriously. We can ask him for a humble heart that honors him, and give thanks that in Christ we receive forgiveness and grace (Romans 6:23).
exp.27:29:
This verse commands offering one male goat, that is, an adult male goat, to make an atonement for the people. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing sin so that you are at peace with God. "You" here refers to the people of Israel.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people, before they enter the promised land. It speaks of the feast of firstfruits, or of weeks, when they celebrated the harvest. Even on a day of joy and thankfulness, the sacrifice for sin had its place. The animals had to be without defect.

For today: Christians believe that Jesus is the complete and final atonement (Hebrews 10:10). When you receive blessings, give thanks, but remember also that you depend on God's forgiveness. Gratitude and humility can go together.
exp.0:17:
This verse tells how Moses and Aaron gathered the whole congregation together on the first day of the second month. Each person was registered by their family and by the houses of their fathers, with the names written down one by one. They counted those who were twenty years old and upward. The word "pedigrees" refers to families with their shared ancestry, and "by their polls" means person by person.

The book of Numbers is narrated in the third person, and tradition attributes it to Moses. God had commanded this census in the wilderness of Sinai. The leaders of the tribes helped Moses and Aaron. According to the text, the men who could go out to war were counted, so the census served to organize the people.

For today: God knows his people by name; no one is just a number to him. We can remember that we have a place in his family. And we can make others feel seen by learning and using their names.
exp.30:1:
God commands Moses that Israel carry out the vengeance against the Midianites. Here, "vengeance" means a just punishment for a wrong received. Then God tells him that he "shall be gathered unto his people," an old way of saying that Moses would die and be reunited with his ancestors.

God speaks, and He does so shortly before Moses' death. In Numbers 25, some Midianite women led many Israelites into idolatry and immorality, and a plague killed thousands. That is why God orders this punishment. Moses obeys and organizes the army, a thousand men from each tribe.

For today: this passage describes a command unique in Israel's history, not an instruction for us to use violence. It reminds us that God takes evil seriously and that justice belongs to Him. We can leave our offenses in His hands and respond with good (Romans 12:19-21).
exp.12:14:
This verse names one of the twelve men chosen to explore the land of Canaan. He represents the tribe of Gad and is called Geuel, son of Machi. The phrase "to spy out the land" means to explore it and observe it. About the name Geuel we know nothing more; the Bible does not mention him again.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator, who lists the names. God had told Moses to send one leader from each tribe (Numbers 13:1-2) to see the land he was going to give them. The list is part of the official record of that mission.

God takes account of each person by name, even those we hardly know. Your service, though it may seem small or little seen, matters to Him. Today you can faithfully carry out what is entrusted to you, without needing applause, trusting that God sees and remembers.
exp.31:2:
This verse is part of a list of towns and regions east of the Jordan River: Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Shebam, Nebo, and Beon. These were the places that the tribes of Reuben and Gad looked at with interest. The word "multitude" refers to a large number of livestock.

The sons of Reuben and Gad speak with Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the leaders of the people. They had many animals and saw that those lands were good for pasture. With this list they point out exactly which area they wanted. Later it will be seen whether their request was wise or hid a risk for the rest of Israel.

For today: before asking for something that suits us, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are also thinking about the good of others and about what God has called us to do together.
exp.17:11:
God tells Aaron that he is giving him the best of Israel's first harvests: oil, new wine (fresh grape juice, freshly made wine), and grain. The "firstfruits" are the first part of the harvest, which the people brought to the Lord. "The finest" speaks of the best portion, not of what was left over.

God speaks to Aaron, the high priest, after telling him that the Levites would receive no land as an inheritance. For this reason God arranged that the priests and their families would live from the offerings of the people. In this way they could devote themselves to the service of the sanctuary.

Today we can learn to give God the first and the best, not what is left over. We can also support generously those who serve full time in teaching and in the spiritual care of the church.
exp.8:7:
Moses says to the men: "Stand still, and I will hear what the Lord will command concerning you." Old words: the word for "hear" in the verse means "listen" or "hear," and the name of God is "the Lord." The word for "command" here means "command" or "order."

These men were ritually unclean because they had touched a dead body, and for that reason they could not keep the Passover on the appointed day. They came with respect before Moses and Aaron to ask why they would be left out. Moses does not make up an answer; he admits that he does not have one and decides to consult God. Afterward, God gives him a solution (a Passover on a later date).

For today: when we do not know what to do in the face of a doubt or a difficult case, it is wise to admit it with humility and to seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word, rather than answering in haste or by mere opinion.
exp.19:28:
It says that when the whole people saw that Aaron had died, all the families of Israel mourned for him for thirty days. "They mourned" means they showed their sorrow with black clothing and weeping. "The congregation" refers to the whole community of Israel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Aaron, the first high priest and brother of Moses, died on Mount Hor, near the end of the journey through the wilderness. God had commanded that he would not enter the promised land (Numbers 20:24). His priestly garments passed to his son Eleazar, so that the service to God would continue. The people, watching the scene from below, acknowledged his death with respect.

For today: honoring those who served us in the faith. Giving time to grieve is healthy and is not a lack of trust in God. Let us accompany with tenderness anyone who is in mourning, without rushing them and without empty phrases.
exp.6:84:
This verse adds up the weight of the silver that the twelve leaders offered. Each dish weighed 130 shekels and each bowl 70. Between the twelve dishes and the twelve bowls, the silver came to 2,400 shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, an official unit of weight for worship. A bowl is a container for liquids, and the word "vessels" here means the items used in worship.

Moses writes this account of the dedication of the altar. Each leader of the tribes brought the same offering, one day after another. Here comes the final summary. Everything is repeated in detail, perhaps to show that no tribe was worth more than another and that God received them all alike.

For today: God notices what we give faithfully and without comparing ourselves to others. We can serve Him with steadiness, without envy or competition, knowing that every contribution counts for Him.
exp.1:15:
This verse gives the total of all the fighting men of the camp of Reuben, which also included the tribes of Simeon and Gad: 151,450. The "divisions" were their groups or units, and "they shall set forth in the second rank" means that, when the people broke camp, they would march out in second place.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. He gives them instructions so that the people camp and travel in good order around the tabernacle, which represented God's presence among them. Each tribe had its place and its banner, and nothing was left to chance.

For today: God is a God of order, and He cares about the details. Ask Him where He wants you to serve, whether in your family, your church, or your work, and do it faithfully, without comparing yourself to others. Your place matters, even if it is not the first.
exp.2:11:
God says that he has taken the Levites, one of the tribes of Israel, so that they will be his. They will take the place of all the firstborn, that is, the first sons, who are described as "those who open the womb." Thus, instead of each firstborn belonging to God, the Levites will belong to him.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The following verses explain that, when God struck the firstborn of Egypt, he set apart for himself the firstborn of Israel. Now he accepts the Levites as substitutes, so that they may serve alongside the priests in the service of the tabernacle.

Everything we have comes from God and belongs to him. We may ask ourselves: what part of my time, my gifts, and my life am I devoting to serving him with gratitude, remembering that he has cared for and redeemed us?
exp.10:1:
This verse says that the people cried out to Moses for help, and Moses prayed to God. Then the fire was quenched, that is, it went out and died down. The people cried out loudly, with fear and desperation.

The Israelites were traveling through the desert toward the promised land and complaining about the hardships of the road. God became angry, and a fire consumed part of the camp. Facing danger, the people turned to Moses, who served as a mediator, and his prayer stopped the punishment. The place was called Taberah.

When you are in trouble, especially because of your own complaints, come to God with humility. It is also good to pray for others, as Moses did. But be careful: the people cried out in danger and soon went back to complaining, so our prayer should come from a grateful heart and not only from fright.
exp.34:26:
This verse says that if someone who killed another person by accident leaves his city of refuge, and the dead person's relative finds him outside and kills him, that relative will not be guilty of murder. The "revenger of blood" is the relative of the dead person, and the city of refuge is the place of protection for the one who caused the death.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. There were cities of refuge for those who caused a death without intention. There the person was protected until there was a fair trial. He had to stay until the death of the high priest. Leaving was a risk, because it meant abandoning the protection God gave him.

For today: God offers protection and cares for justice, but he asks us to stay within the limits he sets. Today we can think about moving away from what protects us, such as wise counsel, the community of faith, or dependence on God, and stay close to him.
exp.4:29:
It says that if a husband is overcome by a "spirit of jealousy," that is, a strong suspicion that his wife has been unfaithful to him, he must bring her before the Lord. "Shall set her" means that he will bring her forward. There the priest will carry out the whole procedure described in this passage.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people of Israel in the wilderness. This law dealt with a case where there were no witnesses and no proof. The matter was not settled by personal revenge, but by bringing it to the priest and to God. It was a practice belonging to that time, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when suspicion or jealousy takes hold of us, let us not act with violence or with hasty accusations. Let us bring the matter to God in prayer and seek honest dialogue and wise help.
exp.6:87:
This verse adds up the peace offerings that the leaders of the twelve tribes presented: twenty-four young bulls, sixty rams, sixty male goats, and sixty lambs in their first year. The offering of peace was a communion offering, in which a meal was shared before God. To be anointed means to be set apart for holy use with oil. So the account of the dedication of the altar comes to its close.

The narrator, in the book of Numbers, summarizes twelve days of offerings. Each tribal leader brought the same gifts, one day at a time, when the altar was consecrated. It was a gesture of gratitude and unity before God. The passage that follows shows Moses hearing the voice of God from the ark, as a sign that God accepted and dwelt among his people.

For today: give God your best with gratitude, without comparing or competing, and seek fellowship with Him and with other believers.
exp.2:23:
This verse names the leader of the Gershonites, one of the three families of the Levites. He was called Eliasaph, son of Lael. The phrase "chief of the house of the father" means that he was the head of that family group, the one responsible before Moses and Aaron.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites were set apart to care for the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people. Each family received a task and a place to camp. The Gershonites were assigned to camp on the west side and to care for the curtains, the coverings, and the cords. The Bible says nothing more about this Eliasaph.

God notices those who serve in what seems small. A faithful leader takes care of what has been entrusted to him, even when no one applauds. Today we can serve with the same steadiness in the church, at home, or at work.
exp.19:3:
Here the people complain angrily to Moses and Aaron. They ask why they brought them into this wilderness, where, as they see it, they and all their animals would die. The word "congregation" refers to the whole gathered people of Israel, and "beasts" means their livestock and pack animals.

The speaker is the people of Israel, now in the wilderness of Zin, toward the end of the forty years of travel. There was no water, and fear turned into complaining. They even remember with grief those who had died before. Moses and Aaron do not answer by arguing, but fall prostrate before God, and God shows them his glory.

When something is lacking and fear grips us, we can imitate Moses and Aaron. Before we complain or argue, let us go to God with humility and in prayer, and place our need before him.
exp.11:13:
God answers Moses with a comparison: if Miriam's father had spit in her face, she would be ashamed for seven days. Therefore she must be shut out of the camp for seven days, and then she may return.

God speaks, responding to Moses' prayer. Miriam, together with Aaron, had spoken against Moses, and God left her with leprosy (a skin disease). Moses asks for her healing. God agrees, but sets a time of shame and separation. This shows that her wrong was serious, but that the punishment would not be forever.

For today: when someone fails you, pray for that person as Moses did, without holding on to resentment. And if you fail, accept correction with humility: God disciplines to restore, not to destroy.
exp.25:27:
This verse introduces the sons of Joseph: Manasseh and Ephraim. The name is given here as "Ephraim," the spelling used in the King James Version. It begins the list of the families of the two tribes that descend from Joseph, within the census of Israel.

The book of Numbers records the second census of the people, taken near the entrance to the promised land. According to the text, God spoke to Moses and Eleazar to count the men of war and to divide the land by families. Almost the whole previous generation had died in the wilderness. For this reason, naming each family confirms that God cared for his people and was still keeping his promises.

God does not forget anyone or any family. Every name matters to him. Today we can remember that our lives count before God, and that we should also value ordinary people whom others overlook.
exp.11:15:
The text of the verse did not come through, but Numbers 12:16 reads in the King James Version: "And afterward the people removed from Hazeroth, and pitched in the wilderness of Paran."

It says that, once the waiting for Miriam was over, the people left Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran. "Pitched" means they set up their camp, that is, they settled in that place.

Miriam had criticized Moses and was kept outside the camp for seven days as discipline. The people did not move forward until she came back. The narrator tells the story, and it shows that God guides the steps of the people: there is a time to stop and a time to move on.

Today we can learn that God's correction is not the end of the story. After the punishment came restoration, and the journey continued. If you have failed, accept correction with humility. And if someone else has fallen, wait patiently for them to be restored, so that you can move forward together.
exp.25:26:
This verse closes the list of the families of Zebulun. It says that, when they were counted, the men of this tribe came to 60,500. Of the Zebulun family lines, the verse uses the word "Zebulunites" for the descendants of Zebulun, and "numbered" means those who were registered in the census.

The LORD spoke to Moses and to Eleazar the priest, after a plague in the wilderness. He commanded that the Israelites of fighting age be counted again, before they entered the promised land. The list shows that God knew each tribe and each family. The numbers appear in the text, but it is not always known how the counts were made; even so, the purpose is clear: to prepare the people and to divide the land.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass, but as families with names. Today you can remember that you too are known by him. Value your place in your family and in your church, and serve faithfully where you are.
exp.27:30:
This verse closes the instructions about the offerings for the new month and for the feasts. It says these animals were to be offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, that is, the daily sacrifice that was burned up completely. The "gifts" were the grain offerings, and the "drink offerings" were the wine that was poured out. "Without blemish" means without any physical flaw.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the people of Israel, who were close to entering the promised land. These rules ordered their worship with a regular calendar. The special offerings did not replace the daily offering, but were added to it. The lamb without blemish shows that God deserves the best, and many Christians see in it a shadow of Christ.

For today: do not reserve your best time and attention for God only on special occasions. Cultivate constant prayer every day, and in the important moments, offer him your best with sincerity.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that the Levites, who received the tithes from the people, were also to give an offering to God. They were to set aside a portion of what they received and hand it over to the priest Aaron. The source's comment about the word for "you" and the word for "offering" is replaced here: the verse itself speaks of you as "ye" and of the offering as a "heave offering," which is a gift lifted up and given to the Lord.

God speaks to Moses and tells him what to say to the Levites. They had no land of their own among Israel, so they lived on the tithes of the people. God asks them to give a tenth of what they received, which is the tithe of the tithes. In this way they too took part in worship with gratitude, and their offering was counted as if it came from their own harvest.

For today: even someone who receives help or support can give with gratitude. Giving God our best, no matter how much or how little we have, is a way of recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.25:4:
This verse begins the census of the tribes of Israel. It starts with Reuben, the firstborn son of Jacob. It names two of his sons, Hanoch and Pallu. From each of them came a family that carried its name: the Hanochites and the Palluites. Here, "family" means a clan, that is, a group of descendants.

Moses and the priest Eleazar speak in the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan. God had commanded them to count the men twenty years old and above. This takes place at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, when a new generation is preparing to enter the promised land.

For today: God knows his people by name and remembers each family. You can thank him that he also knows you, and care for the story of faith you have received by passing it on to your children or to the younger people around you.
exp.30:11:
This verse says that the soldiers of Israel returned from the war against Midian and brought before Moses, the priest Eleazar, and the whole people the captives and everything they had taken. The words "prey" and "spoil" refer to what was seized: people, animals, and goods. All of this arrived at the camp, located on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Earlier, God had commanded Moses to punish Midian because its women had led Israel into idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25). The army returns and presents the result to its leaders. The following verses show that Moses was not pleased with what they had done.

For today: no one should consider a task finished simply because they have done it. It is wise to present our decisions and actions before God and before wise people, and to be willing to receive their correction with humility.
exp.34:4:
God commands that two thousand cubits be measured out in each direction: east, south, west, and north, with the city in the center. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, a little under half a meter. The open lands around the city, used for pasture and animals, are the part that needs explaining here; they were the grazing fields that surrounded the town.

God spoke to Moses on the plains of Moab, before the people entered the promised land. The Levites did not receive territory like the other tribes, so they were to be given 48 cities with room for their livestock. This verse seems to differ from the one before it (a thousand cubits). Some think the thousand cubits were for pasture and the rest for fields, but this is not certain.

God cares that those who serve have what they need to live. Today we can generously support those who dedicate their lives to teaching and caring for others spiritually.
exp.15:22:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God answers Moses and begins to give him new instructions. After the prayer of Moses and Aaron, God does not stay silent but responds.

Context: Korah, Dathan and Abiram had rebelled against the leadership of Moses and Aaron. God had said that he would consume the whole congregation, but Moses and Aaron interceded, saying that not everyone was guilty. Now God answers them and commands that the people be separated from the three rebels. Some see here the mercy of God in response to prayer; the text does not explain this in more detail.

For today: Praying for others has value. Moses and Aaron did not stay quiet in the face of the danger the people faced, but cried out to God, and He heard them. Intercede today for your family, your church or your community.
exp.34:3:
This verse says that around each city given to the Levites there would be an open area of land, called the common land, measuring a thousand cubits from the wall outward. This common land was unbuilt, shared ground used for pasture. A cubit measures about 45 centimeters, so this would be about 450 meters. The following verse speaks of two thousand cubits, and it is not known with certainty how the two measurements fit together. Some think the thousand cubits was the pasture land and the rest was farmland.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before the people enter the promised land. The Levites would not receive a territory of their own, because their inheritance was to serve God. For this reason the people would give them cities and land for their animals.

Today we can generously support those who serve in the church, so that they have what they need to live and work with peace of mind.
exp.21:11:
God tells Balaam two clear things: that he must not go with Balak's messengers, and that he must not curse Israel. The reason is simple: that people is blessed, which means God himself has blessed them.

Here God speaks, answering Balaam. Balak, king of Moab, was afraid because Israel, newly come out of Egypt, was numerous and close by. For that reason he wanted Balaam to curse them so that he could drive them out. God does not allow this, because he had promised to bless this people.

For today: when God has already spoken clearly, we do not need to look for another way out or let ourselves be pressured by fear or by the interests of others. Let us trust that his blessing upon his children is stronger than any threat, and obey without hesitation.
exp.4:28:
This verse sums up the rule God gave for cases of jealousy within marriage. It speaks of a wife who committed betrayal against her husband, that is, who was unfaithful to him, and who became defiled.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel, in the wilderness. This law deals with the case in which a husband suspected infidelity but there were no witnesses. The process brought the matter before God and the priest, not to personal revenge. Interpreters debate how the rite worked in detail, and the text does not explain everything. Also, the law mentions only the jealous husband, which reflects the context of that time.

For today: when suspicion or jealousy arises in a couple, do not act with anger or accusations. Seek the truth calmly, pray, and talk honestly, or ask for help from a wise counselor.
exp.17:6:
God tells Aaron that he and his sons must take care of their priestly duties in everything that concerns the altar and what lies within the veil, that is, the Most Holy Place. Here the word "task" means matter or work. God gives them this service as a gift, and he warns that the stranger, someone who was not from the priestly family, would be put to death if he came near.

God speaks to Aaron after the rebellion of Korah and the people's complaining. God wants to protect Israel from his own anger, and so he makes it clear who is to care for the sanctuary. The Levites help, and the priests serve in the most holy place.

For today: serving God is not a right we earn, but a gift we receive. Do your service with reverence and gratitude, and remember that drawing near to God is always by his grace.
exp.6:65:
On the tenth day, the verse tells us, it was Ahiezer's turn. He was the son of Ammishaddai and the prince, that is, the chief or leader of the tribe of Dan. Here only the person is introduced; his offering is described in the verses that follow.

The book of Numbers tells that when the altar of the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribe brought its offering on a different day. The account is narrated, not spoken by a character. Each leader presents the same thing, and the repetition shows that all the tribes had equal worth before God. Dan was one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

For today: God sees and remembers each person who gives to him sincerely, even when their contribution seems repeated or unremarkable. Serve God with steadiness and do not compare yourself with others; your devotion also counts.
exp.23:13:
Balaam says he is now going back to his own people, but before he goes he wants to tell Balak something important. He announces what the people of Israel will do to the people of Moab in the days to come, that is, in the future, in later times. The word "advertise" here means to let someone know, or to counsel them.

He is a prophet from outside Israel. King Balak hired him to curse Israel, but God allowed him only to bless it. Balaam has already said that he could not speak anything beyond what the LORD speaks. What follows is a prophetic message. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see an announcement concerning King David, and others also see a sign pointing to the Messiah.

For today: we can learn to tell the truth even when it would be more convenient to stay silent or to flatter. Let us ask God for integrity to speak and act according to his word, not according to money or the pressure of others.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that Eliab, son of Helon, was the leader or commander of the tribe of Zebulun. The word "host" here refers to the tribe organized to march, and Eliab was its leader. Zebulun went together with Judah and Issachar under the same banner.

God speaks to Moses, and the people of Israel are leaving Sinai for the first time, on their way to the promised land. Everything is done in order: each tribe has its place and its leader. The text says nothing more about Eliab; it only names him as the one responsible for his tribe.

For today: God notices each person and their place, even when their name appears only once. Ask yourself what specific responsibility God has given you, in your family, your church or your work, and carry it out faithfully and in order, without needing anyone to applaud you.
exp.25:52:
This verse says that the promised land would be divided among the Israelites who were counted in the census. The word "inheritance" means a portion of land that is received and passed down to one's children. The phrase "according to the number of names" means that the division would be made according to the record of the families and their names.

The Lord speaks to Moses after a second census of Israel: 601,730 men were counted. The previous generation had died in the wilderness, and now a new people was preparing to enter Canaan. God reminds them that the land is his promise and that each family would have its place. The verses that follow add that the division would also be made by lot.

For today: God knows our names and does not forget anyone. You can trust that he has a place and a purpose for you. And since each person receives what is theirs, avoid comparing yourself with others and care gratefully for what God has entrusted to you.
exp.10:11:
Moses asks God two questions, and the obvious answer to both is "no." He did not conceive or give birth to this people, so it is not his place to carry them the way a mother carries her baby. Words like "conceive" and "begotten" are rendered in the King James Version as the idea of bringing life into the world, the way a father or mother does. Moses is reminding God that he promised the land to this people's ancestors.

Moses speaks to God worn out and frustrated. The people are complaining and weeping for lack of meat, and God is angry. Moses feels that the burden of all of them is too much for him alone. His prayer is very sincere, almost a complaint. Some see here despair, and others see an honesty that God allows.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by responsibilities, tell God honestly, without pretending to be strong. And seek help from others, because you were not made to carry everything alone.
exp.15:3:
This verse says that when Moses heard the accusation brought by Korah and the leaders who rose up against him, he fell on his face to the ground. The phrase "fell upon his face" is an old way of saying he threw himself to the ground, with his forehead pressed down.

The narrator of the book is recounting Moses' reaction. Two hundred and fifty respected leaders accused him, together with Aaron, of lifting himself up above the people. The Bible does not explain here in words why he fell on his face. Many understand it as a gesture of humility, grief and prayer, leaving the matter in God's hands. Others think it was also a plea on behalf of the people.

When someone criticizes or attacks us, we do not have to respond at once or defend ourselves in anger. We can stop, humble ourselves, and bring the situation before God in prayer before we say a single word.
exp.17:30:
The Levites, together with their families, could eat their portion of the tithes in any place, without having to go to some special location. The word "reward" means payment or wages. It was their pay for serving in the tabernacle of the congregation, which was the tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Aaron through Moses. The Levites did not receive land as an inheritance, so God provided for them through the tithes of the people. They, in turn, set aside the best part of that tithe for the priests. In this way, those who dedicated their lives to serving God were cared for.

Today we can learn to support with gratitude and generosity those who serve in the church, and not to neglect their need. We can also give God our best, and not only what we have left over.
exp.6:22:
This verse ends the list of what Nethaneel, son of Zuar, of the tribe of Issachar, brought. For the peace offering he offered two oxen, five rams, five he goats and five lambs of the first year. The "peace offerings" are the fellowship or thanksgiving offering, part of which was eaten in the presence of God. The "he goat" is a male goat.

Here the narrator of the book follows the order of the dedication of the tabernacle. Each tribal leader brought his offering on a different day, and all of them are nearly the same. The Bible repeats each one to show that God values the giving of each tribe equally, without favoritism.

For today: give to God with consistency and without comparing yourself. Your simple and faithful service matters to him, even if it looks like that of others or no one notices it.
exp.27:20:
This verse says that for each of the seven lambs a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil was to be offered. It was the grain offering that accompanied the sacrifice of the animal. "Offer" here means "present," and the tenth is a measure of flour, a small portion.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to Israel, while the people prepare to enter the promised land. These instructions detail the offerings for the festival days, here those for the new moon, along with the daily sacrifice. Everything was to be done in good order, to worship God as He asked.

For today: God cares about the details of our worship. Today we do not offer animals, for Christians believe that Christ offered himself once for all. But we can present to God the best of our time, our work, and our hearts, with sincerity and steadiness.
exp.0:40:
This verse says that, when the men of the tribe of Asher were counted, there were 41,500 from twenty years old and up. They were the ones who could go out to war, that is, those fit for military service. The phrase "those that were numbered" refers to those recorded in the census.

God himself commanded Moses to take this census in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after Israel came out of Egypt. Each tribe was counted by families and fathers' houses. The census organized the people to march, to camp, and, if needed, to defend themselves. Some scholars debate how to understand these very large figures, but the text presents them as an actual record.

For today: God cares about each person, not only the crowd. Just as every name counted in Israel, you have a place and a service in God's family. Ask him today how you can contribute with what you have.
exp.12:3:
This verse tells us that Moses sent the spies out from the wilderness of Paran, just as God had commanded him. The word "princes" here does not mean sons of kings, but rather leaders or heads of their tribes. "To search out the land" means to explore it.

God speaks to Moses and asks him to send one man from each tribe to explore Canaan, the land that He had already given them. The account in Deuteronomy 1 shows that the people also asked to send spies, so both events are mentioned in the Bible. Here the emphasis is that Moses obeyed and chose respected leaders.

For today: God entrusts us with responsibilities and expects us to fulfill them with obedience. Before taking an important step, it is wise to seek His direction and choose trustworthy people. But let us remember that He had already promised the land: our confidence must rest on His word, not only on what we see.
exp.10:9:
Moses heard the people weeping throughout their families, each man at the door of his tent. Then the anger of the Lord burned hot, and Moses was also troubled.

The narrator tells us that Israel was traveling through the wilderness and eating manna every day. The people grew tired of that food and began to complain, asking for meat and remembering Egypt. Moses felt overwhelmed by carrying so many people, and in the verses that follow he tells God so with complete openness.

When complaint and weariness get the better of us, it is easy to forget what God is already giving us each day. Even so, Moses shows us how to bring our burden directly to God, speaking honestly, instead of letting bitterness grow within us.
exp.23:10:
What it says: Balak, the king of Moab, orders Balaam to go home at once. Balak had promised to give him honor and reward, but now he says that the Lord is the one who kept it from him, because Balaam blessed Israel instead of cursing them.

Context: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, because he was afraid of them. But three times God put blessings into Balaam's mouth. Balak, angry, strikes his hands together and sends him away. Balaam answers that he can only speak what the Lord directs him to say.

For today: We may look for people's applause or benefits, but the word of God cannot be bought or changed. It is better to be faithful to God, even if this costs us the approval of others, because his blessing endures.
exp.12:18:
Moses asks the explorers to look carefully at the land of Canaan: what it is like, and what the people who live there are like. He wants to know whether the people are strong or weak, and whether they are few or many.

Moses speaks to twelve men, one from each tribe, before the people enter the land God had promised to Israel. He wants concrete information to plan the way ahead. Asking for this is not a lack of faith, since the command comes within the frame of God's instruction (Numbers 13:1-2). Later, however, the report of the majority ended up filling the people with fear.

For today: trusting God does not ask us to close our eyes. We can gather information, think, and plan wisely. But when we see the reality around us, let us remember that God's promises weigh more than our fears.
exp.3:48:
This verse says that the Levites were counted just as God commanded through Moses. Each one was given his task, that is, his work, and his burden, meaning the responsibility he had to carry.

Here the narrator of the book closes the count of the men from thirty to fifty years old who served in the tabernacle. The verses before it give the total: 8,580. Moses made the count following God's instructions, so that each Levite family would know what part of the service and transport of the tabernacle belonged to it.

For today: in the church and in life, God cares about order and values every task, great or small. We can ask ourselves what our burden is and carry it faithfully, without envying the burden of others.
exp.30:10:
Israel took everything that was in the Midianite camp. The "spoil" refers to the goods taken from a defeated enemy, and the "prey" is what was captured, both people and animals. "Beasts" are the animals.

The passage describes the end of the war against Midian. According to the chapter, God commanded Moses to carry out this action because of what happened at Peor (Numbers 25), when Israel was drawn into idolatry. The narrator recounts what the army did. It is a hard passage, and scholars interpret it in various ways, but it belongs to a unique moment in Israel's history.

For today: when you read difficult texts, do not use them to justify violence. Read them with humility, ask God for wisdom, and remember that Jesus calls us to love our enemies and to pursue peace.
exp.31:25:
Here the men of Gad and Reuben say that their little children, their wives, their flocks and all their animals will remain in the cities of Gilead, east of the Jordan. The word "animals" in this verse covers working or breeding livestock as well as their herds.

These two tribes are speaking to Moses. They had asked to keep the grazing lands east of the Jordan, and Moses warned them that they must not leave their brothers alone in the war. So they promise to look after their families in those cities, but to cross over armed with the rest of Israel until everyone has received their inheritance.

For today: keeping a promise costs something, and personal blessings must not make us forget others. Before we rest in what God has given us, let us ask whom we can still help.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that God forgives the whole people of Israel, and also the foreigner who lives among them, when the sin was committed "in ignorance," that is, by mistake or without realizing it. Earlier the verse says "shall be forgiven" and "sojourneth" (lives as a stranger among them).

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people, who are now close to the promised land. These rules explain what to do when the community sins without meaning to. A sacrifice was offered for sin, and the priest made atonement, that is, he covered the guilt to restore the relationship with God. Note that the foreigner received the same treatment as the Israelite.

Today, we can remember that God is also concerned with our unintentional failures. It is good to ask him to show us what we do not see, to confess with humility, and to trust in his forgiveness. Moreover, his grace includes everyone, so we should welcome those who come from outside.
exp.2:16:
These verses name the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. From them came the three great families of the Levites.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Levites did not receive land like the other tribes; instead, they were set apart to serve in the tabernacle. That is why Moses counted them by their families, beginning at one month old, as the LORD had commanded. The verses that follow detail each family and its task.

For today: God notices names and services that seem small. Today you can serve in your church or your home faithfully, even when no one applauds you. Your quiet work matters before God.
exp.15:9:
Moses reminds Korah and the other Levites that God had already given them a great honor: He had brought them near to Himself to serve. He asks them, with reproach, whether that was not enough for them, and why they now also wanted the priesthood. The verse's "seek ye" carries the sense of seeking or claiming for oneself.

Moses speaks during Korah's rebellion. Korah, a Levite, and other leaders were questioning the authority of Moses and Aaron. The Levites attended the tabernacle, but only Aaron's family were priests. Moses shows that their complaint, at its root, was against God, who had established these offices.

For today: instead of envying the place of others, let us thank God for the calling He has given us. Serving where He has placed us is a privilege, and proud ambition can make us lose what we have already received.
exp.4:6:
It says that whoever has done wrong to another person must acknowledge it openly, that is, confess it. Then he must make full restitution for the damage and add one fifth more, that is, 20 percent of the value. Everything is handed over to the person who was harmed. Breaking a duty or betraying trust is what this kind of wrong means.

God himself speaks to Moses so that he may tell the people. A sin against a neighbor was also considered an offense against the LORD. For this reason the law required confession, restitution and, according to the verses that follow, a guilt offering. If the injured person was no longer alive and had no relative, the compensation went to the priest.

Today, if you have harmed someone, saying "sorry" is not enough. Acknowledge it honestly, repair what you can, and try to be generous. In this way your repentance becomes visible and helps heal the relationship.
exp.27:8:
This verse says that every Sabbath day an extra offering was to be made to God: two lambs a year old, without defect. Along with them came a grain offering of the finest flour, the very best quality, mixed with oil. That offering is called a grain offering. It also included a drink offering, that is, wine poured out as an offering.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, in the wilderness, near the time of entering the promised land. This chapter sets out the people's regular offerings. The Sabbath lambs were added to the daily burnt offering, so the day of rest had a special place in worship.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not what is left over. We can set apart a time each week, unhurried, to rest, pray, and give thanks, offering him sincerely the best of our time and our hearts.
exp.21:21:
He says that God was very angry because Balaam was going with the princes of Moab. Then the angel of the LORD stood in the way as an adversary, that is, as someone who blocks his path. Balaam was riding on his donkey, accompanied by two servants, who were young attendants.

This is part of the story of Balaam. God had already allowed him to go, but with one condition: to say only what God told him. Why God became angry then is explained in several ways. Many think God saw an improper intention in Balaam's heart, perhaps greed for the reward. The text does not spell this out here.

Today we can ask ourselves not only what we do, but with what attitude we do it. God looks at the heart. Let us ask Him to show us whether any hidden motive is leading us astray, and let us obey Him with sincerity.
exp.15:11:
This verse tells how Moses sent for Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, asking them to come to him. They refused, saying, "We will not come up." The phrase "sent for" simply means that Moses sent messengers to bring them.

Moses is facing a rebellion led by Korah, together with Dathan and Abiram, against his authority and that of Aaron. Moses calls them in order to clear things up, but they reject the dialogue. In the verses that follow, they accuse him of having brought them out of Egypt, which they describe as a land of milk and honey, in order to make them die in the wilderness. They distort the history and harden their hearts.

Today we can learn not to close ourselves off when someone invites us to talk or to correct us. Refusing to listen, out of pride or resentment, can lead us to see reality wrongly and to drift away from God. Let us ask for a humble heart that is willing to dialogue.
exp.32:22:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Kehelathah and camped at mount Shapher. The word "pitched" in the verse means they set up their tents there, and the idea is that they settled there for a time. It is one more stop in the list of their camping places.

Moses is writing down, by God's command, the stages of the journey from Egypt to near the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). It is forty years of travel. Today no one knows with certainty where many of these places were, including mount Shapher, and scholars do not agree. Even so, the record shows that God cared for every stretch of the way.

For today: remember the stopping places in your own life, even the ones that seemed unimportant or slow. Thank God for being with you in each of them, and trust that he is also with you in the next stage.
exp.0:41:
This verse speaks of the counting of the tribe of Naphtali. The men from twenty years old and upward who were able to go to war were counted, organized by tribe, by families, and by the house of their fathers. "According to the number of the names" means that each man was recorded by his name. "Generations" refers to their family line.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, and he, together with Aaron and one leader from each tribe, made this count. Its purpose was to order the people, who had just come out of Egypt, for their march and their camp. The total for Naphtali, which appears in the next verse, was 53,400.

For today: God knows and takes account of each person, not just the crowd. You have a place among his people and something to contribute. Ask him to show you how to serve faithfully where you are.
exp.19:27:
This verse tells how Moses took the sacred garments of the high priest off Aaron and put them on Eleazar, Aaron's son. Then Aaron died on the top of the mountain, and Moses and Eleazar came down alone.

Here the narrator reports that Moses obeyed what God had commanded him. Aaron would not enter the promised land, and God arranged that his service would pass to his son. The garments represented the office of high priest. So the ministry went on, even though the one who held it had died.

For today: God continues his work even when people pass away. We can serve faithfully where we are and prepare with care those who will come after us, trusting that God looks after his work.
exp.12:2:
Here God tells Moses to send some men to explore the land of Canaan, that is, to search it out and observe it. God makes clear that this land is a gift from him to Israel. One man was to go from each tribe, and each one was a leader or chief of his people.

The Lord speaks to Moses when the people are already camped in the wilderness of Paran, near the border of Canaan. God had already promised the land; the exploration would serve to learn about it and prepare for it. Later, Deuteronomy 1 shows that the people also asked for this mission, and some understand that God allowed it for that reason.

For today: God gives us promises, but he also invites us to walk with attention and responsibility. Trusting his word is not being careless; it is moving forward with faith, good judgment, and upright people beside us.
exp.28:24:
This verse says that on the fourth day of the feast, a male goat was also offered as a sin offering. The word "expiation" means covering or cleansing guilt, and that is what the sin offering accomplished. It was added to the continual burnt offering, the daily offering that was burned up completely, along with its grain offering and its drink offering of poured-out wine.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the people of Israel. They are the offerings for the Feast of Tabernacles, in the seventh month. Each day had its own list, and the goat for sin appears every day. In this way the people were reminded that even while celebrating, they still needed forgiveness.

For today: even in days of joy, we should not forget that we need God's mercy. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice for sin. We can celebrate with gratitude and also ask for forgiveness with sincerity, without carrying old guilt.
exp.2:3:
This verse recalls that Nadab and Abihu, the eldest sons of Aaron, died before the Lord for offering "strange fire", that is, fire that God had not commanded. Since they had no children, their brothers Eleazar and Ithamar continued serving as priests under the guidance of their father Aaron. The verse's phrase about "ministered in the priest's office" means that they carried out the priestly duties.

The narrator is introducing Aaron's family before describing the service of the Levites. The account of Nadab and Abihu is told in Leviticus 10. There it is not explained in detail what exactly their wrong was; the emphasis is that they acted without God's command. It is mentioned here to show who remained as priests.

For today: to draw near to God with reverence and obedience, not according to our own ideas. We can ask ourselves whether our way of serving and worshiping seeks to please Him, and not only ourselves.
exp.24:13:
This verse gives the name of the Israelite man who was killed along with the Midianite woman: Zimri, son of Salu. He was the head of a family in the tribe of Simeon.

The narrator of the book makes clear who the dead man was. Israel was at Shittim, and the people had joined in the worship of Baal of Peor. Zimri publicly defied God and Moses, and Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, acted with zeal and stopped the plague. God then promised him a covenant of peace. Naming Zimri shows that not even a leader was exempt from responsibility. How Phinehas's act should be applied today is understood in different ways.

For today: Whoever has influence or leadership has a greater responsibility to set an example. Let us ask God to help us live with integrity, without hiding sin.
exp.31:7:
Moses reminds the sons of Gad and Reuben what their ancestors did. When he sent them from Kadesh-barnea to explore the promised land, they came back and discouraged the people. "Your fathers" refers to the previous generation, and the phrase about going to see the land means exploring it.

Moses speaks with firmness. Gad and Reuben were asking to stay east of the Jordan, where there was good pasture, rather than crossing into Canaan. Moses fears that their decision will discourage the other Israelites, as happened years earlier with the spies, and that God will once again become angry. The following verses recount the punishment of that generation.

For today: our decisions influence the spirit of others. Before we act or speak, let us ask ourselves whether we are encouraging others to trust God or whether, without meaning to, we are spreading fear, comfort, or discouragement. Learning from the mistakes of the past helps us avoid repeating them.
exp.6:42:
Eliasaph, leader of the tribe of Gad, brings his offering: a silver dish and a silver bowl, measured by the "sanctuary shekel," which was the official measure. Both are full of fine flour mixed with oil. This grain offering is here called a "gift."

Moses records how each tribal leader, one day after another, presented offerings for the dedication of the altar. The gifts of all of them are identical. The text repeats every detail, as if God wanted to show that he values each offering equally.

Today we can learn to give to God with consistency and sincerity, without comparing ourselves to others. Your service may resemble that of many, and yet God sees it and remembers it. Offer him what is yours today with a grateful heart.
exp.0:35:
This verse begins the record of the tribe of Benjamin in Israel's census. Each man twenty years old and up who was able to go to war was counted, organized by their generations, their families, and their fathers' households.

The phrase "according to the number of the names" means that each man was recorded by his name.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, at the start of the second year after leaving Egypt. He commands them to count the people so they can be organized into tribes and camps. The result for Benjamin comes in the next verse: 35,400 men. This census prepared Israel for its march toward the promised land.

For today: God knows his people one by one, by name and by family. No one is a lost number to Him. You can rest in the fact that God sees you, and also serve in your place and with your gifts within your community of faith.
exp.9:35:
This verse says that when the ark stopped moving and came to rest in a place, Moses would offer a prayer. He asked God to return to the countless multitudes of Israel, that is, to the uncounted crowds of the people. The word "rested" means that the ark came to settle or stop. The phrase "Return, O Lord" can be understood as "come back to be with them" or "rest among them."

Moses, the leader of Israel, speaks while the people travel through the desert behind the ark of the covenant. When they set out, he asked that God would rise up and lead them. When they stopped, he asked that God would remain in the midst of them. It was a prayer of complete dependence: neither walking nor resting without the presence of the Lord.

For today: we can begin and end our days by asking God to accompany us. Before setting out and also when we rest, a simple prayer reminds us that we do not live alone.
exp.24:17:
It says God commands that the Midianites be treated as enemies, because they troubled Israel with their wiles, that is, with their deceptions and traps. With these tricks they led them into the matter of Peor, an idolatrous cult. It also mentions Cozbi, a Midianite woman from a noble family, who died in the day of the plague.

The Lord speaks and gives the command to Moses. Earlier, in Numbers 25, many Israelites joined themselves with Moabite women and worshiped Baal of Peor, and a plague fell on the people. Cozbi was killed together with an Israelite named Zimri. The text presents the command as a response to the spiritual harm that Midian caused to Israel. It is a difficult passage, and it does not explain every detail of their involvement.

For today: sin often comes disguised as something attractive or harmless. Let us ask God for wisdom to recognize subtle temptations and to flee from them in time.
exp.15:5:
Moses gives an instruction to Korah and all his followers: that they take censers, which were metal containers in which coals and perfume were burned as an offering to God. The word "company" refers to the group of people who accompany and support someone.

Moses speaks after Korah and his followers challenged his leadership and that of Aaron. Hearing them, Moses falls prostrate as a sign of humility and grief. Instead of arguing, he proposes that God himself show whom he has chosen to draw near to him. Burning incense was the work of the priests, so this test would reveal who truly had that calling.

For today: when there are conflicts or envy, we can imitate Moses. Before defending ourselves or striking back, we can humble ourselves before God and let him be the one who judges and confirms what is true.
exp.4:1:
God tells Moses to instruct the people to send three kinds of people out of the camp: those who had a skin disease (the biblical term covered several conditions affecting the skin), those with a discharge from the body, and those who had become unclean by touching a dead body. "Unclean" here means impure according to the law, not necessarily sinful.

The Lord speaks while Israel is camped in the wilderness. God dwells in the middle of the camp, and for that reason he wants the place to remain ritually clean. The separation was temporary, lasting until the person was purified. It also protected the people from contagion, although the text emphasizes the reason of holiness.

For today: God takes his holiness seriously and invites us to live near him with reverence. Today we can examine what things pull us away from his presence and draw close to Jesus, who cleanses and does not turn anyone away.
exp.22:13:
This verse tells how Balak took Balaam to the field of the watchers, on top of Pisgah. There he built seven altars and offered a young bull and a ram on each one. The name of the place seems to mean a high spot for keeping watch, a lookout.
