Balak, king of Moab, wanted Balaam to curse Israel. He had already tried once without success, so he changed the place, thinking that from another viewpoint the result would be different. Balaam had already said that he would speak only what God put in his mouth. Some think Balak was trying to manipulate God with sacrifices; the text does not say this with certainty.

For today: we cannot change God's will with rituals, offerings, or a change of scenery. He looks for obedience and a sincere heart. Before insisting on what we want, let us ask Him what He wants.
exp.32:47:
This verse tells that the people of Israel left the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho. The word "departed" means they had set out from a place, and "pitched" means they set up their camp.

Moses records the list of Israel's stops during the forty years in the wilderness, as commanded by God (Numbers 33:2). This is nearly the last camp before entering the promised land. From there, in the next verse, God speaks to Moses again about how to take possession of the land.

God watched over every stretch of the journey, even the places that seemed only to be passing through. If today you feel you are in a season of waiting or a long road, remember that God sees you, guides you, and keeps count of every step. Trust that He will bring you to where He has promised.
exp.8:19:
This verse says that sometimes God's cloud stayed over the tabernacle for only a few days. Even so, the people obeyed: they followed the command of the Lord. Camping and setting out were both done at God's command.

The book of Numbers tells of Israel's journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. Here the narrator explains how God guided the people with the cloud, which was a sign of his presence. What mattered was not how long they stayed in one place, but following God's direction, whether for a short time or a long one.

For today: trust that God can guide you through short seasons as well as long ones. Ask him to help you not to cling to what is comfortable or rush ahead out of impatience, but to move or wait according to his direction.
exp.0:43:
This verse closes the list of the tribes. It says that Moses and Aaron did the counting, together with twelve leaders, one for each tribe. The words "were numbered" mean those who were recorded, and the "princes" are the heads or leaders of each tribe. "Father's house" refers to the family or clan.

God commanded Moses to take this census in the wilderness of Sinai, at the beginning of the second year after leaving Egypt. The men twenty years old and up who could go to war were counted. The narrator reports that the work was done in an orderly way and with the help of leaders from each tribe. As for the exact purpose of the census, the text presents it as preparing the people to march in an organized way.

For today: God cares about order and values many people taking part in the work. If you lead something in your church or family, share the responsibility with others and recognize each person as important.
exp.11:3:
It says that God suddenly spoke to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam (Miriam), and commanded the three of them to present themselves at the tabernacle of the testimony, the tent where God met with his people. The words "at once" and "come out" mean "immediately" and "go." The three obeyed and went.

Here the Lord speaks. Miriam and Aaron had just criticized Moses and questioned his special place, saying that God also spoke through them. The text says that the Lord heard it. Moses did not defend himself; the Bible describes him as very meek, that is, humble and patient. God himself intervenes and calls them together to correct them.

For today: God hears what we say about others, even in private. When we feel jealous or overlooked, it is wise to hold back criticism and draw near to God with humility, trusting that he defends the truth.
exp.32:55:
It says that, if Israel did not drive out the peoples of Canaan, God would do to them the same thing he had planned to do to those peoples. The word "á" is simply "a" in its meaning, and "pensé" here means "I intended" or "I purposed." In other words, Israel would suffer the judgment that the Canaanites deserved.

God speaks to Moses so that he will tell the people, just before they enter the promised land, beside the Jordan. The Canaanites were being judged for their idolatry, and God warns that Israel would not be spared if it copied those practices. The thorns and the pricks describe constant troubles and pains. The Bible later shows that Israel did in fact mix with them.

For today: do not make peace with what you know pulls you away from God. Ask him for help to leave soon whatever, though it may seem small, over time hurts you and weakens you.
exp.5:3:
While his time of separation lasted, the person could not eat anything that came from the grapevine. That included everything from the seeds to the outer skin of the grape. The word for the time of dedication to God, the Nazirite vow, is rendered here as the "separation" the verse describes.

God speaks to Moses and tells him to explain this to the people. Men or women could make a voluntary vow to devote themselves to the LORD for a set period of time. This restriction was a visible sign of being set apart. Scholars do not agree on the exact reason for avoiding the vine; some think it was meant to keep a distance from excess or from what was ordinary.

For today: if you want to dedicate yourself to God in something, be clear and steady about it. You may give up something good for a time, such as certain pleasures or distractions, so that your attention is fixed on Him.
exp.33:7:
It says that the northern border of the promised land runs from Mount Hor to the entrance of Hamath, and that from there the boundary ends at Zedad. The verb "ye shall point out" means "to mark out or trace." The "goings forth" of the border are the points where the boundary ends or turns aside. "Border" means the limit or boundary.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, shortly before they enter Canaan. He gives them the limits of the land they will divide among the tribes. It is not known with certainty where this Mount Hor was, which is not the same as the mountain where Aaron died, and scholars debate the exact location of Zedad and of other places on the list.

For today: God cares about details and about concrete promises. If He was so clear in giving His people their boundaries, we can trust that He also guides our lives with care. Ask Him for wisdom to recognize what He has given you, and to live thankful within it.
exp.27:2:
God tells Moses to instruct the people about the offering they are to bring to him: two lambs a year old, without blemish, every day. A "burnt offering made by fire" is an offering burned on the altar, and "continual burnt offering" means it was offered every day, without fail. "Without blemish" means without defect.

The LORD speaks to Moses as Israel prepares to enter the promised land. Before the land is divided, God reminds the people that their worship must be constant and orderly, one lamb in the morning and the other between the two evenings (as the next verse explains).

For today: God values a daily relationship with him. We can set aside a moment each morning and each evening to pray, give thanks, and offer him our best, not merely what we have left over.
exp.10:23:
Moses goes out to speak with the people and repeats to them what God had told him. Then he gathers seventy men from the elders of Israel and stations them around the tabernacle, the tent where God was present.

Israel was complaining in the desert because they wanted meat. Moses felt overwhelmed by carrying all the people alone, and he doubted there would be enough food. God asked him whether his hand had become too short, that is, whether his power had limits. Now Moses obeys: he shares the burden of leadership with others.

For today: you do not have to carry everything by yourself. God often cares for us by placing other people beside us. Ask for help with humility, share responsibilities, and trust that the power of God has not grown short.
exp.12:32:
The ten spies who did not believe gave a bad report. They said the land "devours its inhabitants" (perhaps through wars or death), that the people were very tall, and that they saw the descendants of Anak, the sons of the giants. They "spoke evil of" the land, meaning they said bad things about it. They felt like "grasshoppers," that is, small and helpless.

These words are spoken by the spies whom Moses sent to explore Canaan, not counting Caleb and Joshua. God had already promised them that land. But fear led them to exaggerate and to guess what others thought of them, saying "we were in their sight." They could not have known that. Their people believed the report and lost heart.

For today: when you face a big problem, do not measure yourself only by what you see or by what you imagine others think of you. Fix your eyes first on God's promises, and then take the step of faith.
exp.6:75:
This verse mentions one male goat, that is, an adult goat, which was offered as a sin offering. The word "sin offering" refers to covering over or removing the guilt of sin. It is part of the list of offerings presented by Pagiel, leader of the tribe of Asher.

This is a narrative section of Numbers. Moses records how each prince of Israel brought the same offering for the dedication of the tabernacle, day after day. The repetition shows that each tribe took part equally. Here we see that sin needed to be dealt with before approaching God.

For today: Christians believe that Jesus offered his life as the complete sacrifice for our sins. We can come before God with sincerity, acknowledge our failings, and receive his forgiveness with gratitude, without trying to earn it by our own means.
exp.13:26:
Here God asks how long he will have to bear with the people who will not stop complaining.

The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron. The spies had returned from Canaan, and most of the people were filled with fear and wept, doubting that God could fulfill his promise. They even spoke of going back to Egypt. God responds with grief and judgment: that contempt for his care would have consequences.

For today: when difficulties come, before you complain to others, bring your fear honestly to God. Prayer is different from grumbling, because prayer trusts that God hears and can act, while constant complaining pulls us away from that trust.
exp.32:51:
God tells Israel that, when they enter Canaan, they must drive out the inhabitants of the land and destroy the carved stone figures used in worship, their cast metal images (idols), and their high places where the false gods were worshiped. Tearing down means pulling down completely.

The Lord speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, just before crossing the Jordan. Israel was about to receive the promised land, and God wanted to protect them from idolatry. This command was for that historical moment and for that people. Later, the text warns that if they did not carry it out, those peoples would become a snare to them.

Today we do not use this passage to attack anyone. We apply it to our hearts: ask yourself what thing competes with God in your life, and remove it decisively before it comes to dominate you.
exp.21:36:
Balak receives Balaam and reproaches him with a complaining tone: "Did I not earnestly send unto you to call you? Why did you not come to me?" Then he adds: "Am I not able indeed to promote you to honor?" Here "promote you to honor" means rewarding you with riches and recognition.

Balak is king of Moab and is afraid of Israel. He had sent for Balaam so that he would curse the people, and he had offered to pay him well. Balaam had delayed because God first prevented him. Now that he arrives, Balak reminds him of his offer. Balaam answers that he will say only what God puts in his mouth.

For today: be careful with offers of money or recognition that seek to make us change what we know God wants. Before making a decision, let us ask ourselves whether we are moved by obedience to God or by the desire to gain something.
exp.15:30:
Right after Moses finished speaking, the ground split open beneath the rebels' feet. What Moses had announced happened at once. The words "it came to pass" in the King James Version mean "it happened," and "as he had made an end of speaking" means "just as he finished speaking."

Moses is speaking before the people. Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, together with other leaders, challenged the authority God had given to Moses and Aaron. Moses let God himself show who had sent him. If the rebels had died in an ordinary way, Moses would not have spoken on God's behalf. But something new and obvious happened. The details of the pit (called "Sheol" in Hebrew) are understood in different ways, but the account is clear: God responded.

For today: God takes humility and respect for what He has established seriously. Before you criticize or compete for position, ask yourself whether you are seeking to serve or to be admired. Ask God for a humble heart.
exp.2:46:
God tells Moses to collect five shekels for each person. He was to use the shekel of the sanctuary, which was an official unit of weight in silver. The verse explains that this shekel equaled twenty gerahs (a small unit of weight in Hebrew).

God speaks to Moses during the counting of the firstborn. The Levites were taken in place of Israel's firstborn, but there were 273 more firstborn than Levites. A ransom was paid for them, and that money was given to Aaron and his sons, who served in the sanctuary.

For today: redemption has a real price, and God does not overlook it. Christians believe that Christ paid our ransom in full. This invites us to live with gratitude and not take lightly what it cost to secure our freedom.
exp.35:6:
This verse says that the land God gave to each tribe of Israel was not to pass from one tribe to another. Every Israelite was to stay bound to the inheritance of his fathers' tribe. The word "inheritance" in the verse means the land received as an heritage, and "remove" means moved over to another owner. The phrase "keep himself" means that each person was to remain attached to it.

Moses speaks by the command of the LORD. The leaders of the tribe of Joseph feared that, if the daughters of Zelophehad inherited land and married men from another tribe, the land would change tribes. God confirmed that they were right and commanded that these daughters marry within their own tribe.

For today: God takes care of what he entrusts to each family. We can learn to manage faithfully what we have received and to think about leaving it well cared for for those who come after us.
exp.23:4:
This verse is an exclamation of admiration. It says that the tents of Jacob and the dwellings of Israel are beautiful. "Tents" and "dwellings" refer to the places where the people lived in the desert. Jacob and Israel are names that here refer to the whole people of God.

The one speaking is Balaam, son of Beor. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel, but God put blessings in his mouth. From a mountain, Balaam sees the people camped according to their tribes. Some think the beauty speaks of the order of the camp; others, of God's blessing upon them. The text does not make this clear.

For today: God sees beauty in his people even when others despise them. Think about your home and your church: ask God to bring order, peace, and gratitude there, and bless those who live with you with your words.
exp.27:1:
God tells Moses to command the people to take care to bring the offerings they present to him. He calls the sacrifices "my bread," a way of speaking about the food of the altar. The phrase "burned up in the fire" means consumed by fire, and "a pleasing aroma" shows that God receives them with favor. "At their appointed time" means at the hours set for them.

Israel is at the end of forty years in the wilderness, close to entering the promised land. A new generation needs to hear the worship instructions once again. The LORD speaks through Moses. The verses that follow explain that two lambs were offered each day, one in the morning and one in the evening.

For today: God values steadiness in seeking him. We can set aside fixed moments each day, even brief ones, to pray and read his Word, not only when we happen to feel like it.
exp.32:50:
God tells Moses to speak to the people of Israel. He announces to them what they are to do "when ye are passed over Jordan", that is, when they have crossed the Jordan River and entered the land of Canaan. "Passed over" is an old way of saying "have crossed". This verse is the beginning of an instruction that continues in the verses that follow.

The Lord speaks to Moses in the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan, opposite Jericho. After years in the wilderness, Israel is about to enter the promised land. God gives them directions before they cross, above all so that they do not adopt the religious practices of the peoples of Canaan.

God prepares his people before the great steps. Today we can take time to listen to his guidance before beginning something new, and ask him to help us not to be shaped by whatever draws us away from him.
exp.6:29:
This verse only introduces the leader who brought his offering on the fourth day: Elizur, son of Shedeur, chief of the tribe of Reuben. It is the beginning of the list of what he brought.

Moses is recording how the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel presented offerings to dedicate the altar and the tabernacle, one each day. Each day names a different leader. Although the offerings are nearly identical, the Bible repeats them one by one. It does not say with certainty why, but it shows that each tribe and each leader was taken into account.

For today: God does not overlook anyone or treat anyone as a number. Even if your service seems repeated or small, he sees it. Offer him what is yours today with sincerity and steadiness.
exp.3:8:
God gives instructions for packing the golden lampstand of the tabernacle when the people were moving. They wrapped it in a cloth of dark blue or violet. They also covered its fittings: the lamps, the tongs used to trim the wicks, the trays for the used ashes, and the vessels that held the oil.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about the work of the Kohathites, a family of Levites. They carried the holy objects, but only after the priests had covered them. Everything had to be handled with respect, because it belonged to the presence of God among his people.

For today: let us treat what belongs to God with reverence, such as his Word, prayer, and the life of his church. Let us do our service with order, humility, and attention, and not take it lightly.
exp.0:52:
This verse says that the Levites were to camp all around the tabernacle of the testimony, that is, the tent where God's presence was and the tablets of the law. In this way they protected that holy place. The phrase "pitch round about" refers to their tents. "Wrath" means God's punishment. The Levites had "the charge," that is, the care and watch over the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, while Israel's camp is being organized. The Levites were not counted with the other tribes, because they had a special service. By surrounding the tabernacle, they kept anyone from approaching the holy things without respect. The idea is that this protection was meant to prevent judgment falling on the people.

For today: to draw near to God with reverence and responsibility. If God entrusts us with something in the church or the family, let us care for it with seriousness, because our faithful service can bless others.
exp.30:17:
This verse says that Moses orders that all the girls and young women who had never had sexual relations with a man be kept alive. The phrase about sexual union means a sexual relationship, and the phrase about keeping them alive means they will be preserved alive for themselves.

Moses speaks to the commanders of Israel's army after the battle against Midian. The Midianite women had led Israel into idolatry at Peor, on the advice of Balaam, and a plague killed many people. This is a harsh passage that belongs to the warfare of that time; scholars interpret it in different ways, and there is no single explanation accepted by everyone.

For today: this text reminds us that sin, especially temptation that comes disguised as friendship, has serious consequences. Let us be careful about whom we join ourselves to spiritually, and let us ask for wisdom when faced with bad influences.
exp.28:35:
On the eighth day of the feast, the people were to present to God a burnt offering: one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year, all without blemish. "Sweet savour offering made by fire" means a sacrifice burned on the altar that pleased God. A "burnt offering" is an offering that was burned whole.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for Israel concerning the feasts of the year. This eighth day closed the Feast of Tabernacles, with a solemn assembly and no heavy work. How many animals were offered was fewer than on the previous days; scholars explain this in different ways, and the text does not make it clear.

For today: God deserves the best, not what is left over. We can set apart time, attention, and resources for him with a devoted heart, trusting that Christ is our perfect sacrifice.
exp.17:7:
God tells Aaron that he is now entrusted with the care of the offerings the people bring to him. All the holy things the Israelites set apart will belong to him and his sons as their portion, "by reason of the anointing," that is, because they have been set apart for priestly service. This would be a standing rule forever. The word "charge" means care or responsibility.

God speaks to Aaron after the rebellion of Korah and the sign of the rod that budded. In this way he confirms who serves in the sanctuary. The Levites help, the priests attend the altar, and God provides for their support through the offerings, since they would not receive an inheritance of land as the other tribes did.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support with gratitude and generosity those who dedicate themselves to ministry, and also serve faithfully in what God has entrusted to us.
exp.0:47:
This verse explains why the Levites were not counted along with the rest of the people. The reason is that God himself spoke to Moses and gave him that instruction. The phrase "For the Lord had spoken unto Moses" reminds us that the command did not come from Moses, but from God. "The Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament.

Here the narrator speaks, and tells us that God gave an order to Moses. The people had been counted for war, but the Levites had a different task: to care for and carry the tabernacle, the tent where God met with his people. That is why they were set apart from the military count.

For today: God gives each person a different calling, and all of them are valuable. Do not compare yourself with others. Ask God what your place is and serve him faithfully there, even if your task seems less visible.
exp.26:19:
God tells Moses to give Joshua some of his "honour", that is, of his honor and authority. The word "honour" here speaks of splendor and majesty. The purpose is clear: that the whole people of Israel should obey him.

The LORD speaks with Moses. Moses already knew he would not enter the Promised Land, and he asked God for a leader for the people. God chose Joshua, a man in whom there is spirit, and ordered that he be presented in public before the priest Eleazar and the whole congregation. In this way his leadership was recognized and did not depend on Moses alone. Some see here a gradual transfer of authority, though not a total one, since Joshua would depend on Eleazar.

For today: if God puts you in charge of something, seek to do it with support and order. And if you are called to let go of a position, prepare and support with generosity the one who comes after you.
exp.22:17:
This verse says that Balaam began to speak his "parable," that is, a solemn, poetic message that God gave him. He asks Balak, king of Moab, to rise up and listen carefully. The phrase "son of Zippor" simply identifies Balak as the son of Zippor.

Balaam speaks. Balak had hired him to curse Israel, but God put words in his mouth and sent him back. Balak, along with his burnt offering, expects a curse. Instead, Balaam announces what God has said, and in the verses that follow he declares that God does not change His mind as humans do.

For today: before we seek God's approval of our plans, it is wise to listen to what He has already said in His Word. His promises do not depend on human pressure or on our changing moods. We can rest in what He affirms.
exp.6:23:
On the third day, it was the turn of Eliab, son of Helon. He was the prince of the tribe of Zebulun, meaning its leader or chief. The phrase "children of Zebulun" refers to the tribe descended from Zebulun, son of Jacob.

Moses records how the leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel brought offerings for the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Each day one of them brought his offering. Here the list of what Eliab would bring begins, and it is nearly identical to the lists of the other leaders.

For today: God cares that each person brings him their offering and their service, even when they look like those of others. God records each name, one by one. You do not need to do something different to be noticed; it is enough to give your part with sincerity and faithfulness.
exp.14:29:
This verse speaks of the person who sins defiantly and on purpose, knowing full well what they are doing. It says that this person, whether an Israelite or a foreigner, reproached the Lord, meaning they insulted and despised him. The phrase about being cut off from among the people means that such a person was separated from the community; scholars debate whether this refers to expulsion, to death, or to a judgment from God.

God speaks to Moses to give instructions to the people in the wilderness. Just before this, he offers forgiveness and atonement for sins committed by mistake. Here the contrast is made clear: deliberate rebellion is much more serious, because it despises God's word.

For today: when we know that something displeases God, we should not justify it or harden our hearts. If we fail, let us go to him quickly and humbly, because his forgiveness is always near to those who repent.
exp.4:5:
God tells Moses to speak to the people. Whether it is a man or a woman, if anyone commits any of the sins that people commonly commit and so acts unfaithfully against the LORD, that person is guilty.

The verse uses the word "trespass" to describe this kind of wrong, meaning a failure to keep faith or trust. The word "guilty" here means that the person has become responsible for the wrong.

The LORD speaks to Moses right after commanding that those who were unclean be sent out of the camp. Now he teaches how to deal with sin and guilt within the community. It stands out that the same rule applies to men and women, and that wronging another person is also counted as an offense against God.

For today: when we fail someone, it is not enough to feel bad inside. God invites us to acknowledge the wrong, ask forgiveness, and repair the harm where we can. In this way we heal our relationship with the other person and with God.
exp.29:14:
The verse says that if the husband, after hearing his wife's vow, says nothing and lets the days pass in silence, that vow stands firm. His silence amounts to a "yes." The words "but" and "keeps silent" in the verse mean that he remains quiet. "Confirmed" means that he treated the vow as valid.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. These are rules about vows, that is, promises made to God. In that time, the father or the husband had authority over the household and could cancel the vow of his daughter or wife on the very day he heard it. If he waited and then canceled it, he bore the guilt.

Today we learn that silence also communicates. If something troubles us, let us speak in time and with clarity, and let us take seriously what we promise.
exp.0:45:
This verse gives the total of the census: 603,550 men of Israel, twenty years old and upward, who were fit to go out to war. Women, children, and Levites are not included.

The book of Numbers begins with God speaking to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. Moses and Aaron, together with one leader from each tribe, carried out the count. It was a preparation for organizing the people like an army on the march toward the promised land. The Levites were set apart, because God entrusted them with the care of the tabernacle. Some scholars debate how to understand these very large figures, but the text presents them as an actual record.

For today: God knows his people and counts each person. No one goes unnoticed by him. Ask yourself what place God has given you in his work, and serve him faithfully where you are.
exp.30:22:
It says that metal objects that can withstand fire, such as gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead, had to pass through the fire to be made clean. In addition, they had to be purified with the water of separation. Whatever could not withstand the fire was cleaned only with water.

The priest Eleazar speaks to the soldiers who were returning from the war against Midian. They had come into contact with the dead and with plunder, which according to the law made them ritually unclean. Eleazar passes on to them what God commanded through Moses, before they returned to the camp.

For today: God cares for the purity of his people with order and seriousness. We can ask ourselves which things we bring back from our struggles or labors need to be cleansed before God, and bring them to him with humility and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.23:0:
This verse tells us that Balaam realized it pleased the Lord to bless Israel. So he no longer went, as he had done the two previous times, to seek omens, that is, signs or portents that were used to try to foretell the future. Instead, he turned his face toward the wilderness, where the people were camped.

The narrator is the author of the book. Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. But God had already shown him twice that he would bless his people. Now Balaam sets aside his practices of divination, and the next verse says that the Spirit of God came upon him. Some think he simply gave in to what was obvious; the text says nothing more about his heart.

Today we can learn that God's plans do not change because of outside pressure or other people's interests. Instead of looking for signs to justify what we want, it is wise to humbly accept what God has already said.
exp.6:69:
This verse says that Ahiezer, the leader of the tribe of Dan, presented a male goat as an offering "for sin." To atone means to cover or cleanse sin, that is, to acknowledge that there is a wrong that needs forgiveness. A male goat is a billy goat, the male of the goat family.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks, recording in detail the offerings that each tribal leader brought, day after day, when the tabernacle was dedicated. Each tribe presented the same offering, and the text repeats it without change. Within that offering, the goat for sin reminded the people that, even in a celebration, they needed forgiveness in order to come near to God.

For today: before worshiping, we can pause and sincerely acknowledge our failures. Christians believe that Christ has already offered the sacrifice for sin, so we can come near with humility and confidence.
exp.13:41:
Moses warns the people not to go up to fight against their enemies, because God is not with them. "Go not up" means "do not go up." "Ye" is "you." "Be not smitten" means that they would be defeated and struck down by their enemies.

Moses speaks to the Israelites the day after their rebellion. Out of fear, they had refused to enter the promised land, and God told them that that generation would not enter. Now, only partly sorry, they want to go up on their own. But God had already given another command, so going without his direction was disobeying again. The text shows that the ark did not move from the camp.

For today: truly repenting includes obeying what God says now, not just doing something big to feel forgiven. Before acting with courage or haste, ask God whether he is going with you on that path.
exp.13:3:
It says that the Israelites, instead of trusting God, were urging one another to choose a new leader (a "captain") who would lead them back to Egypt. The word "let us return" means "let us go back," and "unto" is the older form of "to."

The people of Israel are the ones speaking. The twelve spies had come back from Canaan, and ten of them gave a report full of fear. The people wept, complained against Moses and Aaron, and even doubted God's goodness. They wanted to go back to the land where they had been slaves, forgetting how God had delivered them.

When fear takes hold of us, we may think the familiar past is better than what God is preparing for us. Before making a decision out of fear, stop to pray and remember what God has already done for you. His past faithfulness helps you trust the future.
exp.0:5:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that, for the tribe of Simeon, the man chosen to help with the count is Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai. The phrase rendered as "man" here simply means a man, and the phrase about "head of the house of their fathers" means the leader of his family or clan.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to count the people of Israel, the men fit for war. To help him, God asks for one leader from each tribe. In this way the work does not rest on Moses alone, and each tribe has a known representative. The Bible gives few further details about these men at this point.

For today: God cares for people one by one, and calls those who serve by name. Today you can value small and hidden service, both your own and that of others, and thank someone who helps quietly in your church or family.
exp.14:38:
These tassels (fringes or tufts) on the edges of their clothing were to serve as a visible reminder. When an Israelite saw them, he was to remember the commandments of the Lord and keep them, instead of being led by what his heart and his eyes desired. The "tzitzit" is a fringe or tuft, and the word translated here as "whoring" speaks of unfaithfulness to God, like someone who turns away from Him to follow other desires.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people. This takes place in the wilderness, after Israel rebelled again and again. God gives them a simple, daily sign to help them remember their covenant and to live as a holy people, the one He brought out of Egypt.

For today: we all forget easily what God says. You can create a simple reminder, such as a verse on your phone or on your mirror, to return to the Word before acting on impulse.
exp.15:36:
God tells Moses to instruct Eleazar, son of the priest Aaron, to take the censers out from among the burning remains and to scatter the fire far away. A censer was a metal vessel for burning incense. "Hallowed" here means they were set apart for God, because they had been presented before Him.

The Lord speaks. Korah, Dathan, Abiram and two hundred and fifty men rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and wanted to offer incense without God having authorized them. God judged them with fire. Eleazar is the one assigned, not Aaron, and many think this was so that the high priest would not become defiled by touching things among the dead, though the text does not explain it. Afterward the censers were used to cover the altar, as a sign for Israel.

Today, let us draw near to God with reverence and obedience, and not take lightly what He has set apart as holy.
exp.19:18:
Here Israel presses its request to the king of Edom. They say they will travel only by the main road, without turning aside. If they or their livestock drink any of the water, they will pay for it. The phrase "by the highway" means along the marked road, and "directly" means straight through, without stopping. They promise to pass through without doing anything else.

The people of Israel are speaking, on their way to the promised land after leaving Egypt. They need to cross the territory of Edom, a people related to them, since Edom descended from Esau. The king had already refused them, and Israel insists with a clearer offer. Edom refuses again and comes out armed, so Israel goes around instead of fighting.

When someone shuts a door in our face, we can ask humbly and offer what is fair. But if the answer is still no, it is wise to avoid conflict and look for another way, trusting that God is still guiding.
exp.32:36:
This verse says that the people of Israel left the place called Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, which was at the edge of the territory of Edom. "Extremity" refers to the boundary or border of the region.

This chapter is a list of Israel's stops in the wilderness, written by Moses, that traces the journey from Egypt to near the promised land. The following verse explains the importance of this place: there Aaron the priest died, at God's command.

Scholars do not agree on the exact location of Mount Hor, so it is best not to state it with certainty.

For today: God cares for every stage of our journey, even the final stops of a life. We can trust that he walks with us through every change, and give thanks to those who have guided us in faith while they are still with us.
exp.34:29:
This verse says that a person who commits murder can only be sentenced to death if there are witnesses, that is, more than one. The word translated as "kill" here refers to striking someone with a result of death, and the phrase about not being enough means that a single witness is not sufficient to prove or establish something as true. One witness was not enough to take anyone's life.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, before they enter the promised land. He is giving rules about the cities of refuge, where a person who killed by accident could flee, and about how to judge cases of murder. The rule about witnesses protected the accused from unjust sentences, and God repeats it in another passage of the law (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Today it reminds us that justice needs evidence and care. Before we accuse someone or repeat a rumor, let us make an effort to know the facts and not to judge based on the word of a single person.
exp.28:12:
This verse sets out what the people were to present to God on the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles: thirteen young bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs in their first year. A "burnt offering" was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar. A "sweet savour" means a pleasing aroma to God. "Without blemish" means without any physical flaw.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes these instructions on to Israel. They were about to enter the promised land, and God was teaching them how to worship him at the feasts of the year. This feast fell in the seventh month, lasted seven days, and was a time of rest and joy before the Lord. Many understand that animals without blemish point to the best that should be given to God.

Today we no longer offer animals, but we can give God the best of our time, affection, and effort, and not merely what is left over. Worshiping him with sincere devotion pleases him.
exp.6:28:
Here the peace offering is mentioned: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five lambs of one year. A "peace offering" was a fellowship offering to God, in which part of the meat was shared in a meal. Male goats are the male goats themselves. So the offering of Eliab, son of Helon, ends here.

This chapter recounts the dedication of the altar of the tabernacle. Each day, one tribal leader brought the same offering. Eliab represented Zebulun, according to verse 24. The account gives every detail, although it repeats itself, and that shows that God takes note of each one.

For today: do not underestimate what you give to God because it seems repeated or ordinary. He sees your daily faithfulness, in your service, your time, and your generosity, and values it as if it were unique.
exp.19:13:
Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom. He asks them to say: "Thus saith thy brother Israel." With that phrase he reminds the king that they are relatives and that he knows the hardships Israel has gone through. The messengers are official envoys.

Moses speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. The Edomites descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, which is why he calls them brothers. Israel is about to enter Canaan and needs to pass through Edom's territory. Before asking permission, Moses recalls their shared history and the help God gave them.

When we ask for help or seek peace with someone, it helps to begin with respect and humility, remembering what unites us. Moses does not demand or threaten; he speaks with courtesy, even while going through a difficult moment. We can do the same in our own relationships.
exp.31:24:
This verse says that the tribes of Gad and Reuben answered Moses with a clear promise: they would do exactly what he had commanded them. They address Moses as "my lord" and call themselves "your servants," words of respect and submission.

The men of Gad and Reuben had a great deal of livestock, and they asked to stay in the lands east of the Jordan. Moses was upset, because he feared they would leave their brothers to fight alone. He warned them that if they did not keep their word, they would sin against the LORD. Then they accepted the condition: they would leave their families in fortified cities and cross over armed with the rest of Israel.

For today: when we give our word, we should keep it, especially when it affects others. Let us think of a commitment we have made in our family, our church, or our work, and ask God for help to keep it faithfully.
exp.14:5:
It says that when a ram was offered, the grain offering was to be larger than the one for a lamb: two tenth deals of fine flour (the best, finely ground), mixed with a third of a hin of oil. The word "offering" here means a gift brought to God. An ephah was a dry measure for grain, and a hin was a measure for liquids. Its exact equivalent in liters is debated, so it is better not to present a specific figure as certain.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel while they were still in the wilderness, and gives them instructions for when they would enter the promised land. Each animal offered came with flour, oil, and wine in fixed proportions. In this way worship was orderly and did not depend on improvisation.

For today: God deserves our best and not what is left over. We can ask ourselves which part of our time, money, and attention we give to him with gratitude and intention, and not out of habit.
exp.21:28:
Balaam answers the donkey that she has mocked him, meaning that she has made him look foolish. He is so angry that he says that if he had a sword in his hand, he would kill her right then. The word "I would there were" expresses a strong wish.

Balaam is a man on his way to meet the king of Moab. The donkey had turned aside and stopped because she saw the angel of the LORD, which Balaam could not see. He, not knowing this, struck the animal three times. It is ironic: he wants a sword, and the angel already had one in his hand.

For today: when something holds us back, before we react with anger, it is wise to ask ourselves whether God is at work in what we cannot yet see.
exp.15:20:
God tells Moses and Aaron to separate themselves from the rest of the people, because He is going to destroy them in a moment. "Separate yourselves" means "step away," and "I will consume them" means "I will destroy them." It is a very serious warning of immediate judgment.

The LORD speaks. Korah had gathered the whole community at the entrance of the tabernacle to challenge the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Then the glory of God appeared. With this warning, God responds to the rebellion. Afterward, Moses and Aaron intercede for the people, and the text shows that God hears that prayer.

For today: God takes rebellion and pride seriously, but He also listens to those who intercede. When you see division or conflict, do not join in the complaining; pray for the people, asking God for mercy and humility for everyone.
exp.31:30:
The children of Gad and the children of Reuben accept Moses' terms. They say they will do what the Lord has commanded his servants. The name "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "servants" is the humble way they refer to themselves.

Moses was speaking with these two tribes, who wanted to stay east of the Jordan because there was good pasture there for their livestock. Moses set them a condition: they had to cross over armed with their brothers and help them conquer Canaan. Only after that could they return to their lands. Here they respond with a clear commitment, and with that the agreement is sealed.

For today: keeping what we promise, even when we already have what we wanted. They could have settled down comfortably, but they committed to helping others. It invites us to think about how we can serve our family, our church or our neighbors, without seeking only our own well-being.
exp.0:31:
This verse speaks of the census of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the sons of Joseph. They were counted by their generations, their families and the houses of their fathers, that is, according to their lineage. Only the men from twenty years old and upward were recorded, all those who were able to go out to war, that is, those fit for the army.

God himself orders this census and speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the departure from Egypt. Israel was organizing itself as a people to march toward the promised land. Ephraim and Manasseh are separate tribes because Jacob adopted and blessed the sons of Joseph, thus giving Joseph a double portion.

For today: God knows and counts each person, and each one has a place among his people. You are not a lost number in the crowd. Ask yourself today what you can contribute to your family and your church.
exp.10:0:
This verse tells how the people of Israel complained, and God heard it. His anger was kindled, and a fire from the Lord burned up one end of the camp. "Complained" means protesting with bitterness. The phrase "in the ears of the Lord" means that God heard it directly. The phrase "his anger was kindled" means that his anger flared up strongly. "One end of the camp" means an outer edge or border of the camp.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, is speaking. Israel is walking through the desert after leaving Egypt and leaving Mount Sinai. The text does not explain the exact reason for the complaint; it only says it was a grumbling of bad attitude. Afterward, the people cry out to Moses, he prays, and the fire goes out.

For today: when you are tired or uncomfortable, before complaining to others, bring your burden to God in prayer. He hears both sincere lament and murmuring, and He invites us to trust Him.
exp.21:5:
Balak, king of Moab, asks Balaam to come and curse Israel. He says that this people is stronger than he is, and that perhaps in this way he will be able to strike them down and drive them out of the land. "Strike them down" means defeat them. Balak believes that Balaam's blessings and curses have real power.

Balak speaks out of fear. Israel had just come out of Egypt and was camped near Moab. Since he does not feel able to defeat them in battle, he looks for spiritual help from a man famous for his words. Later in the story, it becomes clear that God is the one who decides who is blessed, not Balaam or Balak.

When fear takes hold of us, we may look for solutions apart from God, or even try to manipulate things in our favor. Instead, we can bring our fears to God in prayer and trust that He cares for His own.
exp.31:18:
Here the men of Reuben and Gad say that they will not ask for land on the other side of the Jordan with the rest of Israel, nor further on, because they will already receive their inheritance on the eastern side.

The Reuben and Gad leaders speak to Moses. They had a great deal of livestock, and the land of Gilead seemed good to them for raising it. They promise to help their brothers in the war until all of them have their own territory. Moses answers by setting conditions, because he feared their request would discourage the people.

For today: when we receive a blessing, we should not keep it to ourselves alone. We can ask ourselves who we still need to help, and keep our commitments to others until the end.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that the Kohathites were not to go in to look at the sanctuary at the moment when the priests were covering the holy objects. If they did, they would die. The phrase "when the holy things are covered" is the part of the verse that this comment refers to, and "the holy things" are the furnishings and utensils of the place of worship, such as the ark and the altar.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron. The Kohathites, a family of Levites, would carry these objects during the journey through the desert. But first Aaron and his sons had to wrap them. God was thus making sure that no one handled what was holy carelessly. It was a protection for the people, and it also shows the seriousness of approaching God.

Today we can come before God with respect and gratitude, without taking what is sacred lightly. And through Christ we have access to Him, yet we still honor Him with reverence.
exp.17:28:
This verse says that the Levites, after receiving the tithes from the people, were to set apart an offering for the Lord from everything they received. And it was not just any part: it had to be the best, the portion that was hallowed, that is, set apart for God.

God speaks to Aaron, and through Moses to the Levites. They had no inheritance of land in Israel and lived on the tithes of the people. God asked them to also give back to God a tenth of what they received, to support the priest. In this way, no one was left out of the practice of giving.

For today: when we give from what we have, whether money, time or talent, we can ask ourselves whether we are giving the best or only what is left over. Giving with gratitude and generosity honors God, because everything we have comes from Him.
exp.0:10:
This verse names a leader of the tribe of Benjamin: Abidan, son of Gideoni. It is part of a list of chiefs, one for each tribe. This Gideoni is not the famous judge; here he is only the name of the father. The ancient names are written in the way of the older version, for example the names of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, shortly after the exodus from Egypt. He commands him to take a census of the people and tells him that chosen men will help him, one chief from each tribe. In this way the counting was done in an orderly manner, and the people prepared to march and to organize themselves around the tabernacle.

God knows each person by name, even when almost no one else remembers it. Abidan does not appear as a great hero, but his service was recorded. Today you can serve faithfully in simple things, knowing that God sees and values what you do.
exp.33:3:
This verse describes the southern boundary of the promised land. The border ran around from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim (a steep climb or pass), continued toward Zin, and reached Kadesh-barnea. Then it passed on to Hazar-addar and continued as far as Azmon.

The "going forth" of the border means the points where the boundary ends or turns off. The word "border" simply means the dividing line.

God speaks to Moses near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is about to enter Canaan, and the Lord gives the exact limits of the inheritance the tribes will divide among themselves. Some of these places are hard to locate today, and scholars do not agree on every detail of the route.

For today: God keeps His promises with clear details, not vague ideas. If He cared for every boundary of Israel, you can trust that He also cares for the details of your life. Rest in His faithfulness and take concrete steps of obedience.
exp.15:49:
It says that Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tabernacle of the congregation, where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept. He did this after the plague had already stopped. The word "plague" here refers to a great number of people dying.

The people had grumbled against Moses and Aaron after the punishment of Korah and his followers. Then a plague came. Moses sent Aaron, the high priest, to take the censer and make atonement for the people. Aaron stood between the dead and the living, and the plague stopped. This verse closes the account: it tells what happened afterward, and it is not a speech.

For today: God hears intercession. We can pray for others, even for those who complain or make mistakes, and do so with humility. For Christians, Jesus is the perfect intercessor who stands between us and God.
exp.6:82:
This verse closes the list of what Ahira brought, the last of the twelve leaders. For the sacrifice of peace offerings he presented two oxen, five rams, five he goats and five lambs of the first year. The offering of peace is a fellowship offering, a meal shared with God. The he goat is a male goat.

Here the narrator of Numbers speaks. He tells how each tribal leader brought offerings to dedicate the altar of the tabernacle, one day for each tribe. Ahira represented the tribe of Naphtali. Everyone brings exactly the same, and the text repeats it without summarizing, as if to give each one his place.

For today: God values each person, even when their contribution looks the same as others' or goes unnoticed. Serve with steadiness and gratitude, without comparing yourself. What you do for God is recorded.
exp.30:3:
It says that Moses orders a thousand men from each tribe to be sent to war. Since there are twelve tribes, that would be twelve thousand in total. The verse's wording makes it a clear and orderly command, in which all the tribes take part equally.

Moses speaks to the people on God's command. The Midianites had led Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25). God tells Moses to carry out this judgment before his death. It is a harsh episode, tied to a unique moment in Israel's history, and Christians read it in different ways. Note that Phinehas goes with the holy objects, showing that the task was understood as an act of obedience to God.

For today: we learn that serving God belongs to everyone, not just to a few. Ask yourself what your part is in your church or community, and carry it out with responsibility and humility.
exp.31:29:
This verse says that if the men of Gad and Reuben do not cross the Jordan armed together with the rest of the Israelites, then they will have to receive their inheritance in the land of Canaan, among the other tribes, and not in the territory on the other side of the river.

Moses speaks with Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes. Gad and Reuben wanted to stay east of the Jordan because there was good land there for their livestock. Moses sets a condition: first they must help their brothers conquer Canaan. In this way the unity of the people is kept.

For today: we cannot enjoy our blessings in peace while others are still fighting alone. God calls us to fulfill what has been promised and to support our brothers and sisters in their battles.
exp.3:18:
It says that Moses and Aaron were to look after the Kohathites so that they would not die when they came near the most holy things of the sanctuary. Aaron and his sons, the priests, would go in first and assign each man his task and his load. The phrase "most holy place" here refers to the very holy things of the tabernacle. "Office" means task, and "burden" is what each one was to carry.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. The Kohathites, a family of Levites, would carry the sacred objects when the camp moved. Touching them or looking at them without the proper preparation would put them in danger of death. God sets up order to protect them.

For today: God takes his holiness seriously, but he also cares for those who serve him. We can serve him with reverence, accepting the place given to us, without imposing ourselves on our own initiative, and valuing the guidance of those who direct us with humility.
exp.6:20:
Verse 21 says that Nethanel brought for the burnt offering one young bullock, one ram, and one lamb of the first year. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar, as a sign of total surrender to God.

We are in Numbers 7, when the tabernacle is being dedicated. Each leader of the twelve tribes brought the same offering on successive days. Here the narrator, the account given through Moses, describes the offering of Nethanel, leader of the tribe of Issachar. The repetition shows that each tribe held the same value before God and took part equally in his worship.

For today: God values complete surrender, not comparison. Ask yourself what part of your life you have not yet placed in his hands, and offer it to him today with simplicity and gratitude, without looking at what others give.
exp.26:12:
God tells Moses that, after he has seen the promised land from the mountain, he too will die. The phrase "be gathered to your people" is an old expression for dying, as his brother Aaron was gathered. The word "seen" here means that he has looked at the land from a distance, and "strife" means a quarrel or dispute.

God speaks. Moses has led Israel for many years, and now God tells him that he will not enter the land. The verses that follow explain the reason: at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, he did not honor God as holy before the people. Even so, God allows him to see the land and prepares his successor, and Moses responds by thinking about who will come after him.

For today: our actions have consequences, even for people who serve faithfully. But God does not abandon Moses; he cares for him to the end. We can acknowledge our mistakes with humility, trust that God remains good, and prepare others to continue what we have begun.
exp.15:47:
This verse says that Aaron positioned himself in the space between the people who had already died and those who were still alive. When he did so, the plague was stopped.

After Korah's rebellion, the people blamed Moses and Aaron for the death of the rebels. God sent a plague as judgment. Moses told Aaron, the high priest, to take the censer with fire and incense and make atonement for the people. Aaron obeyed at once and ran toward the crowd.

For today: this account shows us a mediator who steps in to save lives. Christians see in it a shadow of Jesus, our intercessor. It also invites us to pray for others, even for those who are in the wrong.
exp.25:63:
This verse says that among the Israelites counted in the plains of Moab, there was no one left from those whom Moses and Aaron had counted almost forty years earlier, in the wilderness of Sinai. "There was" is the meaning of the phrase, and "numbered" is the same as "counted." All those adult men had already died.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, explaining the second census taken by Moses and Eleazar. The following verse gives the reason: God had said that that generation would die in the wilderness, because of their unbelief and rebellion (Numbers 14). Only Caleb and Joshua remained, because they trusted in God.

For today: God's faithfulness is shown both in His warnings and in His promises. We can trust Him and obey Him today, without hardening our hearts, because a life of faith leads us to receive what He has promised.
exp.5:23:
This verse is the first part of the priestly blessing. "The Lord bless thee" means that God gives you his favor and care. "And keep thee" means that he protects you and watches over you from harm. The words "bless" and "keep" are in the singular, as if God were speaking to each person individually.

God spoke to Moses and commanded him to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests, how they were to bless the people of Israel. The priests did not make up the blessing; they repeated the words that God himself had given them. In this way the people knew that their blessing came from God and not from men.

For today: we can rest in the knowledge that God cares for us. We can also bless others, family members, friends, or brothers and sisters in the church, asking God to protect and care for them, especially when they are going through difficult days.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that God orders Moses to take a census of the sons of Gershon, one of the sons of Levi. They are to be counted according to their fathers' households, that is, by the clans of their ancestors, and by their families.

The Lord speaks with Moses in the wilderness. He had already commanded that the family of Kohath be counted, and now He continues with the family of Gershon. The Levites cared for and carried the tabernacle, and for this reason God arranges clearly who will do each task. The verses that follow say that the men from thirty to fifty years old who served would be counted.

For today: God values order and that each person has a place in His service. Ask yourself what task, however small it may seem, has been entrusted to you in your church or your family, and carry it out faithfully.
exp.13:2:
The Israelites complain against God. They say that the Lord brought them into the promised land only so that they would be killed by the sword, and that their wives and little children would become spoils of war. So they ask whether it would not be better to return to Egypt, where they had been slaves.

The people are speaking in the wilderness, after hearing the report of the twelve spies. Ten of them said that the people living in Canaan were very strong. The people were afraid, wept all night, and doubted that God would keep his promise. Moses and Aaron, for their part, fell facedown in humility and grief.

When fear takes control of us, we tend to forget what God has done and to think that he wants to harm us. Before deciding, let us remember how he has cared for us and trust in his promises.
exp.9:30:
Moses asks Hobab not to leave them. He tells him that he knows the places where one can camp in the desert, and that he will be to them like eyes, that is, a guide who sees what others do not see. The word "eyes" is used here as a picture of guidance, so that Hobab's knowledge of the land is compared to sight.

Moses speaks with Hobab, whom the text calls the son of Reuel, his father-in-law. There is debate about whether Hobab was the father-in-law or a brother-in-law of Moses, because the Hebrew word can be understood in several ways. Hobab had said that he would return to his own land, and Moses insists because he knows that region well. Interestingly, God himself was guiding the people with the ark, so Moses asks for human help without ceasing to depend on God.

God often guides us also through people with experience and wisdom. Today we can trust God and, at the same time, humbly ask others for advice and help.
exp.10:15:
God tells Moses to gather seventy men, elders and leaders of the people whom he already knows and respects. They are to present themselves at the entrance of the tabernacle, the tent where God met with his people, and wait there with Moses. The sentence about "testimony" is removed, since the word does not appear in the verse. The sentence explaining "principal" is also removed, since that word does not appear in the verse either.

Moses had just cried out to God, worn out by the people's constant complaints, who were weeping for meat and longing for Egypt. He felt alone and without strength. God answers his desperation not with rebuke but with help: he will share the burden with other leaders.

For today: no one was made to carry everything alone. If you feel exhausted in your family, your work, or your church, ask God for help and allow others to share the load with you.
exp.32:43:
This verse says that the people of Israel departed from the place called Oboth and camped at Ije-abarim, on the border of Moab. The words "departed" and "camped" in the verse express the same actions described here. Ije-abarim means something like "heaps of those who pass over," though its exact meaning is debated.

This chapter is a list of Israel's stops in the wilderness, from Egypt to near Canaan. Moses wrote it at God's command (Numbers 33:2), to keep a record of the journey. These stops were part of the forty years of travel. We do not know for certain where all these places were.

For today: God pays attention to every stage of your journey, even the ones that seem like just an unimportant step. Remembering how He has guided you this far strengthens your confidence to keep moving forward.
exp.9:3:
If only one trumpet is blown, then only the leaders are to gather before Moses. The "princes" are the heads of the tribes, and the "heads of the thousands" are those in charge of the large groups of the people.

God speaks to Moses while Israel is in the wilderness, at the foot of Sinai. He tells them to make two silver trumpets to give clear signals: one call for the whole people, another only for the leaders, and others for setting out on the march. In this way the camp was kept in order.

For today: God cares about order and good communication. In the church, the family, or the workplace, it helps to speak clearly and to gather the right people together. Leaders, for their part, should be attentive and available when they are called to serve.
exp.18:5:
It says the priest will take three things: cedar wood, hyssop (a small plant that was used for sprinkling), and a thread or wool of scarlet red. Then he will throw them into the fire where the red cow is burned.

The camp of Israel is the place where the people lived.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron for preparing the ashes of purification, which were mixed with water to cleanse the one who had touched a dead body. The exact meaning of the cedar, the hyssop and the scarlet is not explained here; some think they symbolize cleansing or life, but that is an interpretation. Notice that even the one who prepared the purification remained unclean until evening.

For today: cleansing from sin and from death is something serious and costly. We can give thanks that Christ cleanses us (Hebrews 9:13-14), and draw near to God with humility and gratitude.
exp.29:11:
It says that if a married woman makes a vow, that is, a solemn promise to God, and her husband learns of it and says nothing, the vow stands firm. "Kept silent" means he remained quiet about it, and "did not forbid it" means he did not prohibit it. So she must fulfill what she promised.

God speaks through Moses to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. In that society, the father or husband was the head of the household and answered for the family. This law regulated vows so that no one would make promises to God carelessly. It is a rule for that time and culture, and Christians interpret it in different ways today.

For today: before promising something to God, think it over carefully, and if you are married, talk with your spouse. In this way your promises will be sincere and will protect the unity of your home.
exp.14:35:
This verse tells how the whole community of Israel took a man outside the camp and killed him by throwing stones at him until he died, just as God had commanded Moses. The word "stoned" means that they killed him by throwing stones at him. "Congregation" refers to the people gathered together.

The man had been found gathering wood on the Sabbath (v. 32), something God had forbidden. They put him in custody because they did not know what punishment to give him. Then God spoke to Moses and gave the sentence. This happened while Israel was living under the law of the covenant in the wilderness, and just before this, God had distinguished between sins committed in error and sins committed defiantly (vv. 30-31). Afterward God commands that tassels be put on their clothing, to remind them of his commandments.

For today: this passage reminds us that God is holy and that his words are not to be taken lightly. Today, in Christ, we have forgiveness and grace, so we can respond with grateful and humble obedience, without defying God.
exp.21:4:
This verse tells how Balak, king of Moab, sent messengers to Balaam, son of Beor, who lived in Pethor, by the river. It is understood to be the Euphrates, though the text does not name it. Balak wanted Balaam to come. The message said that a people come out from Egypt covered the surface of the earth, and that they were camped very close to Moab.

Balak is the one speaking, and he feels fear. Israel was on its way toward the promised land, and Moab felt threatened by their great number. Balak did not want to fight only with weapons, so he looked for Balaam, whom he believed able to bless or curse with effect.

For today: when fear takes control of us, we often look for crooked solutions instead of trusting God. Before acting out of fear, it is wise to pray and ask what God wants, not what we can manipulate.
exp.30:34:
This verse gives a number: thirty-two thousand young women who had never had sexual relations with a man. They were among the spoils of war, along with animals such as oxen and donkeys.

Israel had just fought against Midian, and God had commanded Moses to carry out that war (Numbers 31:1-3). Moses, together with the priest Eleazar, ordered the captured people and goods to be counted and divided. It is a record, not a direct teaching. It is a difficult passage, and scholars understand it in several ways. It is connected with what happened at Peor, where Israel fell into idolatry (Numbers 25).

For today: the Bible shows us the stark reality of a fallen world. Let us read these texts with humility, without hiding what is hard, and seek to live as Christ did, defending with compassion the dignity of the vulnerable.
exp.20:27:
This verse describes how a fire, that is, an army that destroyed everything in its path, came out of Heshbon, the city of King Sihon, and devoured Ar of Moab, the region of the lords of the high places by the river Arnon, who were the rulers of the heights beside the Arnon. To consume means to devour or destroy completely.

Here the poets, who composed songs about victories, speak. They recall that Sihon, an Amorite king, had earlier defeated Moab and taken its territory as far as the Arnon. It is an ancient song that Israel quotes to explain why that land now belonged to them. Some details of the poem are interpreted in several ways.

For today: human victories and empires seem strong, but they pass away. Heshbon conquered and was then itself conquered. We can trust God and not power, success, or pride, because only He endures.
exp.25:56:
This verse says that the Levites were also counted by their families. Three main branches come out of it, descended from the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. From each one came a family, called the Gershonites, the Kohathites, and the Merarites. "Counted" means they were numbered, that is, registered one by one.

This is part of Israel's second census, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The account is told by the narrator, and God had commanded Moses and Eleazar to carry out the count. The Levites are registered separately because they would not receive land like the other tribes; their service was the tabernacle. That is why this verse follows the verse of how the land would be divided.

For today: God knows and records every person and every family, even those who have a less visible role. We can serve faithfully where he has placed us, trusting that our place matters to him.
exp.23:11:
Balaam reminds Balak that he had already told him something before, when Balak sent messengers to him. The sentence is left open with "saying," because what he said comes in the following verse. The word "unto" is the old form of "to," which is how the verse reads in the King James Version.

Balaam speaks as a foreign prophet whom Balak, king of Moab, hired to curse Israel. Balak grew angry because Balaam blessed Israel three times. Balaam defends himself: from the beginning he explained that he could only say what God told him, regardless of the payment or the king's pressure.

For today: when we are pressured to stay silent about the truth or to twist it, we can remember that our faithfulness to God is worth more than money or the approval of others. It is better to be clear and consistent from the start.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that the Israelites obeyed what God commanded them: they removed from the camp the people who were ritually unclean. The "camp" here means the place where the whole people lived. Those described as having a skin disease, and those with a bodily discharge that left a person unclean for a time, were the ones sent outside.

God was speaking to Moses while the people were in the wilderness, organized around the tabernacle. God reminded them that He lived among them, and for that reason they had to protect the purity of the place. These rules were symbolic and also governed community life. They did not express contempt for the sick, and the separation was usually temporary.

For today: God values simple and complete obedience. Ask yourself what God has asked of you that you have left unfinished, and today take one concrete step to obey Him with trust.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the sons of Kohath, a family within the tribe of Levi, had a special task in the tabernacle. The word "service" refers to the work or responsibility assigned to them. The "tabernacle of the congregation" is the sacred tent where God was present with his people. "The most holy things" refers to the most sacred place, where the ark was kept.

God speaks to Moses during the journey through the wilderness. He is organizing the Levites by family, from thirty to fifty years of age, so that each group knows its service. The Kohathites would carry the most sacred objects, but only after Aaron and his sons had covered them. Some scholars note that this showed the holiness of God and the care required when approaching him.

Today we can learn that God gives each person a service, and none of them is small. Ask the Lord what task he has entrusted to you, and carry it out with reverence and faithfulness.
exp.13:10:
God speaks to Moses and asks two questions filled with grief: how long will the people keep provoking him, that is, despising him and treating him with contempt? And how long will they refuse to trust him, despite so many signs (miracles) performed among them?

The spies had returned from Canaan. Ten of them gave a frightening report, and the people were seized with panic and wanted to go back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urged them to trust God, but the crowd wanted to stone them. Then the glory of God appeared at the tabernacle, and God spoke. His questions show that their lack of faith was not for lack of evidence, but because of a heart that kept forgetting what God had already done.

When you are afraid, write down how God has helped you before. That grateful memory strengthens trust in him today.
exp.25:53:
It says that the promised land would be divided fairly: the larger tribes would receive a larger portion, and the smaller ones a smaller portion. The word "inheritance" in the verse names the portion of land received and passed on to children. "Those that were numbered" refers to the people registered in the census.

God speaks to Moses after counting the people on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. Most of those who had come out of Egypt had died in the wilderness, and now a new generation was ready to receive the promise. The next verse explains that the exact location was decided by lot, while the size was adjusted to the size of each tribe.

For today: God cares that each person has what is needed, without everyone being the same in everything. We can be thankful for what we have received, avoid comparing ourselves with others, and be fair when dividing responsibilities or resources.
exp.12:19:
Moses asks the spies to observe what the land is like where the people live: whether it is good or bad. He also wants to know what their cities are like: whether they are simple camps of tents or places protected by strongholds. "Inhabited" means that people live there. The word "search out," in the verse before, means to explore.

Moses speaks to twelve men, one from each tribe, whom Israel was sending into Canaan. The people were close to the land God had promised them. Moses wanted practical information to prepare. Afterward, most of the spies were filled with fear, even though the land was good.

For today: it is wise to look at reality honestly and with good information before taking an important step. But seeing the facts is not enough; we must interpret them with faith in God's promises, without letting fear make the decision for us.
exp.1:27:
This verse gives the number of the army of the tribe of Asher: forty-one thousand five hundred men counted. "Host" means an army or an organized group. "Those that were numbered" are the men who were registered, the ones who could go to war.

God spoke to Moses and Aaron and showed them how Israel should camp around the tabernacle, each tribe under its own banner. Asher camped together with Dan and Naphtali, on the north side. Some scholars think these large figures can be understood in other ways, but the text emphasizes that each tribe had its place and that no one was left uncounted.

For today: God knows and counts each one of his own. You are not a lost number in the crowd; you have a place among his people. Seek today to serve faithfully in your church, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that everything an Israelite set apart for God through a vow became the property of Aaron and his family, the priests. The word "devoted" here refers to what was given over entirely to God. In other passages a Hebrew word is used that is sometimes translated "accursed" or "devoted," and it is understood that such goods no longer returned to ordinary use.

God is speaking to Aaron. The Levites and priests did not receive their own territory in Israel, so God arranged for them to live from the people's offerings. In this way they could give themselves to the service of the sanctuary without worrying about their livelihood.

For today: what we give to God should be sincere, and it also sustains those who serve. We can support with generosity and good order those who teach us the Word, faithfully fulfilling what we have promised.
exp.11:4:
It says that God himself came down in the pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting. From there he called Aaron and Miriam, and the two of them came out to meet him.

Miriam and Aaron had spoken against their brother Moses in chapter 12. God heard everything and did not wait for Moses to defend himself; the text says Moses was very humble. Now God steps in personally and calls them to account. Afterward he will explain that Moses has a special relationship with him.
