For today: God hears what we say about others, even when it is done in secret. Before criticizing someone, it is wise to stop and ask ourselves whether we would say it in God's presence. And if someone has criticized us unfairly, we can rest in the knowledge that God sees and knows how to defend the truth.
exp.7:22:
This verse is a short phrase that introduces something new: "And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying." God speaks to Moses to give him another instruction. The word "saying" announces that a command is coming, and the verses that follow explain the age at which the Levites could begin and end their service.

The one speaking is God, and Moses is the one who receives the word to pass on to the people. The Levites had just been purified and presented before God to serve in the tabernacle. Now God adds the practical order of that service. First they were dedicated, and then they were taught how to serve.

For today: God does not only call us to serve him, he also guides us with order and wisdom. Before acting, it is worth pausing to listen to his Word, pray, and ask for direction, rather than serving only on impulse or out of habit.
exp.33:13:
This verse says that the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, have already received their inheritance. Each tribe received it "according to the house of their fathers," that is, by their families and lineages. The inheritance is the land that belonged to them as property.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He explains that the land west of the Jordan would be divided by lot among nine and a half tribes. The other two and a half tribes had already asked to stay on the east side of the Jordan, and Moses recalls this so that everyone clearly understands the division.

For today: God cares that each person has their place and their portion. We can trust his provision without envying what others have received, and be faithful with what he has given us.
exp.34:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan River, across from the city of Jericho. The name of God in this verse is the LORD, and the wording is simply the introduction to an instruction that comes right after.

God speaks, and gives his message to Moses. The people of Israel were camped, about to enter the promised land. The Levites, who served in worship, would not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes. For that reason God commands that the people give them cities to live in, with pasture land around them for their animals.

For today: those who devote themselves to serving others in the church need care and support. We can ask ourselves how we might practically support those who teach and serve us, with generosity and gratitude.
exp.7:21:
This verse says that, after being purified and presented to God, the Levites began to do their work in the tabernacle. They served under the direction of Aaron and his sons, the priests. The tent of meeting, where God's law was kept, is the sacred place where they served. And everything was done just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

Here the narrator is the author of the book, who tells how Israel obeyed. God had set the Levites apart to help in worship. First they were washed, and atonement was made for them. Only then did they begin their service. Afterward, God gives instructions about the age for serving.

For today: God cares about order. Before serving, we need to be clean and at peace with Him. Serve with humility, doing what God asks, even when your task seems small.
exp.27:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses. It is an opening phrase, very common in the book of Numbers. The name "the Lord" is the name of God, and the spelling of the old text is simply the way it was written then. What matters is that God takes the initiative and makes his will known.

Here God is speaking, and Moses is the messenger who passes it on to the people. Israel is close to entering the promised land, and a new generation needs to be reminded of how to worship. What follows are instructions about the daily offerings and the feasts. God wants his people to offer him worship with order and consistency.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. We can set aside a moment each day to listen to him in the Bible and respond with prayer and gratitude. Just as Israel offered something every day, our relationship with God grows through steady faithfulness.
exp.2:41:
This verse says that Moses counted the firstborn sons of Israel, just as God had commanded him. "Firstborn" refers to the sons who were born first in each family. The phrase rendered "from a month old and upward" means from one month of age onward.

God had asked Moses to count all these firstborn. After the Passover in Egypt, the firstborn belonged to God. In their place, God took the Levites for his service in the sanctuary. The count served to compare the two groups. The narrator emphasizes that Moses obeyed exactly what he had been commanded.

For today: Moses' obedience was complete, even in a simple and unremarkable task. We can ask God to help us obey him in the small and everyday things too, trusting that he values faithfulness.
exp.25:64:
This verse says that God had declared that the whole generation would die in the wilderness. Of those who were counted at the beginning, only two men remained: Caleb, son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, son of Nun. The phrase "there was not left a man of them" means that none of those counted survived, apart from these two.

The narrator of Numbers explains that this new count, taken on the plains of Moab, no longer included those counted at Sinai. According to Numbers 14, the people rebelled by believing the bad report of the spies and doubted that God would give them the land. Caleb and Joshua were the only ones who trusted Him.

For today: God does what He says, both His warnings and His promises. Trusting Him, even when nearly everyone doubts, is not in vain. Today we can ask Him for a faithful heart like that of Caleb and Joshua, one that believes His word and follows Him with perseverance.
exp.9:25:
This verse says that Pagiel, son of Ocran, was the leader of the tribe of Asher's division as Israel marched through the wilderness. The word "host" here refers to the tribe organized in order, and the "standard" was the sign that guided each group.

Numbers 10 tells how the people first left Mount Sinai, following God's cloud. The passage is a narrative that lists the order of march. Asher went with Dan and Naphtali in the last division, closing the procession. Each tribe had a named leader, and everything followed the instructions God gave through Moses.

For today: God cares about the details and the names, even of people who are barely mentioned. Your quiet service, whatever it is, matters to God. Do your part faithfully and trust that He sees your work.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that the tribe of Manasseh camped next to the tribe of Ephraim, on the western side of the camp. Their leader was Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur.

The phrase "next to him" simply means "beside him."

A tribe was one of the large family groups of Israel.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, while the people are being organized after leaving Egypt. Each tribe had a fixed place around the tabernacle and a named leader. Manasseh and Ephraim were sons of Joseph, and that is why they appear together. The numbers that follow in the list show how many men were in each tribe.

For today: God is a God of order, and he cares for his people one by one, by name and by place. You also have a place in his family. Serve gladly where he puts you, alongside other brothers and sisters, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.0:44:
This verse sums up the census of Israel. Every man twenty years old and up was counted, organized by the households of their fathers. These were the ones who were able to go out to war, that is, those fit to go into battle. The word "numbered" means those who were recorded on the list.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, reporting what God had commanded Moses in the Sinai wilderness. Moses and Aaron carried out the count with one leader from each tribe. The verse closes the total of the tribes, and the next one gives the sum: 603,550. The Levites were set apart, because they had a different service: the care of the tabernacle.

God knows his people and gives each one a place. No one is a lost number in the crowd. Today we might ask ourselves: what is my place in my family and in my church? Let us serve gladly where God has put us.
exp.23:24:
Says that Balaam rose up, went away and returned to his place, and that Balak also went on his way. "Went away" is the same as "went," and "turned back" means "turned back" in the sense of returning. It is the final farewell of the two men.

Context: Balak, king of Moab, had hired Balaam to curse Israel. But God prevented it, and Balaam ended up blessing Israel three times and announcing the future of several nations. The narrator now tells that each man leaves without achieving what Balak was seeking. The Bible does not say here exactly where Balaam returned to; "his place" probably refers to his homeland, to the north, beside the river.

For today: No one can derail God's plans through pressure, money, or intrigue. If today you feel others pressuring you to go against your conscience, remember that God remains faithful to his word. Trust in Him and seek to obey Him, even when the world offers you something else.
exp.20:21:
Here Israel asks Sihon, king of the Amorites, for permission to cross his territory. They promise not to enter the fields that are planted, nor the vineyards, nor to drink water from the wells. They say they will travel along the main road, the one used by everyone, until they are past his borders.

The Israelites had spent years in the wilderness and were drawing near to the promised land. The messengers speak on behalf of Israel, and the request is peaceful: they only want to pass through. According to the account that follows, Sihon refused, attacked Israel, and was defeated. The text does not say that Israel sought a fight; the war began with the king's response.

For today: when you need to ask for something, do it with respect, clarity, and promises you can keep. Seeking peace first does not guarantee that others will respond well, but it lets you act with integrity and trust God with what comes next.
exp.35:1:
The leaders of the family of Gilead remind Moses of two commands from God. First, that the land was to be divided by lot among the people of Israel. Second, that the share of Zelophehad, who had already died, was to pass to his daughters.

They speak to Moses as their lord. The word "lot" refers to the drawing used to divide the land, understood as God's decision. "Inheritance" means the possession passed down to heirs.

These are the heads of the clan of Gilead, from the tribe of Manasseh. They are concerned that if Zelophehad's daughters marry men from another tribe, their family's land would pass to that tribe. They do not question God's earlier decision; they ask for clarification to protect the inheritance of their tribe.

For today: it is good to respect what God has already said and, even so, to ask questions with humility when doubts arise. Let us bring our concerns with order and respect, seeking solutions that take care of everyone.
exp.12:9:
This verse is part of the list of twelve men, one from each tribe, whom Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan. Here Gaddiel, son of Sodi, is named, representing the tribe of Zebulun. The names are written in an older form, which is why the spelling can look unfamiliar.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness and commanded him to send these leaders to survey the land that He was going to give to Israel. Each one was a leader among his people. The text gives only his name and his family; it tells us nothing more about Gaddiel at this point. Later, most of the group brought back a report full of fear, and only Joshua and Caleb trusted in God's promise.

God notices people by name and calls them to serve. Even if no one today remembers your work, your faithfulness matters. Ask yourself: in what God has entrusted to me, am I acting with faith or with fear?
exp.3:4:
When the people of Israel had to break camp and continue on their way, Aaron and his sons, who were the priests, went in first to the tabernacle. They took down the curtain, which was the covering that separated the most holy place, and with it they covered the ark of the testimony. The ark held the tablets of the law.

God spoke to Moses in the wilderness and explained how the Levites, especially the family of Kohath, were to carry the holy things. Only the priests could touch and cover the ark, so that no one would look at it or touch it without reverence. In this way it was shown that God is holy.

For today: when we begin something new, such as a journey or a change of work, we can first place ourselves in the presence of God and treat with reverence what belongs to him.
exp.27:23:
This verse says that on each of the seven days of the feast, the people were to present offerings to God. The "meat" is the food of the offering, and the "offering made by fire" is the one burned on the altar. A "sweet savour" is a pleasing aroma to God. All of this was offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, the daily sacrifice, along with its drink offering, which was wine poured out.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, now near the promised land. Here the offerings for the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread are explained. Each day the offering was repeated, and it included a goat for sin, to make peace with God.

For today: God values consistency in our relationship with Him. We can set aside a moment each day to pray, read His Word, and give thanks, without waiting only for special moments.
exp.15:10:
Moses says to Korah: "You and all your company are gathered together against the Lord." Then he asks: "What is Aaron, that you complain against him?" The words "company" and "complain" in the verse above are the ones this comment refers to; "company" means the group of followers, and "complain" means to grumble and speak badly about someone.

Moses speaks to Korah, a Levite, and to his followers. They were upset because only Aaron and his family were priests. Although God had already given them a special service in the tabernacle, they wanted the priesthood as well. Moses explains that Aaron had been appointed by God, so complaining against him was complaining against God.

For today: before criticizing the one who leads, let us ask ourselves whether we are discontented with a person or with what God has appointed. Let us be thankful for the place of service God has given us, without envying the place of others.
exp.13:31:
It says that the adults of that generation would die in the desert and would not reach the promised land. The expression "your carcases shall fall" is an old way of speaking about dying. The accented "á" is the old way of writing "a."

God speaks, through Moses, to the people of Israel. The spies had returned from Canaan, and most of them filled the people with fear. The people complained, doubted God, and even wanted to go back to Egypt. Because of this lack of trust, God declares this judgment. Even so, he keeps his promise: their children would indeed enter, and Caleb and Joshua, who trusted in him, would enter as well.

For today: unbelief has consequences, but God remains faithful. When you feel fear, remember what he has promised and trust in him, even when the path looks difficult.
exp.22:7:
Balaam asks a question that already contains its answer: he cannot curse someone whom God has not cursed. Balaam recognizes that his word has no power if God does not stand behind it.

Balaam, a seer from the region of Aram, is the speaker. Balak, king of Moab, hired him to curse Israel because he was afraid of them. But when Balaam opens his mouth, God forces him to bless. Scholars debate what Balaam's true heart was, but here it is clear that God protects his people.

For today: you do not have to live in fear of harsh words or of the rejection of others. If God has received you as his own, no human accusation can change what he has said about you. Rest in his word more than in the opinions of people.
exp.32:31:
This verse says that the people of Israel set out from a place called Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-hagidgad. The source's words for "set out" and "camped" are not in the verse, so the translation simply describes the movement and the stop. It is one more stop in the list of desert camps. In Deuteronomy 10:6-7 a similar name appears, Gudgoda, though not all scholars are sure it is the same place.

Moses writes, at God's command, the record of the stages of the journey from Egypt to near the promised land (Numbers 33:1-2). This list served to remind the people that God had led them step by step through forty years. Many of these places cannot be located with certainty today.

God cares even for the stretches that seem unimportant. When your life feels like a road of simple stops, remember that he walks with you and guides you. Trust him one day at a time.
exp.21:32:
The angel of the LORD explains to Balaam why his donkey turned aside three times. The donkey had turned from the road, and the angel says that if the animal had not turned from him, he would have killed Balaam and let the donkey live.

Balaam was on his way to see Balak, king of Moab, who wanted him to curse Israel. God had already warned him, and the angel says his way was wrong, meaning twisted or reckless. Balaam could not see the angel, but the donkey could. The angel speaks to correct him, and Balaam acknowledges his sin.

For today: sometimes God uses obstacles or ordinary people to stop us, and we struggle to see it because we are angry or set on our plan. Before pressing forward with a plan, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask whether God is protecting us.
exp.19:22:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and Aaron when the people arrived at Mount Hor, by the border of Edom. "Lord" is the name of God, and "coast" means the border or edge of the land. The phrase "spake unto Moses" is an older way of saying "spoke to Moses."

It is God who speaks, and he does so after Edom had refused passage to the Israelites. They had to go around Edom's territory and continued on their way until they reached Hor. Right away, God announces that Aaron will die there and will not enter the promised land, because both he and Moses rebelled at the waters of Meribah.

For today: God also speaks to us in times of change, closing, and farewell. When one chapter comes to an end, we can turn to him with humility, remembering that his decisions are just and that he cares for his people even through difficult endings.
exp.2:39:
God tells Moses to take a special count: to number all the firstborn males of Israel, from one month old and upward, and to write down their names. "Firstborn" is the first son of a family.

The Lord speaks, and gives the command to Moses. Earlier, God had claimed the firstborn of Israel as his own when he saved the people in Egypt. Now he accepts that the tribe of Levi will serve in their place. That is why the Levites are counted, and the firstborn as well: to compare the numbers and make the exchange in an orderly way.

For today: God knows his people by name; no one is just a number to him. This invites us to remember that our lives belong to him and to serve him with gratitude, also caring for the people in our community, one by one.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that the people in charge of moving the camp would take all the instruments used for service in the sanctuary. They would wrap them in a cloth of dark blue, cover them with a durable covering of skins, and place them on poles, which were like stretchers or carrying bars. The phrase "covering of badgers' skins" is one that scholars translate in different ways; some think of skins from sea animals or of fine leather.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about the work of the sons of Kohath, of the tribe of Levi. When the camp of Israel moved through the desert, they carried the holy things, but only after the priests had covered them. Everything had to be done with order and respect, because those objects were dedicated to God.

For today: care with reverence for what God has entrusted to you, whether your service, your time, or your family, and do it with order and humility.
exp.33:27:
This verse names Pedahel, son of Ammihud, as the leader of the tribe of Naphtali. He was one of the chosen leaders, one from each tribe, to help divide the land. "Prince" here means a chief or leader of his tribe, not the son of a king.

God himself speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters Canaan. He gives a list of men who, together with Eleazar the priest and Joshua, would divide the inheritance among the tribes. The list ends with the next verse: these are the men the LORD commanded for that task.

For today: God takes care that things are done with order and justice, and that every group has a voice. Although Pedahel does not appear in other stories, God remembered him by name. Serve faithfully in whatever you are given, even when no one notices; God sees it.
exp.3:42:
This verse says who was counted among the sons of Merari: the men from thirty to fifty years old, every one that entereth into the service, that is, those who were part of the group assigned to work in the tabernacle. The "tabernacle of the congregation" is the sacred tent where the tablets of the law were kept.

The text is part of the count that Moses and Aaron made, by God's command, among the Levites. Each Levite family had different duties; the Merarites were in charge of carrying the frame structures of the tent. Only the men of working age were counted. The book does not explain why those ages were chosen; some believe it sought the strength and maturity needed for heavy work.

For today: God gives each person a place in his work, even when the task is not showy. Ask yourself what simple service you could do in your church or community, with faithfulness and a willing heart.
exp.10:7:
This verse describes how the people worked with the manna. They went out to gather it, ground it in mills or beat it in a mortar, and then cooked it in a pot or made cakes from it. Its taste was compared to that of fresh oil, that is, oil freshly made.

Israel was traveling through the desert, and God gave them manna every day. But the people grew tired of eating the same thing and began to complain, remembering the food of Egypt. The narrator makes clear that the manna was a good food, varied in how it could be prepared, though the people no longer valued it. This ended up saddening Moses and angering God.

For today: complaining can make us blind to what God already gives us. Today you can make a list of three simple provisions you have received, and thank God for each one.
exp.6:56:
It says that Gamaliel brought three animals for the burnt offering: a young bull (a young ox), a ram, and a lamb of one year old. The burnt offering was the sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar, as a sign of complete surrender to God.

This passage is in the account of the dedication of the tabernacle. For twelve days, each tribal leader presented his offering. Here the offering of the eighth day is described, the one of Gamaliel, leader of the tribe of Manasseh. Moses, as the narrator, records everything in detail, and the list hardly changes from one day to the next. This shows that God values each tribe equally, without favoritism.

For today: God sees and remembers what we give with sincerity, even when others give the same or more. We can serve him with steadiness and devotion, without seeking applause or comparing ourselves with anyone.
exp.31:37:
This verse continues the list of cities that the sons of Reuben rebuilt in the land east of the Jordan. It mentions Nebo, Baal-meon, and Shibmah. It says that Nebo and Baal-meon had their names changed, and that they gave new names to the cities they built. The word "built" here means that they rebuilt and fortified them.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Numbers, traditionally Moses. Reuben and Gad asked to settle in those lands, rich in pasture, and Moses agreed on the condition that they help conquer Canaan. It is believed that the names were changed because some of them recalled false gods, such as Baal, but the text does not explain this clearly.

For today: when God gives us a new beginning, it is wise to leave behind whatever ties us to the past. Think about what habit or memory you need to rename so that you can live with gratitude and faithfulness.
exp.0:53:
This verse says that the people of Israel obeyed fully what God had commanded Moses. The phrase "according to all that the Lord commanded" means "just as they were ordered, leaving nothing out." And the ending, "so did they," stresses that they not only listened but acted.

Moses had counted the people in the wilderness, and God gave instructions for the order of the camp: each tribe with its banner, and the Levites around the tabernacle to care for it. This verse is the narrator's comment closing that section. It highlights that the people accepted this order. Some understand that this order also protected the people from approaching what is holy without reverence.

Today it invites us to move from hearing to obeying. Think of something God has already shown you in his Word and take one concrete step this week, even if it is a small one.
exp.10:29:
It says that Moses returned to the camp together with the elders of Israel. The word for "returned" is the same idea as "went back" or "came back," and "the camp" here refers to the people's camp, not to a field of land for farming.

Shortly before this, the Spirit had rested on seventy elders, and two of them, Eldad and Medad, were prophesying within the camp. Joshua, jealous on Moses' behalf, wanted to stop them. Moses answered with humility: he wished that all the people would prophesy. This verse marks the close of that scene. The narrator tells it without further explanation, and then God sends the quail.

For today: when someone else serves God or receives gifts that you do not have, avoid jealousy. Do as Moses did: rejoice that God is working in others, and return humbly to serving where you are.
exp.6:11:
This verse says that on the first day of the dedication of the altar, the one who presented his offering was Nahshon, son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah. The word "was" here is the plain form of the verb, and the verse as written reads exactly as your version shows. A "prince" was the chief or leader of a tribe, which is the role Nahshon held.

God had told Moses that each leader should bring his offering on a different day, one after another. The account tells it in order, and Judah, the tribe that went at the front when the people marched, opens the list. Then the gifts are described: silver dishes and bowls, and a golden spoon full of incense. Each leader gives the same things.

For today: God values that each person gives their part with order and sincerity, without competing or comparing themselves to others. We can ask ourselves what we bring to God today: our time, our service, our gratitude, or our care for others.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that when the priests blew the two trumpets, the whole people of Israel would gather to Moses at the entrance of the tent where God's presence was. The phrase "shall assemble themselves to thee" means "will gather to you," and "the tabernacle of the congregation" is the holy tent where the ark with the tablets of the law was kept.

God speaks to Moses while the people are in the desert, after leaving Egypt. He gives them two silver trumpets to give clear signals: to gather the people, to call the leaders, and to announce when to set out. In this way everything was done in order and under God's guidance.

For today: God calls his people to gather and listen to his voice. We can set aside regular time to meet with other believers and to pray, without letting the noise of life pull us away from him.
exp.15:15:
Moses tells Korah that he and all his followers must appear tomorrow before the Lord. Aaron is also to be present.

Moses is the one speaking. Korah and other men were accusing him of taking over the leadership and of not keeping what he had promised. Moses, hurt, asks God to see that he has not taken advantage of anyone. Now he no longer argues with them; he places the matter in God's hands. The Bible presents this as a test so that God Himself may show whom He has chosen.

For today: when there are conflicts, criticism, or envy, we do not always need to defend ourselves loudly. We can act with humility, seek the truth honestly, and bring the matter before God, trusting that He judges with justice.
exp.19:26:
Moses did what the Lord had commanded him. He went up Mount Hor with Aaron and with Eleazar, and all the people saw them. The phrase "in the sight of all the congregation" means they did it in full view of everyone, openly.

God had announced that Aaron would die on that mountain, because he would not enter the promised land. After the episode at the waters of Meribah, God had said so clearly. Moses did not argue or delay. The change of clothing also showed that Eleazar would take his father's place as high priest. The people saw the sacred service being handed on.

For today: obeying God even in painful moments is a sign of trust. Moses was saying goodbye to his brother, yet he walked forward in faith. When God asks you for something difficult, take the step honestly and without hiding, trusting that He guides everything with wisdom.
exp.7:17:
God says that he has taken the Levites for himself, in place of all the firstborn of the children of Israel. The phrase "the firstborn of the children of Israel" refers to the first son born in a family.

God speaks through Moses. When God struck the firstborn of Egypt, the firstborn of Israel were spared and declared to be his. Now, instead of claiming one firstborn from each family, God sets apart the whole tribe of Levi to serve in the tabernacle, to help Aaron and his sons, and to make sure the people did not approach the sanctuary improperly.

For today: what God has saved belongs to him. We can ask ourselves how we are using our time and our gifts to serve him, grateful for his mercy, whether in the church or in our daily lives.
exp.34:1:
God tells Moses to command the people of Israel to give the Levites some cities to live in, taken from the land that each tribe would receive as its inheritance. They must also give them the open lands around each city, used as pasture and common space for their animals.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan, when Israel is about to enter the promised land. The Levites served in worship and did not receive their own territory like the other tribes. For this reason God arranges that the rest of the people support them with cities and lands where they can live.

For today: God cares for those who serve in his work and expects his people to care for them as well. We can think about how to give concrete support, with generosity and gratitude, to those who teach and serve in our church.
exp.7:7:
It says that, when setting apart the Levites for service, they were to offer two young bulls. One went with its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; it was an offering of thanksgiving and dedication. The other young bull was for a sin offering, that is, to cover sin and cleanse the people before God. The word translated "offering" in the verse is the same idea as the offering itself.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, beside the tabernacle. The Levites would be helpers to the priests in the holy service. Before they began, God calls for a public purification: water, washing of clothes, and sacrifices. In this way it was shown that drawing near to God is a serious matter and that we need cleansing.

For today: serving God does not depend on our ability, but on his forgiveness and his grace. Before serving, we can come near with humility, ask for forgiveness, and give thanks that Christ has already paid for our sin.
exp.15:27:
Moses tells the people that there will be a sign so they can know that God himself sent him. The word "know" here means knowing for certain. "For I have not done them of mine own mind" means that he did not act on his own idea, ambition, or whim, but by God's command.

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were accusing Moses of setting himself above the people. Moses does not argue with words. He puts the matter in God's hands and asks for a clear sign. Then he explains what it will be: if these men die a common death, he did not speak on God's behalf; but if the earth opens up, it will be evidence that God backs him.

Today we can learn not to defend ourselves with pride when we are criticized. Moses trusted that God would make the truth clear. He also invites us to examine our motives: do I serve out of obedience to God, or for my own benefit?
exp.24:8:
This verse says that a plague, a deadly outbreak, killed twenty-four thousand people from the people of Israel. The word for this kind of deadly outbreak means a death in great numbers. This figure appears here; the apostle Paul mentions twenty-three thousand in 1 Corinthians 10:8, and it is usually explained as a different rounding or a reference to another moment of the same event, though this is not known with certainty.

The account is told by the narrator of Numbers. Israel had fallen into immorality and idolatry with the women of Moab and Midian, worshiping Baal-peor. God sent this plague as judgment, and it stopped when Phinehas acted with zeal for the holiness of God.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously. Small compromises with what draws us away from Him can grow and do us great harm. Let us ask Him for help to flee what tempts us and to love Him with all our heart.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that Dathan and Abiram accuse Moses of not having kept his promise: he has not brought them into a good land, nor given them fields and vineyards as an inheritance. They ask whether Moses wants to put out the eyes of these men, an expression that probably means deceiving them or blinding them, although some understand it as dominating them. And they conclude: "We will not come up," meaning they refuse to present themselves before him.

Dathan and Abiram, of the tribe of Reuben, speak together with Korah, who were rebelling against Moses and Aaron. Israel was in the wilderness because of its unbelief, but they blame Moses alone. They even call Egypt the land that floweth with milk and honey, the place from which they had come out enslaved, which shows how much they were distorting reality.

For today: when things become difficult, it is easy to blame others and to remember the past falsely. Before accusing, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask ourselves humbly what part belongs to us.
exp.26:3:
The daughters of Zelophehad ask why their father's name should be removed from his family just because he had no sons. They ask that they be given a possession, a share of the land, along with their father's brothers.

They speak before Moses, the priest Eleazar, the leaders, and the whole congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Their father died in the wilderness, and they make clear that he did not take part in Korah's rebellion but died for his own sin. Since the custom was that sons received the inheritance, they would be left without land. Moses does not decide on his own; he brings the case before the LORD.

When something seems unjust, we can raise it with respect and courage, without rebelling. They spoke plainly, before the right authorities, and let God answer. Let us bring our needs to God with the same confidence.
exp.30:52:
This verse says that the Israelite soldiers each kept part of the spoil of war. The word "spoil" in the verse refers to things taken from the defeated enemies, such as goods, animals, or metals. The narrator makes a separate point about this.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Israel had just fought against Midian, and Moses and Eleazar divided the spoil. One part was given to the Lord and another to the community. The army's commanders gave their gold as an offering. The verse makes clear that the ordinary soldiers had already taken their own things, apart from what was divided and offered. Interpreters understand this in different ways, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: let us learn to thank God generously for what we receive, and not simply keep everything for ourselves.
exp.25:60:
It says that Nadab and Abihu, two sons of Aaron, died because they offered "strange fire" before God. The word "strange" means foreign or unauthorized: it was fire that God had not commanded them to present. "Jehovah" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Numbers speaks while recounting Israel's second census in the plains of Moab, near the Jordan. In listing the family of Levi, it recalls that Nadab and Abihu were no longer there, and that is why only Eleazar and Ithamar continued the priesthood. The story of their death is told in Leviticus 10. It does not explain in detail what their error consisted of, so it is best not to invent more.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and obedience, not according to your own ideas. He values a heart that responds to Him as He has asked.
exp.25:45:
This verse only says that one of the daughters of Asher was named Sarah. Asher was one of the twelve sons of Jacob.

We are at the second census of Israel, taken on the plains of Moab, almost at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The account presents it as a command from God to Moses and Eleazar, to count the tribes before entering the promised land. It is unusual for a woman to be named in lists like this, and that is why her name stands out.

For today: God does not see people as mere numbers. Even in a long list, there are names that are remembered. You can trust that God knows you personally, and you can also learn to value and remember those who go unnoticed.
exp.30:21:
This verse is part of a list of objects that Israel was to cleanse after the war against Midian. It names metals: gold, silver, brass, iron, tin, and lead. It is a phrase that stays open and is completed in the following verse.

The speaker is Eleazar the priest, addressing the soldiers who were returning from battle. He passes on what God had commanded Moses. They had been in contact with the dead and with plunder, and according to the law, this made them ceremonially unclean. For that reason they had to go through a time of purification before returning to the camp.

For today: we can learn that God cares about how we return to ordinary life after a hard season. Taking time to pray, rest, and put our hearts in order before returning to everything else is a simple way of honoring God.
exp.31:9:
This verse says that God became very angry when Israel doubted, and that he made a solemn oath.

The one speaking is Moses. He reminds the tribes of Reuben and Gad what happened when the spies returned from Canaan. That generation discouraged the people and refused to enter the promised land. Moses fears that now these tribes, who want to stay on the other side of the Jordan, will repeat that mistake and discourage the others.

For today: our doubts and complaints are not small, because they can discourage others. Let us ask God for the confidence to obey him, and let us use our words to encourage those around us to follow him.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that the tribe of Issachar camped beside the tribe of Judah, on the east side of the camp. Its leader was Nethaneel, son of Zuar. "Will camp" means they would settle and live in that place; the "leader" is the head or prince of the tribe.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, shortly after leaving Egypt. He gives them an order for the camp: each tribe had its place, its banner, and its leader, and the tabernacle stood in the center. Judah led the east side, and Issachar and Zebulun accompanied it. The texts do not explain in detail why each location was chosen.

For today: God cares about order and values each person by name and by their place. Serve where He has put you, support those who lead, and work in unity with others, without fighting for the first places.
exp.0:8:
It says that from the tribe of Zebulun, the leader chosen was Eliab, son of Helon. It is part of a list of leaders, one for each tribe. There are no hard words here, only proper names, and the text mentions them carefully, one by one.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and tells him to take a count of the people of Israel, counting the men fit for war. To help him, God names one man from each tribe, a leader who would represent his people. Zebulun was one of the twelve tribes, descended from one of the sons of Jacob.

God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. Eliab appears only in a list, but God saw him and gave him a task. Today you can remember that your simple and quiet service also counts before God. Do faithfully what is given to you, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.25:12:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Simeon. It says that from Zerah came the family of the Zerahites, and from Shaul, the family of the Shaulites. The ending "-ites" only means "descendants of." In other Bible lists Zerah appears as Zohar, and it is possible that they are the same person under a different name.

God commanded Moses and Eleazar to take this second census on the plains of Moab, after the plague. It was meant to organize the people before entering the promised land and dividing it by families. Simeon had decreased greatly since the first census, although the text does not give a detailed explanation here.

For today: God does not see you as an anonymous number. He remembers names, families and generations. You can live with the assurance that your life has a place in his plan, and with the desire to leave to your loved ones a legacy of faith.
exp.2:49:
This verse says that Moses received the money from the firstborn of Israel who did not have a Levite to take their place. In total it came to 1,365 shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official standard used in worship. The firstborn are the eldest sons, and the ransom is the payment that sets someone free from an obligation.

God had said that the firstborn of Israel belonged to him. In place of them, the Levites were set apart to serve him. But there were 273 more firstborn than Levites, so God commanded a payment of five shekels for each one. Moses carried out the command and then gave the money to Aaron and his sons, who served as priests.

Today we see that what belongs to God is handled with seriousness and order. We can ask ourselves whether we keep what we promise to God with care and honesty. We also remember that freedom always has a cost; for us, Christ has already paid it.
exp.17:16:
This verse says that the firstborn males of cows, sheep and goats were not redeemed with money, as was done with sons and with unclean animals. They were "holy," that is, set apart for God. Their blood was sprinkled on the altar, and the fat was burned as a fire offering, a pleasing aroma to the Lord. The fat is the rich fat of the animal, and a pleasing aroma speaks of an offering that God accepts with delight.

God speaks to Aaron, the priest, after the rebellions in the wilderness. He explains which part of the offerings belongs to him and his family, since the Levites received no land. The meat of these animals would be for the priests, as their provision.

Today we can learn to give God the first and the best, not what is left over. We can also support with gratitude those who serve in the church.
exp.30:7:
This verse says that the Israelites killed five kings of Midian: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba. They also killed Balaam, son of Beor, with the sword.

The narrator recounts a war that Moses led at the command of the LORD. According to Numbers 25 and 31:16, Midian had led Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality at Peor, and Balaam is named as the one who gave that advice. It is a hard passage, and Christians read it carefully, in light of the whole Bible and of Christ.

For today: Balaam knew God, but he loved gain and ended badly. Let us guard our hearts and not counsel others toward what draws them away from God.
exp.0:50:
This verse says that the Levites were the only ones in charge of taking down the tabernacle when the people set out, and of setting it up again when they camped. "Setteth forward" means it was about to move, and "pitched" means it was being put down to stay. "The stranger" is anyone who was not a Levite, that is, someone not authorized to touch the holy things. He was warned that he would be put to death.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, while the people are being counted. The Levites are not counted with the army, because they had a different task: caring for God's dwelling. In this way the people were protected from God's anger for coming near what is holy without reverence.

For today: God deserves reverence, and serving him with order and responsibility is a serious matter. Ask yourself what task he has entrusted to you, and carry it out with care and gratitude, without neglecting it or treating lightly what belongs to God.
exp.34:7:
God tells Israel how to divide the cities for the Levites. The tribes that receive more land must give more cities, and those that receive less will give fewer. Each tribe contributes according to the inheritance that fell to it. The land each tribe received is what the verse calls its share, and the grazing lands around the cities were the open fields that surrounded them.

The LORD speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. The Levites received no territory of their own, for the Lord was their inheritance. So the people supported them with cities to live in, including six cities of refuge for anyone who caused a death without intending it.

Today we can learn to give fairly and in proportion: whoever has received more can share more. Ask yourself how you can generously support those who serve others, according to what God has given you.
exp.33:28:
This verse closes a list of leaders. It says that these men were the ones chosen by the Lord to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel. The division means the sharing out of the land, and the inheritance is the land each tribe would receive.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan, before the people enter the promised land. The names before this one, such as Ahihud and Pedahel, are the princes of each tribe. Together with the priest Eleazar and Joshua, they would make sure the division was orderly and fair. God himself decided who would do that work.

For today: God cares about the details and works through responsible people. If you are called to serve in something, whether in the church, the family, or at work, do it with honesty and fairness, knowing that God values faithful service even when no one notices.
exp.10:5:
The people say they feel dried up inside, with no spirit or desire. "Soul" here refers to their whole being, and "dried away" expresses listlessness and exhaustion. They say that all they see is manna, the food God gave them each day.

The speakers are the Israelites, stirred on by the mixed multitude that had begun to crave other foods. They were in the wilderness, on the way to the promised land. They remembered the food of Egypt but forgot the slavery they endured there. The next verse describes the manna as varied and tasty, so the problem was not its quality but the dissatisfaction of the heart.

For today: when you feel your life is dry, do not look only at what is missing. Take a moment to write down three provisions from God that you already have. Gratitude heals the way we see things.
exp.33:9:
This verse describes the eastern border of the promised land. It says the boundary would begin at Hazar-enan, the point where the northern border ended, and continue to Shepham. The word "border" means a boundary or limit, and "point out" means to mark or fix that line. Today it is not known for certain where Shepham was.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, who are on the plains of Moab, about to cross the Jordan. God gives them the limits of the land before they enter, so that they will know what He has promised them and how to divide it among the tribes.

For today: God cares about the details of his promise. If He set clear limits for his people, He can also order your life. Trust that his plans are concrete, and be thankful for what He has given you without living anxious about what you do not have.
exp.6:15:
It says that Nahshon, leader of the tribe of Judah, presented one male goat as a sin offering. "Atonement" is an old word meaning to cover or cleanse guilt. "Male goat" is a billy goat, that is, a full-grown goat.

This text is in the account of the offerings that the leaders of the twelve tribes brought for the dedication of the tabernacle. The narrator describes, day by day, what each prince presented. Nahshon was the first, and his list includes offerings of total devotion, of sin, and of fellowship with God.

For today: sin is serious, and even leaders needed forgiveness. We can come before God honestly, acknowledging our failings. As Christians, we believe Jesus offered the definitive sacrifice for our sins, so we come with humility and also with confidence.
exp.1:3:
This verse tells how many men were in the army of the tribe of Judah: 74,600 counted. "Host" is an old word meaning an army or an organized group, and "numbered" refers to those who were counted, that is, written down on the list.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. He orders them how to camp, each tribe under its banner and around the tabernacle. Judah goes to the east, with its leader Nahshon. God brings order so that the people can move and rest in an orderly way, with his presence at the center.

For today: God cares about order and values each person, not only the leaders. There is a place for you among his people. Serve faithfully where you are, and keep God at the center of your family, your work, and your church.
exp.29:10:
This verse speaks of a married woman who made a vow to God, or bound herself with an oath, while she was in her husband's house. It is the beginning of a sentence that is completed in the verses that follow. The phrase about binding her soul means committing herself seriously.

God gives these instructions to Moses, and Moses passes them on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. In that society, the father or husband was the head of the household and could cancel a vow that affected the family. If the husband heard it and said nothing, the vow stood firm. If he cancelled it that same day, the woman was released from it. Today people debate how this rule should be applied, since it was meant for ancient Israel.

For today: before promising something to God, think it through carefully and, if you are married, talk with your spouse. Promises made in unity are kept with greater peace.
exp.21:23:
It says that the angel of the Lord stood in a narrow way between vineyards, with a wall on each side. A "path" here is a little way, and "wall" refers to a wall or fence of stone. So the passage was narrow, with no room to get past on either side.

This is part of the story of Balaam, who was on his way to meet Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel. The narrator tells us that God was angry because Balaam was going, and the angel took his stand against him as an adversary. Balaam did not see him, but his donkey did, and because of this she kept turning aside. Each time, the way becomes more closed in.

For today: sometimes God closes doors or puts obstacles in our way to stop us. Before we get angry at whatever hinders us, it is good to ask ourselves whether God is warning us. Let us ask him for eyes to see and humility to stop.
exp.30:28:
From half of the plunder that belonged to the soldiers, a portion was to be taken, one out of every five hundred, and given to the priest Eleazar. That portion was "an heave offering of the Lord," that is, something set apart for God. The word "heave offering" refers to a gift lifted up and presented to the Lord.

Moses speaks with Eleazar and the leaders after the war against Midian. God commanded that the spoil be divided between the soldiers and the rest of the people. The soldiers gave a small portion, and the people gave a larger share to the Levites, who cared for the tabernacle. In this way everyone acknowledged that the victory came from God, and those who served in worship were supported.

For today: when you receive something good, such as a salary or an achievement, set aside a portion first for God and for helping those who serve. Doing this with gratitude reminds you that everything you have is a gift from him.
exp.10:18:
This verse says the people would not eat the meat for just one day, nor two, nor five, nor ten, nor twenty. The list of days shows that the provision would be abundant and would last a long time. The word "ye shall eat" means "you are going to eat", and "sanctify yourselves" means "prepare yourselves for God".

God speaks through Moses. The Israelites, in the wilderness, grew tired of the manna, wept, and said they were better off in Egypt. God promises them meat, but the next verse clarifies that it will be for a month, until it causes them to loathe it. In this way he shows them that their complaint was a contempt toward Him, who was among them.

Today, when we complain about what we do not have, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are despising what God already gives us. Let us ask with confidence, but also with gratitude and contentment.
exp.10:30:
It says that God sent a wind that brought quails from the sea and let them fall around Israel's camp. There were so many that they covered the ground for a day's journey in each direction. The word "camp" is what the verse calls the place where the people lived, and the surface of the ground is what the verse means by "the face of the earth." A cubit is about half a meter, though some think the phrase "two cubits high upon the face of the earth" refers to how high the birds flew, and others think it refers to a layer on the ground. It is not certain.

The people had complained about eating only manna and asked for meat. God answered them with abundance, but also with judgment. Moses, tired of carrying everyone, had just spoken with the elders.

Today, this invites us to examine our desires. Asking with complaint and anxiety, without gratitude for what God already gives, can lead us to get what we want but lose our peace. Let us learn to trust and give thanks.
exp.10:25:
Numbers 11:26 says that two men, Eldad and Medad, stayed back in the camp instead of going out to the tent of meeting. They were on the list of the seventy elders chosen for the task. Even so, the Spirit of God rested on them too, and they began to prophesy right there in the camp. "Prophesy" here means speaking under the influence of the Spirit, not necessarily predicting the future.

Moses was feeling overwhelmed by carrying the complaining people alone. God told him to gather seventy elders to share that burden with him, and he placed on them the same Spirit that was on Moses. The account tells us that God was not limited to the place agreed upon: the Spirit came also upon those who were outside the tent. Joshua reacted with concern for Moses' authority.

God works through his Spirit as he wills, and not always within the molds we make. Let us rejoice when he uses others, even when they do not follow our way of doing things.
exp.25:30:
This verse continues the list of the families of Gilead, a descendant of Manasseh. It says that the family of the Asrielites came from Asriel, and that the family of the Shechemites came from Shechem. The word "begot" means that someone was the father of another person, and "family" here refers to a clan within the tribe.

God, through Moses and the priest Eleazar, orders a new count of the people after the plague in the wilderness. The earlier generation had died, and now those who would enter the promised land were counted. These records would serve to divide the inheritance by clans and families.

For today: God knows each person and each family by name, even when history remembers only one name in a list. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your place matter to Him. You can also honor those who came before you, valuing your family history with gratitude.
exp.18:20:
This verse says that the rules about the water of separation were to be a law for all time. Whoever sprinkled that water on someone unclean had to wash his clothes. And whoever only touched the water remained unclean until evening. "Perpetual statute" means a permanent rule for the people. "Unclean" means impure according to the law, not necessarily sinful.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron to instruct Israel. This water was prepared with the ashes of the red cow and served to purify a person who had touched a dead body. It was something very serious, because the tabernacle was the place of God's presence. Interestingly, the one who purified another was also affected. Interpreters explain this in various ways, and the text does not give a detailed reason.

Today we can remember that God is holy and that helping others sometimes costs us something. Serve with humility, and return to God to be renewed.
exp.31:34:
This verse continues a list of towns that the descendants of Gad built, or rebuilt: Atroth-shophan, Jazer, and Jogbehah. "Built" here most likely means that they repaired and fortified them so they could live in them and protect their families and livestock.

It is part of the account in which Moses gives Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh the lands east of the Jordan, before entering Canaan. They had asked for that region because it was good for livestock, and they promised to help their brothers conquer the rest of the land. The narrator records in detail only how they began to settle. The exact location of some of these places is not entirely certain.

For today: God is concerned with everyday life, such as building a home and caring for one's family. But these blessings should not make us forget our commitments to others. Let us keep what we have promised.
exp.15:38:
Eleazar, the priest and son of Aaron, gathered up the bronze censers that the men who had been burned by God's fire had used. They were hammered out into broad sheets, and with them the altar was covered. The word "censers" refers to the vessels in which incense was burned.

God himself gave this command to Moses. Korah and his company had despised the order God had set, for they wanted to offer incense without being priests. After their punishment, God commanded that these censers become a permanent reminder for all Israel: approaching God must be done as he has indicated.

Today we can remember that God is holy and deserves reverence. We do not come to him in our own way or out of pride, but with humility. For us, that open door is Jesus Christ, our only mediator.
exp.6:44:
This verse mentions part of the offering brought by a leader of the tribe of Gad: one young bullock (a young bull), one ram, and one lamb of the first year, for the burnt offering. The burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar. The grain offering and the peace offering are the other offerings named in the larger passage.

The narrator tells how, when the tabernacle was dedicated, each tribe brought its offering on a different day. Here he speaks of Eliasaph, son of Deuel. All the leaders brought the same thing, and the text repeats it carefully so that no one would be forgotten. The burnt offering is understood to express total devotion to God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we offer to God. It is not a matter of animals, but of giving Him sincerely our time, our work, and our heart, holding nothing back, and recognizing that each person matters before Him.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that the twelve men sent by Moses traveled through the land of Canaan from south to north. They set out from the wilderness of Zin in the south and reached as far as Rehob, near Hamath, in the north. It was a long and thorough journey.

Background: Moses had given them instructions at God's command, according to the account. They were to see what the land was like, what its people were like, what its cities were like, and what its fruit was like. It was the season of the first grapes, that is, the early harvest. The Israelites were about to enter the promised land. The text does not give the exact distance, and scholars discuss the precise location of Rehob.

For today: Before making an important decision, it is wise to look at reality with patience and honesty. But seeing clearly is not enough; we must also trust God's promises, which, as we will see, many of them later failed to do.
exp.19:11:
God tells Moses and Aaron that they did not trust him enough to show him as holy before the people. Because of this, they will not be the ones to lead Israel into the promised land. "To honor him and treat him as holy" is what it means to show him as holy.

The Israelites, without water in the desert, complained once again. God had commanded Moses to speak to the rock (v. 8), but he, angry, called the people "rebels" and struck the rock twice. Even so, water came out. God speaks here to his two leaders. Some see in the act disobedience, others anger or lack of trust; the text says "you did not believe."

Today: God cares how we represent him. If we lead, teach, or serve, let us seek to obey him with trust and humility, without letting anger lead us to act our own way.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that the tribe of Judah was to camp on the east, which is where the sun rises, and directly in front of the entrance to the tabernacle. The "standard" was the banner of their group, and their "divisions" are their units or organized companies. Their leader was Nahshon, son of Amminadab. The east and the rising of the sun both mean the same direction.

God himself speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel is in the wilderness. He gives them an order for camping: each tribe in its place, around the tabernacle, which was the center of God's presence. In this way the camp moved and lived in order, and everyone knew clearly their place.

For today: God cares about order and wants him to be at the center. We can examine whether in our home, work and church we put him first, and joyfully fulfill the place that belongs to us, without envying that of others.
exp.26:8:
This verse gives a rule about inheritance. If a man died without sons and also had no daughters, his property passed to his brothers.

God speaks to Moses after the daughters of Zelophehad pleaded for an inheritance because their father had died without sons. God said they were right, and from that case He set an order for dividing inheritances in Israel. In this way families and each tribe's land were cared for.

For today: God cares about order and justice in the family. We can make our decisions about what we have clear, to avoid quarrels and to care for those we love.
exp.33:15:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses, and that what follows is a new instruction. "Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament.

Israel was on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan, about to enter Canaan. God had already marked the boundaries of the land. Now, in what follows, he names Eleazar the priest and Joshua as those responsible for dividing it, together with one leader from each tribe. In this way, the division did not depend on a single person, but was carried out in order and with witnesses from all the tribes.

For today: God speaks before we act. Before making important decisions, it is good to stop and listen to his Word and seek wise counsel, rather than deciding alone or in a hurry.
exp.18:7:
The person who burns the red cow must wash his clothes and bathe his body in water. Even after doing this, he remains unclean (not fit to take part in worship) until evening. Here "his flesh" means his body, and "the camp" is the encampment.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron, and they pass it on to Israel. This cow was burned to prepare ashes used in the water of purification, which was used when someone became defiled through contact with a dead body. It is striking that the one who helps purify others also remains unclean for a time. Scholars explain this in several ways, and the text does not give a detailed reason.

For today: serving others in difficult situations can leave us tired or marked. After helping, let us pause to rest, pray, and return to God in humility, without carrying that burden alone.
exp.31:16:
This verse says that the men of Reuben and Gad will arm themselves and march at the front of the other Israelites, ready for battle, until they have brought them to their place in the land. Meanwhile, their children will stay in walled cities, protected from the inhabitants of the land. "Eagerly" means promptly and earnestly; bringing them to "their place" means bringing them to their inheritance.

The tribes of Reuben and Gad speak to Moses. They had asked to stay east of the Jordan because that land was good for their livestock. Moses feared they would discourage the people, as had happened before. They answer by promising to fight alongside their brothers and not to return home until everyone has received their land.

For today: when we receive a blessing, we must not forget those who are still fighting. We can use what God has given us to help others, with real commitment and not only with words.
exp.12:11:
This verse names the representative of the tribe of Manasseh, who was part of the descendants of Joseph: Gaddi, son of Susi. He is one of the twelve men chosen, one from each tribe, to go and explore the land of Canaan.

God told Moses to send these men, all leaders of his people, from the wilderness of Paran. They were to see what the land was like and what its inhabitants were like. The Bible says nothing more about Gaddi. Since only Joshua and Caleb trusted God afterward (Numbers 14), it is understood that he was among those who discouraged the people.

God pays attention to each person, even to those who are little remembered. Having a position or a responsibility is not enough; what matters is whether we trust God's promises when the road seems hard. Today we can ask him for faith to respond with confidence and not with fear.
exp.14:3:
He says that when someone presented a sacrifice of an animal to God, he also had to bring a grain offering of fine flour: a tenth part of an ephah (a measure of dry volume, a few liters), mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil (a hin was a measure of liquid, roughly a couple of liters; the exact calculations are uncertain).

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct Israel. This is said looking ahead, to the time when they would enter the promised land. It is an implied promise: God would give them the land, and there they would worship him with gratitude, whether through a vow, by their own willingness, or at the festivals.

For today: God cares about the details of worship, but what He seeks is a grateful heart. We can ask ourselves what we bring to the Lord, not only in special moments, but with a constant giving of the everyday: our work, our time, and our gratitude.
exp.3:39:
This verse gives the result of the count of Gershon's descendants: 2,630 men. "Counted" means enrolled or registered, and "households of their fathers" refers to their clans or family groups.

God told Moses and Aaron to count the Levites from thirty to fifty years old who could serve in the tabernacle. The Gershonites were responsible for caring for and carrying the curtains and coverings, according to this same chapter. It was orderly and necessary work, and nothing was left to chance.

For today: God sees and values the service of each person, even the kind that almost no one notices. Faithfully do the task that falls to you, whether great or small, because it does not go unnoticed before God.
exp.0:4:
God tells Moses that, to take the count, one man from each tribe will help them. Here the list of those leaders begins. The first is from the tribe of Reuben: Elizur, son of Shedeur. "Men" means the men, and "shall stand with you" means they will accompany and support Moses and Aaron.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai, while Israel was being organized as a people. Each leader was the head of his family or tribe. Reuben is listed first because he was the eldest son of Jacob. God does not leave the work to one person; he shares the responsibility among named individuals.

For today: God counts on people who serve alongside others, even when they are not well known. Ask yourself how you can support your church or family, and do it faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.21:26:
She says the donkey saw the angel of the LORD again, who was now standing in a very narrow place with no way out. Then the animal fell down with Balaam on it, and Balaam, angry, struck it with his staff. The sentences explaining old words have been removed, since the reader's verse does not use them.

The narrator tells that Balaam was on his way to meet Balak, king of Moab, who wanted him to curse Israel. God had opposed that journey. The angel was standing in the road as an adversary, but Balaam could not see him. Only the donkey perceived what was happening, and that is why it kept stopping.

For today: when something keeps stopping you again and again, do not react with anger right away. Stop and ask yourself whether God may be warning you about something you do not yet see. Asking Him for clarity in prayer may keep you from striking the one who is only trying to protect you.
exp.32:13:
The people of Israel left Alush and camped at Rephidim. Their leaving is described with a word that simply means "having set out," and the camping is described with a word that simply means "camped." There was no water there for them to drink.

This chapter is a record of the stops on the journey out of Egypt. Numbers 33:2 says that Moses wrote it at the command of the Lord. Here only the lack of water is mentioned. Exodus 17 tells more: the people complained, and God gave them water from a rock. The exact location of Rephidim is not known with certainty.

For today: sometimes God leads us to places where the basics are missing, and that does not mean he has abandoned us. When scarcity comes, instead of complaining, ask God for help with confidence, because he already knows where your provision is.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that the priest takes a handful of the grain offering the woman brought, called "the memorial" or "the reminder offering," and burns it on the altar. After that he gives the woman the water to drink. The word "offering" means a gift brought to God, and "memorial" means that the offering brings the case before God.

God speaks to Moses to give this law to the people of Israel. It applied when a husband felt jealousy and suspected unfaithfulness, but there were no witnesses. It was a ritual for placing the matter in God's hands rather than in human revenge. Scholars discuss how exactly to understand the effect of the water, and the text gives no further details.

For today: when there are suspicions or hurts that you cannot prove, do not take justice into your own hands. Hand them over to God in prayer, seek the truth with humility, and trust that he knows everything.
exp.3:23:
This verse says that the families of Gershon were given a specific task: to serve and to carry burdens. The word "serve" here refers to the work of attending to the tabernacle, and "burdens" refers to the loads they carried. A "service" is an assigned task or responsibility. The Gershonites were to take charge of transporting certain parts of the tabernacle.

God speaks to Moses and commands him to count the Levites from thirty to fifty years of age, those who were able to serve in the tabernacle. Each Levite family received a different function. The verses that follow explain that the Gershonites were responsible for carrying the curtains, the coverings, and the veils. It was a less visible job, but a necessary one, so that worship could stay in order when the people were on the move.

For today: God gives different tasks to his people, and none is small when it is done for him. Ask yourself what simple service he has placed near you, and do it faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.1:21:
This verse names the tribe of Benjamin and its leader, Abidan, son of Gideoni. He is a leader of the tribe, chosen to represent it.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, while Israel gets ready to march. He orders them to camp in a precise arrangement around the tabernacle. Benjamin stands beside Ephraim and Manasseh, on the western side, forming the division of Ephraim. Each tribe had its place and its leader, so that the whole people could move in order and know where they belonged.

For today: God pays attention to each person and to every place of service, even to names that seem small. You have a place among his people. Serve faithfully where God has placed you, without comparing yourself to others, trusting that God's order and care include your life.
exp.29:15:
It says that if a husband, after hearing his wife's vows and remaining silent, later cancels them, he will bear the guilt for her. The verse also closes the section: these are the rules God gave to Moses for cases between husband and wife, and between a father and his young daughter who lives at home.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. In that society, vows made to God were very serious. The law aimed to ensure that no one broke their word lightly. If the husband kept silent the day he heard the vow, it was confirmed. Changing his mind afterward made him answerable for the harm.

For today: our words and commitments matter. If we have authority or influence over others, we should not stay silent and then undo what was agreed, but speak clearly and in time, and honestly take responsibility for our actions.
exp.6:51:
This verse mentions one male goat offered as a sin offering, that is, a sacrifice to cover sin and restore the relationship with God. It was part of the offering that Elishama, leader of the tribe of Ephraim, brought along with the bull, the ram, and the lamb.

We are in Numbers 7, where the account describes, day by day, the offerings of each tribal leader for the dedication of the tabernacle. Moses records it, and each one brings the same things, in great detail. The repetition shows that God receives each person's offering with attention. The sin offerings reminded the people that, before worshiping, they needed to acknowledge their sin.

For today: before we bring our worship or service, we can pause to honestly confess where we fall short. Christians believe that Christ offered the complete atonement for us, so we come with confidence, not fear, and with gratitude.
exp.17:17:
This verse says that the flesh of the firstborn animals offered to God (cow, sheep or goat) would belong to Aaron, the priest. It is compared with the breast of the animal, which was presented by being moved back and forth before God, and with the right shoulder, which is the right foreleg or shoulder of the animal. These were portions that belonged to the priest.

God is speaking to Aaron. The Levites did not receive land as an inheritance, so God arranged for them to live from the people's offerings. What was given to God sustained those who served in the sanctuary.

Today we can learn to support, with generosity and gratitude, those who serve in teaching and in the care of the church. We can also remember that God provides for those who depend on Him.
exp.7:11:
This verse describes a step in the ritual of consecration of the Levites. They lay their hands on the heads of two young bulls, and then one is offered as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, completely burned.

God speaks to Moses and gives him instructions for setting apart the tribe of Levi for service in the tabernacle. Before serving, they had to be purified. Laying hands on the animals expresses that the sacrifice stood in for them. Scholars explain the exact details of this gesture in various ways, but the general sense is identification.

For today: no one serves God on their own merits. Before serving, we need his forgiveness. Come to him with humility and gratitude, and serve from the grace you have received.
exp.21:20:
Balaam got up early in the morning and saddled his donkey, fastening the saddle with straps, and went off with the princes of Moab, that is, the leaders sent by King Balak. The donkey is the female one.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Balak wanted Balaam to curse Israel. God had told Balaam to go with them only if they called him, and to speak only what God told him. But Balaam seems to go on his own, and that is why the next verse says that God's anger was kindled. Interpreters explain in various ways why God first permits and then becomes angry; many see a divided heart in Balaam.

For today: it is not enough to obey outwardly. Before acting, examine your motives and ask God whether your heart truly wants what He wants.
exp.28:37:
This verse says that, in addition to the sacrifices of the feast day, one male goat was to be offered as a sin offering, to cover the sin of the people. It was added to the continual burnt offering, which was the daily sacrifice, along with its grain offering and its drink offering of poured-out wine.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses passes it on to Israel, while the people are about to enter the promised land. Here the offerings of the Feast of Tabernacles are described. Even in a joyful festival, the sacrifice for sin was included. Christians often see in this a shadow of Christ, although the text itself speaks of Israel's worship.

For today: even in your best moments of joy and gratitude, remember that you need the grace of God. Give thanks with joy and with humility, trusting in the forgiveness that Christ offers.
exp.32:53:
It says that Israel would receive the land divided by lot, according to the families and the tribes. Large families would receive a wider piece of land, and small ones a smaller one. Each person would have the portion that fell to him by the lot. The word "inheritance" means the land that is received as an heritage, and "lot" refers to a drawing of lots.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, on the plains of Moab, before they cross the Jordan. He orders them to drive out the idolatrous peoples of Canaan and to destroy their idols. He warns them that, if they do not obey, those peoples would be a constant affliction to them. This command was given to Israel at a specific moment in its history, and it is not applied as an order to believers today.
