Today we can learn to receive with gratitude what God gives us, without envying the portion of others. We should also remove from our lives whatever keeps us apart from Him, before it becomes a thorn.
exp.22:10:
Balak is upset and confronts Balaam: "What hast thou done unto me?" He reminds him that he hired him to curse his enemies, but Balaam did the opposite and blessed them. The word "spoken" in the verse means said or uttered aloud. "I took thee" means "I brought you" or "I hired you."

Balak was king of Moab, and he feared Israel, which was close to his territory. He had called Balaam to curse the people. But Balaam could only say what God put in his mouth, and so blessings came out instead. Balak is frustrated because he expected a different result.

Today we can remember that no one can change what God has decided to bless. Sometimes we want God to say what suits us, but it is better to align our plans with his will. Let us speak with honesty and faithfulness, even when we do not please everyone.
exp.3:6:
This verse explains how to cover the table of the showbread when the people were on the move. Over the table a cloth of dark blue, a deep blue-violet, was spread. On top of it they placed the dishes, the spoons, the cups and the bowls for the wine offerings. In addition, the continual bread, that is, the bread that was always present before God, remained on the table.

God gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The Kohathites, a family of the Levites, were to carry the holy objects. First, Aaron and his sons, the priests, covered them so that no one would touch or see them. In this way the respect that holy things deserve was shown.

For today: God cares about details and values order and reverence. We can apply this by setting aside a moment each day to pray or read the Bible with attention and respect, not hurriedly or out of habit.
exp.33:19:
The verse names a man from the tribe of Simeon: Shemuel, son of Ammihud. He was one of the leaders, that is, the chiefs or heads of his tribe. He is part of a list of representatives, one for each tribe.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan, when the people are about to enter Canaan. The Lord commands that each tribe provide a leader to help Eleazar the priest and Joshua divide the promised land. In this way the division would be orderly and fair, with every tribe represented. In other versions the name appears as Semuel.

God attends to the details and works through specific people, even those whom almost no one remembers. This brief name teaches us that every service counts before Him. Ask yourself: what small responsibility, in your family or in your church, can you faithfully carry out today?
exp.2:18:
This verse lists the four sons of Kohath: Amram, Izehar, Hebron, and Uzziel. From each of them a family line would come within the tribe of Levi. The word "and" here simply means "and," and "by their families" means "according to their family groups."

The narrator of Numbers, which tradition attributes to Moses, records these families in order because God had set the Levites apart to serve in the tabernacle. The Kohathites, according to the same book, would also be entrusted with the care of the most sacred objects of the sanctuary.

For today: God knows people by name and values service that seems small or hidden. Ask yourself what simple task you have been entrusted with, in your church or in your family, and do it with faithfulness and joy.
exp.20:7:
God told Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole. The figure of a serpent, which in the following text is made of bronze, is to be raised high on the pole. Whoever has been bitten and looks toward it will live.

The people of Israel were traveling through the wilderness and spoke against God and against Moses. Serpents came among them and many died. Then the people recognized their sin and asked Moses to pray. God answered with a way of salvation, not by removing the serpents, but by giving a remedy to whoever would look upon it in obedience.

For today: when you are wounded by your mistakes or your fears, do not simply keep staring at the problem. Acknowledge your guilt, pray, and trust in what God has shown. He offers salvation to those who believe in his word.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses. It is a short sentence that introduces what God is about to command. The words "Lord" and "saying" show that God himself, the Lord, is about to give clear instructions.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and then God does. The people of Israel were in the desert, without water, and they complained bitterly against Moses and Aaron. They went to the entrance of the tent of meeting, fell facedown on the ground, and the glory of God appeared. Then God responds with a solution: water from the rock.

For today: when you are under pressure or feel criticized, do as Moses and Aaron did: bring your need to God first. Seek him in prayer and listen to his word before you respond. He knows how to care for you.
exp.14:19:
God commands that from the first dough they make with the grain of the new land, they set aside a cake or loaf and offer it to Him. The word "knead" is the one used for preparing the dough, so the verse for that wording is simply that they are to make the dough. The threshingfloor is the place where the grain was beaten out, and its offering was the first part of the harvest. The dough cake was presented in the same way.

God speaks to Moses so that Moses can speak to the people of Israel. They were still wandering in the wilderness, but God promises them that they will enter the land. This law taught them to recognize that the bread came from God and that the first of it belonged to Him. The verses that follow call it the "firstfruits."

For today: before you spend or give away what you receive, whether it is your wages, your time, or your strength, first set aside a part for God with gratitude. In this way you remember that everything comes from His hand.
exp.33:26:
This verse says that the chosen leader of the tribe of Asher was Ahihud, son of Shelomi. The word "prince" does not refer to a king's son, but to a chief or leader of his tribe. He is part of a list of representatives, one from each tribe.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. He gives the boundaries of the land and appoints these leaders, along with Eleazar and Joshua, to divide the inheritance among the tribes. In this way disputes were avoided and the division was made with order and justice. Nothing more is said about Ahihud here.

God works through specific people, including those who are little known, to carry out his work well. Today you can serve faithfully in whatever you are entrusted with, even when no one notices. God does know your name and values your service.
exp.7:5:
God commands Moses to separate the Levites from the rest of the Israelites and to cleanse them. To cleanse here means to purify them, to make them clean and fit to draw near to God. Taking them means setting them apart or choosing them.

The LORD speaks to Moses. Shortly before, the lampstand of the sanctuary was made according to the pattern God showed. Now God also sets out how the Levites are to be prepared, the tribe that would serve in the tabernacle by helping the priests. The next steps include water for purification, washing of clothes, and sacrifices.

For today: serving God is not only doing tasks, it is also living with a clean heart. We can ask God to purify us and prepare us before we serve, trusting that he cleanses us and gives us his grace.
exp.2:4:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the Lord, that is, God, spoke to Moses. The word "saying" announces that instructions will follow right away. In this text, the expression "the Lord spake" shows that what follows is not Moses' own ideas, but commands that come from God.

The one speaking is God, and the one listening is Moses, the leader of the people. Earlier, the sons of Aaron were mentioned, including the death of Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire. Now God arranges the service of the tabernacle and orders that the tribe of Levi be brought forward to help the priests. In this way we see that drawing near to God requires order and reverence.

For today: before serving God, it is wise to listen to him. We can set aside time to read the Bible and pray, asking God to guide our work and our decisions, rather than doing everything our own way.
exp.3:34:
This verse says that the men of the family of Kohath who were between thirty and fifty years old were counted. They were the ones who "entered into the service," that is, those who were part of the serving group. The word "service" here refers to work in the tabernacle, the tent where God dwelt among his people.

The book of Numbers records what God commanded through Moses. Moses, Aaron, and the leaders counted the Levites to organize who would carry and care for the tabernacle during the journey through the desert. Why that age was chosen is not explained here. In Numbers 8:24 another age appears, twenty-five years, and some think there was a period of training before full service.

Serving God requires order, preparation, and responsibility. Today you might ask what your place is in your church or community, and serve there with faithfulness and joy.
exp.21:10:
Here Balaam repeats to God the message from Balak. He says that the people of Israel, who came out of Egypt, are so numerous that they "cover the face of the earth," meaning the surface, all the land in sight. Balak asks that Balaam curse Israel, hoping to be able to fight against them and drive them out of his territory.

The one speaking is Balaam, quoting the words of the king of Moab. Balak was afraid of Israel, which was camped nearby. He thought that a curse spoken by Balaam would have power. But God answers afterward that Israel is blessed, and Balaam cannot go.

For today: fear can lead us to seek wrong solutions against what God has already blessed. Before acting out of fear, it is wise to ask God and to listen to his answer with humility.
exp.21:8:
God comes to Balaam and asks him a question: "What men are these with you?" The old words here are simple: "men" is the plain meaning of the word used, and "said to him" is the same as the verse's "said".

Messengers from Moab and Midian had come with payment for divination, asking Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam asked them to wait one night so he could hear what the LORD would say. God does not ask because he is unaware of anything, for he knows all things. With the question, Balaam has to face what he is doing. In this way, his answer will reveal what is in his heart.

God sometimes leads us to think through simple questions. Before making a decision, it is good to stop and honestly tell him who or what is influencing us, and what we are really seeking.
exp.19:9:
Moses and Aaron gather the people in front of the rock. Moses says to them, "Hear now, you rebels; must we bring you water out of this rock?"

Moses speaks after the people complain about the lack of water in the desert. God had commanded him to speak to the rock, but Moses, angry, scolds the people and speaks as if the miracle depended on the two of them. Then he strikes the rock, and God tells him that because he did not trust Him or honor Him before everyone, they would not enter the promised land.

For today: when we are tired or frustrated, let us seek to obey God just as He said, and give Him the credit, not ourselves.
exp.21:24:
The donkey saw the angel of the Lord again on the road. Since the path had a wall on each side, the animal pressed against the wall and crushed Balaam's foot against it. Balaam, not understanding anything, struck her again.

Here no character speaks; the account simply tells what happens. Balaam was on his way to Moab, summoned by King Balak, to curse Israel. God was displeased with his journey, and the angel stood in the way. The donkey could see the angel; Balaam, the prophet, could not.

For today: sometimes we react in anger when something blocks our path. Before striking out at others or blaming our circumstances, it is wise to stop and ask whether God may be warning us about something we have not yet seen.
exp.6:72:
This verse says that Pagiel, prince of the tribe of Asher, brought one silver plate weighing 130 shekels and one silver bowl weighing 70 shekels, measured by the shekel of the sanctuary, which was the official weight standard of the place of worship. Both were full of fine flour, meaning very fine flour, mixed with oil.

Context: The narrator of the book of Numbers describes the dedication of the tabernacle. For twelve days, each prince of Israel brought the same offering, and the account repeats it in full for each one. This was the eleventh day. The repetition shows that each tribe was taken into account equally, with no tribe placed above another.

For today: God values the giving of each person, not only the actions of the most visible ones. Think of one concrete way to give God your best this week, such as your time, your service, or your resources, and do it with gratitude, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.6:9:
These verses say that the leaders of the tribes of Israel, called "princes," brought their offerings before the altar. They did this on the same day the altar was anointed, that is, set apart with oil for the service of God. Dedication means giving something over for holy use. The old forms of the word for "was" and the word "anointed" are archaic; today we would simply say "was."

Here the narrator of the book describes what happened with the tabernacle. Earlier, the carts and oxen were divided among the Levites to carry the sanctuary. Now the heads of the tribes bring their own offerings. Afterward, God tells Moses that each prince should make his offering on a different day.

For today: giving God what comes first and what is best, freely and in an orderly way, reminds us that our service, whether great or small, is a way of dedicating our lives to him.
exp.32:52:
It says that Israel was to drive out the inhabitants of Canaan, live in that land, and possess it, because God was giving it to them. "Dispossess" means to drive out or remove. "Possess" means to hold it as one's own, as an inheritance.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before crossing the Jordan. He orders them to stay away from the idols and altars of the Canaanite peoples, so that Israel would not be corrupted by their idolatry. The text presents this as a command for that particular moment in Israel's history. Christians have understood it in different ways, but not as permission to use violence today.

Today we can learn that God calls his people not to tolerate in their lives whatever pulls them away from him. Ask yourself what habit, relationship, or custom has become a thorn, and ask God for help in letting it go.
exp.29:0:
This verse says that Moses spoke to the Israelites and passed on everything God had commanded him. The phrase "as the thing which the Lord hath commanded" means "just as" or "according to" what was commanded. Moses does not invent anything; he only conveys what the Lord, that is, Jehovah, told him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of the years in the wilderness. This verse serves as an introduction to the instructions about vows, which follow right after. Moses first speaks to the heads of the tribes, and they would help the people understand. The verse emphasizes that the authority of what is said comes from God.

Today we can learn to take our words seriously. Before promising something, think it through carefully, and if you make a promise, keep it. In this way we honor God and give confidence to those around us.
exp.21:6:
The leaders of Moab and Midian traveled to where Balaam was. They carried "rewards of divination" in their hand, that is, money or gifts to pay for the services of a diviner. When they arrived, they gave him King Balak's message: that he should curse Israel.

Balak, king of Moab, was afraid because Israel was a large people who had come out of Egypt and were camped nearby. He thought Balaam's words could weaken Israel. That is why he sent the elders with payment included. Later on, Balaam asks them to wait for the night so he can consult the LORD.

Today, people sometimes try to buy or manipulate what God has already chosen to bless. Before deciding anything, let us sincerely seek God's will, and not let money or fear move us toward the opposite.
exp.35:7:
It says that every Israelite woman who received an inheritance of land had to marry someone from the family of her father's tribe. In this way, each Israelite would keep the inheritance of their ancestors. "Possess" means "come to possess," and "inheritance" is the land received as a heritage.

The Lord speaks through Moses, almost at the end of the book of Numbers. The daughters of Zelophehad (Salphaad) had already received the right to inherit because their father had no sons. The leaders of their tribe feared that, if they married men from another tribe, the land would pass to that tribe. For this reason the rule was given, and the daughters obeyed it.

For today: God cares for what He entrusts to us and expects us to manage it with responsibility. We can ask ourselves what blessings, teachings, or goods we have received, and how to care for them so that they also benefit those who come after us.
exp.14:12:
Explanation:
It says that every Israelite born in the land must present his offerings in the way indicated, with the correct amounts of flour, oil and wine that go with the animal. "Native" means the one born in that land. "Offering made by fire" is the offering that was burned on the altar, and "of a sweet savour" expresses that God received it with pleasure.

God speaks through Moses to the people, before they enter Canaan. He gives them ordered instructions for worshiping him when they live in the promised land. The following verses add that the foreigner who joins them must follow the same rule, and so will have the same treatment before the LORD.

For today: God values sincere worship done with order and reverence, not carelessly. And among his people there should be no levels of importance; every person who draws near to God is received equally. We can welcome newcomers in the church as equals.
exp.7:13:
God says to separate the Levites from the rest of the people of Israel, and that they will belong to him in a special way. The word "separate" means to set apart, to set aside for a holy purpose. The Levites are the members of the tribe of Levi.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness, when the tabernacle was already in use. The Levites would take the place of the firstborn of Israel, who, having been spared on the night of the Passover in Egypt, belonged to God. Before serving, they were purified and presented before Aaron and his sons as an offering. Animals were offered for atonement, that is, to cover the guilt and cleanse.

For today: everything we are belongs to God, and serving him begins by acknowledging that he sets us apart and cleanses us. Offer him today your work and your time as something that is his.
exp.27:22:
This verse says that the offerings for the festival of Unleavened Bread did not replace the daily offering. First, the morning burnt offering was presented, an animal burned completely on the altar, and it was called the regular offering because it was made every day. The special offerings of the festival were added to this one. "Besides," in the verse, means "apart from" or "together with."

God speaks to Moses, and Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are close to entering the promised land. Here the offerings for the Passover and for the seven days of unleavened bread are explained. God wanted his people not to let their constant worship lapse, not even on festival days.

For today: celebrations and special moments should not push aside our routine of prayer and Bible reading. Seek God every morning, even when your week is very busy or full of festivities.
exp.18:13:
This verse says that when a person dies inside a tent, the death makes the place impure. Everyone who enters that tent, and everyone who is already inside, becomes unclean (ritually impure, not fit to draw near to worship) for seven days.

God gives this law to Moses and Aaron for the people of Israel in the wilderness. It is part of the instructions about the water of purification, prepared with the ashes of the red cow. Death was seen as a sign of the fall of the world, and God wanted his people to come near to his presence with reverence and cleanness. This does not mean that the dead person or those who cared for him had sinned.

For today: death is a serious reality, but we do not have to face it alone. Christians see in Christ the one who overcomes death and cleanses truly. We can accompany someone who is suffering a loss with tenderness and draw near to God with confidence.
exp.8:14:
This verse tells that on the day the tabernacle was set up, a cloud covered it. The "tent of the testimony" is the tent where the tablets of the law were kept, a sign of God's covenant with his people. In the evening, something like fire appeared over the tabernacle, and it stayed there until morning. "Was raised up" means it was set up and made to stand.

The author of the book, traditionally Moses, tells how God guided Israel in the desert. Shortly before, the Passover was mentioned, which everyone was to keep, even the foreigner who lived among them. Now it is shown that God was present and leading them. The cloud and the fire were visible signs of that presence. Afterward it is explained that Israel travelled or camped according to the movement of the cloud.

For today: God does not leave his children without direction. We can seek his guidance with patience, in prayer and in his Word, and move forward or wait as he leads us, trusting that he is with us.
exp.15:33:
This verse tells that all the people of Israel who were around Korah, Dathan and Abiram ran away at the sound of their cries. They were afraid that the earth would swallow them up too. The phrase about being "round about" simply means "around them," and the phrase "fled at the cry of them" means they escaped when they heard the cries of those who were falling.

The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally Moses. Korah, Dathan and Abiram had rebelled against Moses and Aaron, challenging the leadership God had given them. God responded with a very serious judgment, and the people witnessed what happened firsthand.

For today: rebellion and spiritual pride have real consequences. We should examine our hearts with humility, acknowledge those whom God has placed as leaders, and not take his holiness lightly. In this way we learn to fear him and to trust in his mercy.
exp.26:1:
This verse tells us that the five daughters of Zelophehad presented themselves publicly before Moses, the priest Eleazar, the leaders, and the whole people. They did so at the entrance of the tabernacle, the place of the congregation. "Princes" refers to the leaders of the tribes, and "congregation" is the community of Israel.

It is these women who are speaking. Their father had died without leaving any sons, and in that time land was inherited through the sons. They feared that their father's name would disappear from his family. So they brought their request to the place and before the people with authority to hear it.

For today: when you believe something is unjust, raise it with respect, with order, and in the right place. They did not complain in secret or act on their own; they spoke with courage and waited for an answer.
exp.7:23:
This verse says that the Levites, from twenty-five years old and upward, were to begin working in the service of the tabernacle. "Work" here means the task or duty assigned to them. "Tabernacle of the congregation" is the holy tent where God met with his people.

God speaks to Moses. The Levites had already been set apart to help Aaron and his sons, the priests. Here God sets the age for active service. Later, Numbers 4 mentions the age of thirty; scholars explain this in different ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: serving God is a calling with order and purpose. Ask God where he wants you to serve now, and do it with care and steadiness, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.15:6:
Moses says to Korah and his followers that they should put fire and incense in their censers before God the next day. God will show whom He chooses as holy, that is, set apart for Himself. And he tells them, "You take too much upon you," meaning, "That is enough, that is too much."

Here the word "incense" names the spice smoke offered in the censers, and "sons of Levi" refers to the men of the tribe of Levi.

Moses speaks. Korah, a Levite, and other men had rebelled against him and Aaron, because they also wanted the priesthood. Moses does not argue or defend himself; he lets God Himself decide before everyone.

Today, when someone questions us or wants a place that does not belong to them, we can learn not to fight for our position. It is better to be thankful for the service God has given us, to keep a humble heart, and to let Him be the one who confirms His calling.
exp.30:0:
This verse says that God (Jehovah) spoke to Moses. It is only an introductory phrase, and what God says comes in the next verse. The word "spake" is an older form of "spoke."

We are near the end of the book of Numbers. Moses is now an old man, and God tells him that his life is about to end (he will be gathered to his people, that is, he will die). Earlier, in Numbers 25, the Midianites had led many Israelites into idolatry and immorality. This passage is hard, and many readers find it difficult; it is understood within that historical moment in Israel's story, not as a model for today.

For today: God speaks, and his people need to listen. Before acting, let us seek his voice in the Bible and in prayer, with humility.
exp.25:43:
This verse begins to list the tribe of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. It names three of his principal descendants: Jimna, Jesui, and Beriah. From each of them came a family, or clan, that carries his name, such as the Jimnites. "After their families" means "according to their clans."

God, through Moses, orders this second census in the wilderness, near the entrance to the promised land. The previous generation had died because of their unbelief. Now the new generation is counted so that the land can be divided according to the size of each family. The names also show that God remembers every lineage.

For today: God does not see you as a lost number in the crowd. He knows your name and your story. Trust that you have a place in his plan, and care for your own family, passing on the faith to those who come after you.
exp.18:17:
A person who was ceremonially clean was to take a sprig of hyssop (a small plant used in rituals), dip it in the water prepared with the ashes, and sprinkle the tent, the objects, the people who were there, and whoever had touched a bone, a corpse, someone killed in battle, or a grave. "Unclean" means impure according to the law, not necessarily sinful.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron while Israel lives in the wilderness. These rules taught that death is foreign to the holiness of God, whose presence dwelt in the tabernacle. The water with the ashes of the red cow made it possible to return to the community. Christians often see here a shadow of the cleansing that Christ provides (Hebrews 9:13-14), though this is an interpretation.

Today: we do not have to carry our guilt alone, or what defiles us inwardly. God offers real cleansing. Come to Him with sincerity, confess what weighs on your conscience, and receive His forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.0:38:
This verse says that the men counted from the tribe of Dan, those who were twenty years old or more and able to go to war, came to 62,700. After Judah, Dan was the most numerous tribe in the count. "Counted" here means registered or numbered. The words "generations" and "houses of their fathers" refer to the families and lineages of each tribe.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai and commands him to take this census, together with Aaron and the leaders of each tribe. Israel was getting ready to march as an organized people toward the promised land. The numbers show that God had kept his promise to multiply the descendants of Abraham.

For today: God knows and counts each person, and no one escapes his notice. You can rest in the knowledge that you too have a place among his people. And if God is so careful with people, we too should value each brother and sister in the community.
exp.13:14:
It says that if God destroys this whole people in one stroke, as if they were a single person, the nations that have already heard of his renown will start speaking badly of him.

Moses is the one speaking, as he intercedes before God. Israel had rebelled at Kadesh because they were afraid to enter the promised land, and God was speaking of punishing them. Moses does not defend the people on the basis of their merit, but appeals to the honor of God's name and to what the nations would think of him.

When we pray, we can ask God to act in a way that shows his faithful and merciful character. Interceding for others, even when they have done wrong, is an act of love that reflects the heart of God.
exp.3:28:
This verse says that Moses was to take a census of the descendants of Merari, one of the three sons of Levi. He was to count them according to their families and according to the houses of their fathers, that is, by their clans and their family line. The sentence about the counting word is dropped, since the verse reader sees uses "number" rather than the quoted word.

God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The sons of Kohath and of Gershon had already been mentioned, and now it is the turn of Merari. The Levites took care of the tabernacle and carried it. Later it is explained that the sons of Merari were responsible for carrying the boards, bars, pillars, and bases. The counting served to organize the work well, and the men from thirty to fifty years old were the ones who served.

For today: God pays attention to each family and each person, and does not leave service to chance. We can serve in our church with order and devotion, even in simple or little-seen tasks, knowing that God values them.
exp.4:27:
It says that if the woman who was suspected had not been unfaithful, but was clean, the bitter waters would not harm her. She would be free from blame and would be able to have children. The verse of what "defiled" means here is simply that she would be contaminated by adultery, and that "clean" means she could conceive.

God speaks to Moses for the people of Israel. This law dealt with the case of a husband who was jealous and had no witnesses. It was a procedure before the LORD that protected an innocent woman from accusations without proof and placed the judgment in God's hands, not the husband's. Scholars debate exactly how the ritual worked, and the text does not fully explain it.

For today: let us not condemn anyone on the basis of suspicion or gossip. God knows the truth and defends the innocent. When we have doubts, let us seek the truth with humility and justice, and trust in God.
exp.13:24:
God tells the Israelites that the Amalekites and the Canaanites live in the valley, that is, in the area they had wanted to conquer. He commands them to turn around the next day and set out toward the wilderness, by the way of the Red Sea. The verse's wording "turn you" means to go back, and "get you" means to set out on the journey.

God is speaking, addressing Moses and the people. Israel had just believed the fearful report of the ten spies and rebelled against God. Because of their lack of trust, God denies them entry into the promised land at that time. Only Caleb, who trusted God, would receive the promise. Some scholars think that mentioning the enemies emphasizes that the people's fear left them without that ground.

For today: when God calls you to move forward and you draw back out of fear, you may lose blessings that He wanted to give you. Ask Him for the courage to trust and obey Him today.
exp.27:9:
It says that on the sabbath a special burnt offering was offered, and that this did not replace the daily offering. It was added to it. A "burnt offering" is an offering burned completely on the altar. The "drink offering" is the wine that was poured out along with the sacrifice. "Continual" means the one that was made every day.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to the people of Israel, as they were preparing to enter the promised land. Here the calendar of offerings is set out: daily, weekly, and monthly. The sabbath was a day of rest, and even so worship did not stop. It was made more abundant: two lambs in addition to those of the day.

For today: God deserves our constant worship, and also special times of giving ourselves to Him. In addition to praying every day, set aside a weekly moment to rest in Him, give Him thanks, and offer Him your life once again.
exp.28:27:
He says that on the fifth day of the feast, besides the bulls, rams and lambs, a male goat was offered as a sacrifice for sin. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing guilt. The "continual burnt offering" was the daily offering that was burned whole. "Grain offering" is the meal offering, and "drink offering" is the wine poured out.

God speaks to Moses, and Moses to Israel, in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. Here the offerings of the Feast of Tabernacles are detailed, day by day. Each day the male goat was repeated, and the number of bulls went down. God wanted his people to draw near to him with order, gratitude and repentance.

For today: even in times of festival and joy, it is wise to acknowledge our faults before God. Christians believe that Jesus is the final atonement, so we can celebrate with humility and confidence.
exp.3:35:
This verse says that when the men of the family of Kohath (also spelled Coath) were counted by their families, the total was 2,750. They were the men between thirty and fifty years old who could serve in the tabernacle. The phrase "those that were numbered" refers to the men who were recorded in the census.

God commanded this count through Moses. Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of the congregation carried it out. Each Levite family had a different task while the people traveled through the desert. The Kohathites carried the most sacred objects of the tabernacle. That is why so much care was taken to determine who would serve and how many there were.

For today: God knows and values each person who serves him, even in tasks that seem hidden or unremarkable. If your service in the church or in your family seems small, remember that it does not go unnoticed by God. Serve faithfully where he has placed you.
exp.29:13:
If a woman made a vow or pledge that involved "afflicting the soul," that is, some kind of personal sacrifice such as fasting or giving up something, her husband had the authority to confirm it or to cancel it. A vow is a promise made to God, and a pledge is a solemn commitment.

God gives these instructions to Moses for the leaders of Israel. It was a society where the husband or father was responsible for the family. This rule protected the household from commitments that could affect it. Today there is debate about how much of this reflects the culture of that time. Even so, the text shows that God takes promises seriously and also offers forgiveness when a vow is annulled.

For today: before promising something to God, think carefully about how it will affect your family. Talk with your spouse so that spiritual decisions are made with unity, respect, and wisdom.
exp.13:12:
Moses answers God that the Egyptians will hear about what happens. He reminds God that he brought Israel out of Egypt by his power.

Israel had just refused to enter the promised land, because they were afraid after what the spies reported. God, grieved by their lack of trust, spoke of destroying them. Moses, as an intercessor, does not defend the people's conduct, but appeals to the reputation and honor of God's name among the nations.

When we pray for others, we can imitate Moses: asking with humility, remembering what God has already done and what he has promised. Praying this way teaches us to care more about the glory of God than about our own comfort, and to intercede even for those who fail.
exp.17:25:
God tells Moses to speak to the Levites: when they receive from the people of Israel the tithes that God has given them as an inheritance, they too must present a portion to God, the tenth part of what they received, a tithe of the tithe.

The verse here asks readers to notice that the verse speaks of a lifted offering presented before God. Those are the words of the verse above, so no further comment is needed on them.

The Lord speaks to Moses. The Levites did not receive land in Israel; they lived on the people's tithes while they served in worship. Even so, God asks them to give as well. The portion set apart went to the priest Aaron, according to the verses that follow.

For today: everyone, even those who receive from others or have little, can give to God with gratitude. Recognizing that everything comes from Him helps us live with generosity and trust.
exp.31:5:
Moses answers them with a strong question to the tribes of Gad and Reuben: are your brothers going to war while you sit here at rest? The word "brothers" refers to the other tribes of Israel. The word "ye," which appears in the verse above, is how the older form of "you" was written.

Israel had already defeated the kings east of the Jordan. Those lands were good for livestock, and Gad and Reuben asked to settle there. Moses sees this with concern: he feared their decision would discourage the rest of the people, as happened at Kadesh-barnea, when fear stopped the whole nation. Later, they make clear that they will fight alongside their brothers.

Today we might ask ourselves: am I looking only for my own comfort while others carry a heavy burden? God calls us to support our family and the church, sharing the effort and not only the benefits.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that when the cloud stayed still over the tabernacle for many days, the Israelites also remained in their place. "Kept the charge of the Lord" means they carried out what God had commanded them, and "journeyed not" means they did not continue on the road.

The book of Numbers tells of Israel's journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The narrator describes how God guided them with a cloud over the tabernacle. When the cloud moved, they traveled; when it stopped, they camped. It shows that they depended on God at every step, no matter how long the waiting lasted.

For today: when you sense that God is asking you to wait and nothing seems to move forward, do not despair or rush ahead. Trust that his timing is good, and use that waiting to pray and obey in what you already have at hand.
exp.28:6:
This verse speaks of the tenth day of the seventh month, which is the Day of Atonement. God commands a holy gathering, that is, a sacred assembly. It also says "ye shall afflict your souls," an expression that is usually understood as fasting and humbling oneself before God. And it orders that no one do any work, that is, no labor at all.

God speaks through Moses to the people of Israel, now close to entering the promised land. He repeats to them the calendar of feasts and offerings. On this day, the goat offered for sin reminded them that sin needs to be covered and that the people needed to be reconciled with God.

For today: set aside a quiet time to stop, acknowledge your faults without excuses, and give thanks that Christ has already reconciled us to God. Ask forgiveness sincerely and rest in his grace.
exp.2:10:
This verse is a short sentence that introduces what follows: "And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying." In other words, God himself is about to say something important, and Moses is to pass it on to the people.

Here God speaks, and he speaks to Moses. In the verses before, God gave the Levites as helpers to Aaron and his sons, who were the priests. Now God explains why the Levites belong to him: they take the place of the firstborn of Israel, who were God's from the night when the firstborn of the Egyptians died and the Israelites were saved.

For today: God speaks, and it is good for us to listen carefully before we act. Set aside a few minutes to read his Word calmly, ready to obey what he tells you.
exp.22:29:
King Balak did as Balaam had said, and he prepared the sacrifices that Balaam asked for. On each of the seven altars he presented a bullock (a young bull) and a ram (a mature male sheep). The word "offered" here means that he brought them forward as a sacrifice.

The narrator tells of this moment on the third occasion when Balak tries to get Balaam to curse Israel. Balak was king of Moab, and he feared the people of Israel. He had hired Balaam, a foreign prophet, to curse them. But God would only let Balaam say what God put in his mouth, and until now only blessings had come out.

For today: a person can put great religious effort into offerings and rituals and still want to manipulate God into doing what they wish. God is not moved by our sacrifices, but by his own will. Let us come to him with humility, ready to listen to him and to accept his answer.
exp.2:27:
This verse says that when all the Kohathite males were counted, from one month old and upward, the total was eight thousand six hundred. The word "charge" means care or watch: they were the ones responsible for looking after the sanctuary, the sacred place where God was present among his people.

Here the narrator describes how God, speaking through Moses, organized the Levites by family. The Kohathites were one of those families, and they had a specific task in the camp. Some scholars note that the figure in this text can be explained in several ways, and not all of them agree on how to understand it.

For today: God does not work in disorder. Each person had a place and a task that mattered. Ask yourself what service God has entrusted to you to care for, even if it seems small, and do it with faithfulness.
exp.2:40:
God tells Moses to take the Levites for himself, in place of all the firstborn of Israel. The animals of the Levites would likewise take the place of the firstborn of the people's animals. The firstborn is the first son; in this verse, the word "take" means to set apart or separate.

The Lord speaks to Moses in the wilderness. When God delivered Israel from Egypt, he declared all the firstborn to be his (Exodus 13). Now, instead of taking one firstborn from each family, he chooses the tribe of Levi to serve him in the tabernacle. Both groups are then counted: the Levites (22,000) and the firstborn (22,273), and the difference is redeemed with a payment (Numbers 3:46-47).

For today: what God has done for us belongs to him. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, talents, and service we are giving with gratitude, not out of obligation, but because he has redeemed us.
exp.13:36:
This verse tells us that the ten men who gave a bad report about the promised land died from a plague. "Speaking evil of the land" means they discredited it, saying it was impossible to conquer.

The narrator recounts what happened after Moses sent twelve men to explore Canaan. Ten returned full of fear and spread discouragement among the whole people, who grumbled against Moses and against God. Only Joshua and Caleb trusted the promise, and for that reason they were spared.

Our words can encourage or discourage others. Before we speak about a problem, let us ask ourselves whether we are feeding the faith or the fear of those who listen to us. We can be honest about difficulties without ceasing to trust that God keeps what he promises.
exp.10:33:
It says that Moses, or the account, gave that place the name Kibroth-hattaavah. Then it says there they buried the Israelites who had been struck down by the plague. The verse itself gives the meaning of the name, which is "the graves of those who lusted," and the word "lusted" in the verse describes someone who craves something intensely, more than they should.

This is part of the account of the wilderness. The people grew tired of the manna God gave them, asked for meat, and even longed for Egypt. God sent them quail, but also judgment because of their complaining and contempt. The text does not say who gave the name, so the place remained as a reminder of that event.

For today: examine what you desire and how you ask for it. Having desires is not wrong, but demanding with ingratitude, despising what God already provides, harms us. Before complaining, give thanks for what you have, and bring your needs before God with humble trust.
exp.34:2:
This verse says that the Levites would live in the cities that Israel would give them, and that the open land around each city, which the text here calls "ejidos," that is, the grazing lands around each town, would be for their livestock, their herds, and all their beasts.

God speaks to Moses in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, before entering the promised land. The Levites did not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes, because their inheritance was to serve God. That is why the people were to give them cities and land to live in and to support themselves. The verses that follow explain the measurements of those lands, though scholars debate how exactly they were calculated.

For today: God cares for those who serve in his work, and his people share in that care. We can ask ourselves how to support, with gratitude and generosity, the pastors, teachers, and missionaries who dedicate themselves to serving.
exp.22:28:
Balaam asks Balak to build seven altars and to prepare seven young bulls and seven rams. The word "build" is used here in the sense of making or setting up the altars, and the young bulls were offered in sacrifice.

Balaam was a prophet from outside Israel. Balak, king of Moab, had hired him to curse God's people. They had already tried twice in other places, and God allowed Balaam only to bless. Now Balak takes him to a third site, hoping for a different result. Balaam repeats the same ritual, which was a way of seeking God. Scholars debate how sincere Balaam was; the Bible presents him with a mix of partial obedience and doubtful motives.

For today: we cannot change God's will with rituals or persistence. Rather than seeking a place or formula that will give us the answer we want, it is better to come to God with a heart willing to accept what He says.
exp.20:3:
It says that the people of Israel left Mount Hor and took the road toward the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. The phrase about their spirit being "discouraged" means that they became downhearted, worn down inside, during that journey.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just won a battle with God's help, but then the road became long and wearying, because Edom would not let them pass through its land and they had to go around. That discouragement sets up what follows: they complained against God and Moses.

For today: after a victory, weariness can still come. When the road grows long or changes direction, do not let discouragement turn into complaint against God. Instead, remember how He helped you before and ask Him for strength to keep going.
exp.33:22:
This verse names Hanniel, son of Ephod, as the leader or chief of the tribe of Manasseh, which was one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. Here "leader" means the head of the tribe, not a king's son.

God speaks to Moses on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. He instructs that each tribe have a representative to help Eleazar and Joshua divide the land of Canaan. In this way the distribution would be orderly and fair, with the voice of every tribe heard.

Today it reminds us that God cares about order and values each person by name. If you have a responsibility, in the family, the church, or at work, carry it out with honesty and service, thinking of the good of everyone and not only your own.
exp.35:5:
It says that God allows the daughters of Zelophehad to marry whomever they wish, but with one condition: that the husband be within the family of their father's tribe. "Zelophehad" is the name Zelophehad. The phrase "whomever they please" means the same as "whomever they choose" or "to whom they think best." The word "but" introduces the condition.

Moses speaks, passing on what the Lord commanded. The daughters of Zelophehad had no brothers and had received their father's inheritance. The leaders of the tribe of Manasseh feared that if they married men from another tribe, the land would pass to that tribe. God approved their concern and gave this rule to protect each tribe's land.

God cares for both freedom and responsibility. They could choose, within a limit. Today we can choose freely, but seeking that our decisions honor God and care for what He has entrusted to us.
exp.35:8:
It says that the land God divided among each tribe was not to pass from one tribe to another, as if it were a stone rolling from place to place. Each tribe was to keep the inheritance it had received. The "inheritance" is the land received as a family possession, and the wording about being "kept to" it means that it should remain joined to that tribe.

God speaks through Moses at the end of the book of Numbers. The daughters of Zelophehad could inherit land because they had no brothers. The leaders of their tribe feared that if they married men from another tribe, the land would change hands. So they were commanded to marry within their own tribe, and they obeyed.

For today: what God entrusts to us, such as faith, family, or possessions, we should guard faithfully so that it is not lost. Ask yourself what God has entrusted to you and how you can protect it and leave it well for those who come after you.
exp.26:10:
It says that if a man died without sons, without daughters, and without brothers, and also had no uncles on his father's side, his inheritance would pass to the nearest relative in his family. The phrase "statute of judgment" means a legal rule that Israel was to follow. Where the verse says "ye shall give," it is addressed to the whole people.

God speaks through Moses. It all began when the daughters of Zelophehad asked to inherit their father's land, since he had no sons. God answered with a clear order of inheritance. In this way each family's land stayed within its own line and tribe.

For today: God cares about order and justice, and he makes sure no one is forgotten. We can keep our affairs clear and orderly, much like a will, to prevent quarrels within the family and to protect those who depend on us.
exp.6:3:
This verse is a short phrase that introduces an instruction. It says that God spoke to Moses. The name "Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament, and "spake unto" is an older way of saying "spoke to."

The leaders of the tribes had just brought their gifts to the tabernacle: six covered wagons and twelve oxen. Moses did not accept them on his own authority. First he waited for God's word. Then God told him to receive them and distribute them among the Levites, according to the work of each one, since they carried the tabernacle.

For today: before deciding how to use what we have, we can pause to pray and listen to God. He knows best where each resource is needed, and he guides us to serve with order and wisdom.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The name "Jehovah" is God's name, and the phrase "spoke to" is a short phrase that introduces a new instruction.

God is the one who speaks, and Moses is the one who listens. This takes place while Israel is camped in the wilderness, after God had already set apart the Levites to serve him in place of the firstborn. Now God commands that a count be made of the sons of Levi. Before giving the order, the text emphasizes that it comes from God himself and that Moses receives it as his word.

For today: God continues to guide his people with order and purpose. Before organizing your work, your family, or your service in the church, take a moment to listen to God in prayer and in his Word.
exp.30:2:
Moses passes on to the people God's command: some of the men must get ready and arm themselves to go against Midian. The phrase about arming is rendered here simply as "get ready with weapons." The phrase meaning that justice will be carried out in God's name, not out of personal bitterness, is simply part of this verse's sense.

God had just told Moses to act, and after that Moses would die. The Midianites had led Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25), and many Israelites died. Moses repeats the command to the people and organizes the sending of a thousand men from each tribe. This passage is difficult, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: God takes seriously the harm done to his people, and justice belongs to him. That is why we can leave our offenses in his hands, instead of collecting them on our own account (Romans 12:19).
exp.27:21:
It says that, in addition to the other sacrifices, the people were to offer a male goat as an offering for sin.

Dios habla por medio de Moisés a Israel, ya cerca de la tierra prometida.

God speaks through Moses to Israel, now near the promised land. Here he gives instructions about the offerings for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which remembered the departure from Egypt. Along with the thank offerings, one for sin was always included, because the people needed forgiveness to draw near to God.

For today: Christians believe that Jesus is the final sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10:10-14). We can celebrate with joy, but without forgetting to confess our faults and to receive the forgiveness that Christ has already won for us.
exp.18:15:
It says that anyone who touches someone who has been killed in the open field, whether killed by a sword or by natural causes, or who touches a human bone or a grave, was made unclean for seven days. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not necessarily guilty of sin.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives them laws for Israel in the wilderness. These rules accompanied the ritual of the red heifer, whose ashes were used for purification. Many understand that they taught that death is foreign to the holiness of God, although the Bible does not explain every detail.

For today: death is serious and painful, and God offers cleansing. We can come to Christ, who conquered death, with humility and hope.
exp.5:21:
This verse is an introductory line. It says that the Lord spoke to Moses. It does not yet contain the message itself; it only announces that God is about to give a new instruction.

Just before this, the text finished the rules about the Nazarite, a person who set himself apart for God for a special period of time. Now a new section begins. The speaker is God, and Moses is the one who receives his words and passes them on to the people. In the verses that follow, God will tell Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons, the priests, in how to bless Israel.

For today: before doing or saying something important, it is good to stop and listen to God. Reading the Bible and praying calmly helps us receive his guidance, rather than depending only on our own ideas.
exp.4:7:
If someone has wronged another person and wants to make things right, but the injured person has already died and has no close relative to receive the repayment, then the payment is given to the Lord, through the priest. In addition, the offender had to bring a ram for the sacrifice of atonement. "Restored" means repaired or paid back; "wrong" is the harm done; "compensation" is the payment owed.

God speaks to Moses so that he will instruct the people. Earlier it was said that whoever sinned had to confess, make full restitution, and add a fifth part. This law covers a special case: when there is no one to repay. Even so, the debt is not erased. It shows that sin against a person is also an offense against God.

For today: if you have harmed someone, do not stop at asking forgiveness; confess and, when possible, make right the harm. If you can no longer do it directly, bring it humbly to God and seek counsel from a pastor or a mature brother or sister in the faith.
exp.13:25:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that God spoke to Moses and to Aaron, the two leaders of the people. The phrase "spake unto" is older wording; today we would say "spoke to Moses and to Aaron."

Here God is speaking. Israel had rebelled after the spies returned with a bad report about Canaan. The people wanted to go back to Egypt. God had already said that Caleb would enter the land, and now He speaks again to the leaders to give His answer to the people's complaints. What follows is a judgment, but it also shows that God hears what is said against Him.

For today: God hears our words, even the complaints spoken under our breath. Before we grumble, we can bring our fear and weariness to God in prayer, with sincerity and trust.

sum.26: Salfaad's five daughters asked for an inheritance in the land, since their father had died without any sons. God said they were right and set down a law for inheritances. After that, God told Moses that he would see the land from a distance but would not enter it. Moses, following God's command, appointed Joshua as his successor as leader.
sum.9: God tells Moses to make two trumpets of silver to call the people together and to signal when it is time to move on. Then Israel sets out from Mount Sinai in an orderly way, following the cloud and the ark. Moses invites Hobab to travel with them, and as they advance he prays that God will guide and protect them.
sum.23: In Numbers 24, Balaam sees Israel camped below him and, moved by the Spirit of God, blesses them a third time, to the anger of Balak. He then announces that in the days to come a star will rise out of Jacob and a scepter will arise from Israel, one that will defeat Moab, Edom, and other nations. In the end, each of them goes on his own way.
sum.8: In Numbers 9, Israel observes the Passover in the Sinai desert. God allows a second Passover the following month for those who were ritually unclean because they had touched a dead body or who were away on a journey. The chapter also teaches that a foreigner living among them must follow the same rules. In addition, the cloud and the fire over the tabernacle guided when to camp and when to set out.
sum.30: God commands Israel to punish Midian for leading them into sin at Peor. Twelve thousand men go out to fight, and they kill the kings of Midian and Balaam, then bring back captives and plunder. Moses orders further killings among the captives. Rules for ritual purification are established, and the plunder is divided, with one portion set aside for the LORD and the Levites. The leaders also bring gold as an offering of atonement.
sum.19: At Kadesh, Miriam dies, and the people, with no water, complain against Moses and Aaron. God tells Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses strikes it twice; water comes out, though God tells them that they will not enter the promised land. Edom refuses to let Israel pass through, and Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and Eleazar replaces him.
sum.21: Balak, king of Moab, is afraid of Israel and sends for Balaam to curse them. God tells Balaam not to go, but later allows him to go. On the way, his donkey sees the angel with the sword, and God causes the donkey to speak. Balaam arrives with Balak, but he will say only what God tells him to say.
sum.0: God tells Moses and Aaron to count all the men of Israel aged twenty and older who are able to go to war, with the help of one leader from each tribe. The total comes to 603,550. The Levites are not counted, because God assigns them to take care of the tabernacle, carry it, set it up, and camp around it. Israel obeys.
sum.7: God tells Aaron to light the seven lamps of the golden lampstand, and he obeys. Then God orders that the Levites be purified with water, shaved, have their clothes washed, and offer sacrifices, so that they are set apart for his service in place of the firstborn of Israel. They would serve from the age of twenty-five, and from the age of fifty they would help only in guarding duties.
sum.25: After the plague, God told Moses and Eleazar to count the men of Israel again, those who were able to go to war. The total came to 601,730, not counting the Levites. The land would be divided by lot according to the size of each tribe. Of the earlier generation, only Caleb and Joshua were still left.
sum.5: God explains how a man or a woman can set themselves apart for Him by taking a Nazirite vow: they must not drink wine or any product made from grapes, they must not cut their hair, and they must not go near a dead body. It also describes the offerings to be made if a person becomes defiled, and the offerings to be made when the vow is completed. Then God commands Aaron and his sons to bless Israel with a blessing of care, grace, and peace.
sum.2: In Numbers 3, God sets apart the tribe of Levi to serve the priests and take care of the tabernacle, in place of the firstborn of Israel. Moses counts the Levites (22,000) and the firstborn (22,273), and the 273 who are left over are redeemed at five shekels each. That money is handed over to Aaron and his sons.
sum.34: God commands the Israelites to give the Levites forty-eight cities with their pastureland, and that six of these be cities of refuge. There a person who had killed someone unintentionally could flee, and the assembly would judge the case, while a deliberate murderer had to be put to death, with enough witnesses. God asks that the land not be polluted, because He lives among His people.
sum.15: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, together with 250 leaders, rose up against Moses and Aaron, and God judged them: the earth swallowed up the rebels, and fire consumed those who were offering incense. The next day the people complained, and a plague broke out, but Aaron made atonement with the censer and the deaths stopped.
sum.4: God commands that those who were unclean be sent out of the camp, so that the holy place where He dwells would be kept pure. He also orders that a person confess their sin and make restitution for the wrong done, adding an extra fifth to it. In addition, He gives a ritual to be carried out before the priest for cases of marital jealousy, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
sum.33: God tells Moses the boundaries of the land of Canaan that Israel will receive as its inheritance: the south, the west, the north and the east. Nine and a half tribes will divide it by lot, since two and a half tribes already had their portion east of the Jordan. God appoints Eleazar, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe to carry out the division.
sum.11: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of his Cushite wife, and they claimed they were just as important as he was. God rebuked them and defended Moses as his faithful servant. Miriam became leprous. Moses prayed for her, God healed her, and after seven days outside the camp the people continued on their journey.
sum.1: God instructs Moses and Aaron that the tribes of Israel are to camp in order, each one beside its own banner, around the tent of meeting: Judah to the east, Reuben to the south, Ephraim to the west, and Dan to the north. The Levites are to remain in the middle, and the total of those counted is 603,550. The people obeyed, and in this way they camped and marched in good order.
sum.35: The leaders of the family of Gilead are worried that if Zelophehad's daughters marry men from other tribes, their tribe's inheritance will pass to another tribe. God commands through Moses that they marry within the tribe of their father, so that no inheritance is transferred from tribe to tribe. The daughters obey, and the land remains in their family.
sum.16: God asked Moses to take twelve staffs, one from each tribe, with the name of each leader written on it, to show whom he had chosen. The next day, Aaron's staff had sprouted, blossomed, and produced almonds. God commanded that it be kept as a sign against the rebels, and the people, frightened, feared they would die if they came near the tabernacle.
sum.24: At Shittim, Israel fell into sexual immorality and into worshiping Baal of Peor alongside the women of Moab, and the LORD's anger burned against them; a plague killed twenty-four thousand people. Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, stopped the deaths by killing Zimri and the Midianite woman Cozbi. God promised him a covenant of peace and a permanent priesthood, and commanded that Midian be treated as an enemy.
sum.27: God tells Moses that the people are to present offerings to him at the appointed times: two lambs every day, one in the morning and one in the evening, along with flour, oil, and wine. He also calls for larger offerings every Sabbath, at the beginning of each month, at the Passover, and at the Feast of Firstfruits, with rest and a holy assembly.
sum.28: Numbers 29 describes the offerings Israel was to present to the Lord in the seventh month: the Day of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the seven-day feast, followed by a solemn assembly on an eighth day. In all of these, animals without defect were required, and no regular work was to be done. The chapter teaches that God deserves orderly worship, forgiveness, and reconciliation.
sum.10: The people complained about the manna and asked for meat, and God became angry. Yet God also helped Moses by sharing his burden with seventy elders, to whom he gave his Spirit. God sent quail in abundance, but he punished with a plague those who had been greedy. The chapter teaches us to be thankful for what God gives and not to crave with ingratitude.
sum.6: When Moses finished setting up and consecrating the tabernacle, the twelve leaders of the tribes brought wagons and oxen, which Moses distributed among the Levites according to their service. Then each leader, one day after another, presented the same offering to dedicate the altar, showing God's care for order and the generosity of the people.
sum.20: In Numbers 21, Israel defeats the Canaanites of Arad, but on the way the people become discouraged and speak against God and Moses. God sends snakes, and when they repent, He commands them to look at the bronze serpent in order to live. Then God gives them water and victories over Sihon and Og, and Israel takes their lands.
sum.22: Balak takes Balaam to two different places so that he will curse Israel, and at each one they build seven altars and offer sacrifices. But God puts words of blessing in his mouth, and Balaam declares that God does not lie or change his mind, and that he cannot take back what he has blessed. In the end, Balak takes him to a third place to try again.
sum.17: God tells Aaron that he and his sons, the priests, will be responsible for the sanctuary, and that the Levites will help them, but without coming near the altar. God gives the priests the offerings of the people as their provision, and gives the Levites the tithes in place of land, since God himself is their inheritance. The Levites also set aside a tenth of the tithes for the priests.
sum.3: God tells them to count the Levites who are between thirty and fifty years old and assigns them their duties for carrying the tabernacle. The Kohathites carry the holy things, but only after Aaron and his sons have covered them, and they must not touch or even look at them, or they would die. The Gershonites carry the curtains, and the Merarites carry the frames. In total there are 8,580 men. The passage teaches reverence and order in serving God.
sum.13: When they heard the report of the spies, the people rebelled, wept, and wanted to go back to Egypt, even though Joshua and Caleb urged them to trust God. Moses interceded, and God forgave them, but that generation would not enter the land and would wander for forty years. Some insisted on fighting without God, and they were defeated.
sum.18: God commands that a perfect red heifer be sacrificed and burned outside the camp, and that its ashes be kept to prepare the "water of separation." Anyone who touched a dead body was unclean for seven days and had to be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days. In this way the holiness of the tabernacle was protected.
sum.32: Moses wrote down, at the command of the LORD, the list of the places where Israel camped from the time they left Egypt until they reached the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan. Along the way, Aaron died on Mount Hor. God commands them to drive out the inhabitants of Canaan and destroy their idols, to divide the land by lot, and warns that if they do not do this, those peoples will be like thorns in their side.
sum.14: God gives instructions for the offerings that Israel will present when they enter the land, and he says that the foreigner will have the same law as they do. There is forgiveness for sins committed unintentionally, but whoever sins with defiant arrogance is cut off from the people, like the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath. God commands that tassels be put on their clothing as a reminder of his commandments.
sum.12: God tells Moses to send one leader from each tribe to explore Canaan, the land He would give them. The twelve return after forty days carrying enormous fruit, but ten of them speak with fear about the strong peoples living there. Caleb believes they can conquer the land, but the group's fear wins out.
sum.29: Moses taught the leaders of Israel that anyone who makes a vow or oath to the LORD must keep their word. For women, the father (if she was young and living in his house) or the husband could confirm or cancel her vows on the same day they heard them. If they remained silent, the vow stood firm, but widows and divorced women had to keep their own vows.
sum.31: The tribes of Reuben and Gad, who had large herds of livestock, asked to stay on the east side of the Jordan River. Moses reminded them of the sin of the previous generation and warned them not to discourage Israel. They promised to go over armed to help in the conquest, and Moses agreed, warning that if they failed, their sin would catch up with them.
